knowledgeUnits.heading: How can two states carry a message?

leadVisual.title: Three things to keep

coreExplanation: A representation uses one thing to stand for another. If both people agree that a raised hand means “yes”, the hand position carries information. The same physical position could mean something else under a different agreement.

A bit is a binary digit: 0 or 1. A computer can use two distinguishable physical states to represent those alternatives. The printed symbols 0 and 1 describe the states; the computer does not need to store tiny pictures of these digits.
Two bits make four patterns: 00, 01, 10 and 11. We could assign 00 to the letter, 01 to the photograph and 10 to the sound, leaving 11 unused. The order matters: 01 and 10 are different patterns.

A bit pattern has no built-in label saying “number”, “letter” or “colour”. A representation rule tells the receiver how to interpret it. Throughout this section, ask both what is stored and which rule gives it meaning.

learningCycle.observe: An agreed rule could make off mean “letter” and on mean “photograph”. There is no third state left for “sound”. The problem is the number of distinguishable messages, not the brightness of the lamp.

stimulus.title: Three things to keep
items: A letter on a card
The colours and shapes of a leaf photograph
The changing sound of a vibrating tuning fork

learningCycle.question: Could one on/off lamp tell us which of these three things was chosen?

steps.title: Start with an agreed meaning
steps.body: A representation uses one thing to stand for another. If both people agree that a raised hand means “yes”, the hand position carries information. The same physical position could mean something else under a different agreement.

steps.title: Name the smallest binary choice
steps.body: A bit is a binary digit: 0 or 1. A computer can use two distinguishable physical states to represent those alternatives. The printed symbols 0 and 1 describe the states; the computer does not need to store tiny pictures of these digits.

steps.title: Combine bits into ordered patterns
steps.body: Two bits make four patterns: 00, 01, 10 and 11. We could assign 00 to the letter, 01 to the photograph and 10 to the sound, leaving 11 unused. The order matters: 01 and 10 are different patterns.

steps.title: Separate the pattern from its meaning
steps.body: A bit pattern has no built-in label saying “number”, “letter” or “colour”. A representation rule tells the receiver how to interpret it. Throughout this section, ask both what is stored and which rule gives it meaning.

worked.title: Send one choice with two lamps
worked.setup: The left lamp is off and the right lamp is on. Off represents 0 and on represents 1.

steps.title: Record the order
steps.body: Read from left to right: the pattern is 01.

steps.title: Use the agreed table
steps.body: The table assigns 01 to the photograph. Reading the lamps in reverse would give 10 and the wrong message.

worked.conclusion: The two states create a code only when a shared rule defines their meaning and order.

check.prompt: A switch has only two states. Can it uniquely identify three answers without any extra information?
check.answer: No. One bit has two patterns, so two answers can be assigned distinct patterns. Three answers require at least two bits, which provide four patterns.

learningCycle.takeaway: Bits record two alternatives. A shared representation gives an ordered bit pattern its meaning.
learningCycle.bridge: Before representing larger choices, we need a reliable way to count the patterns made by several bits.

workedExample.title: Send one choice with two lamps
workedExample.setup: The left lamp is off and the right lamp is on. Off represents 0 and on represents 1.

steps.title: Record the order
steps.body: Read from left to right: the pattern is 01.

steps.title: Use the agreed table
steps.body: The table assigns 01 to the photograph. Reading the lamps in reverse would give 10 and the wrong message.

workedExample.conclusion: The two states create a code only when a shared rule defines their meaning and order.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Count possibilities before assigning values

leadVisual.title: Add one independent choice

coreExplanation: Each bit can be 0 or 1 independently of the other bits. Three bits therefore give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 patterns. In general, n bits provide 2ⁿ patterns.

If eight patterns label the whole numbers beginning at zero, they label 0 through 7. Zero takes one pattern too. Thus n bits provide 2ⁿ patterns but their largest unsigned integer is 2ⁿ − 1. “Unsigned” means that the representation has no negative values.

A nibble contains four bits. A byte contains eight bits. Lower-case b means bit and upper-case B means byte. One byte therefore holds one of 256 patterns; it is not a container holding 256 separate numbers at once.

learningCycle.observe: Take each two-bit pattern twice: put 0 in front of one copy and 1 in front of the other. No old choice disappears, and every old choice now has two versions.
learningCycle.question: Why does adding one bit double the number of patterns?

prerequisite.title: Read powers as repeated multiplication
prerequisite.body: 2³ means 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8. The raised 3 is an exponent: it counts three factors of 2. It does not mean 2 × 3. We use 2⁰ = 1 later for the rightmost number position.

steps.title: Multiply independent choices
steps.body: Each bit can be 0 or 1 independently of the other bits. Three bits therefore give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 patterns. In general, n bits provide 2ⁿ patterns.

steps.title: Distinguish a count from a largest value
steps.body: If eight patterns label the whole numbers beginning at zero, they label 0 through 7. Zero takes one pattern too. Thus n bits provide 2ⁿ patterns but their largest unsigned integer is 2ⁿ − 1. “Unsigned” means that the representation has no negative values.

steps.title: Group bits into familiar units
steps.body: A nibble contains four bits. A byte contains eight bits. Lower-case b means bit and upper-case B means byte. One byte therefore holds one of 256 patterns; it is not a container holding 256 separate numbers at once.

worked.title: Give each of six team colours a different code
worked.setup: A school needs one distinct bit pattern for each of six colours.

steps.title: Try two bits
steps.body: 2² = 4 patterns. Four codes cannot label six different colours.

steps.title: Try three bits
steps.body: 2³ = 8 patterns. Six can label the colours and two can remain unused. Three bits are sufficient and two are not.

worked.conclusion: Choose the smallest width whose pattern count is at least the number of choices.

check.prompt: How many bits are needed for 20 distinct labels? If five-bit patterns instead represent unsigned integers, what is the largest value?
check.answer: Four bits give only 16 labels. Five bits give 32, so five bits are needed. Five-bit unsigned integers range from 0 to 31; 32 is the pattern count, not the maximum value.

learningCycle.takeaway: n bits provide 2ⁿ patterns. Assigning them to unsigned integers gives values 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
learningCycle.bridge: Files contain many bytes. Prefixes let us describe large byte counts without writing every digit.

workedExample.setup: A school needs one distinct bit pattern for each of six colours.

steps.title: Try two bits
steps.body: 2² = 4 patterns. Four codes cannot label six different colours.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare quantities using the same unit

leadVisual.title: Two labels on the same file

coreExplanation: Kilo, mega, giga and tera use successive factors of 1000. For example, one megabyte is 1000 × 1000 = 1,000,000 bytes. Multiplication expands a large unit into individual bytes.
Kibi, mebi, gibi and tebi use successive factors of 1024. The i in KiB or MiB identifies this scale. One mebibyte is 1024 × 1024 = 1,048,576 bytes.

To compare different sizes, convert them all to bytes. To express a byte count in MB, divide by 1,000,000. To express it in MiB, divide by 1,048,576. Also check b versus B: divide a bit count by eight to get bytes.

Capacity asks how much data fits. After converting the capacity and file size to the same unit, divide. If only whole files may be saved, round down. Include headers or other overhead only when their cost is supplied or already included in the stated size.

learningCycle.observe: First compare a smaller pair: 1 KiB is 1024 bytes, while 1 kB is 1000 bytes. The prefixes follow two different scales. Neither label changes the size of a byte.

stimulus.title: Two labels on the same file
items: File A: 1 MiB
File B: 1 MB
Both use B for bytes. The extra i changes the multiplier.

learningCycle.question: Do these labels describe equal amounts of data?

steps.title: Follow the decimal scale
steps.body: Kilo, mega, giga and tera use successive factors of 1000. For example, one megabyte is 1000 × 1000 = 1,000,000 bytes. Multiplication expands a large unit into individual bytes.

steps.title: Follow the binary scale
steps.body: Kibi, mebi, gibi and tebi use successive factors of 1024. The i in KiB or MiB identifies this scale. One mebibyte is 1024 × 1024 = 1,048,576 bytes.

steps.title: Convert through a common unit
steps.body: To compare different sizes, convert them all to bytes. To express a byte count in MB, divide by 1,000,000. To express it in MiB, divide by 1,048,576. Also check b versus B: divide a bit count by eight to get bytes.

steps.title: Count complete files
steps.body: Capacity asks how much data fits. After converting the capacity and file size to the same unit, divide. If only whole files may be saved, round down. Include headers or other overhead only when their cost is supplied or already included in the stated size.

worked.title: Save complete 600-byte files in 2 KiB
worked.setup: The available capacity is exactly 2 KiB. Each complete file occupies 600 bytes including all overhead.

steps.title: Test complete multiples
steps.body: 3 × 600 = 1800 bytes fits. 4 × 600 = 2400 bytes does not. Three complete files fit.

steps.title: Find the unused space
steps.body: 2048 − 1800 = 248 bytes remain. This is smaller than another 600-byte file.

worked.conclusion: Check both the number of complete files and the remaining capacity.

check.prompt: Which is larger: 2 MB or 1900 KiB? Show a common-unit comparison.
check.answer: 2 MB = 2,000,000 bytes. 1900 KiB = 1900 × 1024 = 1,945,600 bytes. Therefore 2 MB is larger by 54,400 bytes.

learningCycle.takeaway: Keep the prefix, bit/byte unit and calculation together. Different labels can describe the same data quantity.
learningCycle.bridge: We can count stored bits. Next, use their positions to represent whole numbers.

workedExample.title: Save complete 600-byte files in 2 KiB
workedExample.setup: The available capacity is exactly 2 KiB. Each complete file occupies 600 bytes including all overhead.

steps.body: 3 × 600 = 1800 bytes fits. 4 × 600 = 2400 bytes does not. Three complete files fit.

workedExample.conclusion: Check both the number of complete files and the remaining capacity.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Build binary from familiar place values

leadVisual.title: One digit moves one position left

coreExplanation: Denary is base 10. It uses digits 0 to 9 and each place is ten times the place to its right. Thus 304 means 3 × 100 + 0 × 10 + 4 × 1. The zero keeps the hundreds and ones in their correct places.

Binary is base 2. Only 0 and 1 are available, and each place is twice the place to its right. Starting on the right, the weights are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128. Each 1 includes its weight; each 0 leaves it out.
1011₂ = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11₁₀. The symbols 1011 would mean one thousand and eleven in denary. Leading zeros do not change this unsigned value, so 00001011 is also eleven, now written using eight bits.

learningCycle.observe: The position supplies a multiplier. Denary positions are worth 1, 10, 100 and so on. We can use the same idea with positions worth 1, 2, 4 and 8.

stimulus.title: One digit moves one position left

learningCycle.question: Why does moving the 4 change its value when the symbol stays the same?

prerequisite.title: Base and digit
prerequisite.body: A digit is one symbol in a numeral. The base tells us how many digit symbols are available and how place values grow. A subscript such as ₂ or ₁₀ identifies the base; it is not another digit in the value.

steps.title: Read denary as a sum of place values
steps.body: Denary is base 10. It uses digits 0 to 9 and each place is ten times the place to its right. Thus 304 means 3 × 100 + 0 × 10 + 4 × 1. The zero keeps the hundreds and ones in their correct places.

steps.title: Change the base to two
steps.body: Binary is base 2. Only 0 and 1 are available, and each place is twice the place to its right. Starting on the right, the weights are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128. Each 1 includes its weight; each 0 leaves it out.

steps.title: Read the value, not the shape
steps.body: 1011₂ = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11₁₀. The symbols 1011 would mean one thousand and eleven in denary. Leading zeros do not change this unsigned value, so 00001011 is also eleven, now written using eight bits.

worked.title: Decode an eight-bit counter
worked.setup: A counter displays 00101101 as an unsigned binary integer.

steps.title: Write the weights
steps.body: From left to right use 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

steps.title: Include only the set positions
steps.body: The 1s select 32, 8, 4 and 1. Their sum is 45.

steps.title: Check the width
steps.body: 45 fits the eight-bit unsigned range 0 to 255. The leading zeros preserve the stated width.

worked.conclusion: Binary-to-denary conversion adds the weights of the set bits.

check.prompt: Decode 01010110₂. Why is 102₂ invalid?
check.answer: 01010110₂ = 64 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 86₁₀. A binary numeral cannot contain the digit 2 because base 2 permits only 0 and 1.

learningCycle.takeaway: A number system assigns weights to positions. In binary, those weights double towards the left.
learningCycle.bridge: Decoding adds known weights. Encoding reverses the problem: choose weights that make a given value.

workedExample.title: Decode an eight-bit counter
workedExample.setup: A counter displays 00101101 as an unsigned binary integer.

steps.title: Write the weights
steps.body: From left to right use 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.

steps.title: Include only the set positions
steps.body: The 1s select 32, 8, 4 and 1. Their sum is 45.

steps.title: Check the width
steps.body: 45 fits the eight-bit unsigned range 0 to 255. The leading zeros preserve the stated width.

workedExample.conclusion: Binary-to-denary conversion adds the weights of the set bits.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose binary weights for a denary value

leadVisual.title: Make 45 with eight place-value cards

coreExplanation: At each position, write 1 if its weight fits within the remaining amount, then subtract it. Otherwise write 0. For 45, select 32, skip 16, select 8 and 4, skip 2 and select 1. The remainder reaches zero.
Record a digit for every position, including unused weights between selected ones. At eight bits, 45 becomes 00101101. Dropping an internal zero moves later digits to different weights.

Dividing a whole number by 2 leaves remainder 0 if it is even and 1 if it is odd. That remainder is the rightmost binary digit. Repeat with the whole-number quotient until it is zero, then read remainders from last to first.

learningCycle.observe: Start with the largest usable weight. 128 and 64 are too large. Taking 32 leaves 13, so continue deciding from left to right.

stimulus.title: Make 45 with eight place-value cards
items: Available weights: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1
Use each card at most once.
A selected card becomes 1; an unused card becomes 0.

learningCycle.question: Which weights make exactly 45?

steps.title: Choose and subtract
steps.body: At each position, write 1 if its weight fits within the remaining amount, then subtract it. Otherwise write 0. For 45, select 32, skip 16, select 8 and 4, skip 2 and select 1. The remainder reaches zero.

steps.title: Keep every position
steps.body: Record a digit for every position, including unused weights between selected ones. At eight bits, 45 becomes 00101101. Dropping an internal zero moves later digits to different weights.

steps.title: Understand the repeated-division alternative
steps.body: Dividing a whole number by 2 leaves remainder 0 if it is even and 1 if it is odd. That remainder is the rightmost binary digit. Repeat with the whole-number quotient until it is zero, then read remainders from last to first.

worked.title: Encode 13 and check the result
worked.setup: Use repeated division by 2, then express the result in eight bits.

steps.title: Read in reverse order
steps.body: The remainders were 1, 0, 1, 1. Last to first gives 1101.

steps.title: Apply the width
steps.body: Pad on the left to eight positions: 00001101.

steps.title: Decode to verify
steps.body: 8 + 4 + 1 = 13, matching the starting number.

worked.conclusion: Both methods produce the same pattern because both use the same powers of two.

check.prompt: Write 78 as an eight-bit unsigned binary number, then verify it by adding weights.
check.answer: 78 = 64 + 8 + 4 + 2, so the pattern is 01001110. Adding those selected weights returns 78.

learningCycle.takeaway: Encode by choosing weights or reversing division remainders; decode again to check.
learningCycle.bridge: Long binary strings are hard for people to read. Hexadecimal groups them into shorter, exact labels.

workedExample.title: Encode 13 and check the result
workedExample.setup: Use repeated division by 2, then express the result in eight bits.

steps.title: Read in reverse order
steps.body: The remainders were 1, 0, 1, 1. Last to first gives 1101.

steps.title: Apply the width
steps.body: Pad on the left to eight positions: 00001101.

steps.title: Decode to verify
steps.body: 8 + 4 + 1 = 13, matching the starting number.

workedExample.conclusion: Both methods produce the same pattern because both use the same powers of two.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read four binary bits as one hexadecimal digit

leadVisual.title: Two ways to label the same byte

coreExplanation: Hexadecimal is base 16. It uses 0 to 9, then A, B, C, D, E and F for values 10 to 15. Moving left multiplies the place value by 16, giving weights 1, 16, 256 and 4096.

Group binary digits in fours from the right. Add leading zeros to the leftmost group if necessary. Convert each group separately: 1010 is A and 1111 is F. Reversing the conversion, write exactly four bits for every hexadecimal digit, including zeros.

AF₁₆ = 10 × 16 + 15 = 175₁₀. To convert 175 back, 175 ÷ 16 gives quotient 10 and remainder 15, so the digits are A and F. For longer values, keep dividing the quotient by 16 and read the remainders backwards.

Hexadecimal provides a compact, human-readable view of binary values. It is used when displaying memory addresses, diagnostic values and RGB colour values. The shorter written label does not itself compress the underlying data; it changes how a person reads it.

learningCycle.observe: One symbol labels the left group and one labels the right group. There must be a distinct symbol for every value from 0 to 15, so the ten familiar digits are not enough.

stimulus.title: Two ways to label the same byte
items: Binary: 1010 1111
Hexadecimal: AF
A four-bit group has 16 possible patterns.

learningCycle.question: How can two hexadecimal symbols preserve all eight bits?

steps.title: Supply sixteen digit symbols
steps.body: Hexadecimal is base 16. It uses 0 to 9, then A, B, C, D, E and F for values 10 to 15. Moving left multiplies the place value by 16, giving weights 1, 16, 256 and 4096.

steps.title: Convert binary groups without changing the value
steps.body: Group binary digits in fours from the right. Add leading zeros to the leftmost group if necessary. Convert each group separately: 1010 is A and 1111 is F. Reversing the conversion, write exactly four bits for every hexadecimal digit, including zeros.

steps.title: Use hexadecimal place values
steps.body: AF₁₆ = 10 × 16 + 15 = 175₁₀. To convert 175 back, 175 ÷ 16 gives quotient 10 and remainder 15, so the digits are A and F. For longer values, keep dividing the quotient by 16 and read the remainders backwards.

steps.title: Explain why people use it
steps.body: Hexadecimal provides a compact, human-readable view of binary values. It is used when displaying memory addresses, diagnostic values and RGB colour values. The shorter written label does not itself compress the underlying data; it changes how a person reads it.

worked.title: Convert 2D3 between three bases
worked.setup: Interpret 2D3 as hexadecimal.

steps.title: Reverse-check by division
steps.body: 723 ÷ 16 gives 45 remainder 3; 45 ÷ 16 gives 2 remainder 13 (D); 2 ÷ 16 gives 0 remainder 2. Reverse the remainders to recover 2D3.

worked.conclusion: Four-bit grouping and base-16 place values are two consistent ways to check the same conversion.

check.prompt: Convert 1101 0010₂ to hexadecimal and denary. Why is hexadecimal useful when reading a memory address?
check.answer: 1101 = D and 0010 = 2, so the hexadecimal value is D2. In denary it is 13 × 16 + 2 = 210. Hexadecimal gives a shorter, readable label with an exact four-bit correspondence for each digit.

learningCycle.takeaway: One hexadecimal digit labels exactly four binary bits; hexadecimal uses base-16 place values.
learningCycle.bridge: Hexadecimal groups the whole binary value. BCD instead preserves each decimal digit separately.

workedExample.title: Convert 2D3 between three bases
workedExample.setup: Interpret 2D3 as hexadecimal.

steps.title: Reverse-check by division
steps.body: 723 ÷ 16 gives 45 remainder 3; 45 ÷ 16 gives 2 remainder 13 (D); 2 ÷ 16 gives 0 remainder 2. Reverse the remainders to recover 2D3.

workedExample.conclusion: Four-bit grouping and base-16 place values are two consistent ways to check the same conversion.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Keep decimal digits separate with BCD

leadVisual.title: A display shows 59

coreExplanation: Binary Coded Decimal, or BCD, represents each decimal digit with its own four-bit code. For 59, convert 5 to 0101 and 9 to 1001, then keep the digit order. Do not first convert the whole value to ordinary binary.

Split a BCD pattern into groups of four. Each group must represent a digit from 0 to 9, so 1010 through 1111 are unused in the basic BCD digit code. For example, 0010 0111 decodes to the decimal digits 2 and 7, giving 27.

A decimal counter or digital clock can keep a separate BCD code for each displayed digit, simplifying the link to decimal digit displays. Decimal arithmetic systems can also preserve decimal digits exactly when a fixed decimal place is agreed. This uses more bits than ordinary binary for many values; it is a deliberate trade-off.

learningCycle.observe: BCD encodes the displayed 5 and 9 separately. Ordinary binary encodes the whole value fifty-nine. Decide which question each representation answers.
learningCycle.question: Why are the stored patterns different even though the display shows the same number?

steps.title: Encode each denary digit
steps.body: Binary Coded Decimal, or BCD, represents each decimal digit with its own four-bit code. For 59, convert 5 to 0101 and 9 to 1001, then keep the digit order. Do not first convert the whole value to ordinary binary.

steps.title: Decode groups separately
steps.body: Split a BCD pattern into groups of four. Each group must represent a digit from 0 to 9, so 1010 through 1111 are unused in the basic BCD digit code. For example, 0010 0111 decodes to the decimal digits 2 and 7, giving 27.

steps.title: Link the rule to an application
steps.body: A decimal counter or digital clock can keep a separate BCD code for each displayed digit, simplifying the link to decimal digit displays. Decimal arithmetic systems can also preserve decimal digits exactly when a fixed decimal place is agreed. This uses more bits than ordinary binary for many values; it is a deliberate trade-off.

worked.title: Encode the reading 308
worked.setup: A three-digit counter stores one BCD group for each displayed digit.

steps.title: Preserve the middle zero
steps.body: The stored sequence is 0011 0000 1000. Removing the middle group would change the reading to 38.

steps.title: Check the storage cost
steps.body: Three digits × four bits = twelve bits. Decode the three groups to recover 3, 0 and 8.

worked.conclusion: BCD preserves the sequence of decimal digits, including meaningful zero digits.

check.prompt: Decode BCD 0110 0010. Is 0110 1010 valid BCD?
check.answer: 0110 represents 6 and 0010 represents 2, giving 62. 0110 1010 is invalid in the stated basic BCD code because 1010 has value 10 and is not a decimal digit.

learningCycle.takeaway: BCD gives each decimal digit its own four-bit code; it does not encode the whole value as ordinary binary.
learningCycle.bridge: So far the number examples are non-negative. A thermometer needs a rule for values below zero.

workedExample.title: Encode the reading 308
workedExample.setup: A three-digit counter stores one BCD group for each displayed digit.

steps.title: Preserve the middle zero
steps.body: The stored sequence is 0011 0000 1000. Removing the middle group would change the reading to 38.

steps.title: Check the storage cost
steps.body: Three digits × four bits = twelve bits. Decode the three groups to recover 3, 0 and 8.

workedExample.conclusion: BCD preserves the sequence of decimal digits, including meaningful zero digits.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Represent negatives with one’s complement

leadVisual.title: One temperature, two signs

coreExplanation: One’s complement is a fixed-width representation of positive and negative integers. At eight bits, positive values use ordinary binary with a leading 0. For a negative value, first write its positive magnitude at the full width, then invert every bit.

In one’s complement a leading 1 indicates a negative value or the special negative-zero pattern. Invert all the bits, decode the resulting positive magnitude and apply the negative sign. Invert the entire width, not just the first bit.
Eight-bit +0 is 00000000. Inverting it gives 11111111, called −0. Two patterns therefore represent zero. At n bits the range is −(2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1) to +(2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1); at eight bits it is −127 to +127.

The rule provides a systematic binary representation of negative integers: inversion connects a positive value to its negative. The duplicate zero complicates comparisons and arithmetic, helping explain why another signed representation is useful. You do not need one’s-complement arithmetic here.

learningCycle.observe: Each 0 becomes 1 and each 1 becomes 0. This is inversion. To understand the negative value, we must know both the representation and the number of bits.

stimulus.title: One temperature, two signs
items: At eight bits, +5 is 00000101.
In one’s complement, −5 is 11111010.
Compare the patterns one position at a time.

learningCycle.question: What single operation changes every bit of the positive pattern?

prerequisite.title: Positive, negative and fixed width
prerequisite.body: The magnitude is a value’s distance from zero: +5 and −5 both have magnitude 5. Fixed width means every stored number uses the same stated number of bits, such as eight. A negative sign is not stored as an extra printed character in this model.

steps.title: Reserve a signed interpretation
steps.body: One’s complement is a fixed-width representation of positive and negative integers. At eight bits, positive values use ordinary binary with a leading 0. For a negative value, first write its positive magnitude at the full width, then invert every bit.

steps.title: Decode a negative pattern
steps.body: In one’s complement a leading 1 indicates a negative value or the special negative-zero pattern. Invert all the bits, decode the resulting positive magnitude and apply the negative sign. Invert the entire width, not just the first bit.

steps.title: Understand the two zeros and range

steps.title: State its purpose and limitation

The duplicate zero complicates comparisons and arithmetic, helping explain why another signed representation is useful. You do not need one’s-complement arithmetic here.

worked.title: Encode and decode −37 at eight bits
worked.setup: The required representation is one’s complement.

steps.title: Invert every position
steps.body: 00100101 becomes 11011010. Do not add one.

steps.title: Check by reversing
steps.body: Invert 11011010 to recover 00100101 = 37. The original pattern represents −37.

worked.conclusion: Keep the full width and name the representation before changing any bits.

check.prompt: Decode eight-bit one’s complement 11101001. What is the smallest representable value?
check.answer: Invert to obtain 00010110 = 16 + 4 + 2 = 22, so the original value is −22. The smallest eight-bit one’s-complement value is −127.

learningCycle.takeaway: At a stated width, one’s complement represents a negative integer by inverting its positive magnitude.
learningCycle.bridge: Two’s complement changes the rule by one step, giving one zero and a convenient arithmetic system.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Give the leftmost bit a negative weight

leadVisual.title: One pattern, two weight rows

coreExplanation: In n-bit two’s complement, the leftmost bit has weight −2ⁿ⁻¹. The remaining weights are positive powers of two. For eight bits the weights are −128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. Add the selected weights to decode any pattern.

For a representable negative value, write its magnitude as an unsigned working pattern at the required width, invert every bit and add one. Retain the stated width. For −128, the magnitude pattern is 10000000; this intermediate does not claim that +128 fits eight-bit signed storage. The negative-weight rule explains the final pattern.

The smallest eight-bit value is 10000000 = −128. The largest is 01111111 = +127. Zero has only the pattern 00000000. In general, the range is −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1, with one more negative value than positive values.

Two’s complement allows addition involving positive and negative integers to use the same column-addition process. Subtraction can be performed by adding a negative operand. The result still needs a range check: fixed-width arithmetic cannot represent every mathematical total.

learningCycle.observe: The unsigned reading is 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. The signed reading is −8 + 2 + 1 = −5. The pattern has not changed; the leftmost weight has.
learningCycle.question: What value does 1011 have under each row of weights?

steps.title: Use a negative leading weight
steps.body: In n-bit two’s complement, the leftmost bit has weight −2ⁿ⁻¹. The remaining weights are positive powers of two. For eight bits the weights are −128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. Add the selected weights to decode any pattern.

steps.title: Encode a negative magnitude
steps.body: For a representable negative value, write its magnitude as an unsigned working pattern at the required width, invert every bit and add one. Retain the stated width. For −128, the magnitude pattern is 10000000; this intermediate does not claim that +128 fits eight-bit signed storage. The negative-weight rule explains the final pattern.

steps.title: Read the range and single zero
steps.body: The smallest eight-bit value is 10000000 = −128. The largest is 01111111 = +127. Zero has only the pattern 00000000. In general, the range is −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1, with one more negative value than positive values.

steps.title: Connect the representation to arithmetic
steps.body: Two’s complement allows addition involving positive and negative integers to use the same column-addition process. Subtraction can be performed by adding a negative operand. The result still needs a range check: fixed-width arithmetic cannot represent every mathematical total.

worked.title: Store −37 using two’s complement
worked.setup: Use eight bits and check with negative place value.

steps.title: Decode with signed weights
steps.body: −128 + 64 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = −37. Both methods agree.

worked.conclusion: The conversion procedure and the signed weights describe the same representation.

check.prompt: Decode eight-bit two’s complement 11101001. Why is its value different from the one’s-complement check?
check.answer: −128 + 64 + 32 + 8 + 1 = −23. The previous one’s-complement reading was −22 because it used a different representation. The bit pattern alone does not select the rule.

learningCycle.takeaway: Two’s complement uses a negative leading weight, one zero and a fixed signed range.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Ask what the pattern is meant to represent

leadVisual.title: The unchanged pattern 1001 0101

coreExplanation: Identify the source representation, destination representation and any required width. A base conversion preserves a numerical value; changing only how a pattern is interpreted may change its value. These are different tasks.

Unsigned binary permits values 0 to 255 at eight bits. Signed representations use narrower positive ranges. BCD treats each nibble separately and rejects groups greater than 1001. A hexadecimal numeral is a readable base-16 number; it does not by itself say whether a stored byte is signed.

To convert a signed pattern to another signed representation, decode its value first, then encode that value using the new rule and check that it fits. Copying the unchanged bits usually does not preserve a negative value.

learningCycle.observe: Each reading follows a different rule. We should expect different meanings, just as the same word can mean different things in different languages.

worked.title: Interpret 10010101 using four rules

steps.title: Read unsigned and BCD

knowledgeUnits.heading: Carry when a binary column reaches two

leadVisual.title: How many ones fit in one binary digit?

coreExplanation: Write operands at the same width and align them on the right. Add from the least significant bit, the rightmost position, towards the left. Leading zeros help keep corresponding weights together.
At each position add the operand bits and the carry from the previous column. A total of 2 is binary 10: write 0 and carry 1. A total of 3 is binary 11: write 1 and carry 1.

Write or record carries as you go. A correct final pattern alone does not show how you handled a difficult column. Afterward, decode the result to check the arithmetic, and check whether it fits the stated width.

learningCycle.observe: Two ones are exchanged for one two. The same exchange happens in every position: two units of the current weight become one unit of the next weight.

stimulus.title: How many ones fit in one binary digit?

learningCycle.question: Why does 1 + 1 produce 10 rather than a digit 2?

steps.title: Align equal weights
steps.body: Write operands at the same width and align them on the right. Add from the least significant bit, the rightmost position, towards the left. Leading zeros help keep corresponding weights together.

steps.title: Include the incoming carry
steps.body: At each position add the operand bits and the carry from the previous column. A total of 2 is binary 10: write 0 and carry 1. A total of 3 is binary 11: write 1 and carry 1.

steps.title: Show the carry as evidence
steps.body: Write or record carries as you go. A correct final pattern alone does not show how you handled a difficult column. Afterward, decode the result to check the arithmetic, and check whether it fits the stated width.

worked.title: Add 13 and 7 at eight bits

steps.title: Start with the low four columns
steps.body: 1s: 1 + 1 = 2, write 0 carry 1. 2s: 0 + 1 + 1 = 2, write 0 carry 1. 4s: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, write 1 carry 1. 8s: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2, write 0 carry 1.

steps.title: Finish the remaining columns
steps.body: 16s: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1. All higher columns are zero. The result is 00010100.

steps.title: Check the value
steps.body: 00010100 = 16 + 4 = 20, and 13 + 7 = 20. It fits eight-bit unsigned storage.

worked.conclusion: A carry changes the next column, not the already written bit.

check.prompt: Calculate 00101101 + 00010111 and identify one column that receives a carry.
check.answer: 45 + 23 = 68, so the result is 01000100. The 2s column receives a carry from 1 + 1 in the 1s column. Continuing to include each incoming carry produces the result.

learningCycle.takeaway: Binary column addition exchanges two units of one weight for one unit of the next.
learningCycle.bridge: Subtraction reverses this exchange: one unit of a higher weight can be borrowed as two of the next weight.

steps.title: Finish the remaining columns

steps.title: Check the value

knowledgeUnits.heading: Borrow across binary places

leadVisual.title: Subtract 3 from 10

coreExplanation: Align the operands at a stated width. In a column where the upper digit is at least the lower digit, subtract normally. If the column requires 0 − 1, borrow from a higher position.
Borrowing one 2 supplies two 1s; borrowing one 4 supplies two 2s. Reduce the donor by one and record the borrowed amount. A column containing two units after borrowing can produce 2 − 1 = 1.

If the next column is zero, find a higher column containing a 1 and pass the borrow down through each intervening column. Keep each change visible. After completing the operation, add the difference to the subtracted operand to recover the starting value.

learningCycle.observe: The 2s position contains a 1. Borrowing it supplies two ones. The total value of the top row stays ten; we have regrouped it.

stimulus.title: Subtract 3 from 10
items: The rightmost column needs 0 − 1.

learningCycle.question: Where can the missing one be obtained?

steps.title: Subtract from the right
steps.body: Align the operands at a stated width. In a column where the upper digit is at least the lower digit, subtract normally. If the column requires 0 − 1, borrow from a higher position.

steps.title: Exchange a borrowed unit
steps.body: Borrowing one 2 supplies two 1s; borrowing one 4 supplies two 2s. Reduce the donor by one and record the borrowed amount. A column containing two units after borrowing can produce 2 − 1 = 1.

steps.title: Pass a borrow through zero columns
steps.body: If the next column is zero, find a higher column containing a 1 and pass the borrow down through each intervening column. Keep each change visible. After completing the operation, add the difference to the subtracted operand to recover the starting value.

worked.title: Follow 10 − 3 one column at a time

steps.title: Borrow for the 1s
steps.body: Borrow from the 2s column. It becomes 0 and the 1s becomes 2. Calculate 2 − 1 = 1.

steps.title: Borrow across the empty 4s
steps.body: The 2s column now needs 0 − 1. Borrow the 1 from the 8s column into the 4s column, then pass one 4 down as two 2s. The 8s becomes 0 and the 4s retains 1. In the 2s column, 2 − 1 = 1.

steps.title: Finish and verify
steps.body: The 4s column gives 1 − 0 = 1. The result is 00000111 = 7. Check 7 + 3 = 10.

worked.conclusion: Borrowing changes neighbouring columns, so use their updated values.

check.prompt: Subtract 00001001 from 00010010. How can you check the answer?
check.answer: 18 − 9 gives 00001001 = 9. Adding 00001001 + 00001001 returns 00010010, so the subtraction is consistent.

learningCycle.takeaway: Borrowing regroups an existing value; every donor column must be updated.
learningCycle.bridge: A subtraction can also be written as addition of a negative value. Two’s complement makes that useful.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Add positive and negative fixed-width integers

leadVisual.title: A temperature changes by −5

coreExplanation: Positive two’s-complement values use ordinary binary with a leading 0. Negative values use the stated signed rule. For 12 + (−5), the operands are 00001100 and 11111011.

Add bit by bit, including carries. Retain only the stated eight positions. A carry beyond them is outside the stored byte. Separately compare the mathematical signed answer with the signed range; a carry-out alone does not establish signed overflow.
A − B is A + (−B). For 7 − 12, encode +7 and −12, then add. If subtracting a negative, reverse its sign: 7 − (−3) = 7 + 3. The sign of the operand is not the same as the operation symbol.

learningCycle.observe: Encode both operands as eight-bit two’s complement first. The negative operand will look large if incorrectly read as unsigned; keep the signed interpretation throughout.

items: Starting temperature: +12
Change: −5
Final temperature: 12 + (−5)

learningCycle.question: Can ordinary binary column addition calculate this change?

steps.title: Encode each operand at the same width
steps.body: Positive two’s-complement values use ordinary binary with a leading 0. Negative values use the stated signed rule. For 12 + (−5), the operands are 00001100 and 11111011.

steps.title: Use the same column-addition rules
steps.body: Add bit by bit, including carries. Retain only the stated eight positions. A carry beyond them is outside the stored byte. Separately compare the mathematical signed answer with the signed range; a carry-out alone does not establish signed overflow.

steps.title: Turn subtraction into addition
steps.body: A − B is A + (−B). For 7 − 12, encode +7 and −12, then add. If subtracting a negative, reverse its sign: 7 − (−3) = 7 + 3. The sign of the operand is not the same as the operation symbol.

worked.title: Calculate 7 − 12 at eight bits
worked.setup: Use two’s complement for both operands and the result.

steps.title: Decode and check
steps.body: 11111011 = −128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = −5. The mathematical answer 7 − 12 is −5, which fits −128 to +127.

worked.conclusion: The same addition process works because the operands and result use the same signed representation.

check.prompt: Calculate −9 + (−6), then calculate −9 − (−6), using eight-bit two’s complement.
check.answer: −9 = 11110111 and −6 = 11111010. Adding gives 1 11110001; retain 11110001 = −15. For −9 − (−6), add +6 = 00000110 to 11110111, giving 11111101 = −3. Both mathematical results fit the signed range.

learningCycle.takeaway: Encode operands consistently, add columns, decode the retained width and check the signed result.
learningCycle.bridge: The next examples show why a stored pattern can be valid while the intended mathematical answer is out of range.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Decide whether the answer fits its representation

leadVisual.title: Keep only eight bits

coreExplanation: Overflow occurs when the true arithmetic result is outside the range available in the fixed-width representation. The system may retain low-order bits, but those bits no longer represent the required mathematical result.

Unsigned eight-bit addition can produce a ninth bit when its result exceeds 255. That carry shows the result does not fit. Unsigned subtraction also cannot represent a negative difference, such as 3 − 5; check the range rather than assuming that every subtraction is possible.

At eight bits the signed range is −128 to +127. Adding two positive values and obtaining a negative retained result indicates overflow. Adding two negatives and obtaining a non-negative retained result also indicates overflow. Opposite-sign addition cannot exceed the range when both operands already fit.

−1 + 1 produces 1 00000000, with a carry-out, yet signed zero is correct. +127 + 1 produces 10000000 without a ninth-bit carry, yet signed +128 is out of range. The interpretation determines which limit matters.

learningCycle.observe: Unsigned eight-bit storage stops at 255. Signed eight-bit two’s complement stops at +127. Neither row can hold its mathematical answer under the stated rule.
learningCycle.question: Why is a correctly formed eight-bit pattern not always the correct answer?

steps.title: Define overflow using the range
steps.body: Overflow occurs when the true arithmetic result is outside the range available in the fixed-width representation. The system may retain low-order bits, but those bits no longer represent the required mathematical result.

steps.title: Check unsigned addition and subtraction
steps.body: Unsigned eight-bit addition can produce a ninth bit when its result exceeds 255. That carry shows the result does not fit. Unsigned subtraction also cannot represent a negative difference, such as 3 − 5; check the range rather than assuming that every subtraction is possible.

steps.title: Use the signed rule for two’s-complement addition
steps.body: At eight bits the signed range is −128 to +127. Adding two positive values and obtaining a negative retained result indicates overflow. Adding two negatives and obtaining a non-negative retained result also indicates overflow. Opposite-sign addition cannot exceed the range when both operands already fit.

steps.title: Separate carry-out from signed overflow
steps.body: −1 + 1 produces 1 00000000, with a carry-out, yet signed zero is correct. +127 + 1 produces 10000000 without a ninth-bit carry, yet signed +128 is out of range. The interpretation determines which limit matters.

worked.title: Interpret 01111110 + 00000010 twice
worked.setup: The same bit addition is performed at eight bits.

steps.title: Add once
steps.body: The retained sum is 10000000.

steps.title: Apply the unsigned reading
steps.body: 126 + 2 = 128. The range is 0 to 255, so 10000000 correctly represents 128. There is no unsigned overflow.

steps.title: Apply the signed reading
steps.body: 126 + 2 is still mathematically 128, but two’s complement allows at most 127. The pattern 10000000 means −128, so signed overflow occurred.

worked.conclusion: Overflow is about a value failing to fit the chosen representation, not about a pattern looking unusual.

check.prompt: Eight-bit two’s-complement −100 + (−40) retains 01110100. Explain why the pattern cannot be accepted as the answer.
check.answer: The true result is −140, below the minimum −128. The retained pattern represents +116. Two negative operands have produced a positive retained value, confirming signed overflow.

learningCycle.takeaway: Check the mathematical answer against the range of the specified width and representation.
learningCycle.bridge: Numbers are one interpretation of bits. Text uses another: a shared table of character codes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Store the characters, then recover the message

leadVisual.title: A tiny agreed character set

coreExplanation: A character set is an agreed collection of characters with a unique code for each character in the set. Characters include letters, digits, punctuation and spaces. The code allows the computer to identify a character without storing a picture of its printed shape.

To encode text, replace each character with its code and preserve the order. With this table, CAB becomes 010 000 001. The receiver needs the same table and must know that each code contains three bits.

To decode, split the stored data into code groups and look up the corresponding characters. A font then supplies shapes for displaying them. Changing a font can change the appearance without changing the underlying character codes.

learningCycle.observe: Read each three-bit group using the table, keeping the original order. The space has its own code; it is information too. This small teaching table is not ASCII.
learningCycle.question: Which message does 010 000 001 011 100 represent?

steps.title: Define a character set
steps.body: A character set is an agreed collection of characters with a unique code for each character in the set. Characters include letters, digits, punctuation and spaces. The code allows the computer to identify a character without storing a picture of its printed shape.

steps.title: Encode a sequence
steps.body: To encode text, replace each character with its code and preserve the order. With this table, CAB becomes 010 000 001. The receiver needs the same table and must know that each code contains three bits.

steps.title: Decode using the same agreement
steps.body: To decode, split the stored data into code groups and look up the corresponding characters. A font then supplies shapes for displaying them. Changing a font can change the appearance without changing the underlying character codes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use seven-bit ASCII codes

leadVisual.title: A small extract from standard ASCII

coreExplanation: Standard ASCII is a seven-bit character set. Seven bits provide 2⁷ = 128 distinct codes, numbered 0 through 127. The set includes English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes; not every code displays a printable symbol.

Uppercase and lowercase letters have different codes. A file containing A differs from a file containing a even if a chosen font makes them look similar. A code table supplies the mapping; do not guess a code solely from a character’s appearance.

The code for A is 1000001 in seven bits. It can be stored in an eight-bit byte as 01000001. The extra leading zero does not make standard ASCII an eight-bit character set. Use the storage width specified by a file-size question.

learningCycle.observe: In this character table, the digit character 0 has code 48. Its shape looks like a number, but its role in text is a character. Also compare uppercase A and lowercase a.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Add an eighth bit, but keep the table agreed

leadVisual.title: Two illustrative extension tables

coreExplanation: An eight-bit extended-ASCII character set has up to 2⁸ = 256 code values. The additional bit doubles the available patterns compared with standard ASCII. Extensions commonly retain the original ASCII range and use the additional range for extra characters.

“Extended ASCII” does not name one universal extra-character table. Different eight-bit encodings assign different characters to some values from 128 to 255. Extra accented letters or symbols depend on which extension is selected.

Correct reconstruction requires both the stored codes and the matching character table. Choosing the wrong table may display incorrect characters even though no byte was lost. One extension also remains too small to accommodate the many writing systems needed together.

learningCycle.observe: The sender may have preserved the byte perfectly. The receiver can still show the wrong character if it chooses a different extension table.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Represent text across writing systems

leadVisual.title: One message needs more than English letters

coreExplanation: Unicode assigns code points to a much wider range of characters and symbols than ASCII. A code point is a number identifying a character in the Unicode system. The larger repertoire supports text from many writing systems in one consistent system.

An encoding specifies how a sequence of Unicode code points is represented as stored units or bytes. UTF-8, for example, uses a variable number of bytes. Unicode is therefore not accurately described as “every character always takes sixteen bits” or “always thirty-two bits”.

The stored code identifies the character; a font and text-rendering system produce its visible shape. A missing glyph may prevent a correct character from displaying, even when its code was stored correctly. This is different from decoding bytes with the wrong encoding.

learningCycle.observe: A document may need characters from several writing systems at once. Switching among small incompatible tables makes that difficult.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Reconstruct a bitmap from its stored codes

leadVisual.title: A tiny image file

coreExplanation: A bitmap represents an image as a rectangular grid of pixels. Each stored pixel has one colour. Pixels are the smallest individual image elements in this representation; they are not tiny vector shapes with independent smooth boundaries.

Each available colour has a code. The stored pixel data consists of those codes in a defined sequence. In this one-bit example, two codes are enough for white and blue. Real formats may store colour components directly or use a palette that maps codes to colours.

A bitmap file header contains information needed to interpret the image, such as dimensions and colour depth; formats may also record compression or other properties. The decoder uses the file format and this metadata to split and place the codes correctly. Pixel codes and header information perform different jobs.

learningCycle.observe: The six bits alone do not specify whether the image is 3 × 2 or 2 × 3. The dimensions and reading order are needed to reconstruct the intended grid.

learningCycle.takeaway: A bitmap stores ordered pixel colour codes together with information needed to reconstruct their grid.
learningCycle.bridge: The bits allocated to each pixel decide how many different colours can be distinguished.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Give each pixel more colour choices

leadVisual.title: The same gradient, different choices

coreExplanation: Colour depth is the number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel. At n bits per pixel, up to 2ⁿ distinct colour codes are possible. One bit gives two choices; two bits give four; four bits give sixteen.

If the available colours match the source better, each pixel can preserve a more accurate colour. With too few levels, gradual changes may appear as bands or steps. More depth does not add more pixel positions; it adds choices at each existing position.

For a fixed width and height, doubling bits per pixel doubles the uncompressed pixel data. Increasing from 2 to 4 bits doubles storage per pixel but increases the number of codes from 4 to 16, a factor of four. These are different relationships.

learningCycle.observe: With two shades, many different source tones must share the same stored colour. More available shades can distinguish smaller differences in the source.

stimulus.title: The same gradient, different choices

steps.title: Define colour depth
steps.body: Colour depth is the number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel. At n bits per pixel, up to 2ⁿ distinct colour codes are possible. One bit gives two choices; two bits give four; four bits give sixteen.

steps.title: Connect choices to colour accuracy
steps.body: If the available colours match the source better, each pixel can preserve a more accurate colour. With too few levels, gradual changes may appear as bands or steps. More depth does not add more pixel positions; it adds choices at each existing position.

steps.title: Connect depth to data size
steps.body: For a fixed width and height, doubling bits per pixel doubles the uncompressed pixel data. Increasing from 2 to 4 bits doubles storage per pixel but increases the number of codes from 4 to 16, a factor of four. These are different relationships.

steps.title: Count colour choices
steps.body: 2² = 4 possible colours versus 2⁴ = 16.

steps.title: Count pixel-data bits

steps.title: Explain the trade-off
steps.body: The second image can distinguish more colours at each position but needs twice the pixel-data storage. Header and palette costs are excluded here.

worked.conclusion: Colour choices grow exponentially with depth; data size grows in direct proportion to depth.

learningCycle.takeaway: Colour depth controls colour choices per pixel and the number of bits required for each pixel.
learningCycle.bridge: Spatial detail depends on the grid itself. Separate that image grid from the screen used to display it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish the stored grid from the display grid

leadVisual.title: One file displayed on two screens

coreExplanation: Image resolution describes the stored pixel detail, here specified by width and height in pixels. An 800 × 600 image contains 480,000 pixels. At a fixed depicted area, capturing more pixels can preserve finer spatial detail.

Screen resolution is the number of display pixels available across and down the screen. It describes the output device or display setting, not the stored image file. The physical size of the screen and the zoom setting also affect how large an image appears.

Enlarging a bitmap spreads its existing information over a larger display area. The viewer may repeat pixels or interpolate new values, but cannot recover detail never recorded. Creating an image with twice the width and twice the height gives four times as many pixels and, at fixed depth, four times the raw pixel data.

learningCycle.observe: The file still contains 800 × 600 stored pixels. The display can map them onto its own pixel grid in different ways, but reading the file has not added original image detail.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Build the bitmap-size calculation from units

leadVisual.title: A small image specification

coreExplanation: Width × height gives the number of stored pixels. For this image, 120 × 80 = 9600 pixels. Do not add width and height; that does not count the rectangular grid.
Each of the 9600 pixels needs four bits, so pixel data occupies 9600 × 4 = 38,400 bits. This is the origin of width × height × colour depth; it is a count of repeated storage requirements.

Divide by eight to obtain bytes, then use the correct prefix divisor if needed. Keep intermediate values unrounded. Add header or palette bytes only if supplied or required by the question. A compressed file cannot generally be sized from these properties alone.

learningCycle.observe: There are pixels in each row, rows in the image and bits in each pixel. Multiplying these counts produces bits, not bytes.

steps.body: Width × height gives the number of stored pixels. For this image, 120 × 80 = 9600 pixels. Do not add width and height; that does not count the rectangular grid.

steps.title: Multiply by bits per pixel

steps.title: Convert the requested unit
steps.body: Divide by eight to obtain bytes, then use the correct prefix divisor if needed. Keep intermediate values unrounded. Add header or palette bytes only if supplied or required by the question. A compressed file cannot generally be sized from these properties alone.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Draw an image from objects and properties

leadVisual.title: A two-object drawing list

coreExplanation: A vector graphic stores a drawing list of objects or drawing commands. Objects can include lines, rectangles, circles and curves. The list describes how to construct them instead of prescribing a colour for every pixel of one fixed-resolution grid.

A line needs endpoints or equivalent position and direction information, plus properties such as colour and line thickness. A rectangle needs a position, dimensions, fill and outline information. A circle can be described by a centre and radius. Properties depend on the object type.

A renderer interprets the object descriptions and draws the image for an output device. Later objects may cover earlier ones. The screen still uses pixels to display the result; that does not make the source representation a bitmap.

learningCycle.observe: The rectangle description supplies a type, position, dimensions and appearance. The line has endpoints and thickness. Together these descriptions instruct the renderer what to draw.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Turn a continuous signal into stored sample codes

leadVisual.title: Four readings from a changing signal

coreExplanation: An analogue signal varies continuously with time and can take values across a continuous range. A waveform graph shows how its amplitude changes. To store a digital representation, an analogue-to-digital converter produces a sequence of numerical sample values.

Sampling measures amplitude at regular time intervals. In this teaching example the interval is 0.25 seconds, giving four samples per second. Sampling chooses when to measure; it does not yet explain which finite amplitude levels can be stored.

Quantisation maps each measured amplitude to an available discrete level. Use the nearest level in this model. Our levels are −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, +1, +2 and +3. Thus −3.2 becomes −3 and +1.6 becomes +2. The difference from the original measurement is quantisation error.

Assign a three-bit code to each level and store those codes in sample order. This example uses an offset table, not two’s-complement weights: 000 means −4, 001 means −3, through 111 meaning +3. The decoder must use the same mapping.

learningCycle.observe: The measurements include fractional values. Three bits provide only eight patterns, so a model using three bits per sample must choose eight representable levels and a rule for rounding to them.

stimulus.title: Four readings from a changing signal

learningCycle.question: Can a fixed number of bits store every possible amplitude exactly?

prerequisite.title: A waveform is a graph of change
prerequisite.body: Time runs along the horizontal axis and signal amplitude along the vertical axis. Positive and negative amplitudes describe displacement about a reference level; they are not positive and negative loudness. A microphone converts sound into a changing electrical signal.

steps.title: Begin with an analogue signal
steps.body: An analogue signal varies continuously with time and can take values across a continuous range. A waveform graph shows how its amplitude changes. To store a digital representation, an analogue-to-digital converter produces a sequence of numerical sample values.

steps.title: Sample at separate times
steps.body: Sampling measures amplitude at regular time intervals. In this teaching example the interval is 0.25 seconds, giving four samples per second. Sampling chooses when to measure; it does not yet explain which finite amplitude levels can be stored.

steps.title: Quantise each measurement
steps.body: Quantisation maps each measured amplitude to an available discrete level. Use the nearest level in this model. Our levels are −4, −3, −2, −1, 0, +1, +2 and +3. Thus −3.2 becomes −3 and +1.6 becomes +2. The difference from the original measurement is quantisation error.

steps.title: Encode and preserve the order
steps.body: Assign a three-bit code to each level and store those codes in sample order. This example uses an offset table, not two’s-complement weights: 000 means −4, 001 means −3, through 111 meaning +3. The decoder must use the same mapping.

worked.title: Recover what the recording actually contains
worked.setup: Read the stored sequence 001 011 110 111 using the supplied level table.

steps.title: Recover sample order and spacing
steps.body: With a rate of four samples per second, these levels belong to times 0, 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 seconds in the stated interval.

steps.title: Identify what was not stored
steps.body: The original fractions and every between-sample detail were not recorded exactly. Playback reconstructs an analogue output from the stored samples; it does not retrieve the complete original continuous waveform.

worked.conclusion: Sampling selects times, quantisation selects levels, and encoding assigns bit patterns.

check.prompt: In the supplied offset table, how would measured amplitude −1.7 be stored? Which part of the process introduces the rounding error?
check.answer: The nearest level is −2, whose code is 010. Quantisation introduces an error of −0.3 amplitude units relative to the original measurement. Sampling chooses the measurement time; it is not the rounding operation.

learningCycle.takeaway: Digital sound stores ordered codes for quantised amplitude measurements taken at regular times.
learningCycle.bridge: We can change how often samples are taken without changing the available amplitude levels.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Change how often the signal is measured

leadVisual.title: Measure the same one-second interval

coreExplanation: Sampling rate is the number of samples taken per second, measured in hertz (Hz). A rate of 8 Hz gives eight samples each second and an interval of 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125 seconds. Higher rate means shorter time intervals.

More frequent measurements can capture faster changes in the signal and reduce the time detail missed between samples. Increasing rate cannot repair amplitude rounding caused by too few bits per sample. The recording also remains limited by the source and capture process.

For fixed duration, channel count and bits per sample, doubling the rate doubles the number of samples and therefore doubles the raw sound data. Count samples as rate × duration. In the stated one-second interval, do not add a second endpoint sample at time 1.0.

learningCycle.observe: Plan B adds observations in the gaps. It does not make each stored amplitude more precise; its advantage concerns how finely time is sampled.

stimulus.title: Measure the same one-second interval
items: Plan A: samples at 0, 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 seconds.
Plan B: samples every 0.125 seconds, from 0 to 0.875 seconds.
Both plans use the same amplitude levels.

learningCycle.question: Which plan records more information about changes between the original sample times?

steps.title: Define sampling rate
steps.body: Sampling rate is the number of samples taken per second, measured in hertz (Hz). A rate of 8 Hz gives eight samples each second and an interval of 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125 seconds. Higher rate means shorter time intervals.

steps.title: Link rate to waveform detail
steps.body: More frequent measurements can capture faster changes in the signal and reduce the time detail missed between samples. Increasing rate cannot repair amplitude rounding caused by too few bits per sample. The recording also remains limited by the source and capture process.

steps.title: Link rate to data size
steps.body: For fixed duration, channel count and bits per sample, doubling the rate doubles the number of samples and therefore doubles the raw sound data. Count samples as rate × duration. In the stated one-second interval, do not add a second endpoint sample at time 1.0.

worked.title: Compare 4000 Hz with 8000 Hz
worked.setup: Record two seconds of mono sound using eight bits for every sample.

steps.title: Explain what improved
steps.body: The higher rate measures the waveform twice as often. Its amplitude code still has eight bits, so the available amplitude levels are unchanged.

worked.conclusion: At fixed settings, sample count and raw data size grow in direct proportion to sampling rate.

check.prompt: A recording changes from 6000 Hz to 12,000 Hz. Everything else is fixed. Explain both the information change and the raw-size change.
check.answer: Samples are taken twice as frequently, reducing the time interval between measurements and allowing faster changes to be represented. Twice as many samples are stored, so raw data size doubles. The amplitude levels per sample do not change.

learningCycle.takeaway: Sampling rate controls measurements per second and the amount of time detail that can be represented.
learningCycle.bridge: Now keep the sample times fixed and change the number of bits available for each amplitude.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Change the amplitude choices for each sample

leadVisual.title: Measure the same amplitude, round differently

coreExplanation: Sampling resolution, or bit depth, is the number of bits used for each sample. With n bits, up to 2ⁿ amplitude levels can be represented. More bits allow more available levels across the same amplitude range.

More closely spaced levels usually allow a measured amplitude to be rounded to a nearer value, reducing quantisation error. The word “accuracy” needs this mechanism: more bits → more levels → finer amplitude distinctions. A particular value already exactly representable may show no improvement.

At fixed rate, duration and channel count, more bits per sample increase raw data size. Moving from eight to sixteen bits doubles the raw data, while increasing possible levels from 256 to 65,536. It does not double the number of samples.

learningCycle.observe: With two bits, the closest level is 1/3, about 0.333. With three bits it is 3/7, about 0.429. The measurement time has not changed.

stimulus.title: Measure the same amplitude, round differently

Two-bit levels: 0, 1/3, 2/3, 1.

learningCycle.question: Which available level can represent 0.46 more closely?

steps.title: Define sampling resolution
steps.body: Sampling resolution, or bit depth, is the number of bits used for each sample. With n bits, up to 2ⁿ amplitude levels can be represented. More bits allow more available levels across the same amplitude range.

steps.title: Explain the accuracy mechanism
steps.body: More closely spaced levels usually allow a measured amplitude to be rounded to a nearer value, reducing quantisation error. The word “accuracy” needs this mechanism: more bits → more levels → finer amplitude distinctions. A particular value already exactly representable may show no improvement.

steps.title: Explain the storage trade-off
steps.body: At fixed rate, duration and channel count, more bits per sample increase raw data size. Moving from eight to sixteen bits doubles the raw data, while increasing possible levels from 256 to 65,536. It does not double the number of samples.

steps.title: Find the two-bit error

steps.title: Find the three-bit error
steps.body: 0.46 − 3/7 is approximately 0.031 in magnitude.

steps.title: Explain the improvement
steps.body: More levels make the chosen stored value closer to this measurement. The three-bit sample also costs one more bit than the two-bit sample.

worked.conclusion: A more accurate stored amplitude comes from finer level choices, not extra measurement times.

check.prompt: Why is “sixteen-bit sound takes more samples each second than eight-bit sound” incorrect?
check.answer: Bit depth states bits per sample, not samples per second. Sixteen bits allow more amplitude levels than eight bits. Sample frequency is determined separately by the sampling rate.

learningCycle.takeaway: Sampling resolution controls amplitude levels and quantisation error; sampling rate controls the time spacing.
learningCycle.bridge: Combine the independent settings to count the data in a complete recording.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Count samples, bits and channels

leadVisual.title: A recording specification

coreExplanation: Rate × duration gives samples per channel. With 6000 samples every second for three seconds, there are 18,000 samples in one channel. Use seconds if the rate is given per second; convert minutes first.

Multiply samples by bits per sample and by the number of channels. Mono has one channel; stereo has two. Raw bits = sampling rate × duration × sampling resolution × channels, when the stated rate is per channel.

Divide bits by eight for bytes, then by the appropriate prefix multiplier. This gives uncompressed sample data under the stated assumptions. A container header adds information; a compressed audio file may have a different size. Do not invent either cost.

learningCycle.observe: First count the samples in one channel. Then give each sample its bits. A second channel would supply another full sequence of samples.

stimulus.title: A recording specification
items: Duration: 3 seconds.
Sampling rate: 6000 samples per second per channel.
Resolution: 8 bits per sample; one channel (mono).

learningCycle.question: What does each factor count in the size calculation?

steps.title: Count samples in one channel
steps.body: Rate × duration gives samples per channel. With 6000 samples every second for three seconds, there are 18,000 samples in one channel. Use seconds if the rate is given per second; convert minutes first.

steps.title: Count bits across all channels
steps.body: Multiply samples by bits per sample and by the number of channels. Mono has one channel; stereo has two. Raw bits = sampling rate × duration × sampling resolution × channels, when the stated rate is per channel.

steps.title: Convert units and retain the model
steps.body: Divide bits by eight for bytes, then by the appropriate prefix multiplier. This gives uncompressed sample data under the stated assumptions. A container header adds information; a compressed audio file may have a different size. Do not invent either cost.

worked.title: Calculate mono size, then change to stereo
worked.setup: Use the supplied three-second recording.

steps.title: Add a second channel
steps.body: At identical rate, depth and duration, stereo gives 36,000 bytes. It doubles the number of sample sequences; it does not change each sequence’s rate.

worked.conclusion: Every multiplier has a physical meaning: time, measurements, amplitude bits and channels.

check.prompt: Calculate raw bytes for 5 seconds of stereo sound at 8000 Hz and 16 bits per sample. Exclude headers.

learningCycle.takeaway: Raw sound size counts how many sample values are stored and how many bits each value needs.
learningCycle.bridge: Even short recordings and images can need substantial storage. Compression changes how their information is represented.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Reduce the data needed to store or transfer a file

leadVisual.title: A shared folder has room for 20 MB

coreExplanation: Compression represents data using fewer bits when the method is effective. Smaller files use less storage and need less data to be transmitted. At the same usable transfer rate, fewer transmitted bits usually mean a shorter transfer time.

An encoder creates the compressed representation and a decoder interprets it later. Compression and decompression require processing, and the receiver needs a compatible method. A shorter filename or a different unit label does not compress the file.

Before selecting a method, decide whether every original value must be restored exactly. A program, text answer or editable drawing may require exact recovery. Some delivered photos or audio clips can accept controlled differences. This requirement separates the two broad compression approaches.

learningCycle.observe: Two 8 MB files fit into 20 MB, while four 5 MB files fit. A network also has fewer bits to transfer for each compressed copy.

stimulus.title: A shared folder has room for 20 MB
items: One uncompressed resource occupies 8 MB.
A compressed version occupies 5 MB.
Use the stated decimal units and ignore other overhead.

learningCycle.question: What practical difference does the smaller representation make?

steps.title: Define the purpose
steps.body: Compression represents data using fewer bits when the method is effective. Smaller files use less storage and need less data to be transmitted. At the same usable transfer rate, fewer transmitted bits usually mean a shorter transfer time.

steps.title: Recognise the extra processing

steps.title: Ask what must be recovered
steps.body: Before selecting a method, decide whether every original value must be restored exactly. A program, text answer or editable drawing may require exact recovery. Some delivered photos or audio clips can accept controlled differences. This requirement separates the two broad compression approaches.

worked.title: Compare a fixed-rate transfer

steps.title: Transfer the original
steps.body: 8 MB ÷ 1 MB per second = 8 seconds.

steps.title: Transfer the compressed version

steps.title: State the model’s limits
steps.body: The difference is three seconds for data transfer in this model. Encoding, decoding and network overhead may add time in a real use case.

check.prompt: Does renaming an 8 MB file “small.txt” or describing it as 8000 kB reduce its storage requirement?
check.answer: No. The name and unit label do not change the represented file data. Actual compression changes how the information is encoded, producing a different data representation.

learningCycle.takeaway: Compression can reduce storage and transmission requirements by representing the data with fewer bits.
learningCycle.bridge: First examine a method that allows the exact original sequence to be reconstructed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use reconstruction to distinguish the methods

leadVisual.title: Compare the decoded result with the original

coreExplanation: Lossless compression allows the original data to be reconstructed exactly. It can remove redundancy, such as repeated values or repeated sequences, by storing a more compact description. The decoder uses the description to rebuild every original value in order.

Lossy compression discards some information, so decoding cannot guarantee the exact original. Several different inputs may produce the same stored approximation. Once their differences are absent from the file, decoding alone cannot discover which original was used.

A changed symbol in ordinary text or a changed coordinate in a precise drawing may alter its meaning. Those tasks need exact recovery. A delivery image or sound clip may allow less noticeable detail to be removed for a smaller file. State the acceptable change and the intended use.

learningCycle.observe: Version A recovers the original sequence exactly. Version B keeps an approximation but loses the small differences. Decide what a later user could recover from each version.

stimulus.title: Compare the decoded result with the original

learningCycle.question: Which version has preserved every original value?

steps.title: Define lossless compression by exact recovery
steps.body: Lossless compression allows the original data to be reconstructed exactly. It can remove redundancy, such as repeated values or repeated sequences, by storing a more compact description. The decoder uses the description to rebuild every original value in order.

steps.title: Define lossy compression by discarded information
steps.body: Lossy compression discards some information, so decoding cannot guarantee the exact original. Several different inputs may produce the same stored approximation. Once their differences are absent from the file, decoding alone cannot discover which original was used.

steps.title: Choose according to the consequence of a change
steps.body: A changed symbol in ordinary text or a changed coordinate in a precise drawing may alter its meaning. Those tasks need exact recovery. A delivery image or sound clip may allow less noticeable detail to be removed for a smaller file. State the acceptable change and the intended use.

worked.title: Assess an approximate four-value block
worked.setup: A toy lossy method stores one representative value 102 and a count of four, then reconstructs four copies.

steps.title: Decode what was retained
steps.body: The reconstructed block is 102, 102, 102, 102.

steps.title: Compare with the source
steps.body: The source was 100, 101, 102, 103. The decoded first, second and fourth values differ.

steps.title: Explain why the source cannot be recovered
steps.body: The same representative and count could describe many different source blocks. The small original differences are no longer stored.

worked.conclusion: Whether the result looks acceptable is a use-case judgement; whether recovery is exact is a property we can test.

check.prompt: A compression tool makes a text file much smaller. What evidence is needed before calling its process lossless?
check.answer: Decode the compressed data and compare the entire resulting sequence with the original. Every character or byte required by the file must be identical and in the same order. A smaller size alone does not establish losslessness.

learningCycle.takeaway: Lossless reconstructs exactly; lossy sacrifices some information for a potentially smaller representation.
learningCycle.bridge: Run-length encoding provides a small, visible example of an exactly reversible description.
