knowledgeUnits.heading: Encode repeated neighbouring values as runs

leadVisual.title: Read this sequence from left to right

coreExplanation: Run-length encoding, or RLE, replaces a consecutive repetition with its value and repetition count. Start a new run whenever the next value differs. With a fixed-width count, also start a new run if the count limit is reached.

The sequence becomes (4, A), (2, B), (8, C), (2, D). Decode each pair by repeating its value the stated number of times, then join the runs in order. The representation stores all information needed for exact reconstruction.

Assume each original value uses eight bits. The original sixteen values use 16 × 8 = 128 bits. Four encoded runs each need an eight-bit count and an eight-bit value: 4 × 16 = 64 bits. Under these assumptions and with no extra header, RLE halves the data size.

For ABC, the original has three eight-bit values: 24 bits. RLE stores (1, A), (1, B), (1, C), costing 3 × 16 = 48 bits. The counts add overhead without removing repetition. Effectiveness depends on consecutive runs and the format’s actual field costs.

learningCycle.observe: There are four A values followed by two B values, eight C values and two D values. Counting all occurrences without preserving their positions would lose the order.

stimulus.title: Read this sequence from left to right
items: AAAABBCCCCCCCCDD
A run contains consecutive copies of the same value.
In this teaching format, store each run as (count, value), with eight bits for each field.

learningCycle.question: Can a short description reproduce the same sequence in the same order?

steps.title: Find consecutive runs
steps.body: Run-length encoding, or RLE, replaces a consecutive repetition with its value and repetition count. Start a new run whenever the next value differs. With a fixed-width count, also start a new run if the count limit is reached.

steps.title: Encode and decode in the defined order
steps.body: The sequence becomes (4, A), (2, B), (8, C), (2, D). Decode each pair by repeating its value the stated number of times, then join the runs in order. The representation stores all information needed for exact reconstruction.

steps.title: Include the field costs
steps.body: Assume each original value uses eight bits. The original sixteen values use 16 × 8 = 128 bits. Four encoded runs each need an eight-bit count and an eight-bit value: 4 × 16 = 64 bits. Under these assumptions and with no extra header, RLE halves the data size.

steps.title: Test a case that grows
steps.body: For ABC, the original has three eight-bit values: 24 bits. RLE stores (1, A), (1, B), (1, C), costing 3 × 16 = 48 bits. The counts add overhead without removing repetition. Effectiveness depends on consecutive runs and the format’s actual field costs.

worked.title: Decode and evaluate a bitmap row
worked.setup: A row contains 000000111111000000. Each original pixel is one bit; each encoded run has an eight-bit count and one-bit value.

steps.title: Encode the three runs
steps.body: (6, 0), (6, 1), (6, 0). The two zero runs remain separate because the ones occur between them.

steps.title: Decode the pairs
steps.body: Write six zeros, six ones and six zeros. This reconstructs every pixel in the row.

steps.title: Compare costs
steps.body: Original: 18 bits. Encoded: 3 × (8 + 1) = 27 bits. RLE is lossless here but increases the size by nine bits.

worked.conclusion: Reversibility and size reduction are separate properties; calculate both.

check.prompt: Encode AABBAAA as (count, value) pairs. Why can the two A runs not simply become one run of five?
check.answer: The pairs are (2, A), (2, B), (3, A). Joining the A runs would lose the fact that the two B values occurred between them and would change the decoded sequence.

learningCycle.takeaway: RLE preserves ordered consecutive runs using a count and a value; long runs help overcome count overhead.
learningCycle.bridge: The same exact-recovery principle can compress different kinds of files, even when simple runs are not the best pattern to exploit.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Preserve text, pixels, objects and sample values exactly

leadVisual.title: Four kinds of repeated information

coreExplanation: A dictionary method can store a repeated sequence once and replace later occurrences with shorter references. The dictionary and reference rules allow exact expansion, including spaces, punctuation and order. Ordinary text needs lossless recovery because deleting a letter or changing a digit can change the message.

A bitmap with flat areas may contain long runs of the same colour code, making RLE useful. Other lossless methods exploit repeated patterns or predictable relationships. Exact recovery preserves the stored pixels; it does not recover detail already absent from the original capture.

A vector representation may repeat object descriptions, colours, line styles or coordinate patterns. Store reusable descriptions once and retain references plus each object’s required position or other differences. Exact expansion must preserve the drawing order and properties, not just produce a vaguely similar image.

Lossless sound compression reconstructs the original digital sample values exactly. Repeated samples can use runs, while more general methods exploit relationships between nearby values. This does not reverse the sampling or quantisation loss that occurred before the digital source existed.

A dictionary, count field or reference costs storage. Saving repeated content is worthwhile only when the total encoded representation, including required decoding information, is smaller. Short or irregular data may provide little benefit.

learningCycle.observe: Each representation has different values to preserve. A text decoder restores characters or bytes, a bitmap decoder restores pixel data, a vector decoder restores the required object descriptions, and a sound decoder restores the stored sample values.

stimulus.title: Four kinds of repeated information
items: Text: SAVE SAVE SAVE

learningCycle.question: What must each decoder reconstruct for the process to remain lossless?

steps.body: A dictionary method can store a repeated sequence once and replace later occurrences with shorter references. The dictionary and reference rules allow exact expansion, including spaces, punctuation and order. Ordinary text needs lossless recovery because deleting a letter or changing a digit can change the message.

Store reusable descriptions once and retain references plus each object’s required position or other differences. Exact expansion must preserve the drawing order and properties, not just produce a vaguely similar image.

steps.title: Preserve digital sound samples
steps.body: Lossless sound compression reconstructs the original digital sample values exactly. Repeated samples can use runs, while more general methods exploit relationships between nearby values. This does not reverse the sampling or quantisation loss that occurred before the digital source existed.

steps.title: Count all information needed for decoding
steps.body: A dictionary, count field or reference costs storage. Saving repeated content is worthwhile only when the total encoded representation, including required decoding information, is smaller. Short or irregular data may provide little benefit.

worked.title: Compress and restore a short sample sequence
worked.setup: Use the supplied twelve sound samples. Each original sample is eight bits. A run uses an eight-bit count and an eight-bit sample value; exclude other overhead.

steps.title: Calculate the saving
steps.body: Original: 12 × 8 = 96 bits. Encoded: 3 × (8 + 8) = 48 bits.

steps.title: Check exact recovery
steps.body: Expand four 12s, two 13s and six 9s. The result matches every original digital sample, in order.

worked.conclusion: The method is lossless relative to the digital source, even though that source was itself a sampled representation of an analogue signal.

check.prompt: A vector file stores one circle description and three references at different positions. What must remain in the compressed data for exact reconstruction?
check.answer: The circle’s required geometry and style, the definition of each reference, each instance’s position and other differences, and the drawing order must be preserved. References save space only when the shared description and reference overhead cost less than repeating the complete data.

learningCycle.takeaway: Lossless methods exploit repetition or predictable structure while retaining enough information for exact decoding.
learningCycle.bridge: When a delivery copy can tolerate controlled differences, discarding some information may achieve further reduction.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose what a delivery copy may sacrifice

leadVisual.title: Two delivery decisions

coreExplanation: A lossy image method can reduce stored precision or discard fine spatial or colour information that may be less noticeable at the intended viewing size. The decoded image is an approximation. Stronger reduction can produce visible artefacts such as lost detail or blocks, so inspect the actual result for the task.

A lossy audio method can reduce less perceptually significant information, for example some components masked by other sounds. Decoded samples need not match the source. A small spoken delivery clip may tolerate a trade-off that is unsuitable for a recording intended for further audio editing.

Do not apply a lossy media approximation to ordinary text that must retain every character, or to precise vector geometry whose coordinates must survive. A vector drawing can be rendered into a compressed bitmap for delivery, but that changes the representation and loses the original editable object structure.

Keep an appropriate original or lossless master when later editing or alternate exports are required. Re-encoding an edited lossy copy can introduce further loss. Merely copying an unchanged compressed file does not cause additional loss because its bytes remain identical.

learningCycle.observe: The answer depends on visible detail, audible detail and future editing. “Smaller” is a constraint, not enough by itself to justify any amount of quality loss.

stimulus.title: Two delivery decisions
items: A photographic thumbnail must download quickly on a course page.
A spoken revision clip must remain intelligible on classroom speakers.
The original editable photo and recording must also remain available.

A small spoken delivery clip may tolerate a trade-off that is unsuitable for a recording intended for further audio editing.

steps.title: Reject lossy changes when exact values matter

steps.title: Preserve a suitable master

worked.title: Measure one toy lossy trade-off
worked.setup: Four source values, 100, 101, 102 and 103, each use eight bits. A toy block format stores representative value 102 in eight bits and repetition count 4 in eight bits. Ignore other overhead.

steps.title: Compare the sizes
steps.body: The source costs 4 × 8 = 32 bits. The representative and count cost 8 + 8 = 16 bits.

steps.title: Decode and locate the loss
steps.body: The output is 102, 102, 102, 102. The first, second and fourth original values cannot be reconstructed exactly.

steps.title: State what the example does and does not prove
steps.body: This toy method shows how sacrificing distinctions can reduce a representation. It is not a specification of a real image or audio codec, and whether these differences are acceptable depends on what the values represent.

worked.conclusion: A justified lossy choice names both the storage benefit and the information or quality that may be lost.

check.prompt: Choose compression for a text answer sheet, an editable vector diagram, a small photo preview and an audio master. Justify the recovery requirement for each.

A photo preview may use lossy compression if its reduced detail remains acceptable at the intended size; preserve a suitable master for later uses.

learningCycle.takeaway: Choose compression from the required fidelity, data structure and intended use, then verify the decoded result.
learningCycle.bridge: The whole section follows one question: which rules let bits represent the required information, and what do those rules preserve or discard?

knowledgeUnits.heading: What changes when the school connects its devices?

leadVisual.title: One school, one changing timetable

coreExplanation: A network connects devices so that they can exchange data and use resources. A resource can be a file, an application, storage, a printer or a connection to another network. The devices need both a communication path and agreed rules for exchanging information.

If thirty computers can send jobs to one shared printer, the school can buy fewer printers. If authorised students request one centrally maintained timetable, the teacher can update that copy instead of manually replacing thirty separate copies. State the shared resource and the resulting benefit.

Devices can exchange messages and support collaborative work. An administrator can manage user accounts, access permissions and backups centrally where the chosen system provides those services. These are configured services; merely joining cables does not automatically create a backup or protect a file.

Sharing also introduces dependencies. If the printer is unavailable, connected devices cannot print through it. If the shared timetable service cannot be reached, the network does not magically provide a second copy. Later lessons ask which connection or device failed.

learningCycle.observe: The useful object is one current timetable. Connecting devices provides a path for requesting and receiving it. A connection alone does not decide who may change the file.

stimulus.title: One school, one changing timetable
items: Thirty students need the latest timetable.
The teacher has one printer and one updated file.
Students will later open a course page and watch the same lesson video.

learningCycle.question: If the teacher changes the timetable, how could everyone obtain the new version without carrying a storage device around the room?

prerequisite.title: Recall data without assuming expert vocabulary
prerequisite.body: Data is represented using bits, each 0 or 1. A file is an organised collection of stored data. Sending a file means using physical signals to communicate its data so that a receiving system can interpret it.

steps.body: If thirty computers can send jobs to one shared printer, the school can buy fewer printers. If authorised students request one centrally maintained timetable, the teacher can update that copy instead of manually replacing thirty separate copies. State the shared resource and the resulting benefit.

steps.title: Add communication and management
steps.body: Devices can exchange messages and support collaborative work. An administrator can manage user accounts, access permissions and backups centrally where the chosen system provides those services. These are configured services; merely joining cables does not automatically create a backup or protect a file.

steps.title: Notice the new dependence
steps.body: Sharing also introduces dependencies. If the printer is unavailable, connected devices cannot print through it. If the shared timetable service cannot be reached, the network does not magically provide a second copy. Later lessons ask which connection or device failed.

worked.title: Replace thirty timetable copies with one managed copy
worked.setup: The teacher changes Friday’s room from 12 to 18. Every student has permission to read the central timetable, but only staff can edit it.

steps.title: Make one authorised change
steps.body: The teacher updates the managed timetable. This removes the need to replace a separate copy on every student device.

steps.title: Request the current resource
steps.body: A student opens the shared timetable and receives the updated version, provided the service and connection are working.

steps.title: State the benefit precisely
steps.body: Central maintenance reduces duplicated update work and helps students access consistent information. Permissions control editing; backup still needs its own process.

worked.conclusion: A useful explanation connects a network feature to a concrete consequence.

check.prompt: Explain one benefit of sharing a printer and one benefit of centrally backing up school files.
check.answer: A shared printer lets several devices use one printer, reducing duplicated printer purchases. A central backup process can preserve managed copies of school files for recovery, reducing the need to organise separate backups on every device. Neither service is automatic merely because a network exists.

learningCycle.takeaway: Networks exchange data and make resources or services accessible to connected devices.
learningCycle.bridge: The same purpose can apply inside one school or across schools in different cities. Next, describe that change in scale.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish a local site from links between distant sites

leadVisual.title: Extend the school network

coreExplanation: A local area network, or LAN, connects devices within a limited geographical area such as a building or managed school site. It is normally owned or managed by one organisation. It may include several rooms, cables and wireless access points.

A wide area network, or WAN, covers a much larger area and can connect separate LANs. Links between cities commonly use telecommunications-provider infrastructure. Each school can retain its own LAN while participating in the wider network.

LAN and WAN describe geographical and organisational scope. They do not guarantee a speed, a particular signal carrier or whether the public may use them. A carefully designed WAN link can outperform a congested local connection.

learningCycle.observe: WiFi changes the kind of connection. The inter-city link changes the area covered. These are independent descriptions.

stimulus.title: Extend the school network

learningCycle.takeaway: A LAN covers a limited managed area; a WAN links devices or networks over a large area.
learningCycle.bridge: Scope tells us how far the system reaches. It does not tell us which computer supplies the timetable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow a request to the computer that supplies the service

leadVisual.title: Two ways to share a class photograph

coreExplanation: A client requests a service or resource. A server receives requests and provides or manages the service. For the timetable, the student application sends a request, the server obtains the permitted file, and the client receives and displays the response. A server is a role; one computer can run several services.

A client-server system can centralise accounts, permissions, files and backups. Staff can apply one set of access rules and maintain a managed copy. Dedicated server resources and administration cost money, and dependent clients can lose access when the service fails.

In a peer-to-peer system, each participating peer can request and provide resources. A student laptop can receive a photograph from another peer and later provide a different file. A dedicated central server is not required, but sharing, accounts and backups may need separate management on individual peers.

A small trusted group occasionally sharing non-critical files may prefer the lower initial cost of peer-to-peer. A school needing centrally controlled examination documents and consistent backups has reasons to choose client-server. Explain both the requirement and the consequence rather than claiming one model is always better.

learningCycle.observe: The request needs a working provider. The distinction is how service roles and management are organised, not the shape of the cables.

worked.setup: Forty school computers require individual accounts, restricted examination files and a nightly managed backup.

steps.title: Link the requirement to a role
steps.body: Use a server to manage authentication and provide permitted files when clients request them.

steps.title: Explain the alternative
steps.body: With independently managed peers, maintaining consistent permissions and backups across all sharing computers would be harder.

steps.title: State the trade-off
steps.body: Client-server meets the central-management requirement, but the school must fund administration and plan for server or connection failure.

worked.conclusion: A justified choice connects roles, management and availability to the stated scenario.

learningCycle.takeaway: Client-server organises request and service roles centrally; peers may both request and provide resources.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Locate the processing, software and working data

leadVisual.title: The same document in two arrangements

coreExplanation: A thin client relies mainly on server resources for application processing and/or storage. It still handles input, communication and display. Central applications can be updated in one managed place, and the client may need less local processing power or storage.

The server and network must support the users who depend on them. Losing the connection can interrupt the remote application even if the terminal still has power. Central maintenance reduces repeated local work but does not remove the need for adequate server capacity.

A thick client performs substantial application processing locally and normally has more local software or data. It can continue suitable work offline if the required application, data and permissions are available. Maintaining installations and security across many devices creates more distributed work.

A powerful laptop running a local application can still request a centrally stored file and therefore be a client in a client-server system. Thin/thick concerns the location of processing; client-server/peer-to-peer concerns who requests and provides services.

learningCycle.observe: Arrangement B has the application and working data locally. Knowing where processing happens explains the outcome better than knowing how large the device looks.

steps.title: Explain thin-client dependence
steps.body: A thin client relies mainly on server resources for application processing and/or storage. It still handles input, communication and display. Central applications can be updated in one managed place, and the client may need less local processing power or storage.

steps.title: Explain the cost of that dependence
steps.body: The server and network must support the users who depend on them. Losing the connection can interrupt the remote application even if the terminal still has power. Central maintenance reduces repeated local work but does not remove the need for adequate server capacity.

steps.title: Explain thick-client local work

It can continue suitable work offline if the required application, data and permissions are available. Maintaining installations and security across many devices creates more distributed work.

steps.title: Keep the two classifications independent
steps.body: A powerful laptop running a local application can still request a centrally stored file and therefore be a client in a client-server system. Thin/thick concerns the location of processing; client-server/peer-to-peer concerns who requests and provides services.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow each physical link from sender to receiver

leadVisual.title: The same computers, different links

coreExplanation: In a bus topology, devices attach to a shared backbone. A transmission propagates along that shared medium and the addressed receiver accepts the relevant data. Terminators at its ends reduce signal reflections; they do not select a destination. Shared use requires rules for avoiding or handling competing transmissions.

Each star host has a separate link to a central device. With a switch that knows the destination port, A sends to the switch, which forwards towards C: A → switch → C. These are two distinct physical links. Do not draw a direct A–C link that is absent from the network.

A full mesh connects every pair of nodes directly. A partial mesh has only some pairwise links. Mesh connections can provide alternative routes, but using an alternative depends on a working forwarding arrangement; the drawing alone does not configure the equipment.

A hybrid uses more than one arrangement, such as classroom stars connected through meshed links between buildings. Describe the local pattern and the connecting pattern separately. A hybrid label does not tell you which individual host has a spare connection.

learningCycle.observe: A topology is the arrangement of connections. The drawing is evidence about which neighbouring nodes can exchange data directly, not a suggestion that a message may jump between any nearby symbols.

stimulus.title: The same computers, different links

steps.title: Share a backbone in a bus
steps.body: In a bus topology, devices attach to a shared backbone. A transmission propagates along that shared medium and the addressed receiver accepts the relevant data. Terminators at its ends reduce signal reflections; they do not select a destination. Shared use requires rules for avoiding or handling competing transmissions.

steps.title: Use the centre of a star
steps.body: Each star host has a separate link to a central device. With a switch that knows the destination port, A sends to the switch, which forwards towards C: A → switch → C. These are two distinct physical links. Do not draw a direct A–C link that is absent from the network.

steps.title: Distinguish full and partial mesh
steps.body: A full mesh connects every pair of nodes directly. A partial mesh has only some pairwise links. Mesh connections can provide alternative routes, but using an alternative depends on a working forwarding arrangement; the drawing alone does not configure the equipment.

steps.title: Combine patterns in a hybrid
steps.body: A hybrid uses more than one arrangement, such as classroom stars connected through meshed links between buildings. Describe the local pattern and the connecting pattern separately. A hybrid label does not tell you which individual host has a spare connection.

worked.title: Trace a star and count a full mesh
worked.setup: A, B, C and D each connect to switch S. Compare this with a full mesh among the four hosts.

steps.title: Trace the star
steps.body: A sends over A–S. S checks the destination and forwards over S–C. The complete route is A → S → C, not A → B → C.

steps.title: List full-mesh links
steps.body: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD are the six distinct pairwise links.

steps.title: Check the count
steps.body: Each of four nodes has three connections, giving twelve link ends. Each link has two ends, so 12 ÷ 2 = 6 links. More links need more interfaces, cabling and management.

worked.conclusion: State the actual path and count each physical link only once.

check.prompt: In a switched star, explain how data travels from one host to another when the destination port is known. What additional property defines a full mesh?
check.answer: The sending host transmits to the central switch. The switch examines the destination address and forwards through the port leading to the receiving host. A full mesh has a direct link between every pair of nodes; a star does not.

learningCycle.takeaway: Topology describes links; a path is an ordered sequence of existing links.
learningCycle.bridge: Now remove one connection and see which paths still exist.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish a failed host link from a failed centre

leadVisual.title: Two failures that sound similar

coreExplanation: Start with the actual network drawing. Cross out the failed cable or device and its unusable connections. Then trace from the sender using only the remaining links. Do not invent a new connection to make the route work.

A bus backbone is shared, so a break or faulty termination can disrupt the segment. In a star, one host-link failure normally isolates that host while other intact host links remain usable. Failure of the central device removes communication through that centre.

A mesh may retain a route after a link fails. State which route remains and whether the network can activate it. Redundant links need suitable configuration so that they do not produce forwarding loops. Exact configuration methods are beyond this activity.

Compare the required availability, number of links, installation cost, maintenance and traffic. A star can make individual host faults easy to isolate. A mesh adds alternative connections at greater cost. Choose the feature that solves the stated requirement and identify what it does not protect.

learningCycle.observe: Resilience depends on the particular failure. A spare link between switches helps only if the sender can still reach its first switch.

stimulus.title: Two failures that sound similar

Case 2: the central switch fails.
Case 3: one inter-building link fails but another route exists.

learningCycle.question: Does “there are spare links” prove that every device keeps communicating after any failure?

steps.title: Remove the specified component
steps.body: Start with the actual network drawing. Cross out the failed cable or device and its unusable connections. Then trace from the sender using only the remaining links. Do not invent a new connection to make the route work.

steps.title: Compare a bus and a star
steps.body: A bus backbone is shared, so a break or faulty termination can disrupt the segment. In a star, one host-link failure normally isolates that host while other intact host links remain usable. Failure of the central device removes communication through that centre.

steps.title: Evaluate an alternative route
steps.body: A mesh may retain a route after a link fails. State which route remains and whether the network can activate it. Redundant links need suitable configuration so that they do not produce forwarding loops. Exact configuration methods are beyond this activity.

steps.title: Make a justified design choice
steps.body: Compare the required availability, number of links, installation cost, maintenance and traffic. A star can make individual host faults easy to isolate. A mesh adds alternative connections at greater cost. Choose the feature that solves the stated requirement and identify what it does not protect.

worked.title: Keep a building link failure separate from a laptop failure
worked.setup: A connects only to S1. C connects only to S2. S1–S2, S1–S3 and S3–S2 are available, and suitable forwarding can activate the spare path.

steps.title: Use the normal route
steps.body: A → S1 → S2 → C uses the direct S1–S2 connection.

steps.title: Remove S1–S2
steps.body: The available spare route is A → S1 → S3 → S2 → C. It still needs A–S1 and S2–C.

steps.title: Instead remove A–S1
steps.body: A has no remaining attachment, so the inter-switch links cannot restore its communication. A different protection would be needed for that fault.

worked.conclusion: Justify resilience against a named failure, not against the word “failure” in general.

check.prompt: A school wants other classroom computers to continue when one student’s cable breaks. Explain a suitable topology and one failure it still depends on.
check.answer: A star with separate host cables isolates the broken host cable, so other hosts can continue through the working central switch. Those hosts still depend on the centre; failure of that switch prevents communication through it.

learningCycle.takeaway: A design is resilient only against failures for which a usable route and working devices remain.
learningCycle.bridge: A shared connection also needs rules for competing transmissions. Ethernet makes those rules and their limits concrete.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace a school task into remotely supplied resources

leadVisual.title: Save a shared presentation

coreExplanation: Cloud computing supplies computing resources through a network as a service. Resources include processing, storage and applications. Physical computers still do the work; the user obtains access to specified resources rather than personally managing every underlying machine.

The school client sends a request containing the document change. The service checks access, performs the required processing and stores the change according to its application. Its response reports the result. A connection or service failure can interrupt that sequence.

A cloud arrangement can provide or increase resources when needed, within the service’s capacity, configuration and charges. This can avoid buying all possible future capacity at the start. It does not mean unlimited resources or a zero-cost service.

The client still receives input and displays output, and it may perform additional local work. The cloud supplies the remote part. An on-site private cloud may be reached over the local network; an internet-hosted service also depends on a usable internet connection.

learningCycle.observe: Input may exist locally before the remote service accepts it. Trace the request, remote work and acknowledgement instead of treating “cloud” as a place where every action always succeeds.

The service processes changes and stores the shared document.

learningCycle.question: Does a completed-looking page on the teacher’s screen prove that the remote service has saved the latest change?

steps.title: Identify computing resources
steps.body: Cloud computing supplies computing resources through a network as a service. Resources include processing, storage and applications. Physical computers still do the work; the user obtains access to specified resources rather than personally managing every underlying machine.

steps.title: Follow request, work and response
steps.body: The school client sends a request containing the document change. The service checks access, performs the required processing and stores the change according to its application. Its response reports the result. A connection or service failure can interrupt that sequence.

steps.title: Explain resource allocation
steps.body: A cloud arrangement can provide or increase resources when needed, within the service’s capacity, configuration and charges. This can avoid buying all possible future capacity at the start. It does not mean unlimited resources or a zero-cost service.

steps.title: Keep client and service responsibilities visible
steps.body: The client still receives input and displays output, and it may perform additional local work. The cloud supplies the remote part. An on-site private cloud may be reached over the local network; an internet-hosted service also depends on a usable internet connection.

worked.title: Check whether an assignment upload finished
worked.setup: A student selects an assignment file. The application shows “uploading”, then the school connection fails before confirmation.

steps.title: Locate the local state
steps.body: The selected file exists on the student’s device. Selection alone does not prove that the remote service has received it.

steps.title: Locate the uncertain step
steps.body: The transfer or save acknowledgement may have been interrupted. The student needs a confirmed saved result, not simply an open browser window.

steps.title: Recover using evidence
steps.body: When access returns, check the service’s saved assignment status before deciding whether another upload is needed.

worked.conclusion: A remote resource must be reached and the required operation completed before its result can be relied on.

check.prompt: Name three kinds of cloud resource and explain why cloud computing still requires physical computers.
check.answer: Cloud services can supply processing, storage and applications. Physical server hardware executes the processing and stores data, even when allocation and management are hidden from the user. The user accesses the specified resources through a network.

learningCycle.takeaway: Cloud computing supplies remote computing resources as services with identifiable requests, results and dependencies.
learningCycle.bridge: Different cloud arrangements place control and shared infrastructure in different hands.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish public infrastructure from a private document

leadVisual.title: The same confidential document, two deployments

coreExplanation: A third-party provider offers cloud services to multiple customers using its infrastructure. The school obtains the resources it needs without first buying and operating the complete server estate. Customer separation and permissions determine who can access particular data.

A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation. It can be operated on the organisation’s site or hosted elsewhere. The organisation can have greater control over configuration and resource use, but it still needs appropriate administration, capacity and protection.

A public service can reduce initial infrastructure commitment and allow capacity to vary, with continuing charges and provider dependence. A private arrangement can meet specific control requirements but may require more investment and management. Neither label guarantees better security or uninterrupted availability.

Public cloud does not mean publicly readable files. Private cloud does not necessarily mean a server inside the school building. Check which organisation the cloud serves, where it is hosted, who operates it and what access rules are applied.

learningCycle.observe: The deployment model and the document’s access permissions describe different properties. Shared provider infrastructure requires controls that separate customers and users.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Balance access and capacity against specific dependencies

leadVisual.title: The school’s busiest week

coreExplanation: Authorised users can access the same managed resources from suitable connected devices and locations. This supports shared current files and collaboration. A user without a connection or permission cannot obtain those resources merely because they are in a cloud.

A provider may let the school obtain more storage or processing as demand changes and may maintain underlying infrastructure. That reduces some local hardware work. The school still manages its own accounts, data and chosen service settings, and additional use can increase charges.

A school connection outage can block access even while the provider is healthy. A provider outage can block service while the school internet works. Data loss is another problem: recovery depends on an actual backup or version-retention arrangement and on its age.

Choose a deployment using control, confidentiality requirements, workload, available expertise, cost and connectivity. Explain mitigation where needed, such as a verified backup or permitted offline copy. Do not promise that a backup restores work created after the last saved recovery point.

learningCycle.observe: Remote access depends on a working route and permission. Flexible capacity depends on the service’s allocation and charging arrangements. A general advantage needs these conditions to be meaningful.

steps.title: Explain capacity and maintenance
steps.body: A provider may let the school obtain more storage or processing as demand changes and may maintain underlying infrastructure. That reduces some local hardware work. The school still manages its own accounts, data and chosen service settings, and additional use can increase charges.

steps.title: Separate independent failure causes
steps.body: A school connection outage can block access even while the provider is healthy. A provider outage can block service while the school internet works. Data loss is another problem: recovery depends on an actual backup or version-retention arrangement and on its age.

steps.title: Make the choice conditional
steps.body: Choose a deployment using control, confidentiality requirements, workload, available expertise, cost and connectivity. Explain mitigation where needed, such as a verified backup or permitted offline copy. Do not promise that a backup restores work created after the last saved recovery point.

worked.title: Choose an internet-hosted report service
worked.setup: The school has a reliable connection most days, needs parent access and has limited server-management staff. Its chosen service retains a backup made at 18:00.

steps.title: Explain the benefits
steps.body: A hosted service supports authorised access from different locations and reduces the school’s need to run all underlying hardware. Capacity can be arranged for the reporting period.

steps.title: State distinct drawbacks
steps.body: School or provider outages can prevent access. Subscription and extra capacity charges must be budgeted, and permissions and data protection still need management.

steps.title: Test recovery
steps.body: If data is lost at 19:00, an 18:00 backup may restore the earlier state but cannot guarantee recovery of all changes made during the following hour.

worked.conclusion: Choose the service together with explicit availability and recovery expectations.

check.prompt: Give two distinct benefits and two distinct drawbacks of using an internet-hosted school cloud service. Explain the mechanism behind each.
check.answer: Benefits include authorised access to managed resources from different connected locations, and obtaining additional resources without buying all server hardware upfront. knowledgeUnits.heading: Carry the same bits using electrical signals or light

leadVisual.title: Two cables for a school connection

coreExplanation: Copper conductors carry electrical signals. Twisted-pair cable twists pairs of wires to help reduce interference; coaxial cable uses a central conductor and surrounding shielding. Cable type, length and installation affect the signal and the achievable service.

Fibre carries light through a glass or plastic core. An optical transmitter creates the signal and a receiver detects it. Fibre avoids electromagnetic interference in the transmission medium and can support high-capacity links over suitable distances, with appropriate equipment.

Copper can be convenient and economical for many short fixed-device connections. Fibre can suit building-to-building links and electrically noisy routes, but installation, termination and optical equipment affect cost and maintenance. Compare the actual requirement, not an unsupported claim that every fibre service is faster than every copper one.

A wired endpoint needs a physical cable path and connection point. That is useful for a fixed desktop but restricts movement. A cable still needs suitable equipment at both ends; a length of cable by itself does not provide a network service.

learningCycle.observe: The carrier can change while the represented data remains the same. Equipment converts between the link’s physical signals and the data it processes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Connect a moving device through radio coverage

leadVisual.title: Carry a tablet from the front to the back of the classroom

coreExplanation: Wireless radio communication transmits an encoded signal through space. An antenna sends or receives electromagnetic waves. WiFi is a family of technologies used for wireless local networking; it is not another name for the internet.

A tablet can move within usable wireless coverage without maintaining a cable to the tablet. This supports flexible classroom seating and portable devices. Coverage still has limits, and movement can change signal conditions.

Obstacles, distance, interference and competing devices can reduce the usable service. Multiple users may share the available wireless capacity. More users do not create more total capacity merely by joining the network.

A wireless access point connects wireless devices to the local network. It still needs power and an onward connection, often a cable. Wireless access needs authentication and appropriate protection; radio coverage alone is not permission to use school resources.

learningCycle.observe: Wireless does not mean a connection without physical conditions. The data travels using electromagnetic waves, and successful reception depends on the environment and equipment.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Join two fixed locations with a directional radio path

leadVisual.title: Two school buildings with a road between them

coreExplanation: Microwaves are electromagnetic waves in a high-frequency part of the radio spectrum. They are used in several communication systems. Here, consider a terrestrial point-to-point microwave link between directional antennas.

The antennas direct the signal between endpoints. Such links commonly need a suitable line-of-sight path, appropriate antenna height and alignment. An obstruction can weaken or block the path, so the physical route must be checked.

A point-to-point wireless link can cross a route where installing cable is difficult. Equipment, antenna positioning, permitted operation and environmental conditions still constrain the service. Weather effects depend on the frequency and design; do not promise that every microwave link behaves identically.

learningCycle.observe: The proposed link depends on a directed radio path between fixed antennas. The installation needs a suitable clear path rather than merely two devices that support wireless communication.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow the uplink, relay and downlink

leadVisual.title: Connect a school expedition station

coreExplanation: The ground-to-satellite transmission is an uplink. The satellite-to-ground transmission is a downlink. Suitable ground antennas and equipment send and receive the radio signals; a satellite is a relay in the communication path.

Satellite services can connect locations where laying cable or reaching nearby terrestrial infrastructure is difficult. Availability depends on the service coverage, ground equipment and a usable view or radio path to the satellite system.

Signals take time to travel. A longer route adds propagation delay even when the link can carry many bits per second. Satellite altitude and system design matter: do not assign every satellite service the same delay or assume all satellites remain fixed above one place.

Ground equipment, service charges and suitable installation are required. Obstacles and weather can affect some satellite links. Evaluate these conditions against the remote site’s needs instead of promising that satellite access always works everywhere.

learningCycle.observe: Coverage and delay describe different properties. A relay can extend reach while adding signal travel distance and processing or network delays.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Justify the carrier from movement, distance and environment

leadVisual.title: Four links with different jobs

coreExplanation: Identify which endpoints move, the route length, available infrastructure, obstacles, interference, required capacity, acceptable delay, installation cost and maintenance. Use facts supplied by the scenario rather than inventing a universal ranking.

Fibre carries light and avoids electromagnetic interference in its medium. WiFi uses radio and permits movement within coverage. If mobility is the requirement, compare a trailing wired connection with usable wireless coverage. If interference is the problem, compare the signal carriers under that environment. “Fibre is fast; copper is cheap” is incomplete unless those factors are linked to the actual requirement.

A justified answer can prefer an option while stating its installation or service limitation. A mixed school network can use different media for different links; there is no requirement for the whole system to use one carrier.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Connect a computer to its first network link

leadVisual.title: Two entrances to the school network

coreExplanation: A network interface card or controller, NIC, provides an interface between the computer and its network link. It sends and receives data using the link’s signalling and communication rules. A wired Ethernet interface connects through a suitable cable.

A wireless network interface card or controller, WNIC, handles wireless communication using radio. It enables the tablet to communicate with compatible local wireless equipment. It does not mean the tablet itself provides the school’s internet service.

A wireless access point, WAP, gives wireless clients access to a LAN and connects their wireless communication to the wider local network. It needs power and onward connectivity. Its role differs from a server supplying files and a router forwarding between networks.

Ethernet and WiFi interfaces use link-layer addresses commonly called MAC addresses. At this stage, treat them as local interface labels used in frame delivery. They are different from the IP addresses used for routing, which are introduced later.

learningCycle.observe: The network interface joins a computer to a communication medium. Its job differs from storing the requested timetable or deciding a route across distant networks.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate forwarding a frame from answering its request

leadVisual.title: The switch has learned where devices connect

coreExplanation: A frame is a structured unit of link-level communication containing data and control information, including local source and destination addressing. The destination MAC address identifies the intended local interface for the frame.

A switch uses destination MAC information and its forwarding table to select an appropriate outgoing port. In this example the destination is already known, so it sends towards that port rather than sending through every workstation.

The server receives the request, checks any applicable permission, performs the service and prepares a response. Providing the timetable, managing accounts and storing files are service jobs. A switch does not understand the timetable’s meaning in order to forward a frame.

A switch can learn interface locations from received frames. If a destination is unknown, forwarding behaviour differs from this known-port example; do not turn the simplified table into a promise that every frame is always sent through exactly one output. Learning-table details are optional here.

learningCycle.observe: The switch passes communication through a suitable local port. The server performs the requested service. Both participate, but they solve different problems.

steps.title: Forward towards T
steps.body: A sends a frame addressed to T. The switch receives it on port 1 and forwards through port 2.

steps.title: Perform the service

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate segment filtering from signal regeneration

leadVisual.title: Two different problems

coreExplanation: A bridge connects LAN segments and uses MAC-address information to decide whether a frame needs to cross between them. If sender and known destination are on the same segment, it can avoid forwarding the frame into the other segment.

If the known destination belongs to the other segment, the bridge forwards the frame across. This can reduce unnecessary traffic between segments. Unknown and broadcast traffic need appropriate handling; the activity focuses on destinations whose locations are known.

A repeater receives a signal and regenerates or reshapes it for continued transmission. It helps extend a suitable link within the technology’s limits. Its task is not to read a destination address and choose a route, and it cannot repair an arbitrary corrupted message by knowing what the sender meant.

Bridge: inspect link-level addressing and filter or forward between segments. Repeater: regenerate a signal. A switch performs related bridging functions across multiple ports. A router, introduced after addressing, forwards between networks using IP information.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Send a packet towards another network

leadVisual.title: Two destinations from the same classroom

coreExplanation: In the simple LAN model, a client compares the destination address with its local subnet. A destination on that subnet can be reached locally. For a destination outside it, the client normally sends towards a configured router, often called its default gateway.

A router connects networks and examines a packet’s destination IP address. It uses routing information to select an outgoing interface or next hop. The next hop may be another router; one router does not need a direct cable to every final destination.

On the first Ethernet link, the frame is addressed to the local next-hop interface. For a remote destination that is the gateway interface, while the packet inside identifies the remote IP destination. A switch forwards the local frame; the router handles the packet’s onward network delivery.

The server’s response also needs valid addressing and routing back to the client. The route can involve several networks. Successful outgoing transmission does not prove that the service has answered or that every return-path dependency works.

learningCycle.observe: The first local link and the complete IP destination are different parts of delivery. The client must reach its gateway locally before a router can forward onwards.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Package data for an Ethernet link

leadVisual.title: A payload needs delivery information

coreExplanation: Ethernet is a family of standards for wired local-network communication. It defines aspects of physical transmission and link-level frames. It is not a name for every network cable, every internet connection or WiFi.

An Ethernet frame carries data together with control information, including source and destination MAC addresses and error-checking information. The addresses guide local delivery; the payload is the data being transported, which can contain an IP packet.

The sender includes an error-detection value calculated from frame data. The receiver checks the received frame using the corresponding rule. A failed check indicates that the frame should not be accepted as intact; the check does not itself reconstruct any arbitrary damaged data.

Older shared half-duplex Ethernet permits only one successful transmission on the shared medium at a time and uses collision detection. Modern switched full-duplex links can send and receive simultaneously on their separate link and do not use CSMA/CD to arbitrate normal traffic.

learningCycle.observe: Equipment needs boundaries, addressing and error-checking information as well as useful content. A frame puts those different jobs into a structured link-level unit.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Listen, detect a collision, stop and retry after a random delay

leadVisual.title: Two senders share a half-duplex Ethernet medium

coreExplanation: CSMA/CD means Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection. Carrier sense means checking whether the shared medium is busy. Multiple access means several devices may attempt to use it. Collision detection means monitoring for overlapping transmissions while sending.

A device with data checks the shared channel. If it is busy, the device waits; if it is idle, it may begin. Two devices can begin close enough together that their signals overlap before either could sense the other.

When a collision is detected, transmission is stopped and a jamming signal makes the collision evident on the shared medium. Continuing to send the rest of the frame would waste time because this attempt has failed.

Each sender chooses a backoff delay. Different choices help separate their next attempts; an identical fixed delay could make them collide repeatedly. After the delay, the device still checks whether the channel is available before retrying. Random choice reduces repeated conflict but cannot guarantee that the next choices differ.
This procedure belongs to shared half-duplex Ethernet. Do not apply it to WiFi or claim that normal switched full-duplex Ethernet uses collision detection to decide who may transmit.

learningCycle.observe: Signals take time to propagate. Each sender can observe an idle channel before the other transmission reaches it. Listening reduces conflict but does not eliminate that timing possibility.

stimulus.title: Two senders share a half-duplex Ethernet medium

steps.title: Expand the name into actions
steps.body: CSMA/CD means Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection. Carrier sense means checking whether the shared medium is busy. Multiple access means several devices may attempt to use it. Collision detection means monitoring for overlapping transmissions while sending.

steps.title: Start only when the channel is available
steps.body: A device with data checks the shared channel. If it is busy, the device waits; if it is idle, it may begin. Two devices can begin close enough together that their signals overlap before either could sense the other.

steps.title: Stop the failed attempt
steps.body: When a collision is detected, transmission is stopped and a jamming signal makes the collision evident on the shared medium. Continuing to send the rest of the frame would waste time because this attempt has failed.

steps.title: Use a random backoff, then check again
steps.body: Each sender chooses a backoff delay. Different choices help separate their next attempts; an identical fixed delay could make them collide repeatedly. After the delay, the device still checks whether the channel is available before retrying. Random choice reduces repeated conflict but cannot guarantee that the next choices differ.

steps.title: Keep the scope explicit
steps.body: This procedure belongs to shared half-duplex Ethernet. Do not apply it to WiFi or claim that normal switched full-duplex Ethernet uses collision detection to decide who may transmit.

worked.title: Compare equal and different retry delays
worked.setup: A and B collide on a shared half-duplex medium. For this first-collision example each selects zero or one backoff slot; other mandatory Ethernet timing intervals are outside this simplified trace.

steps.title: Try equal waits
steps.body: If both choose zero backoff slots and both find the channel idle when they are permitted to retry, their next starts may overlap again.

steps.title: Try different waits
steps.body: If A chooses zero slots and B chooses one, A may start first. When B is ready it must check the channel and wait if A is still using it.

steps.title: Explain the mechanism
steps.body: Random backoff spreads competing retries over time. The final channel check prevents a completed wait from being treated as permission to interrupt another sender.

worked.conclusion: Both the random delay and the renewed channel check contribute to recovery.

check.prompt: Describe the collision response and explain why two devices should not always wait the same fixed delay.
check.answer: They detect the collision, stop transmitting and send a jamming signal, then wait selected backoff delays before checking the channel and attempting retransmission. The same fixed delay can synchronise retries and cause repeated collisions; different randomly selected delays reduce that risk.

learningCycle.takeaway: Shared Ethernet recovers through collision detection, stopping, random backoff and a checked retry.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Play arriving media before the complete recording is available

leadVisual.title: Two classroom viewing activities

coreExplanation: In bit streaming, media data is delivered as an ongoing sequence and playback can start before the entire resource has been received. Arrival, temporary storage and playback overlap rather than waiting for one complete file download first.

On-demand media has already been recorded. The viewer chooses when to start and may be able to pause or seek within the available resource. Data can be delivered ahead of the current playback position, subject to the application’s buffering choices.

Real-time media is produced and transmitted as the event happens. In a video discussion, capture, encoding or compression, transmission and playback occur continuously. Excessive waiting damages the conversation even if every bit eventually arrives.

A buffer temporarily stores arriving media until playback consumes it. It can absorb short variations in arrival, but it does not create future live content or an unlimited supply. The next concepts quantify its stored amount and changes.

learningCycle.observe: The future part of a live event does not yet exist. Streaming lets playback proceed from available data while more data is transmitted and received.

stimulus.title: Two classroom viewing activities
items: The teacher opens a previously recorded revision clip.
The class joins a live video discussion with a partner school.
In both activities, later media can still be arriving while earlier media plays.

prerequisite.title: Recall compression at the point it becomes useful
prerequisite.body: Digital audio and video contain data represented in bits. Compression reduces the data required for a representation. A lossy delivery version may sacrifice some detail to use fewer bits; lossless compression preserves its source data exactly. The codec details are outside this networking activity.

steps.body: Real-time media is produced and transmitted as the event happens. In a video discussion, capture, encoding or compression, transmission and playback occur continuously. Excessive waiting damages the conversation even if every bit eventually arrives.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare two rates using the same units

leadVisual.title: Two labels on the player

coreExplanation: The incoming media rate is the amount of usable media data received per second. It can change as network conditions and shared use change. A connection’s advertised maximum is not a guarantee of the sustained rate this player actually receives.

Playback consumes encoded media data at a required rate. A higher-resolution or less-compressed version may need more bits per second, but the precise requirement belongs to the actual media representation. Use the supplied playback rate in calculations.
Keep bits and bytes separate and use consistent prefixes. A rate of 500 kB/s is 500 × 8 = 4000 kbit/s = 4 Mbit/s in decimal units. Comparing 500 with 4 without their units gives no useful conclusion.

At a constant rate, amount = rate × time. Receiving 6 Mbit/s for 5 seconds supplies 30 Mbit. Time = amount ÷ rate when the rate remains constant. These are simplified usable-media quantities, so add protocol overhead only when the problem supplies or requests it.

learningCycle.observe: Six million bits arrive while four million are used. The difference is two million bits per second, provided there is space to hold it.

prerequisite.body: A bit rate is a quantity of bits per second. Here Mbit/s uses the decimal multiplier 1,000,000. A byte contains eight bits, so 1 MB of data is 8 Mbit under these decimal units. Storage capacity and transfer rate are different quantities.

steps.title: Define the incoming rate
steps.body: The incoming media rate is the amount of usable media data received per second. It can change as network conditions and shared use change. A connection’s advertised maximum is not a guarantee of the sustained rate this player actually receives.

steps.title: Relate rate and amount

steps.title: Convert the arrival rate
steps.body: 500 kB/s × 8 = 4000 kbit/s = 4 Mbit/s.

steps.title: Compare like units
steps.body: The incoming 4 Mbit/s exceeds the 3 Mbit/s consumption by 1 Mbit/s.

steps.title: Count ten seconds
steps.body: Arrival supplies 40 Mbit and playback consumes 30 Mbit in ten seconds. Stored content would increase by 10 Mbit if the buffer has enough space.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Track what is stored, not just whether the connection is fast

leadVisual.title: A buffer has a starting amount

coreExplanation: The receiver buffer holds media that has arrived but has not yet been consumed. During initial buffering, playback may wait until a chosen threshold is reached. Arrival can then continue while playback removes older content.

While playback runs and neither boundary is reached, new buffer amount = old amount + (incoming rate − playback rate) × time. Equal rates keep the amount unchanged; a positive difference fills it; a negative difference drains it.

The buffer cannot become negative. If it empties and arrival cannot sustain playback, the player must change behaviour, such as pausing to refill or reducing the required media rate. Once playback pauses, its consumption rate is zero until it resumes, so the earlier running-state calculation no longer applies.

A buffer also has a maximum size. Once it is full, the simple unlimited accumulation calculation stops being valid. The application may pause requests or otherwise control delivery. Do not draw more stored data than the specified capacity permits.

Use constant rates only for the stated interval. The experiment uses one-second steps, receiving data before deciding whether to play in each step. It shows the starting threshold and rate balance but does not impose a full-buffer capacity limit. A real buffer is finite; use a supplied capacity when analysing that boundary. Different players can use different pause and restart policies.

learningCycle.observe: No. Previously stored content can cover a temporary shortfall. We need the starting buffer amount as well as the rates and duration.

worked.title: Carry the buffer state from one interval to the next
worked.setup: Start with 4 Mbit buffered. Capacity is 12 Mbit and playback is already running at 2 Mbit/s.

steps.title: Calculate the first interval
steps.body: For 4 seconds, incoming rate is 3 Mbit/s. Change = (3 − 2) × 4 = +4 Mbit, so the buffer reaches 8 Mbit.

steps.title: Use the new starting amount
steps.body: For the next 3 seconds, incoming rate is 1 Mbit/s. Change = (1 − 2) × 3 = −3 Mbit, leaving 5 Mbit.

steps.title: Check the boundaries
steps.body: The amount stays between 0 and 12 Mbit, so neither interval needs a pause or full-buffer adjustment. Playback can continue despite the slower second interval.

worked.conclusion: Every interval starts from the amount left by the previous one.

learningCycle.takeaway: A buffer absorbs a temporary rate mismatch by increasing or decreasing its finite stored reserve.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Explain why a finite buffer cannot solve a permanent deficit

leadVisual.title: The connection settles below the video requirement

coreExplanation: When playback consumes faster than usable media arrives, the buffer decreases by the difference. If those conditions continue, any finite starting reserve eventually runs out. Extra initial buffering buys time rather than changing the ongoing rate balance.

A player may pause to accumulate more content, select a representation with a lower required bit rate, or benefit from a more reliable usable network rate. Each response changes a relevant quantity. Repeating the same fixed-rate playback with an unchanged deficit recreates the problem.

A larger live buffer can smooth some arrival variation but puts playback further behind capture time. In a conversation, that delay may be undesirable. A live source also limits how much future content can be prefetched because it has not yet been created.

Successful DNS resolution or an open page proves neither sufficient throughput nor an available buffer reserve. Check arrival, consumption, stored amount and time. A paused video is not by itself proof that the school’s domain name failed to resolve.

learningCycle.observe: The reserve is being spent at 1 Mbit every second. Doubling the reserve doubles the time it can cover that deficit, but the continuing shortfall remains.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish the network from a service that uses it

leadVisual.title: Three activities on the same connection

coreExplanation: The internet is a global network of interconnected networks that communicate using internet protocols. A school LAN can connect through provider infrastructure to reach other networks. Its paths include physical links and network equipment rather than an invisible cloud with no machinery.

The World Wide Web, or WWW, is a system of linked web resources accessed using web technologies. Browsers request resources from web servers, commonly using HTTP or HTTPS. Web pages may contain text, images and links to other resources.

Email, file transfer and other network applications can use the internet without being the WWW. A webmail interface is itself a web application, so classify the actual activity and interface rather than assuming every instance of the word email must be non-web.

A particular website can fail while the internet connection still supports other services. The school’s internet access can fail while some local LAN services continue. Service availability and network reachability are related but not identical.

learningCycle.observe: The same interconnected networks support different services. Closing one application does not remove the underlying infrastructure or every other service.

stimulus.title: Three activities on the same connection
items: Open the school course page in a browser.
Send an email using an email application.
Use a game service or another non-web network application.

steps.body: Email, file transfer and other network applications can use the internet without being the WWW. A webmail interface is itself a web application, so classify the actual activity and interface rather than assuming every instance of the word email must be non-web.

worked.conclusion: Name the failed service or path as precisely as the evidence allows.

learningCycle.takeaway: The internet connects networks; the WWW is one of the services those networks support.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match data to the signal form required by an access link

leadVisual.title: A communication link expects a carrier signal

coreExplanation: Modem combines modulator and demodulator. Modulation represents data by changing suitable properties of a carrier signal. Demodulation interprets received carrier changes to recover the represented data.

On a traditional analogue telephone access link, the modem converts the computer’s digital data into an appropriate modulated signal for the line. A receiving modem demodulates it back into digital data. This explains the familiar digital-to-analogue and analogue-to-digital description in that context.

Different access technologies use different signal forms and equipment. Do not claim that every internet link is analogue or that every hop converts digital data into analogue form. Explain the conversion required by the link in the stated example.

A modem handles the signal requirements of its access link. A router forwards packets between networks using addressing and routing information. One household or school box may combine roles, but combining hardware does not make the roles identical.

learningCycle.observe: Equipment must use signals that the particular link can carry. A socket shape alone does not convert data into the required signal form.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace communication through the public switched telephone network

leadVisual.title: A traditional telephone-network access route

coreExplanation: PSTN means Public Switched Telephone Network. It is telephone-network infrastructure connecting users through communication lines and switching systems. The switches connect communication through the wider system rather than requiring a dedicated direct line from every user to every other user.

A suitable telephone access service can carry communication towards a provider that connects to wider networks. The exact technology depends on the service; a traditional dial-up example uses modem signals over an analogue access segment.

Telephone infrastructure can contain different line and signal technologies. Apply analogue/digital conversion only where the specific segment requires it. The existence of an analogue access example does not mean every switching centre or long-distance link is analogue.

Identify the user endpoint, required access equipment, local line, switching infrastructure and provider connection. Explain what each contributes to moving communication towards its destination; do not substitute the web server’s content job for a network role.

learningCycle.observe: A complete explanation follows the segments. It does not repeat “telephone line” for every device or assume that the whole route uses one signal form.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare a reserved connection with ordinary shared access

leadVisual.title: The school links two permanent sites

coreExplanation: A dedicated line provides a connection reserved for a particular customer or between specified sites rather than establishing a new ordinary telephone call each time. It can support continuing organisational communication with agreed service characteristics.

An organisation may choose a dedicated arrangement for predictable capacity, persistent connectivity and suitable service support. The actual rate, availability and repair commitments must come from the service specification rather than from the word dedicated alone.

Installation and ongoing charges may be higher than suitable shared access. The arrangement serves planned locations and is not a substitute for a moving device’s radio access. A damaged line or failed endpoint can still interrupt service.

learningCycle.observe: The useful property is an arranged, reserved connection for the customer or sites. Its value depends on the required service and contract, not on a guarantee that no failure can happen.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Connect a moving phone through cells and base stations

leadVisual.title: A teacher travels to a partner school

coreExplanation: A cellular network divides its coverage into service areas called cells. A phone communicates using radio with base-station equipment serving its area. The radio link replaces a fixed cable to the moving phone; it does not replace every cable in the wider network.

The base station connects through the operator’s infrastructure towards other networks and services. For internet use, communication reaches the appropriate external network through the operator. The requested website is not stored in the base station merely because the signal passes through it.

As the phone moves, a handover can transfer its active connection to other suitable serving equipment. Coverage gaps, interference, congestion or failed infrastructure can still interrupt service. Handover supports movement; it is not a promise of uninterrupted communication everywhere.

Cellular access suits a moving teacher or a location with suitable coverage where fixed access is unavailable. Check signal coverage, data capacity, usage charges and reliability. A school’s permanent high-demand link may have different requirements from one mobile device.

learningCycle.observe: The phone has a radio access link into an operator network. As conditions change, the network can arrange a transfer to suitable serving equipment, subject to coverage and capacity.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Associate an IP address with an interface

leadVisual.title: Two readable forms of an IP address

coreExplanation: An IP address is associated with an interface on an IP network and is used in packet delivery. A device can have more than one network interface and address, such as wired and wireless connections. The address is not simply a permanent personal name for the physical computer.

An IPv4 address has 32 bits, commonly written as four decimal groups separated by dots. Each group represents eight bits and ranges from 0 to 255. In 192.0.2.12, the four groups together represent the address; 192.0.2.300 is not valid IPv4 notation.

An IPv6 address has 128 bits. Its full common notation has eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons. Leading zeros in a group may be omitted, and one run of all-zero groups can be compressed using ::. Compression shortens writing, not the underlying 128-bit address.

The example 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0012 can be written 2001:db8::12. Do not compare the two versions by counting visible characters. The example addresses used here are reserved for documentation and are not live service endpoints.

learningCycle.observe: The punctuation helps people read an address representation. The underlying addresses have defined binary lengths; changing the printed notation does not change the bit count.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare the network prefix before choosing local delivery

leadVisual.title: The first three groups are not always enough

coreExplanation: Subnetting divides an IP network into smaller logical network segments. A prefix length or subnet mask identifies the network portion used for comparison. A /24 prefix covers the first three eight-bit groups; a /26 prefix also covers the first two bits of the fourth group.

For this LAN model, compare the client’s network prefix with the destination using the client’s stated prefix length. Matching network portions mean local-subnet delivery. A different network portion requires delivery towards a router or gateway that can forward to another network.

For /26, the last six bits vary, giving blocks of 64 address patterns in the fourth group: 0–63, 64–127, 128–191 and 192–255. These are subnet blocks, not a statement that every address in a block is assignable to an ordinary host. The mask 255.255.255.192 expresses the same 26-bit network portion.

Smaller logical segments can contain local traffic and help administrators isolate faults to a smaller area. Separating staff and student segments can also support different access policies when routers or firewalls enforce the rules. A subnet mask by itself is not a security policy and does not automatically block all traffic.

Use the prefix and topology actually given. These examples teach basic IPv4 same-subnet decisions, not every possible host route or advanced routing arrangement. A numerical match does not prove that a cable, wireless link or destination service is currently working.

learningCycle.observe: No. /26 fixes the first 26 address bits, which includes two bits from the fourth decimal group. We must compare the specified prefix rather than guess from the dots.
