knowledgeUnits.heading: Fetch the instruction, not its operand

leadVisual.title: Fetch the instruction, not its operand

coreExplanation: Register-transfer notation describes copying or changing stored values. The destination is on the left of ←. [PC] means the contents of PC. MAR ← [PC] therefore copies the next instruction address from PC into MAR; PC is not emptied.
With PC = 0, MAR ← [PC] makes MAR = 0. The address bus selects memory location 0. The CU sends a memory-read signal on the control bus. We are asking for the instruction word stored there.

The instruction returns on the data bus into MDR. MDR ← [[MAR]] means read the contents of memory at the address held in MAR. The inner [MAR] supplies address 0; the outer brackets obtain Memory[0]. MDR now contains the encoded instruction displayed as LDD 4.

CIR ← [MDR] copies the instruction into CIR for decoding. PC ← [PC] + 1 makes PC = 1, the next sequential instruction address in this one-location model. Some transfers can overlap in real implementations, but MDR must receive the instruction before CIR can copy it.

Fetch has obtained LDD 4, but it has not yet loaded 18 into ACC. Reading the data at address 4 belongs to executing that instruction. Keeping these two reads separate explains why one load can require more than one memory access.

learningCycle.observe: PC = 0. Memory[0] holds LDD 4 and Memory[4] holds 18. The CPU must obtain the instruction before it knows which operation and operand it requires.
learningCycle.question: Why does fetching LDD 4 first access address 0 rather than address 4?

knowledgeUnits.heading: Decode, execute, then fetch again

leadVisual.title: Decode, execute, then fetch again

coreExplanation: The CU decodes the instruction held in CIR. The operation code, or opcode, identifies the operation. The operand supplies a value, an address or other information required by that operation. In LDD 4, LDD identifies load-direct and 4 identifies the data location.

After fetching LDD 4, MAR receives 4. A memory-read signal causes MDR to receive 18 from that location. ACC ← [MDR] then makes ACC = 18. PC remains 1. This operand read follows the separate instruction read from address 0.
After fetching ADD 5, MAR receives 5 and a read places 24 in MDR. The ALU adds the two values: ACC ← [ACC] + [MDR], giving 42. PC is now 2. The original values in memory remain available.

After fetching STO 6, MAR receives 6 and MDR ← [ACC] places 42 in MDR. The data bus carries 42 towards memory and a write signal stores it: [[MAR]] ← [MDR]. Memory[6] becomes 42. Fetching STO was a read; executing it is a write.

Normally the next fetch uses the advanced PC. A jump instruction can replace PC with another target during execution. In the basic interrupt model, the CPU checks for pending enabled requests at the boundary after the current instruction; the following unit explains this. END finishes our program and returns control to the operating system, the software that manages running programs.

learningCycle.observe: The calculation uses the same fetch pattern three times, but each fetched instruction asks for a different action. Predict whether execution will read memory, calculate or write memory.

steps.body: After fetching LDD 4, MAR receives 4. A memory-read signal causes MDR to receive 18 from that location. ACC ← [MDR] then makes ACC = 18. PC remains 1. This operand read follows the separate instruction read from address 0.

steps.title: Execute the addition
steps.body: After fetching ADD 5, MAR receives 5 and a read places 24 in MDR. The ALU adds the two values: ACC ← [ACC] + [MDR], giving 42. PC is now 2. The original values in memory remain available.

steps.title: Execute the store

steps.title: Choose the next action

In the basic interrupt model, the CPU checks for pending enabled requests at the boundary after the current instruction; the following unit explains this. END finishes our program and returns control to the operating system, the software that manages running programs.

steps.title: Predict the changed states

steps.title: Follow the write

knowledgeUnits.heading: Ask for attention when an event occurs

leadVisual.title: Ask for attention when an event occurs

coreExplanation: Polling repeatedly checks whether a device needs attention. An interrupt allows an event or device to request processor attention when needed. Between requests the processor can carry out other useful work rather than repeatedly checking that one device.

A completed input/output transfer may need the next data block. A timer expiry may require a change of running task. A device error may require corrective action. A software request can ask for an operating-system service. The cause explains why attention is needed; the handler carries out the response.

A request can be pending while the CPU completes the current instruction. Enabled requests are eligible for handling; priority helps decide which eligible work should be handled first. A lower-priority request that remains pending has not necessarily been lost.

For the basic fetch-execute model, check for interrupts at an instruction-cycle boundary, after the current instruction finishes and before the next normal fetch. Processor-specific faults can require different treatment; use the stated model when explaining the sequence.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Save the context, service the request, restore it

leadVisual.title: Save the context, service the request, restore it

coreExplanation: The context is the processor state needed by the interrupted program: the return address, live register values and required status information. Save this before the handler overwrites it. A stack is a storage structure where the most recently placed item is removed first; saved context is commonly held on a stack.

An Interrupt Service Routine, ISR, is code that deals with the accepted event. The CPU transfers control to the appropriate ISR. The routine may read a device, move data or deal with a condition, and it may change working registers while doing so.

In our example the saved program state includes PC = 2 and ACC = 42. The ISR can temporarily make ACC = 0 and set its zero flag without changing the protected saved copy. If an index or flags are needed later, their original values must also remain available.

After service and the required priority checks, restore the saved context. PC = 2 identifies the next instruction, while ACC = 42 supplies the value that STO 6 should write. Restore the original zero flag as well. Continue the interrupted program rather than beginning it again.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Relate assembly to machine code

leadVisual.title: Relate assembly to machine code

coreExplanation: Machine code consists of instructions encoded as binary patterns for a particular processor instruction set. Assembly language uses mnemonics, such as LDD, to represent operations in a form that is easier for people to read. An assembler translates assembly source into machine code.

An opcode specifies the operation. An operand supplies the data or information needed to obtain data or select a target. In LDD 4, the mnemonic denotes the load-direct opcode and 4 is its address operand. END needs no source operand in this example instruction set.

For this teaching example only, each instruction has a 16-bit word: an 8-bit opcode followed by an 8-bit address field. The supplied codes are LDD = 00000001, ADD = 00000010, STO = 00000011 and END = 11111111. END uses a zero-filled operand field. These are classroom encoding choices, not Cambridge-prescribed machine codes.

The assembler looks up the operation code and encodes its operand using the target format. It does not obtain the LDD opcode by adding the character codes of L, D and D. A different processor instruction set may use different encodings or support different operations.

learningCycle.observe: The readable instruction LDD 4 means load the contents at address 4. Compare this meaning with a supplied binary encoding for the same operation.
learningCycle.question: Why can a person write LDD while the processor executes a bit pattern?

knowledgeUnits.heading: Give locations names without changing their contents

leadVisual.title: Give locations names without changing their contents

coreExplanation: A label is a name assigned to a location. In START: LDD FIRST, START followed by a colon defines an instruction label. FIRST is used as the instruction’s operand; its definition appears later. The numbers in the left margin below are address annotations, not source instructions.

The form label: opcode operand names the address of an instruction. START names address 0. If an instruction has no operand, as with END, none is required after the opcode. A later branch can use an instruction label to identify its target.

The form label: data names a location that contains the given data. FIRST: 18 puts 18 at the location named FIRST. Here FIRST is address 4. TOTAL is address 6, initially containing 0; after the program runs, the same address contains 42.

A data declaration reserves and initialises a location; it is not a load instruction. END occurs before the declarations so normal execution finishes before the CPU would fetch them as instructions. A forward reference uses a label before its definition appears; FIRST in the first line is an example.

learningCycle.observe: Rewrite the calculation with START for the first instruction and FIRST, SECOND and TOTAL for the three data locations. Each listed item still occupies one location, starting at 0.
learningCycle.question: Does FIRST mean address 4 or the value 18?

steps.title: Read a definition and a use
steps.body: A label is a name assigned to a location. In START: LDD FIRST, START followed by a colon defines an instruction label. FIRST is used as the instruction’s operand; its definition appears later. The numbers in the left margin below are address annotations, not source instructions.
steps.code:
000  START: LDD FIRST
001  ADD SECOND
002  STO TOTAL
003  END
004  FIRST: 18
005  SECOND: 24
006  TOTAL: 0

steps.title: Name an instruction address
steps.body: The form label: opcode operand names the address of an instruction. START names address 0. If an instruction has no operand, as with END, none is required after the opcode. A later branch can use an instruction label to identify its target.

steps.title: Name a data address
steps.body: The form label: data names a location that contains the given data. FIRST: 18 puts 18 at the location named FIRST. Here FIRST is address 4. TOTAL is address 6, initially containing 0; after the program runs, the same address contains 42.

steps.title: Keep data out of the execution path
steps.body: A data declaration reserves and initialises a location; it is not a load instruction. END occurs before the declarations so normal execution finishes before the CPU would fetch them as instructions. A forward reference uses a label before its definition appears; FIRST in the first line is an example.

worked.title: Resolve names before running
worked.setup: Addresses start at 0 and each instruction or data declaration takes one location.

steps.title: Replace operand names with addresses
steps.body: LDD FIRST becomes LDD 4. ADD SECOND becomes ADD 5. STO TOTAL becomes STO 6.

steps.title: Distinguish symbol and data
steps.body: The symbol table records TOTAL = 6. Running the program changes Memory[6] from 0 to 42 but does not change that symbol-table entry.

worked.conclusion: A label names an address; reading or writing through it accesses the contents at that address.

check.prompt: After the calculation, does TOTAL mean 42?
check.answer: No. TOTAL still denotes address 6. Its contents are now 42; the symbolic address does not change when data is stored there.

learningCycle.takeaway: Instruction labels name instruction addresses. Data labels name data locations.
learningCycle.bridge: A first scan can discover every label before a second scan resolves forward references.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Find addresses first, emit code second

leadVisual.title: Find addresses first, emit code second

coreExplanation: In the taught two-pass process, the first pass reads source lines, removes irrelevant comments or extra spacing, and checks their form. It starts a location counter at the supplied origin, here 0. Every instruction or data item in this model advances that counter by one.

When a label definition is reached, record the current address for that name. The first pass records START = 0, FIRST = 4, SECOND = 5 and TOTAL = 6. It can continue past the first use of FIRST because resolution will happen after all definitions have been found.

The second pass reads the source again, replaces label operands with their addresses, looks up the machine opcode and emits the encoded word. Data declarations also emit their initial data words. Both passes read source lines; generating object code belongs to the second pass in this taught model.

The output includes four instruction words and three data words. Here data uses a full 16-bit unsigned word. Address 4 receives the binary representation of 18, while the operand in the instruction at 0 encodes the address 4.

Defining FIRST twice is a duplicate-label error. Using MISSING without a definition is an undefined-symbol error when the operand cannot be resolved. Guessing an address would hide the source error. The assembler translates the program; executing the resulting program is a separate step.

learningCycle.observe: Read the labelled program from top to bottom. At its first line, START is known but FIRST has not yet been defined. Track a location counter as the scan continues.
learningCycle.question: How can the first line use FIRST before the assembler reaches FIRST: 18?

worked.title: Move the program to origin 10
worked.setup: Keep the same seven source items but start the location counter at 10.

steps.title: Repeat pass one
steps.body: START = 10, FIRST = 14, SECOND = 15 and TOTAL = 16.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use the operand itself or read a location

leadVisual.title: Use the operand itself or read a location

coreExplanation: An immediate operand supplies the value itself. LDM #4 copies the denary value 4 into ACC without a data-memory read for that value. Fetching the instruction is still a separate memory access. The # prefix means denary in the supplied syntax.

Direct addressing uses the operand as the address of the data. LDD 4 selects address 4, then loads its contents, 18. The selected location is called the effective address. The effective address and the value obtained there are different things.

The example instruction set uses # for denary, B for binary and & for hexadecimal immediate values. #15, B00001111 and &0F all represent the value fifteen. With an instruction that accepts those forms, they provide the same immediate value.
A load copies a value. LDD 4 does not empty Memory[4]. A later STO 6 copies ACC into Memory[6] without clearing ACC. Record only the destination that the instruction changes.

learningCycle.observe: Memory[4] contains 18. One instruction gives the processor the number 4 directly; the other uses 4 to find a stored value. Predict ACC after each instruction independently.
learningCycle.question: Why do LDM #4 and LDD 4 give different answers?

steps.body: An immediate operand supplies the value itself. LDM #4 copies the denary value 4 into ACC without a data-memory read for that value. Fetching the instruction is still a separate memory access. The # prefix means denary in the supplied syntax.

steps.title: Read a directly addressed value
steps.body: Direct addressing uses the operand as the address of the data. LDD 4 selects address 4, then loads its contents, 18. The selected location is called the effective address. The effective address and the value obtained there are different things.

steps.title: Recognise three immediate notations
steps.body: The example instruction set uses # for denary, B for binary and & for hexadecimal immediate values. #15, B00001111 and &0F all represent the value fifteen. With an instruction that accepts those forms, they provide the same immediate value.

steps.title: Keep the source
steps.body: A load copies a value. LDD 4 does not empty Memory[4]. A later STO 6 copies ACC into Memory[6] without clearing ACC. Record only the destination that the instruction changes.

worked.setup: Memory[15] = 24. Reset ACC before each case.

steps.title: Immediate
steps.body: LDM #15 sets ACC to 15.

steps.title: Direct
steps.body: LDD 15 sets ACC to 24 because it reads the contents at address 15.

worked.conclusion: Read the instruction and operand form before using the digits in a calculation.

check.prompt: Are #15 and B00001111 different immediate values?
check.answer: No. They are denary and binary representations of the same value, fifteen.

learningCycle.takeaway: Immediate supplies a value. Direct supplies the address of the value.
learningCycle.bridge: An address can itself be stored in memory, or calculated from a base and an index.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow a pointer or add an index

leadVisual.title: Follow a pointer or add an index

coreExplanation: A pointer is a value used as the address of another location. LDI 100 first reads Memory[100], obtaining pointer 150. It then reads Memory[150], obtaining 7 for ACC. The first read gives the effective address; the second gives the data.

Indexed addressing adds the index register to the instruction’s base address. LDX 100 with IX = 2 forms effective address 102 and reads the value 9. It does not follow the pointer 150 at address 100, and it does not load 102 as the final data value.

If a list starts at address 100, IX = 0 selects the first item, IX = 1 selects the next, and IX = 2 selects the third in this one-location-per-item model. Changing IX allows the same LDX instruction to access a different item.
Reset the example before each independent load. Direct uses the specified address; indirect follows the stored pointer; indexed calculates a location using IX.

learningCycle.observe: In this separate addressing example, Memory[100] = 150, Memory[150] = 7 and Memory[102] = 9. IX = 2. Compare direct, indirect and indexed loads using operand 100.
learningCycle.question: Does the first memory read give the data, or tell us where the data is?

steps.title: Follow an indirect address
steps.body: A pointer is a value used as the address of another location. LDI 100 first reads Memory[100], obtaining pointer 150. It then reads Memory[150], obtaining 7 for ACC. The first read gives the effective address; the second gives the data.

steps.title: Add an index
steps.body: Indexed addressing adds the index register to the instruction’s base address. LDX 100 with IX = 2 forms effective address 102 and reads the value 9. It does not follow the pointer 150 at address 100, and it does not load 102 as the final data value.

steps.title: Walk along adjacent items
steps.body: If a list starts at address 100, IX = 0 selects the first item, IX = 1 selects the next, and IX = 2 selects the third in this one-location-per-item model. Changing IX allows the same LDX instruction to access a different item.

steps.title: Compare from the same initial state
steps.body: Reset the example before each independent load. Direct uses the specified address; indirect follows the stored pointer; indexed calculates a location using IX.

worked.title: Change the pointer without changing the instruction
worked.setup: Keep LDI 100, but change Memory[100] from 150 to 102.

steps.title: Resolve the new effective address
steps.body: The first read now supplies address 102.

steps.title: Obtain the contents
steps.body: The second read supplies Memory[102] = 9, so ACC becomes 9.

worked.conclusion: Indirect addressing follows the current stored pointer each time.

check.prompt: With IX = 2, why does LDX 100 load 9 rather than 102?
check.answer: 102 is the effective address formed by 100 + 2. LDX then reads that location, whose contents are 9.

learningCycle.takeaway: Indirect: follow a stored address. Indexed: add IX to the base, then read the selected contents.
learningCycle.bridge: Other instructions change IX or calculate a target relative to the program counter.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Change the index and locate a relative target

leadVisual.title: Change the index and locate a relative target

coreExplanation: LDM #n places n into ACC. LDR #n places n into IX. MOV IX copies ACC into IX, leaving ACC unchanged. The instruction’s defined effect determines the destination; MOV IX does not mean copy IX into ACC.

After LDR #2, an indexed load uses offset 2. If MOV IX then copies ACC = 9 into IX, the next indexed load uses offset 9. Resolve the effective address using the current IX, not the value it had at the start of the program.

Relative addressing adds a signed displacement to a stated PC base. A displacement is an offset that can be positive or negative. If the given PC base is 40 and the displacement is −5, the target address is 35. For a relative branch, this target selects the next instruction rather than loading Memory[35] into ACC.

Use the PC value specified by the question, including any fetch increment already included in it. The example instruction list does not supply a separate relative-jump mnemonic, so these calculations name the base and displacement explicitly. Without the base, an offset alone does not determine a unique target.

learningCycle.observe: ACC = 9 and IX = 0. LDR #2 puts an immediate value into IX; MOV IX then copies ACC into IX. Follow the destination, not just the number in the instruction.
learningCycle.question: Which register changes when the instruction says LDR #2 or MOV IX?

steps.title: Distinguish register destinations
steps.body: LDM #n places n into ACC. LDR #n places n into IX. MOV IX copies ACC into IX, leaving ACC unchanged. The instruction’s defined effect determines the destination; MOV IX does not mean copy IX into ACC.

steps.title: Recalculate after a change
steps.body: After LDR #2, an indexed load uses offset 2. If MOV IX then copies ACC = 9 into IX, the next indexed load uses offset 9. Resolve the effective address using the current IX, not the value it had at the start of the program.

steps.title: Form a relative address
steps.body: Relative addressing adds a signed displacement to a stated PC base. A displacement is an offset that can be positive or negative. If the given PC base is 40 and the displacement is −5, the target address is 35. For a relative branch, this target selects the next instruction rather than loading Memory[35] into ACC.

steps.title: State the base convention
steps.body: Use the PC value specified by the question, including any fetch increment already included in it. The example instruction list does not supply a separate relative-jump mnemonic, so these calculations name the base and displacement explicitly. Without the base, an offset alone does not determine a unique target.

worked.title: Keep copies and destinations distinct
worked.setup: ACC = 9, IX = 0 and Memory[109] = 24.

steps.title: Set and replace IX
steps.body: LDR #2 sets IX = 2. MOV IX then sets IX = 9 while ACC remains 9.

steps.title: Read and store
steps.body: LDX 100 reads Memory[109], giving ACC = 24. STO 120 writes 24 to Memory[120]; ACC stays 24 and IX stays 9.

worked.conclusion: Resolve the operand from the current state and change only the defined destination.

check.prompt: The given PC base is 40 and the relative displacement is +6. What is the target, and is it a loaded data value?
check.answer: The target address is 46. For a relative branch it is the next instruction address, not the contents loaded from Memory[46].

learningCycle.takeaway: Copy to the specified destination. For relative addressing, add the signed displacement to the stated PC base.
learningCycle.bridge: Now use the resolved values in arithmetic and character input/output.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate a value and output its character

leadVisual.title: Calculate a value and output its character

coreExplanation: ADD and SUB combine ACC with an immediate value or the contents of a direct address and keep the result in ACC. With ACC = 10, ADD B00000101 gives 15 and SUB &03 then gives 12. ADD 330 would instead add Memory[330].

INC increases the named register by one; DEC decreases it by one. INC IX changes IX, while DEC ACC changes ACC. Retain the other register’s value in a trace. Do not assume an unspecified word width or wrap rule.

IN reads one character and stores its ASCII value in ACC. OUT outputs the character represented by the value in ACC. Input A supplies 65; ADD #1 makes 66; OUT emits B. This OUT instruction does not convert a number to printed decimal digits.
END finishes the program and returns control to the operating system. A complete trace includes this executed instruction and does not continue into later data or unused instructions.

learningCycle.observe: Recall that a character code represents a character using a number. In the supplied ASCII subset, A = 65, B = 66 and C = 67. Predict the effect of reading A, adding 1 and outputting the result.
learningCycle.question: If ACC contains 66, does OUT print B or the digits 66?

steps.title: Resolve before adding or subtracting
steps.body: ADD and SUB combine ACC with an immediate value or the contents of a direct address and keep the result in ACC. With ACC = 10, ADD B00000101 gives 15 and SUB &03 then gives 12. ADD 330 would instead add Memory[330].

steps.title: Change only the named register
steps.body: INC increases the named register by one; DEC decreases it by one. INC IX changes IX, while DEC ACC changes ACC. Retain the other register’s value in a trace. Do not assume an unspecified word width or wrap rule.

steps.title: Read and output one character
steps.body: IN reads one character and stores its ASCII value in ACC. OUT outputs the character represented by the value in ACC. Input A supplies 65; ADD #1 makes 66; OUT emits B. This OUT instruction does not convert a number to printed decimal digits.

steps.title: Terminate explicitly
steps.body: END finishes the program and returns control to the operating system. A complete trace includes this executed instruction and does not continue into later data or unused instructions.
steps.code:
0  IN
1  ADD #1
2  OUT
3  END

worked.title: Trace a character conversion
worked.setup: PC = 0, ACC = 0, IX = 0; input is A. The program above uses no data-memory operands.

steps.title: Carry the state forward
steps.body: IN gives ACC = 65, then ADD #1 gives 66. IX remains 0.

steps.title: Record the actual output
steps.body: OUT emits B and leaves ACC = 66. END returns to the operating system.

worked.conclusion: The code value in ACC and the character produced by OUT are two representations of the same character.

check.prompt: ACC = 66 and IX = 2. What changes after INC IX followed by OUT?
check.answer: IX becomes 3. ACC remains 66 and OUT emits B. It does not print 3 or the two digits 66.

learningCycle.takeaway: ADD/SUB update ACC; INC/DEC update the named register; IN/OUT use character codes.
learningCycle.bridge: A comparison can choose which instruction path is followed before the output.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Make a comparison, then choose a path

leadVisual.title: Make a comparison, then choose a path

coreExplanation: CMP compares ACC with an immediate value or a directly addressed value. CMI compares ACC with an indirectly addressed value. Both record whether the values are equal; neither loads the compared value into ACC. Keep a separate last-comparison entry in a trace.

JPE jumps to its target when the preceding comparison is True, meaning equal. JPN jumps when that comparison is False, meaning not equal. If the condition is not met, execution continues at the next sequential address. JMP is unconditional and always chooses its target when executed.

The source below reads a character. CMI 340 follows Memory[340] = 341 to Memory[341] = 65. Equal input follows the addition path; unequal input goes to REJECT. SEND names the shared output instruction.

For input A, CMI gives True, so JPN is not taken. ADD #1 gives 66; CMP #66 gives True; JPE SEND goes to 187 and skips the rejection assignment. For input B, the first comparison is False and JPN selects 186 immediately.

Record a row for each instruction that executes. A skipped line has no row and no effect. The comparison column records the last explicit CMP or CMI; do not replace it with a guess about a different processor’s flags.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow a loop through its final test

leadVisual.title: Follow a loop through its final test

coreExplanation: A trace records the state after each executed instruction. Here PC = 20, ACC = 0, IX = 0 and Memory[90] = 67. No input is needed. Each instruction occupies one address. The initial values belong above the table; do not invent zero for unspecified registers in another question.

LDM #2 gives ACC = 2. DEC ACC gives 1. CMP #0 records False. JPN LOOP therefore sets PC to 21. Record all four executed instructions; the next row returns to address 21 rather than moving down the printed listing.

The second DEC gives 0. CMP #0 now records True. JPN is still executed, but its branch is not taken, so PC becomes 24. A loop trace must include this final condition test; otherwise it does not show why repetition ends.
LDD 90 replaces the zero counter with 67. OUT emits C and END terminates. ACC is therefore 67 at the end, even though it was zero at loop exit. IX stays 0 and Memory[90] stays 67.

For every row: obtain the instruction at the current PC, resolve its operand using the current registers and memory, apply only its defined changes, and select the next PC. Record stores and output when they occur. Repeated addresses produce repeated rows; skipped addresses produce none.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Classify instructions by their effects

leadVisual.title: Classify instructions by their effects

coreExplanation: Data-movement instructions copy values between registers and memory. Arithmetic instructions calculate a new value. STO is movement because it copies ACC into a memory location; ADD is arithmetic because it changes the working result.
CMP and CMI compare values. JMP, JPE and JPN control which instruction executes next. A comparison may support a decision, but it is not itself a conditional jump.
IN obtains a character and OUT emits a character, so they belong to input/output. Writing a value into ordinary working memory with STO does not make STO a character-output instruction.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Move bits and see what falls out

leadVisual.title: Move bits and see what falls out

coreExplanation: A byte has eight bits. For an unsigned byte, positions from left to right have weights 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. Here 00110100 represents 52. Fixed width matters because outgoing bits cannot remain in the result.

LSL #n moves the bits in ACC n places left. Zeros enter on the right and outgoing left bits are discarded. LSL #1 changes 00110100 to 01101000. The value doubles from 52 to 104 because this example does not lose a significant 1 bit.

LSR #n moves the bits in ACC n places right. Zeros enter on the left and outgoing right bits are discarded. Applied after the previous instruction, LSR #2 changes 01101000 to 00011010, giving 26. Use the updated ACC in a sequence.

Starting independently from 10000001, logical left gives 00000010. Logical right of that result gives 00000001, not the original byte: the discarded leading 1 cannot be recovered. Right shifting an unsigned odd value also discards its remainder bit.

learningCycle.observe: Use eight boxes containing 00110100. Move every bit one place left, discard the bit that leaves the byte, and fill the empty right-hand box with 0.
learningCycle.question: If we shift left and then right, must the original byte return?

steps.title: State the width and interpretation
steps.body: A byte has eight bits. For an unsigned byte, positions from left to right have weights 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. Here 00110100 represents 52. Fixed width matters because outgoing bits cannot remain in the result.

steps.title: Shift logically left
steps.body: LSL #n moves the bits in ACC n places left. Zeros enter on the right and outgoing left bits are discarded. LSL #1 changes 00110100 to 01101000. The value doubles from 52 to 104 because this example does not lose a significant 1 bit.

steps.title: Shift logically right
steps.body: LSR #n moves the bits in ACC n places right. Zeros enter on the left and outgoing right bits are discarded. Applied after the previous instruction, LSR #2 changes 01101000 to 00011010, giving 26. Use the updated ACC in a sequence.

steps.title: Check information loss
steps.body: Starting independently from 10000001, logical left gives 00000010. Logical right of that result gives 00000001, not the original byte: the discarded leading 1 cannot be recovered. Right shifting an unsigned odd value also discards its remainder bit.

steps.body: LSR #1 discards the final 1 and introduces 0 on the left, giving 00000010.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.body: The result is 2. The original value divided by two is 2.5, so the discarded low bit matters.

worked.conclusion: Move the bits according to the rule before interpreting the resulting value.

check.prompt: What fills a vacated position in a logical shift?
check.answer: Zero, on the right for a logical left shift and on the left for a logical right shift.

learningCycle.takeaway: Logical shifts discard outgoing bits and fill vacated positions with zeros.
learningCycle.bridge: Signed values and rotations need different rules for the incoming bit.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Preserve a sign or wrap a bit around

leadVisual.title: Preserve a sign or wrap a bit around

coreExplanation: In two’s complement, a leading 1 indicates a negative value. Arithmetic right shift copies the original sign bit into the new left-hand position, preserving the sign. For 10010111 it gives 11001011, which represents −53.

Arithmetic right shift of a negative odd value rounds down: −105 divided by two is −52.5, and the result is −53. Logical right instead inserts zero and gives 01001011, or positive 75. The two rules therefore have different meanings for this bit pattern.

Arithmetic left shifts the bit pattern like logical left and inserts zero on the right. From 10010111 it gives 00101110, or 46. The intended signed double would be −210, outside the eight-bit range −128 to 127: overflow has occurred. Left shift only behaves as multiplication when the result fits.

A cyclic shift rotates the outgoing bit to the opposite end instead of discarding it. Cyclic left of 10010111 gives 00101111; cyclic right gives 11001011. Its rule is wrapping, even when a particular result happens to equal an arithmetic result.

learningCycle.observe: Start each comparison afresh from 10010111. As unsigned it is 151. As eight-bit two’s complement it is −105: the leftmost bit has weight −128, so −128 + 16 + 4 + 2 + 1 = −105.
learningCycle.question: What should enter the left-hand position when a negative number shifts right?

steps.title: Recover the sign rule
steps.body: In two’s complement, a leading 1 indicates a negative value. Arithmetic right shift copies the original sign bit into the new left-hand position, preserving the sign. For 10010111 it gives 11001011, which represents −53.

steps.title: Check the numerical consequence
steps.body: Arithmetic right shift of a negative odd value rounds down: −105 divided by two is −52.5, and the result is −53. Logical right instead inserts zero and gives 01001011, or positive 75. The two rules therefore have different meanings for this bit pattern.

steps.title: Check arithmetic left
steps.body: Arithmetic left shifts the bit pattern like logical left and inserts zero on the right. From 10010111 it gives 00101110, or 46. The intended signed double would be −210, outside the eight-bit range −128 to 127: overflow has occurred. Left shift only behaves as multiplication when the result fits.

steps.title: Wrap with a cyclic shift
steps.body: A cyclic shift rotates the outgoing bit to the opposite end instead of discarding it. Cyclic left of 10010111 gives 00101111; cyclic right gives 11001011. Its rule is wrapping, even when a particular result happens to equal an arithmetic result.

steps.title: Cyclic right

worked.conclusion: Equal results for one input do not make two shift rules identical.

check.prompt: How many 1 bits are lost in a cyclic shift?
check.answer: None. Bits wrap around, so the number of 1 bits remains unchanged. Their positions can change.

learningCycle.takeaway: Arithmetic right repeats the sign bit; cyclic shifts wrap; left-shift arithmetic needs an overflow check.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Apply one logic rule at every bit position

leadVisual.title: Apply one logic rule at every bit position

coreExplanation: AND produces 1 only when both input bits are 1. OR produces 1 when at least one is 1. XOR produces 1 when exactly one is 1. Bitwise operations apply these rules separately to every corresponding pair of bits.

A mask is a bit pattern used to select positions. AND with 1 preserves a bit and AND with 0 clears it. OR with 0 preserves a bit and OR with 1 sets it. XOR with 0 preserves a bit and XOR with 1 toggles it, changing 0 to 1 or 1 to 0.

AND, OR and XOR each accept immediate #n, Bn or &n operands, or a direct memory address. AND #15, AND B00001111 and AND &0F use the same immediate mask. AND 700 reads Memory[700] and only uses that same mask if the location contains 15.
For each row below, start again from 10100110. The result replaces ACC. The AND result is not the input to the following OR row unless a program explicitly gives that sequence.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Test readiness, then change one control bit

leadVisual.title: Test readiness, then change one control bit

coreExplanation: A memory-mapped interface can be read or written using a memory address. Here a read of address 900 gives the current byte and a write replaces it. Assume the device does not independently change this byte during the short sequence. Real interfaces can have different write rules.

Load the byte into ACC, then AND B00010000 to select bit 4. The result is either 00010000, value 16, or 00000000. CMP #0 followed by JPE DONE skips the update when the ready bit is clear. A successful bit test need not produce denary 1.

The AND test cleared other positions in ACC, including the original bit 0. Reload the original byte with LDD 900. OR B00000100 then sets bit 2 while preserving every other position. STO 900 writes the resulting 00010101 back to the interface.

DONE names the END instruction at address 107. The not-ready branch reaches it without executing a store. The ready path reloads, sets and stores before reaching the same ending. A label identifies an instruction address; it is not an extra instruction.

To clear bit 2, AND with 11111011; to toggle it, XOR with 00000100. To test whether an unsigned integer is odd, select bit 0 using AND B00000001: only its weight 1 can make the number odd. The other binary place values are even.

A source declaration such as FLAGS: 17 names a data location initially containing 17, binary 00010001. LDD FLAGS loads those contents and STO FLAGS changes them. The label continues to name the same address after the stored byte changes, just as TOTAL did in the addition program.

learningCycle.observe: An eight-bit interface value at address 900 contains 00010001. Bit 4 means ready and bit 2 enables a motor. Number bits from 7 on the left to 0 on the right. We must enable the motor only when ready and preserve all other bits.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Who connects the application to the computer?

leadVisual.title: Who connects the application to the computer?

coreExplanation: An application is software for a user task: a document editor arranges text, while a music player chooses and plays a track. Both need common operations such as opening files and using devices. Requiring every application to control every device separately would duplicate this work.

An operating system, or OS, is system software that manages computer resources and provides services to applications. The editor requests a file or print operation. The OS checks and coordinates that request, then communicates with the relevant hardware. The OS also provides a user interface, such as windows and menus or a command line.

Selecting Save is an application action. The requested file must be located or created, access must be permitted, and data must reach storage. The OS supplies these common services. The application still decides which document content to save.

Several applications may request the same resource. The OS coordinates their requests and controls permitted access. For example, one printer can service a waiting sequence of jobs, while a protected file can reject a write from an account without permission. Managing the request is different from creating the document content.

learningCycle.observe: Look at the computer and printer. The editor lets a student change words on a page. The printer makes marks on paper. Something must carry the request between them and coordinate access when another application also wants to print.
learningCycle.question: When you select Print in a document editor, what makes the separate printer respond?

prerequisite.title: Hardware, software and resources
prerequisite.body: Hardware is the physical equipment. Software is the instructions that run on it. A resource is something programs need to use, such as processor time, working memory, storage or a printer.

steps.title: Separate the user task from the shared work
steps.body: An application is software for a user task: a document editor arranges text, while a music player chooses and plays a track. Both need common operations such as opening files and using devices. Requiring every application to control every device separately would duplicate this work.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Give running programs working space

leadVisual.title: Give running programs working space

coreExplanation: Memory management keeps track of which parts of main memory are in use and which are available. The OS allocates working space when a process starts or needs more memory. In this simplified map, the new process can receive the two available units.

Different processes can occupy RAM at the same time. Memory protection restricts access to their allocated areas so that one process cannot freely overwrite another process’s instructions or data. The issue is which memory a process may access, even if both processes belong to the same user.

When a process ends, the OS can release its allocation and record that memory as available for reuse. This lets another process use the space later. Releasing RAM does not create a saved file: a document needs a separate save operation before its working changes can be relied on after shutdown.

learningCycle.observe: Imagine a small RAM map with eight equal teaching units. Process A uses three units, process B uses three, and two remain available. A new process requests two units. Follow which units are occupied, released and protected.
learningCycle.question: Where can the editor keep a sentence while the student is still changing it?

prerequisite.title: RAM, storage and a process
prerequisite.body: RAM is the working memory used during execution; it normally loses its contents when power is removed. Storage retains saved files. A program is a set of instructions; a process is a program in execution, with its current working state.

steps.title: Record allocated and available memory
steps.body: Memory management keeps track of which parts of main memory are in use and which are available. The OS allocates working space when a process starts or needs more memory. In this simplified map, the new process can receive the two available units.

steps.title: Protect one process from another
steps.body: Different processes can occupy RAM at the same time. Memory protection restricts access to their allocated areas so that one process cannot freely overwrite another process’s instructions or data. The issue is which memory a process may access, even if both processes belong to the same user.

steps.title: Release space when work finishes
steps.body: When a process ends, the OS can release its allocation and record that memory as available for reuse. This lets another process use the space later. Releasing RAM does not create a saved file: a document needs a separate save operation before its working changes can be relied on after shutdown.

worked.conclusion: Memory management allocates, protects and releases working memory.

check.prompt: After closing the editor, three units of RAM become available. Does that prove the latest document edits were saved?

learningCycle.takeaway: Track available memory, allocate space to processes, protect their allocations and release space for reuse.
learningCycle.bridge: The saved document needs a name, a storage location and rules about who may read or change it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Locate the document and check the requested access

leadVisual.title: Locate the document and check the requested access

coreExplanation: A file is named data stored for later use. A directory, often shown as a folder, organises entries for files and other directories. The path Classes/Friday.txt identifies Friday.txt inside Classes. File management maintains information such as names, locations, sizes and ownership and supports create, open, read, write, rename and delete operations.

An application can supply the path without knowing the physical position of each block on a storage device. The OS uses directory and file-system information to locate the file and coordinate the requested operation. Reading brings data into working memory; writing records supplied data in storage.

Authentication checks who is requesting access, for example by checking login credentials. Successful authentication identifies the account. It does not decide that every operation is allowed. The next decision depends on the resource and the account’s access rights.

Permissions specify what an account may do. In this example the OS allows the student to read the timetable but rejects the student’s write request. The teacher has both rights. Security management enforces these rules; activity logging and security updates can also support system protection.

learningCycle.observe: A teacher owns a shared timetable. Both the teacher and student have successfully signed in. The student may read it; the teacher may read and change it. Follow an Open request and then a Save request from the student.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Let different devices work at their own speed

leadVisual.title: Let different devices work at their own speed

coreExplanation: A device driver is software that lets the OS communicate with a particular device. It turns general requests into the commands that the device understands and handles device responses. Applications can use a consistent OS interface while a suitable driver handles the printer-specific details.

A queue holds work awaiting service. If the printer is busy, later print jobs wait rather than all sending their pages at once. The job currently being serviced can finish before the next one starts. The queue organises waiting requests; it does not physically print pages.

A buffer is an area of memory holding data temporarily while it is transferred. It helps equipment operating at different rates exchange data. A queue records waiting work, whereas a buffer holds data for a transfer. A print system may use both, and neither performs the driver’s device-specific translation.

A device can use an interrupt, a signal requesting processor attention, to report completion or a condition that needs service. The OS arranges the appropriate response. Hardware management therefore includes coordinating requests, drivers and transfers, not simply detecting that the printer is connected.

learningCycle.observe: Three applications submit jobs to one printer. The computer can prepare data much faster than paper moves through the printer. Separate the job waiting for its turn, the data being transferred and the commands understood by this printer model.

learningCycle.takeaway: Hardware management coordinates device access through drivers, queues, buffers and appropriate responses to device events.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Share processor time while a program waits

leadVisual.title: Share processor time while a program waits

coreExplanation: A running process currently has processor time. A ready process can run when selected. A waiting process needs an event, such as completed input, before it can continue its dependent work. Keeping these states lets the OS distinguish useful work from work that cannot progress yet.

Process management schedules which ready process receives processor time. When A waits for input/output, the OS can select B instead of leaving the core idle. Switching between processes over successive intervals can make several applications appear to progress together.

Before switching away from a process, the system preserves the execution information needed to resume correctly, such as its current instruction position and working register values. When A’s input completes, A becomes ready again and can later resume. It does not have to restart the document-editing task from the beginning.

On this single-core model, selected processes take turns. The appearance of simultaneous progress comes from switching; it does not mean two instructions from different processes execute at the same instant on the same core. Memory management keeps their working data available and protected; process management allocates processor time.

learningCycle.observe: Use a single CPU core. Process A is the editor and process B is the music player. A starts running, then needs data from a slow device before it can continue. B already has work ready to execute.

steps.title: Schedule another ready process

steps.title: Preserve enough state to resume

steps.title: Explain multitasking precisely
steps.body: On this single-core model, selected processes take turns. knowledgeUnits.heading: Prepare empty storage; investigate damaged organisation

leadVisual.title: Prepare empty storage; investigate damaged organisation

coreExplanation: A disk formatter prepares a medium or volume with the file-system structures needed to organise files. It creates allocation records that track which storage areas belong to files; a File Allocation Table, or FAT, is one example used by some file systems. A full-format operation may also check the disk for errors. The result is a volume ready to create and locate new files, not a restoration of previous documents.

Disk contents analysis can report which files or categories occupy space. That evidence can explain why a disk is nearly full. Finding one large folder is a different result from finding an error in the structures that record a file’s location.

Disk checking and repair tools examine file-system records and may identify lost allocation information or unreadable sectors. A repair tool attempts corrections it supports and may mark unsuitable areas to avoid further use. It cannot guarantee recovery of physically damaged or missing data.

Use formatting to prepare the known-empty volume. Investigate Volume B with checking and repair tools because its existing files matter. Reformatting a volume that contains needed work can make that work inaccessible. A separate recoverable copy is valuable before a fault occurs.

learningCycle.observe: Volume A is known to be empty and has no file system. Volume B contains work, but a check reports inconsistent allocation information. Both involve storage, yet the desired outcomes are different.

knowledgeUnits.heading: See why separated HDD blocks require more movement

leadVisual.title: See why separated HDD blocks require more movement

coreExplanation: A magnetic hard disk, or HDD, has rotating platters and moving read/write heads. To read a required area, the drive positions a head over the relevant track and waits for the required sector to rotate into position. Mechanical movement and rotational waiting contribute to access time.

A file is fragmented when its parts occupy separate areas rather than one contiguous sequence. Saving and deleting files can leave gaps into which later file parts are placed. Reading the separated parts can require more head movement between their locations.

Defragmentation software relocates file blocks into fewer, more contiguous groups and can consolidate free space. Reading A1, A2 and A3 can then need less seeking between separated areas. The file’s three blocks still contain the same data; the utility changes where those blocks are stored.

The performance explanation depends on mechanical head movement in an HDD. A solid-state drive, or SSD, has no moving read head. Routine HDD-style defragmentation is therefore not the same performance treatment for an SSD. Defragmentation also does not compress file data or repair every disk fault.

learningCycle.observe: A magnetic hard disk stores a file in blocks. Label the three blocks of one file A1, A2 and A3. Other files occupy B1 and C. In the simplified block map, A’s blocks are separated by other occupied or free positions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Detect harmful code and keep a recoverable copy

leadVisual.title: Detect harmful code and keep a recoverable copy

coreExplanation: A virus checker examines files, memory or activity for evidence of malicious software. It may compare known signatures, which are recognisable patterns, and look for suspicious behaviour. Detection information needs updates because an old signature set may not recognise a newly identified threat.

The utility can quarantine a suspect item, isolating it from normal use, or remove or attempt to repair infected content. A scan does not guarantee that every threat will be detected. Handling the malicious program also does not automatically reconstruct a document it has already damaged.

Back-up software creates recoverable copies of files or system data. It can schedule jobs, select changed files and retain versions. Restoring means copying a saved version back into use after deletion, corruption or equipment failure. The needed version must have been captured before it was lost.

If the separate device holds V1 and the failed disk held the only V2, recovery gives V1. The changes made after the last successful backup are absent. A copy on the same physical disk is also lost if that disk fails. Restore checks establish that the saved copy is readable and usable.

learningCycle.observe: Yesterday’s version V1 was copied to a separate backup device. Today the working document becomes V2, then the computer’s main disk fails. First follow the malicious-file case; then follow recovery after the failed disk.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use fewer bits and choose the correct utility

leadVisual.title: Use fewer bits and choose the correct utility

coreExplanation: A file-compression utility encodes data in a representation that can require fewer bits. For suitable data, the smaller result needs less storage and less transfer time over the same connection. Compression changes how data is represented; it does not rearrange HDD blocks to reduce head movement.

Lossless compression allows decompression to reproduce the original data exactly. This is essential for a folder of source code: losing or changing one character can alter or invalidate a program. An archive can package files and may compress them; extracting restores the stored file data.

Some data has useful redundancy and some is already compressed or difficult to compress. The result may shrink very little, and format overhead can even make a small result larger. The utility cannot promise the same reduction for every file.

Name the problem before naming the tool. Compression seeks a smaller representation; backup provides recovery; defragmentation changes HDD placement; a formatter prepares organisation; analysis and repair investigate storage use or faults; a virus checker handles evidence of malware. A compressed file is not automatically encrypted or stored as a separate backup.

Compare the compact description with reconstructing the exact original sequence. Real archive formats use specified encodings and include overhead.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Call a tested routine instead of rewriting its algorithm

leadVisual.title: Call a tested routine instead of rewriting its algorithm

coreExplanation: A program library is a collection of pre-written or pre-compiled routines or modules that other programs can use. A routine is a named section of code that performs a task. A library can supply specialist operations such as mathematical calculations or reading an image format.

The interface tells the caller how to use the routine: its name, arguments, returned result and conditions for use. An argument is a value supplied in a call. Here SQRT(Value) supplies Value and returns its square root; the chosen routine requires Value to be non-negative.

INPUT supplies Value. The condition checks it before the call. Assignment stores the returned result in Result, then OUTPUT displays it. This is Cambridge-style pseudocode using a documented library operation, not a claim that an unspecified real compiler accepts the listing.

Reusing suitable tested code reduces implementation and testing effort and can improve reliability. It gives access to specialist routines without writing their algorithms from scratch. The calling program still needs testing: valid library code can be supplied with unsuitable data or have its result ignored or misused.

learningCycle.observe: The supplied routine SQRT accepts a non-negative number and returns its square root. The caller needs to supply 81, receive 9 and use that result in the rest of the program.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Share a separate library and track the dependency

leadVisual.title: Share a separate library and track the dependency

coreExplanation: With static linking, required library code is incorporated into the built executable. An executable is a built program that can be launched in its target environment. With dynamic linking, a Dynamic Link Library, or DLL, remains a separate file and its routines are linked when the program is loaded or when needed during execution.

Several applications can use one compatible DLL rather than each containing its own incorporated copy. Their executable files can be smaller, disk duplication can be reduced and loaded library code can be shared in memory where supported. The library code still exists in the separate file.

A compatible correction can be made to the DLL without recompiling each calling application. Recompiling means translating the application’s source code again to rebuild it. Each caller must load the corrected library version; a running application may need restarting or reloading. Compatibility means that required routine names, arguments and expected behaviour remain usable by the caller.

The DLL must be available and compatible when needed. If MakeLabel is removed or its parameter requirements change, an unchanged caller can fail even if the filename is still Label.dll. A missing library can also prevent loading or execution. Test the callers after an update.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Translate assembly mnemonics for a target processor

leadVisual.title: Translate assembly mnemonics for a target processor

coreExplanation: In the Cambridge teaching instruction set, LDM #6 loads the immediate value 6 into the accumulator, a working register. ADD #4 adds the immediate value 4. STO 200 stores the result at address 200, which we reserve as a writable result location. END finishes the program. The # marks an immediate value.

An assembler translates assembly-language mnemonics and operands into target machine-code encodings. It must understand the relevant processor’s instruction set. A high-level language such as Java needs a different translation route; an assembler does not translate arbitrary Java statements.

Translating ADD #4 creates an encoding of an addition instruction. It does not itself carry out the program’s addition. When the translated program later executes, the accumulator changes from 6 to 10 and 10 is written at address 200.

Assembler output may be object code, a translated module that still requires linking, or a complete executable. A linker combines required modules and resolves references between them. This connects to libraries: a translated call must be connected to the routine it uses before or during execution, according to the linking approach.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Build one version, then execute that version

leadVisual.title: Build one version, then execute that version

coreExplanation: Both variables start at 0. Each loop body adds 2 to Total and 1 to Count. The body runs while Count is 0, 1 and 2; it stops when Count becomes 3. The last statement displays Total, which is 6. The listing is Cambridge pseudocode used to model behaviour, not source for an unspecified real compiler.

In the native compilation model, a compiler translates a high-level program or compilation unit into target code before it executes. A build can include linking object modules and required routines into an executable. The native executable must be suitable for the target processor and system.

Editing and saving source changes the source file. It does not automatically replace an existing executable. A successful rebuild of version B produces the new program; Run must launch that new build to show 12.

Translation diagnostics describe detected source problems. A successful build does not prove the algorithm correct: subtraction can be valid syntax when addition is required. A later runtime failure can also occur. If a build fails, any retained old executable is still the older version, not a successful translation of the invalid edit.

prerequisite.body: DECLARE introduces a variable. The assignment arrow <- stores a value. WHILE checks its condition before each repetition; ENDWHILE returns to that test. Count increases on each repetition, so this loop eventually finishes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Translate and execute along the selected path

leadVisual.title: Translate and execute along the selected path

coreExplanation: An interpreter is software that carries out the program as execution progresses. In this high-level interpretation model, statements are translated and executed along the selected control path instead of first saving a separate permanent native executable for the whole source. The interpreter itself runs on the computer.

A loop can revisit the same statement; a branch can skip one. Therefore “line by line” should not be read as “each displayed line exactly once from top to bottom”. For the same complete version A listing, the condition is checked four times and the body runs three times.

If the limit is 0, the initial check 0 < 0 is false. No loop body runs and Total stays 0. In the lab’s additional branch, choosing false skips its marked branch action. The loop still follows its own limit; a skipped branch does not automatically skip everything after it.

An interpreting environment can provide prompt feedback while trying usable parts of a developing program. Earlier statements may execute before a later runtime failure. For example, with numeric input 0, the complete program below outputs Starting and then encounters division by zero in the stated environment; it never reaches the last output. This is a runtime error example, not a rule about when all interpreters detect syntax errors.

In the usual introductory comparison, a compiler produces an executable file from source code before execution. The interpreter instead works as execution proceeds, stops when it encounters an error and supplies immediate feedback. An interactive environment can let the programmer correct the problem and continue supported work; another environment may require a restart. Follow the conditions given in a question rather than assuming every implementation resumes in the same way.

A completed native executable can be reused without retranslating the original source for each run and can be distributed without that source. Interpretation requires a suitable execution environment and may repeat translation-related work. These are reasons tied to the taught models, not guaranteed speed measurements for all language implementations.

A correction to compiled source needs a successful rebuild and distribution of the corrected executable. An interpreting environment can execute the corrected source it is given. In either case, a correction needs testing against the expected result, and the users must receive the intended version.

Use “because” to join requirement, mechanism and benefit. For Team A, prompt feedback on usable sections supports frequent corrections. For Team B, a suitable compiled executable can be repeatedly run and supplied without source. A compiler can also support debugging, and an interpreter is not always the best choice during development; the stated reasons decide whether a recommendation is justified.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compile Java source; run bytecode with a JVM

leadVisual.title: Compile Java source; run bytecode with a JVM

coreExplanation: Save the following as Hello.java. Its public class is named Hello, main is the starting method and the print statement displays the quoted message. The surrounding Java syntax makes a complete runnable example; this is Java source, not Cambridge pseudocode. Development requires tools providing javac and java, such as a JDK.

The command javac Hello.java invokes the Java compiler. It translates the source into bytecode stored in Hello.class. The bytecode targets the Java Virtual Machine, or JVM; it is not universal native machine code understood directly by every physical CPU.

The command java Hello launches the class through a suitable runtime. The JVM provides the host-specific execution of the bytecode. This illustrates partial compilation followed by interpretation; real JVMs may also compile frequently executed bytecode just in time for the host. The second computer needs a compatible runtime to run this already built class, but it does not need javac merely to perform that run.

Change the message to Hello, Class! and save the source. The old class file still contains the earlier bytecode. Running java Hello before recompiling therefore displays Hello, World! A successful javac Hello.java updates the class file; the next run displays Hello, Class!

If javac is missing, the development tools are unavailable. If the destination lacks a compatible JVM, it cannot execute this bytecode by the stated route. Producing another class file does not install the missing runtime. Use java Hello without the .class extension and run from an environment that can locate the class.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use suggestions and syntax feedback while entering code

leadVisual.title: Use suggestions and syntax feedback while entering code

coreExplanation: Context-sensitive prompts use the language and current editing position to suggest suitable keywords, names, methods or parameters. At a library call, a prompt may show the routine’s name and required arguments. It reduces typing and recall work while leaving the intended operation for the programmer to choose.

The following program is complete and grammatically valid in the teaching notation, but it multiplies by Delivery. The result is 3 × 2 = 6 instead of the required 3 × 4 = 12. Merely accepting a known identifier did not establish the correct meaning.

Dynamic syntax checking examines source while it is entered and highlights rule violations. For example, Cost <- Quantity * is an incomplete expression because it lacks the right operand. A missing required keyword can also be flagged. The message and location guide inspection, including surrounding lines where the cause may have begun.

Completing the expression with Delivery can remove that grammar error while preserving the wrong calculation. Syntax checking tests language rules; it does not prove that the result meets the requirement. Correct the example to Cost <- Quantity * UnitPrice, then run and compare the result with the independently predicted 12.

coreExplanation: The requirement is quantity multiplied by unit price, so the expected cost is 3 × 4 = 12. Read the complete source and select a point immediately before the suspect assignment. That puts both the input values and the effect of the operation within reach.

A breakpoint tells the debugger to pause execution at a selected source location. In this model it pauses before the selected calculation. At that pause, Quantity is 3, UnitPrice is 4 and Delivery is 2; Cost has not yet been assigned. Reaching a breakpoint is different from executing the statement on that line.

Variable inspection shows stored values at the current pause. An expression watch can evaluate Quantity * UnitPrice as 12 using those values. This pure arithmetic expression does not assign 12 to Cost and does not execute OUTPUT. It supplies evidence for comparison.

Single stepping executes one statement and pauses again. Stepping Cost <- Quantity * Delivery sets Cost to 6. The operands explain why: the program used 3 and 2. OUTPUT has not yet executed. A second step executes OUTPUT Cost and makes 6 appear in the program-output window.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Security, privacy and integrity

leadVisual.title: One record, different protection needs

coreExplanation: Security protects against unauthorised access, loss and damage; privacy concerns appropriate use and disclosure of personal data.
Integrity concerns accuracy, completeness and consistency. Judge each consequence; one incident can affect several properties.

teachingBlocks.text: Data security protects data against unauthorised access, loss or damage. Privacy concerns who may access personal information and whether its collection, use or disclosure is appropriate. Data integrity concerns accurate, complete and consistent information during storage, processing and transfer. A security control may support privacy or integrity, but the terms describe different questions.
teachingBlocks.title: Ask a different question about each property

teachingBlocks.text: If an unchanged medical record is sent to an unauthorised advertiser, its disclosure affects privacy and security even though its contents have not been corrupted. Conversely, a permitted employee can enter the wrong date in a protected file. The access restriction worked, but the stored date is inaccurate. Do not infer an integrity failure merely because an incident was serious.
teachingBlocks.title: Use consequences rather than exclusive labels

teachingBlocks.text: Check accuracy against the intended fact, completeness against the required information, and consistency between values that should agree. A missing examination mark makes the result set incomplete; two stored totals that should agree but differ are inconsistent. Rules, source comparisons and controlled updates address different causes. Lesson 037 develops the checking methods.
teachingBlocks.title: Unpack integrity

workedExample.title: Four independent events involving a source mark of 46

knowledgeUnits.heading: Protect the data and its processing system

leadVisual.title: Two independent protection targets

coreExplanation: Protect every relevant data copy and the computer system that processes it.
Confidentiality, a functioning service and recoverable data require complementary measures.

teachingBlocks.text: Data is the information being protected; the computer system supplies the hardware, operating system and applications needed to use it. Protecting a file alone does not keep that processing environment trustworthy or available. Malware could stop an application, or misuse an already authenticated session to read data after the application decrypts it.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep both protection targets in view

teachingBlocks.text: Also follow the copies. A locked server room protects one physical location, not a readable export on a lost removable drive. Controls must suit data at rest, data in transit and data in use. These describe where or how the data is being handled, not three new encryption algorithms.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow data beyond the original computer

teachingBlocks.text: Recovery needs a usable copy and a functioning destination. A backup left on the failed disk may be unavailable with the working data. A tested separate backup can restore a chosen saved state, but not later changes it never captured. Lesson 029 teaches backup operation; here the point is why protection must include continued use and recovery.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain why recovery belongs alongside prevention
