knowledgeUnits.heading: User accounts and passwords

leadVisual.title: Establish an identity before checking what that identity may do

coreExplanation: An account identifies the claimed user; a password supplies secret evidence for authentication.
After authentication, check the requested resource and operation against access rights.

teachingBlocks.text: A user account associates an identifier with permissions and recorded activity. At login the identifier selects the claimed identity; knowing the identifier alone does not prove that the person is its owner. Separate staff accounts make it possible to associate actions with distinct identities instead of one shared label.
teachingBlocks.title: Claim an identity, then supply evidence

teachingBlocks.text: A password is secret knowledge. The system checks the supplied password against the stored verifier for that account and accepts or rejects the login. The verifier is information used to check the secret; it need not be a readable stored copy of the password. Hard-to-guess passwords and restrictions on repeated attempts reduce guessing, while a disclosed password can still be used by an impostor.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain what the password check establishes

teachingBlocks.text: Authentication evaluates the identity claim. Authorisation checks whether that identity may perform a particular operation on a resource. A valid login can therefore lead to a denied deletion. Lesson 028 introduced this OS service; Lesson 036 develops the data-permission decisions. An activity log records the account used, not infallible proof of which human used stolen credentials.
teachingBlocks.title: Do not stop at successful login

workedExample.title: Three independent requests for Marks.csv

knowledgeUnits.heading: Create and verify a digital signature

leadVisual.title: Digital signature: sender and receiver

coreExplanation: Hash the message and sign using the sender’s private key; send the message and signature together.
The receiver checks with the sender’s trusted public key and the received message. A valid signature supports origin and unchanged signed content, not secrecy.

teachingBlocks.text: A hash algorithm produces a digest, a short fixed-length value derived from a message. The same message and algorithm give the same digest. A cryptographic hash is designed to make finding different messages with the same digest infeasible in practice; it is not a reversible encryption of the message. The fingerprint icon in the visual is an analogy for a message digest, not a scan of the sender's finger.
teachingBlocks.title: First understand the digest

teachingBlocks.text: The signer keeps a private key secret and makes the corresponding public key available for verification. These keys have different roles: the public key does not give its holder the ability to create that signer's valid signature. Before trusting the claimed origin, the receiver must have a reliable association between the public key and the sender. A public key supplied by an unknown impostor does not establish that association.
teachingBlocks.title: Know which key belongs to whom
Create, send and check the signed message
items: Sender calculates
Apply the chosen hash algorithm to the exact message to obtain its digest.
Sender signs
Use the private key to create a signature tied to the digest. Send the message and signature; retain the private key.
Receiver calculates
Hash the received message with the same algorithm.
Receiver verifies
Use the trusted sender public key to verify the signature against the digest of the received message. Accept the signature only when verification succeeds.

teachingBlocks.text: A simplified teaching model describes signing as encrypting the digest with the private key and checking as recovering it with the public key for comparison. Actual signature algorithms differ; some verify without recovering a digest from the signature. The invariant is a check of the signature, key and received message. H(M), h1 and h2 below denote supplied conceptual values, not computed outputs of a specified cryptographic implementation.
teachingBlocks.title: Interpret the simplified comparison model

teachingBlocks.text: A valid signature does not conceal the accompanying plaintext, prove the sender's statements true, or compensate for a stolen signing key. An attacker can edit a message while leaving its signature bytes unchanged; the verification then fails for the altered content. Hashing alone cannot establish origin because an attacker could replace an unprotected message and its plain digest together.
teachingBlocks.title: State what the evidence supports

workedExample.title: A purchase order, checked in the simplified digest model

knowledgeUnits.heading: Biometric authentication

leadVisual.title: Capture and match a biometric

coreExplanation: Enrol a reference template, then compare features from a new capture with it.
False acceptance admits an impostor; false rejection denies a legitimate user. A match does not grant every access right.

teachingBlocks.text: Biometrics use a physical or behavioural feature, such as a fingerprint, iris, voice or typing pattern, as identity evidence. The sensor captures a feature and software derives a template containing information useful for matching. This need not be a raw photograph of the feature.
teachingBlocks.title: From a feature to a reference
Separate enrolment from later authentication
items: Enrol
Register the legitimate user under the correct account, capture suitable samples and store a protected reference template.
Capture again
At a later login, capture the claimed user’s feature and extract a new comparison template.
Compare
Compare the new features with the enrolled reference and apply the system’s match requirement.
Decide
Accept a sufficient match or reject/request a supported retry. If authenticated, still apply the resource permissions.

teachingBlocks.text: Two scans need not be pixel-for-pixel identical: lighting, finger placement, noise or illness can change the capture. A false rejection occurs when the legitimate user is rejected; a false acceptance occurs when an impostor is accepted. Sensors, protected templates and an appropriate recovery method are needed. A compromised biological feature is harder to replace than a password.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain both kinds of wrong decision

workedExample.title: Check the system decision against the actual user

knowledgeUnits.heading: Firewalls on a PC and at a network boundary

leadVisual.title: Traffic decisions and firewall placement

coreExplanation: A firewall allows or blocks traffic by configured rules on the paths it controls.
Host and network firewalls differ in placement; permitted connections may still carry harmful content.

teachingBlocks.text: A firewall checks traffic against a policy, using properties such as addresses, direction, protocol, port or connection state. A port identifies a service endpoint, not a physical cable socket. The firewall permits or blocks the traffic and may record the decision. It does not decide solely from the name of the sender or from whether a packet is described as dangerous.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect a rule to observable traffic properties

teachingBlocks.text: A host firewall protects one computer's traffic. A network firewall filters the traffic routed through a boundary, for example between a LAN and the internet. Internal traffic that stays within the LAN need not cross that boundary. The protection therefore depends on placement as well as configuration; the device cannot filter a path that bypasses it.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow the actual path

teachingBlocks.text: For the classroom policy below, use the first matching rule and stop; the final rule denies everything else. This is a stated simplified policy, not universal default behaviour. Rule 1 permits traffic recognised as part of a previously allowed connection. Rules 2 and 3 distinguish new inbound and outbound connections.
teachingBlocks.title: Apply a complete policy
Policy for the worked traffic trace
rows: Traffic belongs to an already permitted connection
New inbound TCP connection to the public web server, destination port 443
New outbound TCP connection to destination port 443

teachingBlocks.text: An allowed connection can carry a deceptive message or an infected download. Content checking, authentication, patching and user decisions still have separate jobs. Conversely, an overly restrictive rule can block legitimate work. Explain both the chosen rule and its consequence for the stated traffic.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate connection permission from content trust

workedExample.title: Apply the policy, including a permitted unsafe download

knowledgeUnits.heading: Anti-virus software

leadVisual.title: Respond to a suspicious executable

coreExplanation: Scan for recognised virus patterns or suspicious behaviour; block, quarantine, remove or repair detected infection as supported.
Update detection information. A clean scan is evidence of no detection, not proof of no malware.

teachingBlocks.text: A virus is malicious code that infects a host file or program and can replicate when that host executes. Anti-virus software checks files, memory or activity for known patterns and suspicious behaviour. A virus signature here means a detection pattern; it is different from a digital signature used to authenticate a message.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain what is being detected

teachingBlocks.text: A detected file can be prevented from executing, isolated in quarantine, removed, or repaired where the tool supports it. Quarantine preserves a restricted copy for investigation instead of letting it run normally. The choice depends on the detected object and tool; removal of an infected file may also remove useful content that needs restoring.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow detection through to a usable system

teachingBlocks.text: Updates add or improve detection knowledge as threats become known. New, concealed or modified malware can evade existing checks, and a benign file can be flagged incorrectly. Inspect the result and use trusted recovery copies where necessary. Lesson 029 introduced the utility; Lesson 035 follows the infection route that it helps interrupt.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain the limits of the result

workedExample.title: From a suspect executable to checked recovery

knowledgeUnits.heading: Anti-spyware software

leadVisual.title: After detecting a keylogger

coreExplanation: Anti-spyware detects and stops, isolates or removes covert monitoring components.
Removal cannot retrieve information already disclosed; address exposed credentials and the entry route as well.

teachingBlocks.text: Spyware covertly monitors activity or collects information, for example by recording keystrokes or the screen. Anti-spyware looks for recognised components and suspicious monitoring behaviour. It may be part of a broader anti-malware product, so two named functions do not necessarily require two separate installed products.
teachingBlocks.title: Match the function to covert collection

teachingBlocks.text: Detection can lead to blocking, quarantine or removal. Keep detection information current because newly identified components may not match older rules. Removing a detected keylogger interrupts its future collection, but a remote recipient can retain logs it already received.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish the local component from disclosed information

teachingBlocks.text: After exposed credentials are identified, replace them using a trusted device and repair the installation route, such as an unauthorised download. Changing a password on a still-monitored device can reveal the new value too. This explains the order of response, not a promise that one tool reverses every consequence.
teachingBlocks.title: Resolve the remaining consequence

workedExample.title: Use the timeline to choose the response

knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine controls for different risks

leadVisual.title: A travelling employee's computer

coreExplanation: Select controls from the threat route and the property needing protection.
Authentication, traffic filtering, malware detection, encryption and recovery perform complementary jobs.

teachingBlocks.text: Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key. An application with the required decryption key can recover the readable contents. This protects a stolen or intercepted copy from a person without the key; Lesson 036 develops the data transformation and key-protection requirements.
teachingBlocks.title: Introduce the confidentiality layer

teachingBlocks.text: Start a recommendation with the exposure: a guessed password calls for stronger authentication, disallowed traffic for a filtering policy, and infected code for detection and containment. A list of product names does not show that the mechanisms fit. State what each control checks or changes and how that reduces the stated risk.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose a mechanism for each risk

teachingBlocks.text: Layering combines measures that address different routes or consequences. If malware executes in a user's unlocked session, encryption of the disk alone may not stop access to data that the application has already decrypted. Recovery adds a way to regain a usable saved state when prevention fails; it does not prevent disclosure that has already happened.
teachingBlocks.title: Test the combination against a changed condition

knowledgeUnits.heading: Viruses attach to a host and replicate

leadVisual.title: An infected host can carry replication to other files

coreExplanation: A virus infects a host file or program; executing the infected host can run the viral code and spread infection.
Explain arrival, execution, replication and possible damage separately.

teachingBlocks.text: A virus attaches to or modifies a host file or program. A shared or downloaded infected host provides a route to another computer, but the arrival of the file and the execution of its code are different events. In the executable-host model used here, running the infected program runs the attached code.
teachingBlocks.title: Identify the host and activation event

teachingBlocks.text: The virus can copy its code into additional hosts, creating further opportunities to execute and spread. Its payload may alter or delete data or disrupt normal processing. Replication describes how it spreads; the payload describes harmful actions it performs. A virus need not immediately erase every file to count as an infection.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate spread from impact

teachingBlocks.text: Avoiding untrusted execution and controlling software installation reduce opportunities for the code to run. Updated anti-virus can detect and isolate recognised infection; a trusted backup may support recovery after damage. None of these precautions can be justified merely by saying that it makes the computer safe: identify the stage it interrupts.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain the link to a precaution

workedExample.title: Follow one infected shared program

knowledgeUnits.heading: Spyware monitors and discloses

leadVisual.title: Trace a captured password to its recipient

coreExplanation: Spyware secretly collects activity or information and may disclose it to a third party.
Covert collection, not self-replication, defines the behaviour; one program can have several malicious behaviours.

teachingBlocks.text: Spyware can log keystrokes, record the screen or collect browsing activity without the user's informed awareness. Identify what is collected: a typed password, a visible customer record, or activity history. Merely saying that information is stolen omits the mechanism. Not every openly declared monitoring or analytics function is automatically spyware.
teachingBlocks.title: Name the captured information

teachingBlocks.text: A monitoring component can store a log and send it to a third party. A keylogger may therefore expose credentials for another service, even though the spyware is installed on the local computer. The recipient can try to impersonate the user. Removing the local component does not erase that separate log.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow collection into disclosure

teachingBlocks.text: Spyware need not infect other executable hosts. A single program can both replicate like a virus and collect secrets like spyware; classify the behaviours rather than forcing a mutually exclusive label. Controlled installation reduces entry, and anti-spyware addresses detected monitoring components. L034 explains the response after exposure.
teachingBlocks.title: Use behaviour to distinguish threats

workedExample.title: A local keylogger affects a separate email service

knowledgeUnits.heading: Unauthorised access by hackers

leadVisual.title: Entry route and consequence

coreExplanation: Unauthorised access may exploit stolen or guessed credentials, exposed services or software flaws.
Match authentication, patches and restricted permissions to the relevant route or consequence.

teachingBlocks.text: In this syllabus security context, hackers attempt or gain unauthorised access to systems or data. Access is unauthorised because the person lacks legitimate permission, even if the system accepts a guessed or stolen password. The label refers here to an access threat rather than every possible use of the word hacker.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate accepted credentials from legitimate permission

teachingBlocks.text: A weak password permits guessing; a disclosed password permits impersonation; an unpatched vulnerability can allow unintended actions through a software flaw. These are different entry routes. Replacing a password does not repair a vulnerable service, and a patch does not automatically invalidate a previously stolen credential.
teachingBlocks.title: Diagnose the entry route

teachingBlocks.text: After access, permissions determine which records and operations the compromised account can reach. Least privilege limits unnecessary access but does not make the intrusion legitimate. Restrict exposed services, apply relevant patches and strengthen authentication according to the stated cause. Record the remaining risk instead of claiming complete prevention.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish preventing access from limiting its impact

workedExample.title: A receptionist account is impersonated

knowledgeUnits.heading: Phishing persuades the user

leadVisual.title: Phishing succeeds by persuading a person to act

coreExplanation: A phishing communication impersonates a trusted source and induces disclosure or an unsafe action.
Verify the request using independently known contact details or a known service, not the message’s supplied route.

teachingBlocks.text: Phishing uses a deceptive email, text message or other communication to impersonate a trusted person or organisation. Urgency, a familiar logo and a plausible sender name can persuade the recipient to disclose private information or act unsafely. The message may direct the user to a copied sign-in page, but installing malware is not necessary for credential theft.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain persuasion and the requested action

teachingBlocks.text: Trace where the action sends information. If a user submits credentials to an attacker-controlled form, they reach the attacker rather than the intended service. If the message requests a payment change, the harm can result from following that instruction even without a fake login page. Describe the stated route instead of assuming every phishing attempt works identically.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow the information or instruction

teachingBlocks.text: Use an independently known address or trusted contact record to verify the request. A phone number or reply address inside the suspicious message may also belong to the attacker. Filtering and training reduce exposure, and an additional authentication factor can reduce some consequences of a stolen password; it does not make every deceptive instruction harmless.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain why the independent channel matters

workedExample.title: Two outcomes for the same support message

knowledgeUnits.heading: Pharming changes the destination

leadVisual.title: Two routes to an imitation page

coreExplanation: Pharming redirects a user to a fraudulent destination, for example through corrupted DNS or local name-resolution information.
A correctly typed name can still be misdirected; protect resolution settings and investigate certificate or hostname warnings.

teachingBlocks.text: Normally the browser needs an address for the intended domain name before contacting its server. Lesson 014 separates DNS name resolution from the later web request. Pharming manipulates the destination, for example by corrupting a DNS record or local name-resolution entry, so the intended name leads to an attacker-controlled server.
teachingBlocks.title: Recall the normal resolution step

teachingBlocks.text: The user may type the correct name and receive a convincing imitation page. Unlike the phishing route taught alongside it, no deceptive link is needed to start this redirection. Merely advising the user to type the address does not repair a corrupted mapping. The two routes can also be combined in a wider attack.
teachingBlocks.title: Locate the change before the page is returned

teachingBlocks.text: Restrict unauthorised changes to resolution settings, maintain relevant software and investigate unexpected certificate or hostname warnings. An HTTPS indicator describes an encrypted connection and its certificate context, not a guarantee that every site or request is honest. Certificate acquisition and TLS protocol details are outside this AS explanation.
teachingBlocks.title: Match the precaution to the destination problem

workedExample.title: The correctly typed payroll address

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match precautions to the threat

leadVisual.title: Choose from the mechanism

coreExplanation: A justified precaution interrupts a threat route or reduces a specified consequence.
Combine prevention, detection and recovery; state what each measure does and what remains.

teachingBlocks.text: Start with the mechanism rather than a product. Ask what permits entry, what the attacker or code then does, and which data or service is affected. Map a control to that stage: patches repair known flaws, limited installation reduces unapproved execution, and independent confirmation challenges a deceptive request.
teachingBlocks.title: Build a reasoned recommendation
Different purposes in a response
rows: Restrict new software installation or unnecessary access.
A permitted program or compromised account may still be misused.
Identify and quarantine recognised malicious code.
Unknown threats may escape detection; earlier damage may remain.
Restore a trusted saved state to a usable system.
The backup cannot prevent prior disclosure or recover changes it never captured.

teachingBlocks.text: Physical protection, staff procedures and technical controls can complement each other. For a lost drive, restricting server permissions is insufficient for a readable independent copy; encryption and key protection fit that exposure. For a fake payment request, an encrypted disk does not authenticate the instruction. Reconsider the recommendation when the scenario changes.
teachingBlocks.title: Test whether the proposed control reaches the risk

knowledgeUnits.heading: Encryption and decryption

leadVisual.title: From readable data to a protected copy

coreExplanation: Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext; the correct decryption method and key recover the plaintext.
Protect the key as well as the copy. Encryption alone does not prevent deletion, control every authorised action or prove source truth.

teachingBlocks.text: Plaintext is readable original data. Encryption applies an algorithm using a key to produce ciphertext. Decryption uses the corresponding method and required key to recover the original data. An intercepted or stolen encrypted copy should not reveal its readable content to someone without the required secret. Encryption does not prevent the copy from being intercepted.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow both directions

teachingBlocks.text: Protect the key separately from the exposed copy. An unprotected decryption key on the same lost drive can give the finder both ciphertext and the means to recover it. A legitimate recipient who has the key can read the sent content; possession of that key does not automatically grant permission to edit the original database.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate the copy, the key and the service

teachingBlocks.text: The small character example illustrates reversible transformation only. It uses uppercase letters A–Z, shifts forward by three for encryption and backward by three for decryption, wrapping at either end. Its rule is deliberately simple and is not a secure cipher for real records or an algorithm to memorise for this syllabus. Cryptographic key-system comparisons belong to later study.
teachingBlocks.title: Use a fully specified teaching model
Complete the stated character transformation

teachingBlocks.text: The model turns ZOO into CRR and restores ZOO with the inverse rule. It is not a hash: the purpose is recovery of the original. If ciphertext is erased, encryption cannot recreate it. If the original data is false, decrypting it faithfully restores the same false information. Keep confidentiality, availability and integrity judgements separate.
teachingBlocks.title: Check the result and its limits

workedExample.title: A protected archive: normal delivery and loss

knowledgeUnits.heading: Apply access rights to data

leadVisual.title: Personnel-file permissions

coreExplanation: Access rights specify permitted operations for users or roles on particular resources.
Least privilege limits unnecessary actions; authenticated users can still be denied an operation or make an authorised mistake.

teachingBlocks.text: After identifying the user, the service checks the resource and requested operation against its permissions. Read permits viewing, modify permits changing existing data, and delete permits removing it. Other systems may distinguish creation or record-level permissions too; use the rights and resource scope actually stated in the problem.
teachingBlocks.title: Evaluate a complete request

teachingBlocks.text: A role groups users with similar responsibilities. Least privilege gives each role only the access needed for its work. A reviewer who checks marks can have read access without modification or deletion rights. Restricting reads supports confidentiality, while restricting updates reduces unauthorised alteration. Neither establishes that an allowed update is factually correct.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect each right to its consequence
Teaching matrix: rights on one mark record
Sequential operations; initial stored mark = 46
rows: Teacher changes mark to 48 after checking the source

teachingBlocks.text: The previous operations concern a resource controlled by the service. If a readable copy has already been exported, an outsider may read it without consulting that service's matrix. Read-only access is not a promise that no external copy can be made. Protect disclosure and exported copies as well. Lesson 044 applies these principles to database users and groups.
teachingBlocks.title: State the enforcement boundary

knowledgeUnits.heading: Validation and verification answer different questions

leadVisual.title: A source mark of 46 is entered as 64

coreExplanation: Validation checks stated acceptability rules; verification checks faithful entry or transfer relative to a source.
An acceptable wrong value or two matching wrong copies can pass a check. Neither proves the original fact true.

teachingBlocks.text: Validation tests whether input satisfies stated rules and is reasonable for its purpose. Verification checks whether information has been entered, copied or transferred accurately relative to its source. They support integrity by detecting different kinds of error. First ask whether the task needs rule compliance, faithful copying, or both.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose the question the check must answer

teachingBlocks.text: A source mark of 46 entered as 64 can pass the range 0–75 while failing comparison with the source. A source age of 200 copied correctly can pass that source comparison but fail a permitted range of 0–120. If a wrong source says 12 and both copies say 12, neither a matching copy nor a reasonable age proves the person is actually 12.
teachingBlocks.title: Separate acceptable, copied correctly and true
Use independent checks in a data-entry process
rows: Does each field satisfy the specified bounds, pattern, required entry and lookup rules?
Flag the relevant field and request correction.
Does the entered information agree with the original form?
Investigate the difference against the source, correct and check again.
Have the required checks passed for this submission?
Do not silently store the rejected submission as an accepted record.

teachingBlocks.text: The next units first choose and apply individual validation methods, then combine them on one form. The second stage adds a check digit and source comparisons. The final stage follows checking information from sender to receiver. This is a progression from rule decisions to complete checking processes, not a requirement to implement a program here.
teachingBlocks.title: Follow the three learning stages

workedExample.title: Validate and verify a submitted mark

knowledgeUnits.heading: Range and limit checks

leadVisual.title: Apply the written bounds

coreExplanation: A range specifies lower and upper bounds; a limit specifies one bound.
Follow the stated inclusive or strict comparisons and test the endpoints as well as values just outside.

teachingBlocks.text: A range check compares a value with both ends of an allowed interval. For integer marks with 0 <= Mark <= 75, both 0 and 75 are allowed. The two conditions must both hold. Replacing the upper <= with < excludes 75, so the exact comparison matters.
teachingBlocks.title: Read both bounds

teachingBlocks.text: A limit check uses one upper or lower bound, such as UploadSize <= 10 MiB or Temperature >= -20. A lower limit alone does not impose an unstated upper limit. When a problem already supplies non-negative file sizes, that is an input condition; do not pretend the upper-limit comparison itself checked non-negativity.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish the rule from supplied conditions
Test the actual boundary

teachingBlocks.text: Use values just inside, at and just outside the relevant boundary to expose a wrong comparison. For a whole-number mark, 74, 75 and 76 distinguish an inclusive maximum of 75 from a strict maximum. For continuous or measured data, choose test values according to the stated precision rather than always adding one.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose a discriminating test

workedExample.title: Test an inclusive temperature range

knowledgeUnits.heading: Format and length checks

leadVisual.title: Code rule: two uppercase letters, then four digits

coreExplanation: Length counts characters; format checks their required arrangement.
Preserve leading zeros in string identifiers and apply each stated check separately.

teachingBlocks.text: A length check tests the number of characters, such as exactly six or at most twenty. A format check tests the required arrangement, such as two uppercase letters followed by four digits. A format may imply a length, but the tests still ask distinguishable questions: 123456 has six characters yet fails the specified letter-and-digit pattern.
teachingBlocks.title: Count characters, then inspect positions

teachingBlocks.text: Read the full pattern. AB0123 fits two uppercase letters and four digits, while A10123 has a digit where the second uppercase letter is required. AB123 has only five characters and too few trailing digits. A stored identifier is often a string: converting 001234 to a number would lose its leading zeros and change the representation being checked.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep the representation needed by the rule

teachingBlocks.text: Do not infer factual meaning from appearance. A correctly formatted date string may still describe an impossible date, and a correctly shaped customer code may not occur in the customer file. A format rule needs to be stated precisely; use an additional appropriate check for conditions the pattern does not establish.
teachingBlocks.title: Identify what remains unchecked

knowledgeUnits.heading: Presence and existence checks

leadVisual.title: Stored customer IDs: C102, C107, C115

coreExplanation: Presence requires an entry; existence tests membership in the stated stored set.
A non-blank correctly shaped value can still fail existence. Give the lookup data needed to decide.

teachingBlocks.text: A presence check rejects an absent required entry. It does not test whether a supplied identifier corresponds to a real record. An existence check searches a specified stored lookup or file for the supplied value. The correct source matters: finding a customer code in an unrelated product file would not establish that the customer exists.
teachingBlocks.title: State the required field and lookup

teachingBlocks.text: In the simple examples, Blank means no characters were entered. If a real form also treats spaces-only input as empty, that must be a stated rule. Once a required field fails presence, the form can flag that error before trying its format or lookup. A skipped lookup is not a successful existence check.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain the order of checking
Complete form specification for the worked example
rows: Required; two uppercase letters followed by three digits; must be in {AB012, CD345}
Exactly six characters; two uppercase letters followed by four digits
An integer already supplied; 5 to 18 inclusive
A non-negative size in MiB already supplied; at most 10 MiB

teachingBlocks.text: All required checks must pass for this form to be accepted under its input rules. Report the failed field and request correction rather than silently replacing an unknown customer or inventing an age. Leading zeros in the two codes are characters and must remain. Passing every rule still does not prove agreement with an original form.
teachingBlocks.title: Combine checks without changing their meaning

workedExample.title: Apply all stated rules and finish the submission

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate and check an identifier's check digit

leadVisual.title: Weighted check digit: a complete calculation

coreExplanation: Derive a check digit using the specified rule; on entry recalculate and compare with the supplied digit.
A mismatch detects an error but does not identify the intended identifier. Some wrong identifiers still pass.

teachingBlocks.text: A check digit is a digit calculated from the other digits in an identifier and stored with them. The system repeats the stated calculation when the full code is entered or scanned. It can compare the expected final digit with the supplied final digit or apply the equivalent rule to their combined total.
teachingBlocks.title: Distinguish generation from checking

teachingBlocks.text: For this example only, use four data digits with weights 3, 1, 3, 1. Multiply corresponding digits and weights, add the products, then choose a digit from 0 to 9 that makes the total a multiple of 10. If the total already is a multiple of 10, choose 0; do not choose 10, which is not one digit. Different schemes use different weights and rules.
teachingBlocks.title: Use a complete stated algorithm
Generate three check digits under the same rule

teachingBlocks.text: 47269 and 42769 both satisfy this rule even though their data digits differ. The totals 31 and 41 both need a final 9. This is a concrete undetected transposition, not proof that check digits are useless. They detect many errors cheaply, but cannot establish that an accepted identifier is the one intended or that its record exists.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain a passing wrong value

workedExample.title: Check the scanned identifier and resolve an error

knowledgeUnits.heading: Verify entered data

leadVisual.title: Source code: BK209

coreExplanation: A visual check compares the entry with its source; double entry compares two independently entered copies.
Resolve differences against the source and recheck. Identical copies can contain the same mistake.

teachingBlocks.text: Visual verification means that a person compares the entered information with the original source. Looking at the entry alone and deciding it seems plausible is not that comparison. The original form, document or other stated source must be available, and the person must check the relevant characters or values.
teachingBlocks.title: Make the comparison reference explicit

teachingBlocks.text: For double entry, enter the value independently twice and let the computer compare the copies. The second entry should not simply copy the first displayed entry. A mismatch identifies disagreement but does not say which entry is right; consult the original source, correct and compare again.
teachingBlocks.title: Complete the mismatch-resolution process

teachingBlocks.text: If source 640 is entered as 604 twice, both copies agree despite the repeated error. If the source itself is wrong, perfect copying preserves its error. These limitations explain why agreement is evidence from a particular check and why verification differs from validation of permitted values.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain both agreement and disagreement

workedExample.title: Resolve a double-entry disagreement completely

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use parity on a byte

leadVisual.title: Build an even-parity byte

coreExplanation: Choose the parity bit to make the total count of 1 bits, including that bit, meet the agreed odd/even convention.
Byte parity detects an odd number of bit flips; an even number can pass. It cannot locate the erroneous bit.

teachingBlocks.text: The sender and receiver agree a parity convention. Count the 1 bits in the data, then choose a parity bit so the whole transmitted group has an even or odd total as required. The example uses seven data bits followed by one parity bit to make an eight-bit group. Other questions may specify a different data width or bit position; follow the supplied arrangement.
teachingBlocks.title: Fix the convention and the bit positions
Build both conventions for the same seven data bits

teachingBlocks.text: The receiver checks the whole received group, including its received parity bit. If 10110010 becomes 10100010, the count falls from four to three and even parity fails. The changed bit could instead have been the parity bit itself; this check alone cannot identify which position changed. Reject or request retransmission rather than guessing a correction.
teachingBlocks.title: Trace the receiving decision

teachingBlocks.text: Each bit flip changes the count of 1s by one in either direction. An odd number of flips changes whether the count is odd or even; an even number preserves it. Flipping the first two bits gives 01110010, still with four 1s. Therefore a passed parity check means no parity error was detected, not that the data is necessarily unchanged.
teachingBlocks.title: Derive the limitation from the count

workedExample.title: A parity failure followed by successful retransmission

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use row and column parity

leadVisual.title: Construct the transmitted block, then locate an error

coreExplanation: Append row parity bits and a column-parity row, then transmit that checking information with the block.
Under a single-bit error assumption, one failed row and one failed column locate the bit; correct and recheck.

teachingBlocks.text: Two-dimensional parity adds checking information in both directions. Start with the three seven-bit data rows below and use even parity throughout. Append one row-parity bit to each row. Then count each column of these complete rows to form a final column-parity row, often called a parity byte. This last row is transmitted, not invented by the receiver after an error.
teachingBlocks.title: Construct the sender’s complete block
Sender construction

teachingBlocks.text: For data column 4, the sender's rows contain 1, 0, 0: one 1, so the final parity row needs 1 in that column. For column 1 they contain 1, 0, 1: two 1s, so the final bit is 0. Repeating across all eight columns gives 00010100. In this construction the lower-right bit completes the parity information consistently; it is not another original data bit.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain how a column value is obtained
Check all column totals including the transmitted last row

teachingBlocks.text: After exactly one bit changes, its row and column each have the wrong parity. Their intersection locates the bit; flip it and check the complete block again. This reasoning depends on the one-bit assumption. Multiple errors can produce several failed lines, ambiguous intersections or no parity failure. Do not promise correction from every pattern.
teachingBlocks.title: State the correction condition

workedExample.title: Check, correct and recheck every direction

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate and compare a checksum

leadVisual.title: An eight-bit sum checksum

coreExplanation: Calculate a checksum from the data, send it with the block, recalculate from the received data and compare.
Use the specified algorithm. A mismatch detects an error; a match does not prove that the data is unchanged.

teachingBlocks.text: A checksum is a value calculated from a block using an agreed algorithm. The sender transmits the data and its checksum. The receiver repeats that algorithm on the received data and compares the newly calculated value with the received checksum. For this example, the checksum is not included as another data byte in the receiver's sum.
teachingBlocks.title: Keep the two compared values distinct

teachingBlocks.text: The stated rule adds the data bytes and keeps the remainder after division by 256. This is called sum modulo 256. For 84, 121 and 77, the sum is 282. Since 282 = 1 × 256 + 26, the remainder and eight-bit checksum value are 26, not the quotient 1 and not 282. Other checksum algorithms use different operations; do not substitute this rule when a question supplies another.
teachingBlocks.title: Explain the remainder calculation

teachingBlocks.text: If the received data is 84, 120, 77, its sum is 281 and its remainder is 25. Comparing 25 with the received 26 detects an error somewhere in the data/checking information. A mismatch does not locate the incorrect byte. The system can reject or request retransmission according to its protocol.
teachingBlocks.title: Continue from mismatch to a decision

teachingBlocks.text: Changing the data to 85, 120, 77 preserves the sum 282 and checksum 26. The two changes cancel, so this algorithm misses them. It is not a digital signature and supplies no authenticated origin: an attacker who can replace both an unprotected block and its checksum can recompute the check. A check digit instead accompanies an identifier under its stated validation rule.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why does technical knowledge create responsibility?

leadVisual.title: Why does technical knowledge create responsibility?

coreExplanation: A computing professional is someone whose work uses specialist computing knowledge, such as a developer, systems analyst or consultant. A student may depend on the reading assistant without understanding its source code. The developer can investigate faults and recognise limitations that the student cannot independently discover.

Ethics concerns principles about right and wrong conduct. Professional ethics guides decisions about how specialist knowledge and control should be used. Here, the developer must consider whether the student can rely on the output, not merely whether the program starts and produces sound.

Suppose the developer knows that blurred pages can produce incorrect words. Concealing this limitation leaves the school with an incomplete basis for deciding how to use the tool. Explaining the limitation lets the teacher check uncertain readings or use a different resource. The professional has a responsibility because others depend on knowledge that the professional controls.

Ethics helps protect the public interest, encourages honest and competent work and makes professionals accountable for their decisions. Accountability means being answerable for what was done and why. These purposes support justified trust: people can rely on evidence and responsible conduct instead of an impressive claim alone.

learningCycle.observe: Compare the printed instruction with the spoken output in the diagram. A student may rely on the spoken words because they cannot easily read the page. The developer has recorded a failure, but the student may not know about it. Decide who needs that evidence before the tool is used.
learningCycle.question: The assistant speaks confidently. Who knows whether it read the page correctly?

prerequisite.title: Use what you know about data and access
prerequisite.body: A digital image represents pixels; text represents characters; an audio output represents sound. You do not yet need to know how the assistant converts between them. Recall also that an account can allow a person to access data without deciding whether every possible use of that access is appropriate.

steps.title: Begin with people depending on an output
steps.body: A computing professional is someone whose work uses specialist computing knowledge, such as a developer, systems analyst or consultant. A student may depend on the reading assistant without understanding its source code. The developer can investigate faults and recognise limitations that the student cannot independently discover.

steps.title: Explain ethics in this situation
steps.body: Ethics concerns principles about right and wrong conduct. Professional ethics guides decisions about how specialist knowledge and control should be used. Here, the developer must consider whether the student can rely on the output, not merely whether the program starts and produces sound.

steps.title: Connect knowledge to a duty
steps.body: Suppose the developer knows that blurred pages can produce incorrect words. Concealing this limitation leaves the school with an incomplete basis for deciding how to use the tool. Explaining the limitation lets the teacher check uncertain readings or use a different resource. The professional has a responsibility because others depend on knowledge that the professional controls.

steps.title: State the purposes of professional ethics
steps.body: Ethics helps protect the public interest, encourages honest and competent work and makes professionals accountable for their decisions. Accountability means being answerable for what was done and why. These purposes support justified trust: people can rely on evidence and responsible conduct instead of an impressive claim alone.

worked.title: A confident reading of an uncertain page
worked.setup: During a trial, the assistant sometimes changes a printed instruction from “Do not enter” to “Do enter”. The developer has recorded the failure. The school is about to use the assistant for safety signs.

steps.title: Identify the dependence
steps.body: A student who relies on speech may act on the spoken instruction without checking the original sign. The developer knows the demonstrated limitation, while the student and school may not.

steps.title: Choose a responsible action and explain it
steps.body: Report the failed readings and advise against relying on this version for safety instructions. Arrange a checked alternative while the fault is investigated. This gives the school relevant evidence and protects people who might otherwise follow an incorrect instruction.

worked.conclusion: The need for ethics follows from how professional decisions affect people who depend on specialist work.

check.prompt: Change the case: the same error appears in a poem rather than a safety sign. Does the professional responsibility disappear?
check.answer: No. Honest reporting and appropriate use remain necessary. The likely harm and urgency change, so the response can be proportionate: a checked reading may be sufficient for the poem, while safety information needs a more restrictive response. Do not pretend that both contexts have identical consequences.

learningCycle.takeaway: Professional ethics guides the use of specialist knowledge to protect people, support honest work and establish accountability.
learningCycle.bridge: We now need to turn these broad purposes into actions a professional can take.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Turn professional duties into practical actions

leadVisual.title: Turn professional duties into practical actions

coreExplanation: Competence means having the knowledge and skills required for the work. A developer who has not tested a language should not claim expertise or accuracy for that language. They should state the limitation and seek a suitably qualified review. Recognising a limit is part of competent practice.

Honesty means reporting results, limitations and uncertainty accurately. An observed failure should be described as a failure, while an unconfirmed report should be described as a concern requiring investigation. Meeting a deadline does not justify changing a failed result into a passed one.

Confidentiality means avoiding inappropriate disclosure of information entrusted to the professional. The school needs the failure evidence, but an unrestricted public post containing student records can create a separate harm. Integrity also requires disclosing a personal interest, such as a commission from the recommended supplier, so that advice can be evaluated fairly.

Law sets enforceable requirements. An employer gives work instructions, and a professional code sets expectations of conduct. These may support the same action, but obeying a manager or finding no explicit prohibition does not settle whether an action is responsible. Equally, identifying an ethical concern does not by itself prove that a law has been broken.

learningCycle.observe: The reading assistant failed three tests, but the manager wants the report to say “all tests passed” so that delivery is on time. Name the fact that would be hidden and the person who needs it. Then consider a second issue: the report contains identifiable student reading records.
learningCycle.question: What should a developer do when a manager asks for a misleading test report?

steps.title: Work within your competence
steps.body: Competence means having the knowledge and skills required for the work. A developer who has not tested a language should not claim expertise or accuracy for that language. They should state the limitation and seek a suitably qualified review. Recognising a limit is part of competent practice.

steps.title: Report evidence honestly
steps.body: Honesty means reporting results, limitations and uncertainty accurately. An observed failure should be described as a failure, while an unconfirmed report should be described as a concern requiring investigation. Meeting a deadline does not justify changing a failed result into a passed one.

steps.title: Protect confidentiality and disclose conflicts
steps.body: Confidentiality means avoiding inappropriate disclosure of information entrusted to the professional. The school needs the failure evidence, but an unrestricted public post containing student records can create a separate harm. Integrity also requires disclosing a personal interest, such as a commission from the recommended supplier, so that advice can be evaluated fairly.

steps.title: Separate law, instructions and ethical judgement
steps.body: Law sets enforceable requirements. An employer gives work instructions, and a professional code sets expectations of conduct. These may support the same action, but obeying a manager or finding no explicit prohibition does not settle whether an action is responsible. Equally, identifying an ethical concern does not by itself prove that a law has been broken.

worked.title: Report the fault without exposing student records
worked.setup: A developer must respond to the request for an “all passed” report. The cause of the reading failure has not yet been confirmed.

steps.title: Record what is known
steps.body: Keep the actual test conditions and results. State that failures occurred and that their cause remains under investigation. Do not invent a diagnosis or remove the failed cases from the summary.

steps.title: Choose the appropriate audience and material
steps.body: Notify the responsible school and development leads using a report with only the information they need. Protect identifiable student records and use a suitable authorised reporting route.

steps.title: Follow the concern through
steps.body: Recommend correction and retesting before relying on the affected function. If further expertise is needed, request it. Record the new evidence rather than promising that no future error is possible.

worked.conclusion: Competence, honesty, confidentiality and integrity need specific actions, recipients and reasons.

check.prompt: A consultant receives an undisclosed commission for recommending the assistant. The assistant works correctly. Is there still an ethical concern?
check.answer: Yes. The financial interest can affect the independence of the recommendation even when the software functions. Disclose the commission and arrange an impartial comparison with the school’s requirements. A conflict of interest does not require a defective product.

learningCycle.takeaway: Explain the duty, the action it requires and the person it protects.
learningCycle.bridge: Professional bodies provide shared standards and support for applying these duties.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use professional standards and support

leadVisual.title: Use professional standards and support

coreExplanation: BCS is the British Computer Society. IEEE is the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. They are professional organisations that support standards and professional practice. They are different from a software supplier, an employee’s manager or the team testing a particular product.

A professional code states the behaviour and standards expected of members. It gives professionals and the public a reference against which conduct can be judged. Associated conduct procedures provide accountability and consequences for breaches. Program source code, in contrast, contains instructions for a computer.

Continuing professional development helps a member keep knowledge and skills current. Technical information and professional contacts help a developer recognise limits and obtain advice. Ethical guidance helps them explain why hiding a known fault conflicts with professional responsibilities. State how a benefit helps the person’s work instead of listing a benefit without a reason.

Membership can support professional recognition and public confidence, but it does not certify that every member’s decision is ethical. The member still chooses how to act. The assistant still needs appropriate design, testing and review; a membership logo is not evidence that it reads every page correctly.

learningCycle.observe: Compare three kinds of help: a written conduct standard, a training event and advice from an experienced professional. Identify which helps establish expected behaviour, which develops competence and which helps someone respond to a difficult situation.
learningCycle.question: Where can a new developer find recognised standards when an employer asks them to hide a fault?

steps.title: Identify the two professional bodies
steps.body: BCS is the British Computer Society. IEEE is the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. They are professional organisations that support standards and professional practice. They are different from a software supplier, an employee’s manager or the team testing a particular product.

steps.title: Explain what a code of conduct does
steps.body: A professional code states the behaviour and standards expected of members. It gives professionals and the public a reference against which conduct can be judged. Associated conduct procedures provide accountability and consequences for breaches. Program source code, in contrast, contains instructions for a computer.

steps.title: Explain why membership helps a practitioner
steps.body: Continuing professional development helps a member keep knowledge and skills current. Technical information and professional contacts help a developer recognise limits and obtain advice. Ethical guidance helps them explain why hiding a known fault conflicts with professional responsibilities. State how a benefit helps the person’s work instead of listing a benefit without a reason.

steps.title: Keep support separate from proof
steps.body: Membership can support professional recognition and public confidence, but it does not certify that every member’s decision is ethical. The member still chooses how to act. The assistant still needs appropriate design, testing and review; a membership logo is not evidence that it reads every page correctly.

worked.title: Use membership when the work becomes unfamiliar
worked.setup: A new programmer is asked to approve a speech feature in a language they do not understand and to sign an inaccurate test report.

steps.title: Connect learning and advice to competence
steps.body: Training and technical contacts can help the programmer understand the feature and find a suitably qualified reviewer. The programmer should still disclose their present lack of expertise.

steps.title: Connect the code to the conduct problem
steps.body: The programmer can refer to the expected honesty and public-interest standards when explaining why the actual test results must be reported. Guidance supports that response; it does not make the inaccurate report acceptable or transfer responsibility to the body.

worked.conclusion: A code states expected conduct. Membership provides ways to maintain competence and obtain professional support.

check.prompt: Give one reason to join a professional body and one purpose of its code. Explain why neither guarantees that the reading assistant is safe.
check.answer: Membership can provide training that keeps the programmer’s skills current. The code states expected professional behaviour and supports accountability for breaches. The programmer may still make poor decisions, and the product’s behaviour must be established through relevant evidence and testing.

learningCycle.takeaway: Know BCS and IEEE, distinguish a code’s purpose from membership benefits, and explain each benefit in context.
learningCycle.bridge: With the duties established, we can compare the effects of different actions on specific people.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Identify who is affected and what they need

leadVisual.title: Identify who is affected and what they need

coreExplanation: A stakeholder is a person or group affected by a decision or with an interest in it. Here the decision is whether to disclose or conceal a known limitation and whether to credit the person who found it. Starting with the actual decision prevents a vague list of people with no explained connection.

Fair treatment, recognising contributions, constructive criticism and helping colleagues develop are professional responsibilities. Acknowledge who found the fault. Discuss the test evidence and suggest specific improvements to the work. A personal attack or removing deserved credit can discourage people from raising future concerns.

Students need realistic claims and reliable information about the tool’s limits. Their safety, privacy and fair treatment matter even when they did not purchase the product. A parent can also be a stakeholder because a decision affects their child, although the parent never operates the assistant.

The school needs competent advice to decide how to spend money, support students and manage the release. Reporting a limitation lets it plan a correction or alternative. A deadline matters to the school, but it does not remove responsibilities towards colleagues or the public.

learningCycle.observe: A colleague discovers that the tool misreads small print. The project leader proposes removing the failed result and the colleague’s name from the report. List the separate effects on the colleague, students and the school before deciding what should happen.
learningCycle.question: Who is affected when a colleague finds a fault in the reading assistant?

steps.title: Name the decision before naming people
steps.body: A stakeholder is a person or group affected by a decision or with an interest in it. Here the decision is whether to disclose or conceal a known limitation and whether to credit the person who found it. Starting with the actual decision prevents a vague list of people with no explained connection.

steps.title: Include responsibilities towards colleagues
steps.body: Fair treatment, recognising contributions, constructive criticism and helping colleagues develop are professional responsibilities. Acknowledge who found the fault. Discuss the test evidence and suggest specific improvements to the work. A personal attack or removing deserved credit can discourage people from raising future concerns.

steps.title: Include users and the wider public
steps.body: Students need realistic claims and reliable information about the tool’s limits. Their safety, privacy and fair treatment matter even when they did not purchase the product. A parent can also be a stakeholder because a decision affects their child, although the parent never operates the assistant.

steps.title: Include the client or employer without ignoring other duties
steps.body: The school needs competent advice to decide how to spend money, support students and manage the release. Reporting a limitation lets it plan a correction or alternative. A deadline matters to the school, but it does not remove responsibilities towards colleagues or the public.

steps.title: Develop the colleague point

check.prompt: The colleague never uses the finished assistant. Does that remove them from the stakeholder analysis? Give one responsibility towards them.

steps.body: The programmer should be honest about the small-print limitation so that students and teachers do not trust the assistant for a reading it has not reliably produced. This addresses the people using or depending on the output.

workedExample.conclusion: An explained responsibility identifies an action, its recipient and why the action matters.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace the consequences of two actions

leadVisual.title: Trace the consequences of two actions

coreExplanation: A consequence explains how an action changes what happens to someone. Reporting the steps allows the route label to be corrected or withdrawn; a wheelchair user can then avoid an unsuitable route. The phrase “good reputation” skips this mechanism. Explain why honest information provides a better basis for trust.

Investigating and correcting the route may delay launch and require staff time. An ethical response can therefore impose an immediate cost. That cost belongs in the comparison, together with the benefit of avoiding a foreseeable misleading claim.

Concealment may allow the operator to meet the launch date. A traveller may then reach steps, need assistance or be unable to complete the journey. Complaints and loss of confidence may follow if users learn that the fault was known. These are plausible consequences supported by the situation, not guaranteed outcomes for every journey.

Do not make the error disappear in one branch unless the chosen action corrects it. Do not assume a delay automatically removes all future risk. Compare actions using the evidence supplied and distinguish immediate effects from later possibilities.

learningCycle.observe: Move to an independent example: a route labelled wheelchair-accessible includes steps. The developer knows this before launch. Compare disclosing and correcting the label with concealing the fault and publishing it unchanged. Keep the original fault the same in both branches.

worked.setup: The school can delay a small-print feature and supply a checked transcript, or advertise the current feature as fully reliable despite known failures.

steps.title: Explain the responsible branch
steps.body: Disclosing the limitation and keeping a checked transcript takes preparation time. Students retain a usable source, and teachers can avoid relying on the uncertain output.

steps.title: Explain the concealment branch
steps.body: Claiming complete reliability avoids the immediate correction work but can cause students to learn or act on incorrect text. The school may later have to correct materials and rebuild confidence in its claims.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose an action and test it against changed conditions

coreExplanation: Begin with the actual aim: making the current text accessible. Establish what information the function requires and what is known about its use. “It may be useful one day” is too vague to explain why identifiable images must be retained indefinitely.

A less intrusive option must still meet the stated purpose. If the assistant can read a page without retaining a permanent identifiable copy, that offers the immediate benefit with less stored personal information. If a separate improvement study needs examples, assess that purpose and its conditions explicitly instead of treating all future use as already justified.

Restricting access reduces who can view stored images. A retention limit reduces how much old information remains available. Removing unnecessary identifiers can reduce exposure, but does not automatically make every image anonymous. Checking and correcting an inaccurate output addresses a different risk. Explain the mechanism of each safeguard.

Proportionality means matching the action to the need. State who should do what, why the action fits the evidence and what uncertainty remains. A reasonable conclusion can be to proceed under specific controls, run a limited trial, obtain further evidence or reject the proposed use.

worked.title: Change the purpose: attendance or an emergency?
worked.setup: A college proposes tracking students’ phones all day and night to confirm arrival at lessons. Later, one student becomes separated from a supervised outdoor trip.

steps.title: Decide for ordinary attendance
steps.body: A classroom check-in can meet the attendance purpose without retaining an off-site movement history. Use that narrower method, restrict access and provide a correction route for failed check-ins.

steps.title: Reconsider for the missing student
steps.body: A classroom check-in cannot locate the missing student. A suitable available location service may now meet an urgent safety purpose within the trip’s authorised arrangements. Limit access to the responsible search team and check whether the location is current.

steps.title: Limit the changed decision
steps.body: End the emergency collection when it is no longer needed and handle remaining records according to the justified follow-up purpose. The emergency does not establish a reason for permanent tracking of everyone.

worked.conclusion: The justified action can change when the purpose and evidence change. The duty to explain necessity, effects and limits remains.

check.prompt: A proposal adds “human review” to the assistant’s output. What must you establish before treating this as an effective safeguard?

learningCycle.takeaway: Justify the action from its purpose, evidence, affected people, realistic alternatives and workable controls.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate owning software rights from using a copy

leadVisual.title: Separate owning software rights from using a copy

coreExplanation: Software requires skill, time and investment to create, while finished copies can be reproduced cheaply. Copyright legislation gives a basis for controlling restricted copying and distribution and for acting against unauthorised use of protected work. This supports creators in deciding the terms on which their work is made available.

The copyright holder controls relevant rights in the protected software expression. A licence grants permission to perform specified acts under stated conditions. Buying a copy normally grants the licensed use; it does not automatically transfer ownership of the copyright or every right to modify and distribute the program.

Running a program, modifying its source and redistributing copies are different activities. A licence can permit one and restrict another. For the school, permission to run an assistant on one device does not answer whether a modified version may be supplied to ten other schools.

A copyright holder can grant broad permissions while requiring notices to be retained. Publishing source therefore does not automatically remove copyright. Protection concerns the program’s expression; do not treat it as ownership of every general idea that another programmer might implement independently.

learningCycle.observe: The programmer has spent months writing the assistant. Copying the completed files takes seconds. Consider who controls the work and what a school actually receives when it downloads or buys a copy.
learningCycle.question: If the school buys one copy, can it automatically change the code and send copies to every partner school?

worked.title: Read a short set of offered terms
worked.setup: A fictional licence permits use on two school computers and redistribution of unchanged copies if the copyright notice remains. It does not grant permission to modify the source.

steps.title: Separate the acts
steps.body: Running on two computers is within the stated permission. Redistributing an unchanged copy must retain the notice. Modifying the source requires additional permission under this offer.

steps.title: Explain what stays with the owner
steps.body: The recipient has the stated permissions, while the rights holder retains copyright. The school cannot remove the notice merely because it paid for a copy or is allowed to share it.

worked.conclusion: A licence states permitted acts and conditions; receiving a copy does not automatically transfer copyright.

check.prompt: A programmer allows anyone to share unchanged copies while retaining a copyright notice. Is that permission inconsistent with copyright protection?

learningCycle.takeaway: Explain why creators need protection, then check which acts the licence permits.
learningCycle.bridge: Some licences grant broad user freedoms, including studying, changing and sharing software.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Understand what “free” means in free software

leadVisual.title: Understand what “free” means in free software

coreExplanation: The Free Software Foundation, or FSF, promotes software freedom. In its approach, “free” concerns what users are permitted to do, not necessarily whether they pay for a copy. FSF is an organisation; an individual software licence supplies the actual terms.

The school can run the program for any purpose. It can study how the program works and change it to meet its needs. It can redistribute copies to others. It can distribute modified versions so others benefit from the changes. Study and modification require access to the source.

A downloadable executable lets users run a program, but does not by itself provide its human-readable source. The school needs both source access and the relevant permission to make an authorised source change. Possessing one without the other does not meet that requirement.

A supplier can charge for distribution, maintenance or support while preserving software freedoms. Conversely, a no-charge download may restrict modification or redistribution. Users must still follow the licence’s conditions, such as retaining notices; free software is compatible with continuing obligations.

learningCycle.observe: Offer A costs nothing but forbids source modification. Offer B charges for a copy and support while allowing users to run, study, change and share it under its terms. Decide which information concerns price and which concerns freedom.
learningCycle.question: Can software cost money and still be free software?

knowledgeUnits.heading: Check permissions as well as visible source

leadVisual.title: Check permissions as well as visible source

coreExplanation: The Open Source Initiative, or OSI, maintains the Open Source Definition and approves licences that meet it. Open-source software makes source available under terms that provide the required permissions, including modification and redistribution. The OSI is an organisation, not the name of one universal licence.

A source-visible product may allow inspection while forbidding changes or sharing. Inspection helps someone understand the code, but those restrictions do not provide the necessary open-source freedoms. Read the distribution terms as well as checking whether a source download exists.

If an offer permits modification for school use but prohibits all business use, it restricts a field of endeavour and does not meet open-source criteria. Conditions such as preserving copyright notices are different: a licence can impose such conditions while allowing the required activities.

Many licences satisfy both free-software and open-source definitions. The FSF emphasises users’ freedoms; the OSI maintains open-source criteria and a licence approval process. These are overlapping approaches with distinct organisations. For a concrete choice, identify the permissions the user needs and check the actual licence.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate a trial, a price and a business model

leadVisual.title: Separate a trial, a price and a business model

coreExplanation: Shareware lets a user evaluate software before paying for continued or complete use. An offer may limit time, features or other uses. Thirty days is the condition in this example, not a universal rule. Users benefit by checking suitability before purchase; developers can use trial feedback to improve the software and may gain users through recommendations.

The trial supplies evidence of suitability under the tested conditions. It does not authorise unlimited later use. Before the permitted evaluation ends, obtain appropriate rights for the planned use or stop using the restricted offer. Check whether work can be exported and whether the trial includes the relevant permissions.

Commercial software is developed or distributed as a business activity. A business may earn money from copies, subscriptions, maintenance or support, including services for open-source software. Proprietary software restricts users’ freedoms, commonly limiting modification or redistribution. A no-charge proprietary product is possible, as is a paid open-source product.

Charging for software can provide income to fund development. Users can benefit from support that helps resolve difficulties, and commercial products are often tested before distribution. These describe possible or usual benefits, not guarantees: check the offered support and testing evidence. The business model alone does not prove that a particular product is reliable.

Check how many users or devices are covered, how long permission lasts and which acts are allowed. Then check the service agreement. A promised response within four hours does not necessarily mean a completed repair within four hours. Paying for a copy does not by itself establish either source access or a particular quality of support.

leadVisual.title: Match the complete plan to the offered terms

coreExplanation: The school must run the assistant, inspect and modify its source, and distribute modified copies. Zero licence fees are a financial constraint. Available maintenance staff are a practical resource. Separate these from a preference such as liking a familiar product name.

An option that fails a mandatory permission is unsuitable for the stated plan even if it is cheap. Modification requires source access and permission. Distribution to partners is a further act that needs permission. A licence covering one school cannot be silently treated as covering ten.

A school needing an unmodified tool and a guaranteed support response may favour a different offer from one needing extensive source adaptation. Justify the choice using the actual terms. Open-source permissions do not automatically supply a support service, and a support contract does not automatically supply modification rights.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Recognise the intelligent task

leadVisual.title: Recognise the intelligent task

coreExplanation: Artificial intelligence enables computers to perform tasks associated with human intelligence, such as recognising patterns, interpreting language, reasoning and predicting likely events. In the assistant, interpreting an image as words is the relevant task. Simply storing a typed string or playing an audio file does not by itself demonstrate AI.

A rule-based AI system applies expert-written knowledge to supplied facts to infer a conclusion. A data-driven approach learns patterns from examples. These are ways to explain where the system’s knowledge comes from; not every AI application learns from examples or changes its knowledge while being used.

In a data-driven pump-monitoring example, past vibration and temperature readings are paired with known fault outcomes. A learning procedure adjusts a model to patterns in those examples. Separate known-outcome cases are then used to check its predictions. Checking only the examples used for learning would give insufficient evidence about new cases.

Inference means using the resulting model or knowledge to produce a conclusion from supplied input. A new pump reading can produce a predicted fault risk without updating the model. The future outcome is not known merely because past examples had known outcomes. A prediction can be wrong and should be interpreted with the relevant evidence.
