knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow a page from pixels to spoken words

leadVisual.title: Follow a page from pixels to spoken words

coreExplanation: The camera supplies pixel data representing the printed sign. At this point the program has an image of the word; it does not yet have a recognised character sequence. Lighting, focus and framing can affect the quality of the input.

Optical character recognition, or OCR, locates character patterns and interprets them as text. Here it should produce the characters in “Sortie”. Recognising a character is different from translating its meaning into another language.

Natural language processing uses information about words, phrases and context to interpret the recognised sequence. Translation produces corresponding text in the chosen language. In this sign context, the French text “Sortie” becomes the English text “Exit”. These are distinct conceptual tasks even if one product performs them together.

Text-to-speech generates an audio waveform representing the translated words. The speaker turns the output signal into sound, so the student hears “Exit”. Speech-to-text works in the reverse direction, recognising words from audio; it is not the final conversion used here.

If a blurred letter becomes the wrong recognised word, later translation and clear speech can carry that error forward. Retaking the image or verifying the recognised text addresses the early problem. Increasing volume cannot repair a wrong word. If translated text is already correct but no audio is heard, investigate the later speech and output stages.

learningCycle.observe: A camera photographs a clear sign reading “Sortie”, and the user selects English output. Follow the information after each stage. Predict which stage first produces text and which later stage produces an audio waveform.
learningCycle.question: Which transformations are needed before the student can hear a French sign in English?

prerequisite.title: Keep representations distinct
prerequisite.body: Pixels describe the image. Recognised characters represent text. An audio waveform represents sound. A camera supplies an image; a speaker produces sound. A clear sound does not tell us whether the earlier text was correct.

worked.title: Trace the expected output and a changed condition
worked.setup: The clear sign reads “Sortie”. The target is English. In a second attempt, the photograph is too blurred for a checked recognition.

steps.title: State each intermediate representation
steps.body: Camera: pixels showing the sign. OCR: text “Sortie”. Language processing and translation: interpreted French sign text and English text “Exit”. Text-to-speech: an audio waveform. Speaker: audible English speech.

steps.title: Locate the uncertainty in the second attempt
steps.body: The blurred image makes character recognition uncertain before translation. Stop treating the output as a checked reading. Retake the photograph or compare the recognised text with a reliable reading of the sign.

steps.title: Explain the consequence
steps.body: A polished voice can speak an incorrect translation derived from incorrect text. The quality of the final sound therefore cannot establish that all earlier transformations were accurate.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Transfer the input-to-use method

leadVisual.title: Transfer the input-to-use method

coreExplanation: Name the input representation, the task performed, the output and how someone uses it. “AI is used in healthcare” names a sector but does not explain an application. A precise description might explain that a model recognises suspicious patterns in a medical image and flags an area for a clinician to inspect.

A maintenance model may estimate that a pump is likely to fail. The technician then inspects it and schedules work. The prediction is information supplied to a decision; the inspection is a subsequent action. Their separation matters when deciding who checks an uncertain result.

A fraud system can compare a new payment with transaction patterns and flag unusual activity for investigation. A recommendation system ranks items using preferences and item features. An autonomous vehicle interprets sensor data about roads and obstacles to support control decisions. The input and consequence differ, even though each uses recognition or inference.

A false pump alert can cause an unnecessary inspection; a missed fault can allow a breakdown. A mistaken fraud flag can delay a legitimate payment. These are different consequences of particular outputs. State the error, affected person and result rather than saying only that AI sometimes fails.

learningCycle.observe: A pump produces a vibration reading that differs from its usual pattern. The model raises a fault-risk alert, and a technician decides whether to inspect it. Locate the model’s output and the separate action taken using that output.

worked.title: A recycling sorter makes a wrong classification
worked.setup: A camera photographs an item on a sorting belt. A model classifies its material, and a controller directs it to a bin.

steps.title: Describe the recognition
steps.body: The image is the input. The model interprets visual patterns to infer a material category. The resulting category is used by the controller to choose a bin.

steps.title: Explain the error’s consequence
steps.body: If a non-recyclable item is classified as recyclable, the controller may place it into a recyclable-material stream and contaminate that stream. The physical movement alone does not establish AI; the image interpretation is the relevant task.

worked.conclusion: A useful application explanation names both the inference and the decision that uses it.

check.prompt: A fraud model flags a payment. Explain why “the customer committed fraud” is a stronger claim than the evidence supports.
check.answer: The flag indicates a pattern associated with risk, not proof of wrongdoing. The payment needs investigation using relevant evidence. A false flag can affect a legitimate customer, so the response should account for that possibility.

learningCycle.takeaway: Describe the AI task precisely, then explain how its output is used and what an error would change.
learningCycle.bridge: The reading assistant’s value depends on which people it helps and whether its errors affect them equally.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Who gains access, and who still faces a barrier?

leadVisual.title: Who gains access, and who still faces a barrier?

coreExplanation: Social effects concern participation, access and treatment. A visually impaired reader can hear information they cannot easily see. A reader who does not understand the printed language can hear a translation in a language they understand. These are distinct benefits because they remove different barriers.

In this invented caption test, accent A has 90 correct captions out of 90 and accent B has 5 out of 10. Overall, 95 out of 100 are correct, or 95%. For B, however, only 50% are correct. The larger group dominates the overall result.

Users relying on captions for group B receive less reliable access in this test. Different training examples, audio quality or operating conditions might contribute, but these counts alone do not prove the cause. Investigate representative cases and the conditions before claiming why the difference occurred.

A correction route helps only if someone can identify the error and supply accurate text in time. Human reviewers need relevant skills, evidence and authority to act. Privacy is a separate concern: recordings and photographed pages can reveal personal information, so limit unnecessary collection and retention and restrict access.

A short practice caption and an emergency instruction have different consequences if wrong. Compare performance and correction arrangements with the actual users and task. A high average alone cannot justify removing an existing accessible, checked resource.

A camera-based system might analyse classroom behaviour to identify students who need extra support. This could improve access to help. Constant observation or sharing recorded behaviour may also intrude on privacy and cause stress. Explain the affected people and the mechanism of the effect; calling the system simply “good” or “unethical” leaves the impact unexplained.

worked.setup: The school’s assistant photographs a notice in French, translates it into English and reads it aloud.

steps.title: Explain the sight-related benefit
steps.body: A visually impaired student can hear the notice instead of depending on being able to read its small print. The spoken result provides another route to the information.

steps.title: Explain the language-related benefit
steps.body: A student who understands English but not French can receive the meaning in a language they know. This is a different barrier from the ability to see the print.

steps.title: State the condition for access
steps.body: Both benefits depend on sufficiently accurate reading and translation and a usable correction alternative. Incorrect output can leave the student with confidently delivered but misleading information.

worked.conclusion: Explain who is helped, what barrier is reduced and what conditions affect that benefit.

learningCycle.bridge: Access matters, but a deployment also needs resources and staff time. Compare its economic effects next.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare useful work with the complete cost

leadVisual.title: Compare useful work with the complete cost

coreExplanation: Productivity concerns output from resources such as staff time. Automated transcription may let a teacher prepare more accessible material in the same time. In a factory, a useful prediction may avoid an unplanned shutdown. Explain the task that changes and the resulting saving instead of claiming that all AI reduces costs.

Costs can include purchase or development, integration, data preparation, subscriptions, computing, maintenance, staff training and review. Incorrect output can cause rework or other losses. The same activity and time period must be compared with the previous method.

These are invented teaching values in currency units. The previous method costs 1200 per month for the same work. The new service costs 500, review costs 400, maintenance costs 100 and rework costs 100. The recurring saving is 1200 − 500 − 400 − 100 − 100 = 100. If setup costs another 600, the first-month change is 100 − 600 = −500: a net additional cost of 500.

Putting a value on released staff time does not necessarily reduce the salary bill. Staff may use that time for other work. Automation can reduce some tasks while creating demand for oversight, maintenance or specialist support. Some people may need retraining or lose work, even when the organisation as a whole becomes more productive.

learningCycle.observe: The school expects fewer hours of routine transcription. It also needs a service subscription, someone to check output, repairs to incorrect material and an initial setup. Separate recurring changes from the one-off setup before comparing totals.
learningCycle.question: If the assistant saves preparation time, does it necessarily save money?

In a factory, a useful prediction may avoid an unplanned shutdown. Explain the task that changes and the resulting saving instead of claiming that all AI reduces costs.

steps.title: Include the added work and expenditure
steps.body: Costs can include purchase or development, integration, data preparation, subscriptions, computing, maintenance, staff training and review. Incorrect output can cause rework or other losses. The same activity and time period must be compared with the previous method.

steps.title: Work through a stated monthly example
steps.body: These are invented teaching values in currency units. The previous method costs 1200 per month for the same work. The new service costs 500, review costs 400, maintenance costs 100 and rework costs 100. The recurring saving is 1200 − 500 − 400 − 100 − 100 = 100. If setup costs another 600, the first-month change is 100 − 600 = −500: a net additional cost of 500.

steps.title: Distinguish saved time from cash and employment
steps.body: Putting a value on released staff time does not necessarily reduce the salary bill. Staff may use that time for other work. Automation can reduce some tasks while creating demand for oversight, maintenance or specialist support. Some people may need retraining or lose work, even when the organisation as a whole becomes more productive.

worked.title: Change the review and correction workload
worked.setup: Use the monthly teaching example: the previous method costs 1200, while the AI-assisted method has service 500, review 400, maintenance 100 and rework 100. Setup is a separate one-off cost of 600.

steps.title: Establish the recurring comparison
steps.body: The recurring total is 500 + 400 + 100 + 100 = 1100. Compared with 1200 for the previous method, the recurring net saving is 100 under these assumptions. Over six months, 600 of operating savings offsets the 600 setup cost; other unchanged costs are excluded equally.

steps.title: Change the workload
steps.body: If review rises to 700 and rework rises to 250 each month, the recurring total becomes 500 + 700 + 100 + 250 = 1550. That is 350 more per month than the previous method, before setup. Increased checking and correction can reverse the economic conclusion.

steps.title: Limit a real-world financial claim
steps.body: The example treats the figures as costs. In a real proposal, establish whether claimed avoided work actually reduces expenditure or merely releases staff time for other useful tasks. Include setup when evaluating the initial period.

worked.conclusion: A credible economic comparison includes recurring costs, initial costs, errors and what actually happens to released staff time.

check.prompt: The assistant saves a teacher four hours of transcription each week. Does this prove the school spends less on salaries or that a job is lost?
check.answer: No. The teacher may use the time for other work and receive the same salary. Compare actual expenditure and the use of released time with the new system and review costs. Fewer hours on one task do not alone establish lower total spending or fewer jobs.

learningCycle.takeaway: Explain productivity through the changed task, then compare all relevant costs and effects on work.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare resource savings with the system’s footprint

leadVisual.title: Compare resource savings with the system’s footprint

coreExplanation: AI-assisted irrigation can avoid unnecessary watering and pumping. Route planning may reduce vehicle travel, and predictive maintenance may extend equipment life. Each claimed environmental benefit needs a mechanism and a comparison with the previous or simpler method serving the same need.

Learning and inference use computing equipment and electricity. Cooling can use energy and water. Manufacturing, replacing and disposing of sensors and computing hardware use materials and create environmental impacts. The amount depends on the particular system and its lifetime.

Under comparable monthly watering conditions, the baseline is 1000 kWh. With pumping at 850 kWh and added AI plus cooling at 80 kWh, the new total is 930 kWh and the operating saving is 70 kWh. If the added use rises to 180 kWh, the total is 1030 kWh: 30 kWh more than the baseline.

These invented values establish operating-electricity differences within the stated boundary. They do not measure manufacturing impacts, water use, disposal or emissions per kWh. Do not subtract litres of water from kWh of electricity. A broader environmental judgement needs evidence about each relevant measure and the system lifetime.

The activity below compares 12 months and adds an illustrative 1200 kWh for making the new hardware, allocated evenly across its assumed lifetime. A 60-month lifetime allocates 1200 × 12 / 60 = 240 kWh to the comparison. For case A, 12 × 930 + 240 = 11400 kWh, compared with the baseline 12000. If the lifetime is only 12 months, all 1200 kWh is allocated and the total becomes 12360. This is an accounting assumption for comparison; manufacturing electricity is used when the hardware is made.

steps.title: Locate the incomplete boundary
steps.body: The claim counts only pumping. The added system consumes 180 kWh, so the combined operating total is 850 + 180 = 1030 kWh.

steps.title: State the supported conclusion
steps.body: Operating electricity increases by 30 kWh compared with the stated baseline. Other benefits, such as water savings, might still exist, but these values do not quantify them or establish an overall environmental improvement.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Decide how the school should use the assistant

leadVisual.title: Decide how the school should use the assistant

coreExplanation: Adding an optional checked reading aid is different from replacing the only accessible resource. Identify the input, AI task, output and intended use, then state what changes for the users. The consequences of an error depend on that use.

Social evidence concerns access, unequal errors and privacy. Economic evidence concerns useful time released, integration, operation, review and correction costs. Environmental evidence concerns the additional equipment and resource use compared with the previous method. Include relevant effects rather than inserting an unrelated stock advantage from another application.

A reviewer needs access to a reliable original, sufficient language knowledge, time and authority to correct the output. An inaccessible complaints form is not an effective correction route. Check samples beyond the cases already flagged as uncertain, because confidently wrong outputs may otherwise be missed.

The school could retain checked transcripts while running a limited assisted pilot. It should define which uses are permitted, who checks output, what information is retained and how errors are reported. Evidence from representative users, correction capacity and practical costs can then support expansion, revision or stopping the pilot.

A recommendation should identify remaining uncertainty and the evidence that would resolve it. If the assistant works well for all intended groups and corrections are timely within available resources, a wider controlled deployment may become justified. If it repeatedly leaves some students without reliable access, the school should change the arrangement rather than rely on an average score.

Students using connected tools also make decisions that affect others. Respect other people’s privacy, avoid bullying through the network and acknowledge work created by someone else. Do not present another person’s work as your own. Each action connects to a person’s information, wellbeing or contribution, rather than simply repeating that the network should be used responsibly.

An AI tutor can offer additional explanations and practice at a student’s own pace, which may build confidence. Reliance on supplied answers can reduce the student’s own reasoning practice, while replacing discussion with individual screen use may reduce collaboration and social contact. Access can also be unequal if some students lack suitable equipment. These are possible effects of how the tool is used, not inevitable outcomes for every student.

worked.setup: Use the invented caption evidence: group A has 90/90 correct results and group B has 5/10. Checked transcripts exist. The proposed reviewer cannot reliably understand group B’s speech.

steps.title: Identify the benefit and the specific risk
steps.body: Captions could appear faster, but B currently receives a correct caption in only half of its tested cases. Removing checked transcripts would remove a working alternative for those users.

steps.title: Test the proposed safeguard
steps.body: The named reviewer cannot reliably compare B’s speech with the generated text. Their presence therefore does not establish an effective correction process for the observed problem.

steps.title: Reach a supported conclusion
steps.body: Retain checked transcripts and use a limited assisted pilot while arranging competent correction and representative testing. Do not replace the checked material solely because the overall result is 95%.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why does the library need shared records?

leadVisual.title: Why does the library need shared records?

coreExplanation: These two records describe different activities but repeat the same member contact detail. The phone number belongs to the member, so changing it should not require finding every past loan and every separate application copy.

Data redundancy is unnecessary repeated storage of the same fact. It uses storage and creates extra update work. Data inconsistency occurs when copies that should agree contain different values. Repetition creates the opportunity for this disagreement; two identical copies have redundancy even before they disagree.

A relational database organises data into related tables. Store Asha’s current phone once in Member. Each Loan stores MemberID 1 to identify whose borrowing event it records. When an application needs the phone, it retrieves the shared Member value. Repeated identifiers preserve links; they do not duplicate the phone itself.

Separate application files may have different formats and duplicated validation or access-control code. A DBMS provides shared definitions, query facilities and centrally enforced rules. Related data can be retrieved consistently through those facilities. These benefits depend on a suitable design: merely calling a collection of files a database does not remove bad duplication.

learningCycle.observe: Imagine a loans file and an overdue-notices file. Both store Asha’s name and contact number beside each borrowing event. The loans desk changes its copy, but the notices desk uses yesterday’s number. Predict what happens when the next reminder is sent.

When an application needs the phone, it retrieves the shared Member value. Repeated identifiers preserve links; they do not duplicate the phone itself.

worked.setup: Initially both files store 020 1111. Asha’s correct new number is 020 2222.

steps.title: Trace the failed update

learningCycle.takeaway: Store shared facts with the object they describe and use identifiers to connect related records.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read a table as facts about things and events

leadVisual.title: Read a table as facts about things and events

coreExplanation: An entity is a type of thing or concept about which the organisation stores data. Member represents people registered with the library. Loan represents borrowing events. An event can be an entity even though it is not a physical object.

A table stores records about occurrences of its entity. A record, also called a tuple, is one row: (1, Asha) describes a particular member. A field or attribute is a named property represented by a column. MemberName is the attribute; Asha is a value in that field.

Rows 201 and 202 are two different loans by member 1. They share a member reference, but remain different borrowing events. Giving each loan a row lets the library retain both events instead of overwriting the earlier one.

Later the catalogue will use Book for a title and Copy for a physical item with its own barcode. Two physical copies can have the same title while only one is currently borrowed. Introduce those extra tables when the business question needs them; our first query tables deliberately show only Member and Loan.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose a key that really identifies one record

leadVisual.title: Choose a key that really identifies one record

coreExplanation: A name appearing once today is not guaranteed unique. A candidate key is a minimal field or combination of fields that uniquely identifies a record under the business rules. Both MemberID and SchoolEmail are candidate keys under the stated guarantees.

MemberID plus MemberName is unique when MemberID is unique, but it is not minimal: remove MemberName and identification still works. Therefore that unnecessary combination is not a candidate key. Minimal means no component can be removed while preserving the uniqueness guarantee.

Select one candidate key as the primary key. Choosing MemberID gives a short identifier that need not change when a name changes. Primary-key values must be unique and must not be null. Other candidate keys remain possible identifiers; the choice of primary key does not erase them.

A secondary key is an additional retrieval key, such as TutorGroup when finding everyone in 8A. It need not identify only one record. Secondary key does not mean the second candidate key or an unchosen alternative primary key.

coreExplanation: Every non-null foreign-key value must match an existing value of its referenced key. Loan.MemberID 9 would point nowhere, so the declared foreign-key constraint rejects it. Having a new LoanID does not repair that missing member.

Other designs can explicitly define a referential action, such as a coordinated cascade. Such behaviour must be declared; it is not an automatic promise that every DBMS deletes all related data.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Find records through an index

leadVisual.title: Find records through an index

coreExplanation: A scan examines rows and checks the condition. If the question requests every member named Asha, finding one Asha does not justify stopping because another may exist. A scan may be appropriate for a small table or a request matching much of the table.

An index associates indexed values with record locations or suitable record references. A name lookup can identify members 1 and 5 as matches for Asha, then retrieve their requested fields from the table. The displayed IDs stand for record references in this simplified model.

The index occupies additional storage. When member 5 changes name to Esha, update the table and move that reference from the Asha index entry to Esha. Inserts, deletes and changes to indexed values may add work.

An index can improve a suitable access path; it does not guarantee every query is faster. The activity counts illustrative inspections, not milliseconds or a benchmark of a real database. An index does not enforce the truth of a name or establish result ordering; use ORDER BY when order matters.

coreExplanation: These teaching rules apply throughout the example: each product appears at most once in an order; each order has one customer; each product has one current name and fixed current price; each customer has one stored name. Historical prices are not being recorded here.

First Normal Form requires atomic field values and no repeating groups. Atomic means a value is treated as one item for the application’s operations. The product list fails because its items and quantities must be queried separately. Product1, Product2 and Product3 columns also repeat the same group and impose an arbitrary item limit.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Move facts that depend on only part of a key

coreExplanation: X → Y means each permitted X value determines one Y value under the business rules. ProductID → ProductName and UnitPrice. OrderID → CustomerID and CustomerName. Only (OrderID, ProductID) determines the line’s Quantity. The arrow describes determination, not a processing step.

Second Normal Form requires 1NF and no non-key attribute depending on only part of a candidate key. In this example the candidate key is the pair. ProductName depends on ProductID alone, while customer facts depend on OrderID alone. These are partial dependencies.

Product stores P1 once as Pen with price 2 and P2 once as Pad with price 5. This avoids changing the same product price separately in several order rows. The fixed current-price rule is essential; a price agreed separately for each order line would belong to that line instead.

steps.body: Second Normal Form requires 1NF and no non-key attribute depending on only part of a candidate key. In this example the candidate key is the pair. ProductName depends on ProductID alone, while customer facts depend on OrderID alone. These are partial dependencies.

steps.title: Move product facts to Product
steps.body: Product stores P1 once as Pen with price 2 and P2 once as Pad with price 5. This avoids changing the same product price separately in several order rows. The fixed current-price rule is essential; a price agreed separately for each order line would belong to that line instead.

steps.title: Keep order facts and line facts separate
steps.body: SalesOrder at 2NF stores (501, C7, Amina) and (502, C7, Amina). OrderLine retains both identifiers and Quantity. Repeated foreign keys are required to reconnect the records.

worked.title: Change the price of P1
worked.setup: Before decomposition the two P1 lines each store price 2. The correct current price changes to 3.

steps.title: Show the original anomaly
steps.body: Changing only the order 501 copy leaves P1 priced at 3 and 2 simultaneously. Removing the last P2 order line would also remove the only stored Pad description. A product without an order has no suitable line key for insertion.

steps.title: Apply the 2NF design
steps.body: Update Product P1 once to price 3. OrderLine remains (501, P1, 3), (501, P2, 1), (502, P1, 2); its final values are quantities, not prices. A new product can now exist without an order.

worked.conclusion: Move each fact to its determinant; preserve the linking fields and the whole-key line fact.

check.prompt: Why does Quantity stay in OrderLine rather than Product or SalesOrder?
check.answer: P1 has different quantities in different orders, and order 501 has different quantities for its two products. Neither identifier alone determines Quantity. The complete (OrderID, ProductID) pair does under the stated rules.

learningCycle.takeaway: 2NF removes partial dependencies while keeping facts that depend on the complete composite key.
learningCycle.bridge: The 2NF order table still repeats the customer’s name. Follow the remaining dependency.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate a customer fact from an order fact

leadVisual.title: Separate a customer fact from an order fact

coreExplanation: OrderID determines CustomerID, and CustomerID determines CustomerName. Therefore OrderID → CustomerID → CustomerName is a transitive dependency through a non-key attribute. A single-field primary key does not rule out this problem.

Third Normal Form requires 2NF and, in these simple designs, no non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute. Move CustomerName to the table identified by CustomerID. The exact determinant is the reason for splitting, rather than a general desire for more small tables.
Customer contains (C7, Amina). SalesOrder retains OrderID and CustomerID, so orders 501 and 502 still identify their customer. Removing CustomerID from SalesOrder would lose that association.
SalesOrder has two rows: (501, C7) and (502, C7). A new customer can now be registered without an order. Deleting an order and its lines need not delete the customer’s independent record.

learningCycle.observe: The 2NF SalesOrder table contains (501, C7, Amina) and (502, C7, Amina). Each order has one customer, but the customer’s name is a fact about C7 rather than the order.

steps.title: Update the fact where it belongs
steps.body: Change only Customer C7 to Amina Patel. SalesOrder 501 and 502 keep CustomerID C7, while Product and OrderLine remain unchanged.

steps.title: Retrieve each order’s customer
steps.body: For order 501, read CustomerID C7, then the Customer name Amina Patel. Repeat for order 502 and reach the same updated record. Both retrievals agree without separate order-name updates.

worked.conclusion: The customer name is stored once, and both orders retain the reference needed to find it.

check.answer: No. ParcelID → DepotID → DepotName is a transitive dependency. Use Parcel(ParcelID PK, DepotID FK) and Depot(DepotID PK, DepotName), retaining DepotID to retrieve each parcel’s depot name.

learningCycle.takeaway: Remove transitive dependencies by storing the dependent fact with the entity that determines it.
learningCycle.bridge: A finished design must pass both a dependency check and a reconstruction check.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Prove that the new tables still tell the whole story

coreExplanation: First check atomic values and repeating groups. Then identify all stated candidate keys and test partial dependencies. Customer owns CustomerName; SalesOrder connects an order to its customer; Product owns ProductName and UnitPrice under the fixed-price rule; OrderLine owns Quantity for each order-product pair. Every original attribute has a defined home.

Different prices in a small sample do not prove price uniquely identifies products.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Turn the library model into a logical schema

leadVisual.title: Turn the library model into a logical schema

coreExplanation: Data modelling identifies entities, attributes and relationships from requirements. A modelling tool can draw Member and Loan, mark their keys and record a one-to-many association. It helps document and revise the design, but cannot decide whether the real library permits several responsible members per loan.

The logical schema defines tables, attributes, types, keys, relationships and other constraints. Here MemberID and LoanID are INTEGER fields, MemberName is limited to 40 characters, and Loan.MemberID must refer to Member. A schema describes the permitted structure even when the tables contain no records.

The schema permits Member (1, Asha, TRUE), but does not itself state that Asha is registered. Inserting Dara changes the contents while leaving the same table definition. Adding a new Email field changes the schema.

The logical schema does not tell a user which disk sector holds a loan. The DBMS manages storage and retrieval behind the table interface. A file move or different storage device need not change the meaning of MemberID or the application’s logical queries.

learningCycle.observe: The library’s rule says that every loan has one registered member. An ER diagram expresses the association. The software also needs exact field names, types and constraints. Compare these two descriptions of the same rule.
learningCycle.question: What must a developer specify before the database can accept its first loan?

steps.title: Revise the conceptual relationship

steps.body: Define the association’s fields, key and references, and decide how existing loans map to it. Merely drawing another line without changing the definitions does not implement the new rule.

check.prompt: Classify each change: add member Dara; add a Member.Email attribute; move the physical database files to another device.

learningCycle.takeaway: Separate the organisation’s model, the logical definitions and the records currently stored.
learningCycle.bridge: The DBMS records those definitions as metadata in its data dictionary.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read the data about the data

leadVisual.title: Read the data about the data

coreExplanation: A database management system is software that manages database definitions, storage, retrieval and controlled changes. It provides a shared way for applications and users to work with data. The database is the managed collection; the DBMS is the software managing it.

The data dictionary stores metadata: descriptions of tables, fields, data types, lengths, keys and constraints. MemberName has a declared maximum length of 40; MemberID is the primary key. These descriptions differ from records such as member 1 being named Asha.

A query requesting MembrName contains a field name absent from the schema. The DBMS cannot treat it as MemberName just because the intended spelling seems obvious. A declared length or key constraint also provides rules for proposed data changes.

The dictionary records definitions that tools and processing components can consult. A developer’s field inspector can show the same type and key information used to check requests. Central definitions reduce the need for each application to invent its own incompatible interpretation.

learningCycle.observe: Compare Asha’s actual record with the definition MemberName: VARCHAR(40). One tells us a fact about a member; the other tells the system what kind of field exists.

learningCycle.bridge: Developers use DBMS tools to turn these definitions into forms, queries and reports.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Build forms and reports from defined fields

leadVisual.title: Build forms and reports from defined fields

coreExplanation: A DBMS developer interface can provide table designers, SQL editors, query builders, form tools and report designers. A developer can specify a field type or key without entering application records at the same moment.

The member picker displays a readable name but supplies the selected MemberID. A checkbox supplies a Boolean Returned value. Clear field labels and choices help the librarian produce a valid request; they do not replace the database’s constraints.

A developer defines which fields and query a report uses and how the output is arranged. Later, running the report retrieves the current records. A well-designed report therefore changes when the underlying data changes, without rebuilding the report layout.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Check valid values before accepting a change

leadVisual.title: Check valid values before accepting a change

coreExplanation: Entity integrity includes unique, non-null primary keys. Referential integrity preserves valid links. Domain or validation rules restrict field values, such as a numeric non-negative Fee or the declared type and length of a name. These checks solve different problems.

A rule defined in the DBMS can apply to requests from forms, scripts and other authorised interfaces. A rejected change must leave the affected database state consistent; do not display success after only part of an intended operation was accepted.

A fee of 20 satisfies a non-negative numeric rule even if the librarian meant 2. Constraints check declared properties; they cannot independently know every real-world fact. Verification against the borrowing record is still needed.

worked.title: Compare two incorrect entries
worked.setup: The correct fee for a new loan is 2. One attempt enters −2 and another enters 20. All identifiers are otherwise valid.

steps.title: Apply the declared rule
steps.body: The DBMS rejects −2 because it is outside the allowed range. No new loan should be added by this attempt.

steps.title: Identify the undetectable copying error
steps.body: The value 20 passes the given type and range rules. Acceptance does not prove it matches the real charge. A source check or suitably justified additional rule is needed to detect this error.

worked.conclusion: State both what a constraint prevents and what it cannot establish.

check.prompt: Why is “the DBMS guarantees that all stored information is true” too strong?
check.answer: It enforces the constraints that have been defined. A plausible but incorrect name, fee or date may satisfy all of them. Validity under declared rules is different from agreement with the real event.

learningCycle.takeaway: Integrity rules enforce defined identities, references and permitted values across request routes.
learningCycle.bridge: A structurally valid request must also come from a user allowed to perform it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Decide who may perform each operation

leadVisual.title: Decide who may perform each operation

coreExplanation: Authentication establishes the account identity. Access rights specify which data and operations that account may use. A known account is not automatically allowed to read every field or perform every update.

Rights can be assigned to an individual or to a group. Adding a new librarian account to the Librarians group applies the configured shared rights and avoids repeating each grant manually. Removing an account from a group changes inherited rights; it does not change the data constraints.

Permissions may be restricted to particular tables, fields or operations. A pupil helper who checks a catalogue need not receive contact details or permission to delete members. A request may be denied even when its proposed values would be valid.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Recover a known consistent state

leadVisual.title: Recover a known consistent state

coreExplanation: A backup is a protected copy from which data can be restored. Schedule copies according to how much recent work the library can afford to lose. Keep recovery copies separate from the live system’s failure risk, restrict access and periodically test that restoration works.

Member and Loan must be backed up as a coherent database state. Copying Loan after a new member is referenced but Member before that member was added could create an inconsistent recovery set. Use the DBMS’s supported backup procedure.
Restoring the 18:00 backup restores the values saved at 18:00. Loan 203 is FALSE again, and loan 206 is absent. Those later changes are not recreated simply because they happened before the failure.

Check that required tables open, expected counts and values match the saved state, and references remain valid. Later committed changes can be recovered only when a suitable additional recovery source and procedure exist. A supported log may permit replay after the backup; it must actually be available.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow a request from SQL to its result

leadVisual.title: Follow a request from SQL to its result

coreExplanation: The query processor interprets SQL, checks its syntax and resolves referenced tables and fields using metadata. The DBMS also checks applicable permissions. A request containing Ffee instead of Fee cannot be evaluated as the intended field.

The processor plans how to carry out the query, considering available access paths such as scans and indexes. Different plans can produce the same logical result. An index is useful only when it suits the request and the data.

The DBMS carries out the chosen operations, tests conditions and returns the requested columns in the specified order. Here loans 202, 203 and 205 qualify. This SELECT does not remove non-matching stored loans.

Checking, planning and executing is a conceptual explanation of responsibilities. It is not a claim that every database performs all internal checks in one fixed sequence. A query builder helps construct a request; the processor executes it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate changing a structure from using its records

leadVisual.title: Separate changing a structure from using its records

coreExplanation: Data Definition Language creates or changes database structure. CREATE DATABASE establishes a named database; CREATE TABLE defines fields and constraints; ALTER TABLE changes an existing definition. Creating Loan does not itself record a borrowing event.

Data Manipulation Language works with records in a defined structure. SELECT retrieves information; INSERT INTO adds records; UPDATE changes field values; DELETE FROM removes records. Retrieval counts as DML in this syllabus even when no stored value changes.

Structured Query Language is the industry-standard language used to express both DDL and DML requests. SQL is the language, DDL and DML describe roles within it, and the DBMS is the software that processes the requests. They are not three competing database products.

“Change” alone is ambiguous. Changing the definition of DueDate is structural; changing loan 201’s current date is a record operation. A SELECT result looks like a table but does not define a new persistent table in these examples.

coreExplanation: SELECT and FROM are SQL keywords. Member and MemberName are identifiers naming a table and a field. In a condition such as MemberName = 'Asha', the quoted text is a literal value to compare with the field. MemberName and 'MemberName' therefore mean different things.

The condition Fee >= 3 includes 3, while Fee > 3 excludes it. AND requires both conditions; OR permits either. Do not paraphrase “at least” as “more than”. Explain what exact records satisfy a condition using the supplied data.

In CREATE TABLE Member (MemberID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, MemberName VARCHAR(40)); INTEGER is a data type, 40 is the permitted maximum text length, and PRIMARY KEY imposes unique non-null identity. This statement defines an empty structure; it does not create forty members.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose types that match the facts

leadVisual.title: Choose types that match the facts

coreExplanation: CHARACTER(n) stores fixed-length character data, such as a one-character initial. VARCHAR(n) stores variable-length text up to n characters, such as a name of up to 40 characters. A phone number is normally text even when its characters are digits, because leading zeroes and symbols matter and arithmetic is not its purpose.

BOOLEAN represents logical TRUE or FALSE. INTEGER stores whole numbers such as identifiers or counts. REAL stores numbers that may have fractional parts. Type choice defines what values and operations make sense; REAL may use approximate numeric representation, so it is not a promise of exact decimal arithmetic.

DATE represents a calendar date and TIME a time of day. They allow suitable validation and comparison instead of treating every input as arbitrary text. Quoted ISO-style values such as '2027-03-01' make the examples unambiguous.

Place the field definitions inside parentheses, separate them with commas and end the statement with a semicolon. This teaching Visit table includes all seven syllabus types and refers to an existing Member. The shorter Member and Loan tables remain the query fixtures. The next concept explains the key declarations line by line.

learningCycle.bridge: The table also needs explicit constraints that identify rows and preserve references.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Declare primary and foreign keys in SQL

leadVisual.title: Declare primary and foreign keys in SQL

coreExplanation: Define Member and declare PRIMARY KEY (MemberID). The key is unique and non-null. A table-level constraint names the field to which it applies; an inline MemberID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY declaration expresses the same single-field intention.

FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) names the local Loan field. REFERENCES Member(MemberID) names the target table and key. Matching names alone would not declare a reference. Compatible field types and an appropriate referenced key are required.

NOT NULL is included to express our explicit rule that every loan must have a member. REFERENCES checks that a supplied member exists. The primary key prevents repeated LoanIDs while the foreign key permits several loans for the same member.

For Membership with one member-group association per pair, use PRIMARY KEY (MemberID, GroupID). Do not declare two independent primary keys: the combination identifies the association, and each component remains a separate foreign key to its parent.

learningCycle.observe: An INTEGER field can store the number 9 without knowing whether member 9 exists. Compare a plain type declaration with the explicit REFERENCES clause.
learningCycle.question: Which part of a CREATE TABLE statement makes Loan.MemberID a reference?

steps.title: Create the referenced table first
steps.body: Define Member and declare PRIMARY KEY (MemberID). The key is unique and non-null. A table-level constraint names the field to which it applies; an inline MemberID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY declaration expresses the same single-field intention.

steps.title: Name both sides of the foreign key
steps.body: FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) names the local Loan field. REFERENCES Member(MemberID) names the target table and key. Matching names alone would not declare a reference. Compatible field types and an appropriate referenced key are required.
steps.code:
CREATE TABLE Loan (
    LoanID INTEGER,
    MemberID INTEGER NOT NULL,
    Fee REAL,
    Returned BOOLEAN,
    PRIMARY KEY (LoanID),
    FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) REFERENCES Member(MemberID)
);

steps.title: Separate required-value and reference rules
steps.body: NOT NULL is included to express our explicit rule that every loan must have a member. REFERENCES checks that a supplied member exists. The primary key prevents repeated LoanIDs while the foreign key permits several loans for the same member.

steps.title: Declare a composite key together
steps.body: For Membership with one member-group association per pair, use PRIMARY KEY (MemberID, GroupID). Do not declare two independent primary keys: the combination identifies the association, and each component remains a separate foreign key to its parent.

check.prompt: In FOREIGN KEY (BorrowerID) REFERENCES Member(MemberID), must the two field names be identical? What does each name mean?

learningCycle.takeaway: Declare identity with PRIMARY KEY and a reference with FOREIGN KEY … REFERENCES; required values are explicit.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Change a definition while preserving its records

leadVisual.title: Change a definition while preserving its records

coreExplanation: ALTER TABLE Loan ADD DueDate DATE; adds a field to the existing definition. It does not insert a new loan, assign a date to loan 201 or recreate every row as a new borrowing event.

With this nullable field and no supplied default, the existing loan has no due date value, represented as NULL. The LoanID and Returned values remain. A later UPDATE can supply a date for a selected loan.

If a legacy Loan table already has MemberID but no reference constraint, an ALTER statement can declare the foreign key. Existing non-null values must satisfy the new rule; adding the constraint is not a repair of unmatched values.

The table and required fields must exist. Adding DueDate twice generally fails because the name is already present. The SQL laboratory resets its own exercise state so that a repeated demonstration starts from a known schema.

ADD FOREIGN KEY (MemberID) REFERENCES Member(MemberID);

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose the information a result should show

leadVisual.title: Choose the information a result should show

coreExplanation: MemberID identifies the member, MemberName stores the name, and Active records a Boolean membership status. Chen remains a stored member even though Active is FALSE. There is no filtering in our first query.
SELECT MemberName names the requested output field. FROM Member names the source table. SELECT * requests every field, which is different from requesting only the names.

The result contains Asha, Ben, Chen and Dara. Reading the names does not delete the other columns or remove inactive members. Without ORDER BY, no particular output order is guaranteed; use the sorted version when comparing exact displayed sequences.
Use a comma-separated list such as SELECT MemberID, MemberName FROM Member;. The result shows those fields in that order. A misspelled identifier does not become a new field automatically.

learningCycle.observe: Member contains MemberID, MemberName and Active. The librarian wants a simple list of names. Predict which columns appear in the result and which remain stored afterwards.
learningCycle.question: Can we display member names without changing the Member table?

steps.body: MemberID identifies the member, MemberName stores the name, and Active records a Boolean membership status. Chen remains a stored member even though Active is FALSE. There is no filtering in our first query.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Test each row against a precise condition

leadVisual.title: Test each row against a precise condition

coreExplanation: Returned FALSE means the loan has not been marked returned. Fee is numeric. WHERE retains a row only when its condition is true; the other stored rows remain in the table.
Returned = FALSE AND Fee >= 3 requires both tests to pass. Loan 203 passes with FALSE and 6; loan 205 passes with FALSE and 3. Loans 201 and 202 each fail one test.
Returned = FALSE OR Fee >= 3 accepts either test. It returns loans 201, 202, 203 and 205. A row passing both appears once; OR does not mean concatenate two copies of the row.

(MemberID = 1 OR MemberID = 2) AND Returned = FALSE requests unreturned loans belonging to either member. It gives 201, 203 and 205. Without the parentheses, AND binds more tightly than OR, so returned loan 202 also qualifies through MemberID = 1.

learningCycle.observe: Read all five Loan rows. Loan 202 has fee 4 but was returned. Loan 201 is unreturned but its fee is only 2. Predict whether either belongs in a result that requires both conditions.
learningCycle.question: Which loans are both unreturned and have a fee of at least 3?

steps.title: Read the source and the Boolean field
steps.body: Returned FALSE means the loan has not been marked returned. Fee is numeric. WHERE retains a row only when its condition is true; the other stored rows remain in the table.

steps.title: Combine required conditions with AND
steps.body: Returned = FALSE AND Fee >= 3 requires both tests to pass. Loan 203 passes with FALSE and 6; loan 205 passes with FALSE and 3. Loans 201 and 202 each fail one test.
steps.code:
SELECT LoanID, Fee
FROM Loan
WHERE Returned = FALSE AND Fee >= 3
ORDER BY LoanID;

steps.title: Compare OR without treating it as equivalent
steps.body: Returned = FALSE OR Fee >= 3 accepts either test. It returns loans 201, 202, 203 and 205. A row passing both appears once; OR does not mean concatenate two copies of the row.

steps.title: Use parentheses to state grouped conditions
steps.body: (MemberID = 1 OR MemberID = 2) AND Returned = FALSE requests unreturned loans belonging to either member. It gives 201, 203 and 205. Without the parentheses, AND binds more tightly than OR, so returned loan 202 also qualifies through MemberID = 1.

worked.title: Evaluate one row at a time
worked.setup: Use the initial loans and the condition Returned = FALSE AND Fee >= 3.

steps.title: Record both truth values
steps.body: Loan 201: true and false → reject. Loan 202: false and true → reject. Loan 203: true and true → keep. Loan 204: false and false → reject. Loan 205: true and true → keep.

steps.title: Project only the requested fields
steps.body: The result shows LoanID and Fee for 203 and 205. MemberID and Returned were used or available in the source but are not requested output columns.

worked.conclusion: Translate the complete requirement into a condition, then test borderline and near-matching records.

check.prompt: Why does loan 205 qualify for the AND query, and what changes if the comparison becomes Fee > 3?
check.answer: Loan 205 is unreturned and its fee equals 3, which meets >= 3. With > 3 it no longer qualifies; only loan 203 meets both conditions. Neither query changes the stored loan.

learningCycle.takeaway: WHERE filters rows; AND, OR, comparison boundaries and parentheses determine which rows qualify.
learningCycle.bridge: The qualifying set still needs an explicit rule if its display order matters.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Arrange the result and resolve ties

leadVisual.title: Arrange the result and resolve ties

coreExplanation: ORDER BY Fee DESC sorts by decreasing fee. ASC means increasing order and is the default. It arranges result rows without changing their stored values or selecting a smaller set.
Fees decrease as 6, 4, 3, 2, 0, so LoanIDs appear as 203, 202, 205, 201, 204. The initial table happens to contain no tied fees.

ORDER BY Fee DESC, LoanID ASC first compares Fee. Only rows with equal fees are then compared by LoanID in increasing order. It does not sort the whole result again by LoanID and erase the fee ordering.

In a separate sample Charge has (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 3). ORDER BY Fee DESC, ChargeID DESC gives (2, 6), (3, 3), (1, 3). Reversing only ChargeID to ASC swaps the two fee-3 rows; the fee-6 row stays first.

learningCycle.observe: The initial fees are 2, 4, 6, 0 and 3. Predict the LoanID order for decreasing fees, then consider what should happen when two fees are equal.
learningCycle.question: How can the librarian see the largest fees first?

steps.title: Name the sort field and direction
steps.body: ORDER BY Fee DESC sorts by decreasing fee. ASC means increasing order and is the default. It arranges result rows without changing their stored values or selecting a smaller set.

steps.title: Read the sorted initial result
steps.body: Fees decrease as 6, 4, 3, 2, 0, so LoanIDs appear as 203, 202, 205, 201, 204. The initial table happens to contain no tied fees.

steps.title: Use later fields only for ties
steps.body: ORDER BY Fee DESC, LoanID ASC first compares Fee. Only rows with equal fees are then compared by LoanID in increasing order. It does not sort the whole result again by LoanID and erase the fee ordering.

steps.title: Test a tie explicitly
steps.body: In a separate sample Charge has (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 3). ORDER BY Fee DESC, ChargeID DESC gives (2, 6), (3, 3), (1, 3). Reversing only ChargeID to ASC swaps the two fee-3 rows; the fee-6 row stays first.

check.prompt: Does ORDER BY Fee DESC remove loans with fee zero? What clause would remove them?
check.answer: No. It places the zero-fee loan after larger fees. A WHERE condition such as Fee > 0 filters out that row; ORDER BY only arranges the retained result.

learningCycle.takeaway: ORDER BY controls output order; later fields resolve ties under earlier fields.
learningCycle.bridge: Instead of returning every matching row, a query can calculate a summary of their values.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate a total, count and mean

leadVisual.title: Calculate a total, count and mean

coreExplanation: SUM(Fee) adds known fees, COUNT(*) counts rows, and AVG(Fee) calculates the mean of the included non-null fees. Without GROUP BY, these aggregate expressions produce one summary for the selected set.
The five fees sum to 15. There are five rows and five known fees, so the mean is 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Zero contributes a known value to the denominator even though it adds nothing to the sum.
AS TotalFee, AS LoanCount and AS MeanFee name the result columns. These aliases make the summary readable; they do not create new stored fields in Loan.

For a separate sample of fees 2, NULL and 4, COUNT(*) is 3 while COUNT(Fee) is 2. SUM is 6 and AVG is 3 because the unknown fee is ignored by those value aggregates. If no rows qualify, COUNT(*) is 0 and SUM/AVG are NULL in the laboratory SQL engine; there is no known mean to report as zero.

learningCycle.observe: Add 2, 4, 6, 0 and 3 by hand. Count how many known values you included, then calculate their mean. Predict how an unknown fee differs from a fee of zero.
learningCycle.question: What single summary describes the five loan fees?

steps.title: Aggregate one selected set
steps.body: SUM(Fee) adds known fees, COUNT(*) counts rows, and AVG(Fee) calculates the mean of the included non-null fees. Without GROUP BY, these aggregate expressions produce one summary for the selected set.

steps.title: Calculate before using SQL
steps.body: The five fees sum to 15. There are five rows and five known fees, so the mean is 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Zero contributes a known value to the denominator even though it adds nothing to the sum.
steps.code:
SELECT SUM(Fee) AS TotalFee, COUNT(*) AS LoanCount, AVG(Fee) AS MeanFee
FROM Loan;

steps.title: Read output labels
steps.body: AS TotalFee, AS LoanCount and AS MeanFee name the result columns. These aliases make the summary readable; they do not create new stored fields in Loan.

steps.title: Distinguish NULL, zero and an empty set
steps.body: For a separate sample of fees 2, NULL and 4, COUNT(*) is 3 while COUNT(Fee) is 2. SUM is 6 and AVG is 3 because the unknown fee is ignored by those value aggregates. If no rows qualify, COUNT(*) is 0 and SUM/AVG are NULL in the laboratory SQL engine; there is no known mean to report as zero.

worked.title: Summarise only unreturned loans
worked.setup: WHERE Returned = FALSE retains loans 201, 203 and 205 with fees 2, 6 and 3.

steps.title: Choose the input set first
steps.body: The known total is 2 + 6 + 3 = 11; COUNT(*) is 3; AVG is 11 ÷ 3, approximately 3.667. Do not include the returned loans’ fees.

steps.title: Express the same calculation
steps.body: Use the aggregate expressions with the filter. The displayed precision of AVG can vary, but it represents 11 divided by 3.

worked.conclusion: Determine the selected rows, then calculate the aggregate over that set.

check.prompt: For fees 2, 4 and 0, is AVG(Fee) 3? How does the answer change if the zero is instead NULL?
check.answer: With zero it is (2 + 4 + 0) ÷ 3 = 2. With NULL it is (2 + 4) ÷ 2 = 3 because only two fee values are known. COUNT(*) remains 3, but COUNT(Fee) changes from 3 to 2.

learningCycle.takeaway: Calculate over the correct rows and distinguish counting records from counting known field values.
learningCycle.bridge: The library may need one summary per member instead of one summary for everyone.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Make one summary for each member

leadVisual.title: Make one summary for each member

coreExplanation: GROUP BY MemberID puts Loan records with the same MemberID into one group. The initial table has three groups: member 1 has two rows, member 2 has two, and member 3 has one. Member 4 has no Loan row, so this source contributes no group for Dara.
COUNT(*) is now evaluated inside each member group instead of once across all five rows. SELECT returns the grouped identifier and the aggregate, producing one row per represented member.

Non-aggregated selected fields should be included in GROUP BY for the queries taught here. Selecting a single arbitrary LoanID beside the member’s count would not represent the group: member 1 has both 201 and 202.

WHERE restricts source rows before they contribute to group calculations. GROUP BY forms the summaries. ORDER BY arranges the resulting group rows; it does not create groups. Without a separate order requirement do not infer a guaranteed sequence.

learningCycle.observe: Place loans 201 and 202 together, 203 and 205 together, and 204 on its own. Identify the common field value within each collection.
learningCycle.question: How many loans belong to each member represented in Loan?

steps.title: Form groups using shared values
steps.body: GROUP BY MemberID puts Loan records with the same MemberID into one group. The initial table has three groups: member 1 has two rows, member 2 has two, and member 3 has one. Member 4 has no Loan row, so this source contributes no group for Dara.

steps.title: Calculate one aggregate per group
steps.body: COUNT(*) is now evaluated inside each member group instead of once across all five rows. SELECT returns the grouped identifier and the aggregate, producing one row per represented member.
steps.code:
SELECT MemberID, COUNT(*) AS LoanCount
FROM Loan
GROUP BY MemberID
ORDER BY MemberID;

steps.title: Give each selected value an unambiguous meaning
steps.body: Non-aggregated selected fields should be included in GROUP BY for the queries taught here. Selecting a single arbitrary LoanID beside the member’s count would not represent the group: member 1 has both 201 and 202.

steps.title: Keep filtering and sorting distinct
steps.body: WHERE restricts source rows before they contribute to group calculations. GROUP BY forms the summaries. ORDER BY arranges the resulting group rows; it does not create groups. Without a separate order requirement do not infer a guaranteed sequence.

worked.title: Count only outstanding loans per member
worked.setup: Filter Returned = FALSE before grouping by MemberID.

steps.title: Identify the retained records
steps.body: LoanIDs 201, 203 and 205 remain. Member 1 contributes one row; member 2 contributes two; members 3 and 4 contribute none.

steps.title: Write and check the grouped result
steps.body: The result is (1, 1), (2, 2). These counts are for outstanding loans, not all borrowing history.
steps.code:
SELECT MemberID, COUNT(*) AS Outstanding
FROM Loan
WHERE Returned = FALSE
GROUP BY MemberID
ORDER BY MemberID;

worked.conclusion: Choose the rows first, group by the identity you mean, then calculate one result per group.

check.prompt: Why does grouping Loan by MemberID not display Dara with a count of zero?
check.answer: There is no Loan row with MemberID 4, so that table provides no group for Dara. The query summarises groups present in its source; it does not invent a row for every possible member.

learningCycle.takeaway: GROUP BY partitions the selected records and lets aggregates produce one result for each group.
learningCycle.bridge: To display names alongside loan information, reconnect Member with Loan.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match a loan with its member

leadVisual.title: Match a loan with its member

coreExplanation: Member has four records. Loan has five records. The shared meaning of MemberID and the declared reference justify matching these fields; matching arbitrary equal numbers such as MemberID and LoanID would not represent the relationship.
Loan 201 has MemberID 1 and matches Asha. Loan 202 also has MemberID 1 and matches the same member. Each matching pair can contribute a row, so a join is not automatically one result per member.

FROM Member INNER JOIN Loan identifies the two sources. ON Member.MemberID = Loan.MemberID gives the match rule. Qualifying names with the table makes the two MemberID fields unambiguous. SELECT chooses the fields from the matching pairs.

Asha appears with 201 and 202; Ben with 203 and 205; Chen with 204. Dara has no matching Loan and contributes no result row to this INNER JOIN. The manual pairing explains the logical result, not the exact internal algorithm used by every DBMS.

learningCycle.observe: Member contains Asha and Ben. Loan contains borrowing events 201–205. Match Loan 201’s MemberID to a Member row, then repeat for Loan 202. Predict how often Asha appears and whether Dara appears at all.
learningCycle.question: Which table contains the name, and which contains the loan number?

steps.title: Keep both sources in view
steps.body: Member has four records. Loan has five records. The shared meaning of MemberID and the declared reference justify matching these fields; matching arbitrary equal numbers such as MemberID and LoanID would not represent the relationship.

steps.title: Match the child record to its parent
steps.body: Loan 201 has MemberID 1 and matches Asha. Loan 202 also has MemberID 1 and matches the same member. Each matching pair can contribute a row, so a join is not automatically one result per member.

steps.title: Write INNER JOIN with its ON condition
steps.body: FROM Member INNER JOIN Loan identifies the two sources. ON Member.MemberID = Loan.MemberID gives the match rule. Qualifying names with the table makes the two MemberID fields unambiguous. SELECT chooses the fields from the matching pairs.
steps.code:
SELECT Member.MemberName, Loan.LoanID
FROM Member INNER JOIN Loan
ON Member.MemberID = Loan.MemberID
ORDER BY Loan.LoanID;

steps.title: Read omissions and repetitions
steps.body: Asha appears with 201 and 202; Ben with 203 and 205; Chen with 204. Dara has no matching Loan and contributes no result row to this INNER JOIN. The manual pairing explains the logical result, not the exact internal algorithm used by every DBMS.

steps.title: Combine matching and filtering
steps.body: The ON condition finds the matching member-loan pairs. WHERE Loan.Returned = FALSE keeps only loans 201, 203 and 205. SELECT asks for MemberName and LoanID.
steps.code:

FROM Member INNER JOIN Loan
ON Member.MemberID = Loan.MemberID
WHERE Loan.Returned = FALSE
ORDER BY Loan.LoanID;

steps.title: Verify every output pair
steps.body: The result is (Asha, 201), (Ben, 203), (Ben, 205). Each name comes from Member and each event identifier from Loan. Ben appears twice because two outstanding loans match.

check.prompt: Asha has two matching loans. Does INNER JOIN remove one because the displayed name repeats?
check.answer: No. The loans are distinct matching records, so both row pairs contribute. A repeated displayed name is not a duplicate loan. A member with no matching Loan contributes no row to this INNER JOIN.

learningCycle.takeaway: INNER JOIN returns matching record pairs according to ON; parent values can repeat across different children.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Build a complete two-table summary

leadVisual.title: Build a complete two-table summary

coreExplanation: MemberName comes from Member. Fee and Returned come from Loan. Count one row per outstanding loan, then return one summary per member. An INNER JOIN is appropriate because this task requests only members who have matching outstanding loans.

Join by MemberID and retain FALSE in Returned. Asha contributes loan 201 with fee 2. Ben contributes 203 and 205 with fees 6 and 3. Chen’s returned loan and Dara’s lack of loans contribute no selected record.

Group by both MemberID and MemberName so distinct people with the same name remain separate while the displayed non-aggregated name has a defined group. Order by total fee descending, with MemberID ascending as a tie-breaker.

Ben has count 2, total 9 and mean 4.5. Asha has count 1, total 2 and mean 2. ORDER BY places Ben first. This reasoning order describes the logical calculation; the DBMS may choose another internal execution plan.

learningCycle.observe: The required result must name each member with outstanding loans, count those loans and calculate their total and mean fees. The largest total should appear first. Predict Ben’s and Asha’s summaries before writing SQL.
learningCycle.question: Who has outstanding loans, and whose outstanding fees total the most?

steps.title: Translate the output requirement
steps.body: MemberName comes from Member. Fee and Returned come from Loan. Count one row per outstanding loan, then return one summary per member. An INNER JOIN is appropriate because this task requests only members who have matching outstanding loans.

steps.title: Trace the selected matching rows
steps.body: Join by MemberID and retain FALSE in Returned. Asha contributes loan 201 with fee 2. Ben contributes 203 and 205 with fees 6 and 3. Chen’s returned loan and Dara’s lack of loans contribute no selected record.

steps.title: Group by identity and write the statement
steps.body: Group by both MemberID and MemberName so distinct people with the same name remain separate while the displayed non-aggregated name has a defined group. Order by total fee descending, with MemberID ascending as a tie-breaker.
steps.code:
SELECT Member.MemberName, COUNT(*) AS LoanCount,
       SUM(Loan.Fee) AS TotalFee, AVG(Loan.Fee) AS MeanFee
FROM Member INNER JOIN Loan
ON Member.MemberID = Loan.MemberID
WHERE Loan.Returned = FALSE
GROUP BY Member.MemberID, Member.MemberName
ORDER BY SUM(Loan.Fee) DESC, Member.MemberID ASC;

steps.title: Calculate and inspect the exact result
steps.body: Ben has count 2, total 9 and mean 4.5. Asha has count 1, total 2 and mean 2. ORDER BY places Ben first. This reasoning order describes the logical calculation; the DBMS may choose another internal execution plan.

worked.title: Change a source value and predict the whole effect
worked.setup: Reset to the initial data, then suppose loan 205 is marked returned. Re-run the same query.

steps.title: Rebuild the selected groups
steps.body: Loan 205 no longer qualifies. Ben’s outstanding group contains only loan 203 with fee 6. Asha’s group is unchanged.

steps.title: Recalculate instead of reusing a fixed answer
steps.body: Ben now has count 1, total 6 and mean 6; Asha still has count 1, total 2 and mean 2. Ben remains first. A real query result must reflect this changed data.

steps.title: Test identity separately
steps.body: If another member is also named Asha, grouping by MemberID and MemberName keeps the two people separate. Grouping only by MemberName could merge their loans and answer a different question.

worked.conclusion: Trace the input set, match rule, filter, group identity, calculation and output order.

check.prompt: Why is SELECT MemberName, COUNT(*) with GROUP BY MemberName alone unsafe for counting loans per person?
check.answer: Different members can share a name, so grouping only by name can merge their records. Include MemberID as the identifying group field and MemberName as the displayed non-aggregated field, keeping each person’s group distinct.

learningCycle.takeaway: Build a combined query from a precise output requirement and verify each stage against the data.
learningCycle.bridge: Now consider how the DBMS can find matching records efficiently, then define and maintain the structure yourself.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Add a new record in the defined field order

leadVisual.title: Add a new record in the defined field order

coreExplanation: INSERT INTO Member (MemberID, MemberName, Active) lists the fields receiving values. VALUES (5, 'Elena', TRUE) supplies corresponding values in the same order. Text is quoted; the integer and Boolean are expressed according to their types.
MemberID 5 must not already exist. An insertion into Loan would also need a valid MemberID reference and any required fields. INSERT does not silently turn a duplicate identity into an update.
A valid insertion adds one row and leaves members 1–4 unchanged. SELECT can inspect the new state. Repeating the statement unchanged then fails because MemberID 5 is already present.

learningCycle.observe: Member currently contains IDs 1–4. Elena needs a new identity, name and Active value. Predict the five-row state after one valid insertion, and what happens if the identical insertion is repeated.
learningCycle.question: Which existing records should change when Elena registers?

steps.title: Name target fields explicitly
steps.body: INSERT INTO Member (MemberID, MemberName, Active) lists the fields receiving values. VALUES (5, 'Elena', TRUE) supplies corresponding values in the same order. Text is quoted; the integer and Boolean are expressed according to their types.
steps.code:
INSERT INTO Member (MemberID, MemberName, Active)
VALUES (5, 'Elena', TRUE);

steps.title: Check the new identity and any references
steps.body: MemberID 5 must not already exist. An insertion into Loan would also need a valid MemberID reference and any required fields. INSERT does not silently turn a duplicate identity into an update.

steps.title: Inspect the complete effect

steps.title: Move the corresponding values too
steps.body: Use INSERT INTO Member (MemberName, MemberID, Active) VALUES ('Elena', 5, TRUE);. The value positions correspond to the explicit field list, not a guess about visual table order.

steps.title: Verify exactly one addition
steps.body: Run a retrieval ordered by MemberID. Check the new row and confirm that Asha, Ben, Chen and Dara retain their previous values. Reset before trying another independent version with MemberID 5.

worked.conclusion: Match field and value positions, satisfy constraints and inspect the resulting records.

check.prompt: Will repeating the same INSERT for MemberID 5 refresh Elena’s existing record?
check.answer: No. With MemberID as the primary key, the repeated insertion attempts a duplicate identity and must be rejected. UPDATE is the operation for changing a field of an existing record.

learningCycle.takeaway: INSERT adds records; the field list and values must correspond and all declared constraints still apply.
learningCycle.bridge: Use UPDATE when a stored borrowing event changes status.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Change a value without losing the event

leadVisual.title: Change a value without losing the event

coreExplanation: UPDATE names the table. SET gives the replacement field value. WHERE identifies which rows receive it. UPDATE Loan SET Returned = TRUE WHERE LoanID = 203; targets one event.

A SELECT with the same WHERE condition should identify loan 203 before the change. If the condition instead uses MemberID = 2, both 203 and 205 qualify. The shared member identifier is too broad for this instruction.
Loan 203 remains present, with MemberID 2 and Fee 6 unchanged, while Returned becomes TRUE. Loan 205 stays FALSE. A successful update does not mean every displayed column should change.

Without WHERE, UPDATE targets every row, subject to constraints. A condition matching no row changes nothing. Several values can be assigned with commas in SET, but every assignment still applies to the rows selected by the one WHERE condition.

learningCycle.observe: Both loans belong to member 2, but they represent separate events. The instruction names LoanID 203. Predict the exact fields and records that should change.
learningCycle.question: Ben returns loan 203. Should loan 205 also become returned?

steps.title: Separate target, replacement and restriction
steps.body: UPDATE names the table. SET gives the replacement field value. WHERE identifies which rows receive it. UPDATE Loan SET Returned = TRUE WHERE LoanID = 203; targets one event.

steps.body: A SELECT with the same WHERE condition should identify loan 203 before the change. If the condition instead uses MemberID = 2, both 203 and 205 qualify. The shared member identifier is too broad for this instruction.

steps.title: Verify changed and unchanged values
steps.body: Loan 203 remains present, with MemberID 2 and Fee 6 unchanged, while Returned becomes TRUE. Loan 205 stays FALSE. A successful update does not mean every displayed column should change.

worked.title: Record a return and waive its fee
worked.setup: The instruction now explicitly says loan 203 is returned and its fee becomes zero.

steps.title: Write both requested assignments
steps.body: Use UPDATE Loan SET Returned = TRUE, Fee = 0 WHERE LoanID = 203;. Both changes belong in SET; the unique loan identifier belongs in WHERE.

steps.title: Check the resulting event
steps.body: Loan 203 becomes (203, 2, 0, TRUE). Loan 205 remains (205, 2, 3, FALSE). Ben’s identity is unchanged, and no record has been removed.

worked.conclusion: Choose the record by the task’s identity, then change only the requested fields.

check.prompt: Which clause says what changes, and which says which records change? What if LoanID = 999 matches nothing?
check.answer: SET specifies replacement values and WHERE restricts the records. If 999 is absent, no record is updated; the statement does not insert a new loan. INSERT is needed to add a record.

learningCycle.takeaway: UPDATE preserves records while replacing specified values in the rows selected by WHERE.
learningCycle.bridge: Deleting a completed event is a different decision from changing its status.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Remove the intended record and explain the whole solution

leadVisual.title: Remove the intended record and explain the whole solution

coreExplanation: DELETE FROM Loan WHERE LoanID = 204; removes the complete matching Loan row. It does not mean clear only the fee or mark the event returned. Those would be different value changes.

SELECT LoanID FROM Loan WHERE LoanID = 204; identifies the intended event. After deletion, loan IDs 201, 202, 203 and 205 remain. Member 3 Chen remains registered even though that member now has no Loan row.

Without WHERE, DELETE targets all rows of the named table, subject to constraints. Deleting a child Loan does not normally delete its Member. Deleting a referenced parent can be rejected or follow a declared referential action; inspect the schema rather than assuming a cascade.

In a new scenario, identify entities and rules, choose keys, design the relationships, assign each fact to its determinant, define constraints and rights, then query or maintain precisely targeted records. Check the actual final state and account for recovery of intended data.
