knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 1: Information representation

leadVisual.title: Three questions for every representation

coreExplanation: Recover meaning using a stated representation, then show the calculation or reconstruction and check its boundary.

teachingBlocks.title: Retrieve a method and produce evidence
rows: Explain 2ⁿ patterns versus maximum 2ⁿ − 1; convert prefixes through bytes.
Convert both ways; decode signed values; show carries or borrows and judge overflow.
Use supplied codes to encode and decode a string; distinguish a code point from its stored bytes.
Reconstruct the grid or object list, calculate data size, and justify scaling behaviour.
Quantise numerical measurements, encode and decode them, then calculate raw data size.
Decode every run or reference and compare the complete stated storage costs.

teachingBlocks.text: In the independent tasks below, first name the width, representation and any storage assumptions. A familiar bit pattern can have different meanings; a repeated source can still grow after encoding. Check your intermediate steps before opening the answers.
teachingBlocks.title: Use a consistent checking method

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 2: Communication

leadVisual.title: Four independent diagnosis tasks

coreExplanation: Justify designs from their constraints and trace packets, frames and responses through named devices.
Calculate buffer and subnet decisions with supplied values; distinguish failed dependencies before proposing recovery.

teachingBlocks.text: A mobile museum terminal retrieves an exhibit record from a hosted service. Diagnose the complete system by locating each responsibility: local access, onward link, addressing, remote service and returned content. A correct name must be connected to the stated requirement or failure.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect the section as one system
Follow the request and identify evidence
rows: Choose LAN/WAN scope, client-server/P2P roles, thin/thick processing, topology and carrier from separate requirements.
A suitable service model does not create a spare physical link or guarantee radio coverage.
WNIC → WAP → switch; MAC and known ports guide local frames, while routers handle other networks.
A device, cable or central switch can fail; shared half-duplex collision handling has a separate scope.
Use the prefix to choose local/gateway delivery; distinguish scope from assignment; resolve the domain before requesting a resource.
DNS success, network delivery and an existing server resource are different conditions.
Compare arrival and playback rates, current reserve and capacity; follow the hosted request and response.
A finite buffer cannot cover an indefinite deficit. A backup captures only retained state and requires a usable recovery service.

teachingBlocks.text: Use the four Section 2 diagnosis questions below to test design, forwarding and collision behaviour, rate calculations, and address-to-resource flow. For revision, return to Lessons 007–014 when a step depends on a label you cannot yet explain.
teachingBlocks.title: Apply the complete chain

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 3: Hardware

leadVisual.title: Section 3 application route

coreExplanation: Trace physical and data changes before assigning a fault or choosing hardware.
Use the full rule, actual state and all input combinations when checking control and logic.

teachingBlocks.text: An environmental recorder measures conditions, stores observations and controls a pump. Diagnose it by separating the physical measurement, data representation, temporary workspace, persistent files and corrective action. A component’s name alone does not demonstrate that the full system is working.
teachingBlocks.title: Connect the hardware responsibilities
Choose evidence that separates possible faults
rows: A saved reading returns after restart but an unsaved edit disappears.
Separate non-volatile saved data from volatile working memory.
A burst can be accepted but a sustained excess eventually blocks transfer.
Compare waiting content and finite capacity; apply the full-buffer policy.
A motor receives a command but the pressure stays unchanged.
The command is not the physical outcome; use actual feedback and investigate the actuator.
An alarm triggers under a supposedly rejected input.
Translate the stated condition, trace intermediate logic and identify a counterexample.

teachingBlocks.text: Use the three hardware diagnosis tasks and the retained logic task below. Return to Lessons 015–020 to reconstruct any missing physical stage or Boolean relationship. The logic task’s complete eight-row answer is a check on the supplied expression, not a substitute for independently deriving the table.
teachingBlocks.title: Demonstrate the chain independently

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 4: Processor fundamentals

leadVisual.title: Section 4: produce evidence for each claim

coreExplanation: Trace addresses, values and control flow; preserve context across interrupts and unrelated bits during a conditional device update.

teachingBlocks.text: Diagnose the state that made a result wrong. Separate the instruction address from its contents, a comparison from a branch, a pending request from an accepted one, and a test mask from the status byte that must be stored.

For each task, identify the initial state and trace the relevant transfers or decisions to the final state. Explain the correction and check a different path, such as unequal input or a clear ready bit. These tasks connect processor structure to assembly behaviour.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 5: System software

leadVisual.title: Retrieve the complete S5 chain

coreExplanation: Separate the job from the software responsible for it: the OS coordinates resources, utilities perform maintenance or protection tasks, and libraries supply reusable code. Explain the actual operation before claiming a benefit.

Track what is translated, when execution occurs and which environment is required. Match compilation or interpretation to the workload, follow Java through bytecode and the JVM, and use IDE evidence to check behaviour rather than assuming a successful translation proves correctness.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 6: Security, privacy and data integrity

leadVisual.title: Retrieve the process, then apply it

coreExplanation: Classify the consequence, follow the threat route and justify controls by their mechanisms.
Trace validation, source comparison and transfer checks; a passed check does not prove truth or authenticated origin.

teachingBlocks.text: Begin with what happened to the record or service: unauthorised disclosure, wrong values, lost records or unavailable processing. Then separate identity authentication, operation-specific permission, encryption, signature verification, filtering and malware detection. One incident may need several controls because each checks a different condition.
teachingBlocks.title: Reconstruct the protection argument

teachingBlocks.text: For integrity, decide which question needs answering. Validation applies input rules. Visual comparison or double entry checks copying. Transfer parity and checksums compare calculated evidence under an agreed rule. Work from supplied data, complete the receiving decision, and explain a relevant way the check can miss an error.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose and execute the check

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 7: Ethics and ownership

leadVisual.title: Retrieve the complete S7 reasoning

coreExplanation: Connect duties and rights to the actual people and acts; a category name is not a justification.
Trace an AI application, interpret its evidence and give a conditional decision with a workable safeguard.

teachingBlocks.text: Separate the professional duty, the code that supports it and the actual response. Include colleagues as well as the public. Compare the consequences of each proposed action for named people; alter the judgement when the legitimate purpose or evidence changes.
teachingBlocks.title: Reconstruct the responsibility argument

teachingBlocks.text: For software, distinguish ownership from permissions, then check source access, modification, redistribution, deployment terms and support against the scenario. A no-charge or commercial label cannot replace that comparison. State continuing obligations and explain why an alternative fails a requirement.
teachingBlocks.title: Read the terms

teachingBlocks.text: For AI, follow input through recognition or inference to the output and its use. OCR, translation and text-to-speech do different jobs. Examine relevant group results, complete operating costs and a consistent resource baseline; a useful aggregate number may conceal a limitation. Match the safeguard to the error and state evidence that would change the recommendation.
teachingBlocks.title: Use mechanisms and evidence in an evaluation

knowledgeUnits.heading: Section 8: Databases

leadVisual.title: Retrieve and apply the S8 methods

coreExplanation: Use business rules to choose keys and dependencies, then preserve references through normalisation.
Connect DBMS controls to exact operations; trace DDL structure and DML results against supplied data.

teachingBlocks.text: Identify which entity owns each fact. Test candidate keys against the permitted records, not only a convenient sample. For normalisation, state the repeating group or dependency, decompose it, then match retained identifiers to recover the original facts. A positive 3NF verdict needs reasons as well as a rejected example.
teachingBlocks.title: Reconstruct a design argument

teachingBlocks.text: Separate metadata from records, permissions from integrity and backup state from later changes. A logical schema is the definition being represented; the dictionary records its metadata. A developer interface builds objects, while the query processor handles requests for their use.
teachingBlocks.title: Choose the responsible facility

teachingBlocks.text: For SQL, first decide whether structure or records must change. Read each DDL type and key explicitly. For a combined query, match two tables, filter rows, form groups, calculate and order results. Verify which stored records remain unchanged after a maintenance statement.

pastPaperCoverageNotes.E067: Directly tests selecting information for a stated purpose and justifying those choices. It does not ask for a complete abstract model or a general explanation of the benefits of abstraction; the preceding teacher-written tasks assess those separately.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Give the ticket seller instructions that can be followed

leadVisual.title: Give the ticket seller instructions that can be followed

coreExplanation: Read the requested quantity, multiply it by 25.00 and tell the buyer the result. For two tickets the result is 50.00. Another volunteer should obtain the same result from those instructions.

“Sell tickets” names a goal but leaves the method open. “Read the quantity; multiply the quantity by 25.00; display the result” supplies operations and their order. A solution expressed as a sequence of defined steps is an algorithm.

Changing the quantity from two to three changes the total. Changing the poster background from blue to green does not change this calculation. Keep quantity and price when representing this particular task.

Abstraction removes unnecessary detail while retaining essential features. Its purpose here is to make the price calculation easier to understand. Removing the price would make the representation unusable, even though it would contain less information.

learningCycle.observe: Two people want to attend a school performance. Tickets cost 25.00 each. The volunteer has a poster, a list of seats and a note saying “work out the price”. Explain what the volunteer can determine and what the note still leaves unstated.

stimulus.title: The first ticket desk
items: Request: 2 tickets
Price: 25.00 per ticket
Poster: blue background and a photograph
Task: tell the buyer the total price

learningCycle.question: Could a new volunteer sell the correct tickets using only your instructions?

prerequisite.title: Start with an ordinary calculation
prerequisite.body: You only need multiplication and the idea of following instructions in order. This first version assumes that the requested tickets are available. Discounts, payment and repeated orders will be added later, one rule at a time.

steps.title: Carry out the task before naming it
steps.body: Read the requested quantity, multiply it by 25.00 and tell the buyer the result. For two tickets the result is 50.00. Another volunteer should obtain the same result from those instructions.

steps.title: Replace an aim with defined actions
steps.body: “Sell tickets” names a goal but leaves the method open. “Read the quantity; multiply the quantity by 25.00; display the result” supplies operations and their order. A solution expressed as a sequence of defined steps is an algorithm.

steps.title: Ask which facts can change the answer
steps.body: Changing the quantity from two to three changes the total. Changing the poster background from blue to green does not change this calculation. Keep quantity and price when representing this particular task.

steps.title: Name abstraction after making the choice
steps.body: Abstraction removes unnecessary detail while retaining essential features. Its purpose here is to make the price calculation easier to understand. Removing the price would make the representation unusable, even though it would contain less information.

worked.title: Change the request, keep the same method
worked.setup: The next buyer wants three tickets at 25.00 each. The poster now has a red background.

steps.title: Select the relevant facts
steps.body: Keep quantity 3 and unit price 25.00. The new colour has no role in the stated price rule.

steps.title: Follow the ordered operations
steps.body: Obtain 3 before calculating 3 × 25.00 = 75.00. Display 75.00 after calculating it; do not guess the total before reading the request.

steps.title: Check the model against the purpose
steps.body: A second volunteer can reproduce 75.00. If the task changes to printing matching posters, colour becomes relevant; relevance belongs to a purpose, not permanently to a fact.

worked.conclusion: Defined steps make the calculation repeatable; abstraction keeps the information those steps need.

check.prompt: A model keeps the poster colour and quantity but removes the ticket price. Can it calculate the total? Explain the missing information.
check.answer: No. Quantity alone does not determine the total. The model must retain the price or a rule that supplies it. Keeping an unrelated colour does not repair that omission.

learningCycle.takeaway: An algorithm solves a problem using defined steps. Abstraction retains the details essential to the stated purpose.
learningCycle.bridge: Next, turn the selected facts into a model another person can inspect.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Build and challenge an abstract model

leadVisual.title: Build and challenge an abstract model

coreExplanation: This model answers whether enough places remain for a specified performance and quantity. It does not allocate named seats or take payment. State these limits so that a reader knows which decisions the model can support.
Record a performance identifier and its available places. Record the requested performance and quantity separately. The identifier connects the request to the correct availability record.
Find the requested performance, then check that quantity is at least one and does not exceed its places left. In ordinary words, request 2 for A fits within 8; request 2 for B does not fit within 0.

If the model stores only a total of eight places across all performances, it could wrongly accept a request for B. A useful abstraction removes unrelated detail while preserving distinctions that change the answer.

learningCycle.observe: Performance A has eight places left and performance B has no places left. A buyer requests two tickets for A. A model saying only “the school sells tickets” cannot distinguish this request from one for B.

stimulus.title: Two requests with different outcomes
items: A: 8 places left; request 2
B: 0 places left; request 2
Both performances have the same poster
Decision: can this request be accepted?

learningCycle.question: What must a model show to decide whether a ticket request can be met?

prerequisite.title: Choose a purpose before choosing fields
prerequisite.body: A field is one named item recorded in a model, such as the performance identifier. You can write values in an ordinary table; you do not need database commands or programming syntax.

steps.title: State the exact question
steps.body: This model answers whether enough places remain for a specified performance and quantity. It does not allocate named seats or take payment. State these limits so that a reader knows which decisions the model can support.

steps.title: Represent the facts, not only their names
steps.body: Record a performance identifier and its available places. Record the requested performance and quantity separately. The identifier connects the request to the correct availability record.

steps.title: Add the relationship needed for a decision
steps.body: Find the requested performance, then check that quantity is at least one and does not exceed its places left. In ordinary words, request 2 for A fits within 8; request 2 for B does not fit within 0.

steps.title: Test omissions with contrasting cases
steps.body: If the model stores only a total of eight places across all performances, it could wrongly accept a request for B. A useful abstraction removes unrelated detail while preserving distinctions that change the answer.

worked.title: Model a new performance
worked.setup: Performance C has five places left. Requests R1 and R2 ask for four and six tickets respectively. Ignore seat positions and assume whole-number quantities.

steps.title: Produce the representation
steps.body: Add the row C, 5. Record R1 as performance C, quantity 4, and R2 as performance C, quantity 6. Keep the two trial requests independent.

steps.title: Use the model
steps.body: R1 can be met because 4 is positive and no greater than 5. R2 cannot be met because 6 exceeds 5. No payment or stock change is being performed in this model test.

steps.title: Explain a limit and a benefit
steps.body: Omitting seat positions makes the availability decision easier to inspect, but the model cannot tell a buyer their seat number. That limitation is acceptable only because named-seat allocation is outside the stated task.

worked.conclusion: An abstract model must show retained data and useful relationships, with limits that match its purpose.

check.prompt: Create a model for hiring devices: D1 is available and D2 is already hired. The task is to identify a device that can be hired now. Give fields, both rows and one assumption.
check.answer: Use DeviceID and Availability: D1, Available; D2, Hired. Select D1. A suitable assumption is that both devices work and there are no reservations. A list of field names without the two states is incomplete.

challenge.prompt: The purpose changes to emailing buyers about a cancelled performance. Which information must be added, and why?
challenge.answer: Add a way to associate each booking with its performance and a contact email address. Availability alone cannot identify affected recipients or deliver the message. Explain each additional field through the new purpose.

learningCycle.takeaway: Produce a representation containing essential details, and test whether it can answer the stated question.
learningCycle.bridge: The names and values in a model become the data used by an algorithm.

pastPaperCoverageNotes.E068: Tests named submodules and their responsibilities in a text-message task. It supports decomposition into modules, but does not directly test the difference between a returned value and displayed output.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Give each module a clear responsibility

leadVisual.title: Give each module a clear responsibility

coreExplanation: Decomposition divides a complex problem into manageable sub-problems. CheckQuantity decides whether the requested number fits availability. CalculateCharge determines the amount due. CompletePayment handles success or failure according to the payment rule.

CalculateCharge receives Quantity and Student, uses fixed TicketPrice 25.00 and returns Total. CompletePayment needs Quantity, PlacesLeft, Total and Paid. Naming a module without stating its job or needed data leaves the design incomplete.

A charge function can return 45.00 so the caller can evaluate Paid >= Total. Merely printing 45.00 does not return it. DisplayReceipt can be a procedure because its required effect is presenting information.

The parts together must satisfy the original rules. Rejected payment must not reduce places; receipt generation must not recalculate a different price. Giving one part ownership of a calculation makes a changed rule easier to apply consistently.

learningCycle.observe: The desk must check a quantity, calculate an amount, accept or reject payment and report a result. Giving every piece the name “process tickets” hides the different work each one performs.

stimulus.title: Follow information between responsibilities
items: CheckQuantity needs Quantity and PlacesLeft
CalculateCharge needs Quantity and Student
Payment needs the calculated Total and the amount Paid
Receipt needs the confirmed result

learningCycle.question: Which pieces of the ticket task can be understood and checked separately?

prerequisite.title: Recall returned values and effects
prerequisite.body: A function returns a value that its caller can use, such as an amount in a later comparison. A procedure performs a task when called, such as displaying a receipt. Here we design responsibilities and data flow without requiring full subroutine-declaration syntax.

steps.title: Break the whole task into smaller problems
steps.body: Decomposition divides a complex problem into manageable sub-problems. CheckQuantity decides whether the requested number fits availability. CalculateCharge determines the amount due. CompletePayment handles success or failure according to the payment rule.

steps.title: State what each part receives and supplies
steps.body: CalculateCharge receives Quantity and Student, uses fixed TicketPrice 25.00 and returns Total. CompletePayment needs Quantity, PlacesLeft, Total and Paid. Naming a module without stating its job or needed data leaves the design incomplete.

steps.title: Choose a returned value when later processing needs it
steps.body: A charge function can return 45.00 so the caller can evaluate Paid >= Total. Merely printing 45.00 does not return it. DisplayReceipt can be a procedure because its required effect is presenting information.

steps.title: Check cooperation and completeness
steps.body: The parts together must satisfy the original rules. Rejected payment must not reduce places; receipt generation must not recalculate a different price. Giving one part ownership of a calculation makes a changed rule easier to apply consistently.

rows: Reports result and updates places only on success

worked.title: Pass the result to the next responsibility
worked.setup: Quantity 2, PlacesLeft 8, Student TRUE and Paid 50.00. TicketPrice is 25.00.

steps.title: Check the request
steps.body: CheckQuantity determines that 2 is at least one and no greater than 8. The caller may continue to charging.

steps.title: Return the amount due
steps.body: CalculateCharge obtains subtotal 50.00, applies the student rule and returns 45.00. The caller keeps this numeric value as Total and displays the amount due.

steps.title: Complete the accepted sale
steps.body: CompletePayment compares 50.00 with 45.00, calculates change 5.00 and changes PlacesLeft to 6. A receipt can use those confirmed values without repeating the charge calculation.

worked.conclusion: A useful decomposition gives each part a distinct job and connects the data required by the other parts.

check.prompt: Decompose a device hire into availability checking, charge calculation and receipt output. The charge is Quantity × 4.00 + 10.00. Identify a suitable function and its inputs and returned value.
check.answer: An availability module checks the requested quantity against devices available. CalculateCharge can be a function receiving Quantity and returning Quantity * 4.00 + 10.00. A receipt procedure receives the accepted hire details and calculated amount and outputs them. Printing the amount alone does not supply the numeric result to a payment comparison.

challenge.prompt: Two modules separately calculate a charge. One is updated when the discount changes; the other is not. Explain the defect and improve the design.
challenge.answer: The same order can receive inconsistent amounts. Put the charging rule in one calculation module and let other modules use its returned result. Test that module and the connections after a rule change.

learningCycle.takeaway: Decomposition creates cooperating sub-problems that can be represented as modules with defined inputs and results or effects.
learningCycle.bridge: A module name still hides internal work. Next, expand that work until every step is programmable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Give changing values meaningful names

leadVisual.title: Give changing values meaningful names

coreExplanation: Quantity holds 2 for Mina and later holds 3 for Arun. It is a variable because its stored value can change during execution. Using the meaningful name Quantity lets the same instructions work for both buyers.

BuyerName is text, so use STRING. Quantity is a whole number, so use INTEGER. A paid amount can contain a fractional part, so use REAL. Student records TRUE or FALSE, so use BOOLEAN; it does not store the word “student”.

TicketPrice is fixed at 25.00 for this version of the program. A named constant states the value once and prevents reassignment during the run. A programmer can change that definition for a later version with a new price.
An identifier names a data item. Record its name, type and purpose, not just an example value. A declaration gives a variable a type; it does not by itself read a buyer’s name or initialise a count.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace input, assignment and output

leadVisual.title: Trace input, assignment and output

coreExplanation: INPUT Quantity waits for a supplied value and stores it in Quantity. For this run the value is 2. TicketPrice does not need another input because the task already defines it as a constant.

In Total ← Quantity * TicketPrice, read the current values 2 and 25.00, multiply them to obtain 50.00, then store that result in Total. The arrow points to the destination on the left; the calculation uses the right-hand side.

OUTPUT Total displays the current numeric value. OUTPUT "Total" displays the literal word Total instead. The quotation marks distinguish text supplied directly by the program from the name of a stored value.

Read Quantity before calculating Total and calculate Total before displaying it. Group these effects as input, process and output. A declaration can appear before them to establish types, but it does not perform any of these three actions.

learningCycle.observe: The buyer requests two tickets. A desk calculator displays 2, then 50.00. The printed receipt still says nothing until a separate print action. Distinguish obtaining a value, calculating with it and communicating the result.

stimulus.title: Three separate actions
items: Read the requested quantity: 2
Calculate 2 × 25.00: 50.00
Display the amount due: 50.00
Assume a positive whole-number quantity; tickets are available

learningCycle.question: When does the computer first know the total, and when does the buyer see it?

prerequisite.title: Use named values and a fixed price
prerequisite.body: Quantity is an INTEGER variable; Total is REAL; TicketPrice is the constant 25.00. A variable must receive a value before an expression reads it. We introduce one statement at a time.

steps.title: Obtain data with INPUT
steps.body: INPUT Quantity waits for a supplied value and stores it in Quantity. For this run the value is 2. TicketPrice does not need another input because the task already defines it as a constant.
steps.code: INPUT Quantity

steps.title: Evaluate first, then store
steps.body: In Total ← Quantity * TicketPrice, read the current values 2 and 25.00, multiply them to obtain 50.00, then store that result in Total. The arrow points to the destination on the left; the calculation uses the right-hand side.
steps.code: Total ← Quantity * TicketPrice

steps.title: Communicate a result with OUTPUT
steps.body: OUTPUT Total displays the current numeric value. OUTPUT "Total" displays the literal word Total instead. The quotation marks distinguish text supplied directly by the program from the name of a stored value.

steps.title: Keep the dependency order visible
steps.body: Read Quantity before calculating Total and calculate Total before displaying it. Group these effects as input, process and output. A declaration can appear before them to establish types, but it does not perform any of these three actions.

worked.title: Work out the change after a sufficient payment
worked.setup: For this separate trace, Cost is 75.00 and Paid is 100.00. Both are non-negative REAL values and Paid is at least Cost.

steps.title: Read the values in the stated order
steps.body: INPUT Cost stores 75.00; INPUT Paid stores 100.00. Change has not yet been assigned a value.

steps.title: Calculate and store the result
steps.body: Change ← Paid - Cost evaluates 100.00 - 75.00 and stores 25.00. Paid and Cost keep their values; using them in the subtraction does not remove them.

steps.title: Report and check
steps.body: OUTPUT Change displays 25.00. Reversing the subtraction gives -25.00 and violates the meaning of change. For exact payment of 75.00, the correct output is zero.

worked.conclusion: A trace records how the current values change and which outputs are actually produced.

check.prompt: Write a complete small algorithm to read a positive INTEGER Quantity, calculate its cost at 25.00 per ticket and output the text "Amount due" followed by the result. Include declarations.
check.answer:
CONSTANT TicketPrice = 25.00
DECLARE Quantity : INTEGER
DECLARE Total : REAL
INPUT Quantity
Total ← Quantity * TicketPrice
OUTPUT "Amount due", Total

challenge.prompt: A rental desk charges 4.00 per device plus one 10.00 deposit per order. Read Quantity and output AmountDue. State the result for 3 devices.
challenge.answer: Declare Quantity as INTEGER and AmountDue as REAL. INPUT Quantity; AmountDue ← Quantity * 4.00 + 10.00; OUTPUT AmountDue. For 3 devices the output is 22.00. Adding the deposit once per device would implement a different rule.

learningCycle.takeaway: Input obtains data, processing transforms it, and output communicates the result. Assignment stores the evaluated right-hand side.
learningCycle.bridge: We can now translate an ordinary written rule into statements without changing its meaning.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Let a condition choose the ticket price

leadVisual.title: Let a condition choose the ticket price

coreExplanation: Read Quantity and Student, then calculate Subtotal ← Quantity * 25.00. Doing this before the decision gives both possible branches the same undiscounted amount.
IF Student THEN selects the discounted calculation when Student is TRUE. ELSE selects the full subtotal when it is FALSE. Only the selected branch runs on one execution.

Place OUTPUT Total after ENDIF. Either branch assigns Total, so the output can use it whichever branch was selected. Two unconnected IF statements are not automatically equivalent to one IF with an ELSE.

Paid >= Total is TRUE when payment is sufficient, including exact payment. For Total 45, Paid 44 is FALSE and Paid 45 is TRUE. The symbols >= include the boundary; > would wrongly reject exact payment.

learningCycle.observe: Two buyers each request two tickets. Mina is a student and pays 45.00 after a 10% discount. Arun is not a student and pays 50.00. The quantity and unit price are the same; student status selects the calculation.

stimulus.title: Two routes from one subtotal
items: Student TRUE: pay 90% of 50.00
Student FALSE: pay the full 50.00
Expected totals: 45.00 and 50.00

learningCycle.question: How can one program charge students and other buyers differently?

prerequisite.title: A condition has a truth value
prerequisite.body: A BOOLEAN value is TRUE or FALSE. IF uses that value to choose an action. A 10% discount removes one tenth of the subtotal, leaving 90%, so multiply by 0.90. Inputs have the stated types and requested tickets are available.

steps.title: Calculate what both cases share
steps.body: Read Quantity and Student, then calculate Subtotal ← Quantity * 25.00. Doing this before the decision gives both possible branches the same undiscounted amount.

steps.title: Choose one branch
steps.body: IF Student THEN selects the discounted calculation when Student is TRUE. ELSE selects the full subtotal when it is FALSE. Only the selected branch runs on one execution.
steps.code:
IF Student THEN
    Total ← Subtotal * 0.90
ELSE
    Total ← Subtotal
ENDIF

steps.title: Continue after the decision
steps.body: Place OUTPUT Total after ENDIF. Either branch assigns Total, so the output can use it whichever branch was selected. Two unconnected IF statements are not automatically equivalent to one IF with an ELSE.

steps.title: Build conditions from comparisons
steps.body: Paid >= Total is TRUE when payment is sufficient, including exact payment. For Total 45, Paid 44 is FALSE and Paid 45 is TRUE. The symbols >= include the boundary; > would wrongly reject exact payment.

worked.title: Trace both student-status inputs
worked.setup: Quantity is 3 and TicketPrice is 25.00. Compare independent runs with Student TRUE and Student FALSE.

steps.title: Calculate the shared subtotal
steps.body: Both runs read Quantity 3 and calculate Subtotal = 3 × 25.00 = 75.00.

steps.title: Take the selected branch
steps.body: TRUE assigns Total = 75.00 × 0.90 = 67.50. FALSE assigns Total = 75.00. The other branch is skipped in each run.

steps.title: Follow the join and output
steps.body: Each execution continues after ENDIF and outputs its own Total once. The student run displays 67.50; the other displays 75.00.

worked.conclusion: Selection uses a truth-valued condition to choose which operations are executed.

check.prompt: Read a non-negative INTEGER Age. Output "Adult" when Age is at least 18 and "Minor" otherwise. Write the selection and give outputs for 17, 18 and 19.
check.answer:
DECLARE Age : INTEGER
INPUT Age
IF Age >= 18 THEN
    OUTPUT "Adult"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Minor"
ENDIF
// Outputs for 17, 18, 19: Minor, Adult, Adult

learningCycle.takeaway: Selection chooses a branch according to a condition. Preserve inclusive and exclusive boundaries.
learningCycle.bridge: Draw the same decision so that its possible paths can be followed visually.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Replace repeated additions with a FOR loop

leadVisual.title: Replace repeated additions with a FOR loop

coreExplanation: Starting from zero, add 2 to get 2, then 1 to get 3, then 3 to get 6, then 2 to get 8. The repeated actions are reading the next quantity and adding it to the current total.
FOR OrderNumber ← 1 TO 4 repeats its body for 1, 2, 3 and 4. The upper bound is included. OrderNumber is the loop counter; TotalTickets records a different quantity.
Initialise TotalTickets to zero before the loop. Put INPUT Quantity and the addition inside it. Put OUTPUT TotalTickets after NEXT OrderNumber so that only the completed total is displayed.
Record the new input and new total on each iteration. Resetting TotalTickets inside the loop would discard earlier additions. Reading Quantity only before the loop would repeatedly add one old value.

learningCycle.observe: Four valid requests contain 2, 1, 3 and 2 tickets. We want the total number requested. These quantities are teaching inputs for a count-controlled calculation; payment and available capacity are outside this small task.

stimulus.title: Four quantities, one running total
items: Inputs in order: 2, 1, 3, 2
Start with zero tickets counted
Read and add one new quantity at a time
Display the final total once

learningCycle.question: How can the desk total four requests without writing the same instructions four times?

prerequisite.title: Update from the old value
prerequisite.body: In TotalTickets ← TotalTickets + Quantity, evaluate the right side using the old TotalTickets, then replace it with the new value. This is an update, not an algebraic claim that a number equals itself plus another number.

steps.title: Perform the repeated work manually
steps.body: Starting from zero, add 2 to get 2, then 1 to get 3, then 3 to get 6, then 2 to get 8. The repeated actions are reading the next quantity and adding it to the current total.

steps.title: State the repetition count with FOR
steps.body: FOR OrderNumber ← 1 TO 4 repeats its body for 1, 2, 3 and 4. The upper bound is included. OrderNumber is the loop counter; TotalTickets records a different quantity.

steps.title: Place operations before, inside and after
steps.body: Initialise TotalTickets to zero before the loop. Put INPUT Quantity and the addition inside it. Put OUTPUT TotalTickets after NEXT OrderNumber so that only the completed total is displayed.

steps.title: Check the state after each pass
steps.body: Record the new input and new total on each iteration. Resetting TotalTickets inside the loop would discard earlier additions. Reading Quantity only before the loop would repeatedly add one old value.

worked.title: Write and trace the four-request total
worked.setup: Use the inputs 2, 1, 3, 2. All inputs are positive integers and the task requests one final total.

steps.title: Prepare the state
steps.body: Declare the three INTEGER variables and initialise the accumulator once. Its zero means no quantities have yet contributed.

steps.title: Write the repeated body
steps.body: Use one input and one addition per iteration. The same statements operate on each newly obtained Quantity.
steps.code:
DECLARE OrderNumber, Quantity, TotalTickets : INTEGER
TotalTickets ← 0
FOR OrderNumber ← 1 TO 4
    INPUT Quantity
    TotalTickets ← TotalTickets + Quantity
NEXT OrderNumber
OUTPUT TotalTickets

steps.title: Verify input count and final output
steps.body: The loop consumes four quantities and produces a final total of 8. The output is after the loop; 2, 3 and 6 are intermediate stored values, not required outputs.

worked.conclusion: Use a count-controlled loop when the required number of repetitions is known.

check.prompt: Read exactly three REAL payments and output their total once. Write the pseudocode and trace payments 25.00, 45.00 and 50.00.
check.answer:
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Paid, TotalPaid : REAL
TotalPaid ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 3
    INPUT Paid
    TotalPaid ← TotalPaid + Paid
NEXT Index
OUTPUT TotalPaid
// Running totals: 25.00, 70.00, 120.00. Final output: 120.00.

learningCycle.takeaway: Initialise once, repeat the input and update the specified number of times, then output the final aggregate.
learningCycle.bridge: The next total includes only inputs that meet a condition.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Add only the inputs that qualify

leadVisual.title: Add only the inputs that qualify

coreExplanation: For the small trial, use three iterations even though one value is negative. The negative entry still uses one input position. Reading until three positive values arrive would implement a different requirement.
After obtaining the new value, evaluate Value > 0. If it is TRUE, add Value to Total. If it is FALSE, leave Total unchanged and continue to the next iteration.
Total ← Total + Value adds the accepted amount. AcceptedCount ← AcceptedCount + 1 would count qualifying entries instead. With 2, -1, 3, the sum is 5 but the number of positive entries is 2.

Include required declarations and any requested input prompt. Initialise before repetition and output after it. For E086, extend the count to exactly 100 integers and prompt before each input; do not change the positive-value condition.

learningCycle.observe: A trial input list contains 2, -1 and 3. The rule for this small exercise is to total positive INTEGER values and ignore zero or negative values. It is a data-processing exercise, not a completed sale or a change to ticket availability.

stimulus.title: Predict the changing total
items: Read exactly 3 integers: 2, -1, 3
Initial total: 0
Add a value only when it is greater than 0
Expected final total: 5

learningCycle.question: How can the desk read every entry but add only positive quantities?

prerequisite.title: Keep loop count and accepted total separate
prerequisite.body: A FOR loop controls how many inputs are read. An IF inside the loop controls whether the current input contributes. The number of iterations is not the number of accepted inputs and neither is automatically their sum.

steps.title: Read every required input
steps.body: For the small trial, use three iterations even though one value is negative. The negative entry still uses one input position. Reading until three positive values arrive would implement a different requirement.

steps.title: Test the current value inside the loop
steps.body: After obtaining the new value, evaluate Value > 0. If it is TRUE, add Value to Total. If it is FALSE, leave Total unchanged and continue to the next iteration.

steps.title: Distinguish counting from totalling
steps.body: Total ← Total + Value adds the accepted amount. AcceptedCount ← AcceptedCount + 1 would count qualifying entries instead. With 2, -1, 3, the sum is 5 but the number of positive entries is 2.

steps.title: Prepare a complete response to the question
steps.body: Include required declarations and any requested input prompt. Initialise before repetition and output after it. For E086, extend the count to exactly 100 integers and prompt before each input; do not change the positive-value condition.

worked.title: Build the three-input algorithm
worked.setup: Read exactly three integers, prompt before each one and output the sum of the positive values once. Use 2, -1, 3.

steps.title: Initialise and choose the loop
steps.body: Declare Index, Value and Total as INTEGER. Set Total to zero before FOR Index ← 1 TO 3. This establishes one running total for the whole task.

steps.title: Place input and selection in the repeated body
steps.body: Each iteration prompts, reads a new Value and selects whether to add it. The indentation shows which operations belong to the loop.
steps.code:
DECLARE Index, Value, Total : INTEGER
Total ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 3
    OUTPUT "Input an integer value"
    INPUT Value
    IF Value > 0 THEN
        Total ← Total + Value
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total

steps.title: Check normal and empty-contribution cases
steps.body: The trial produces three prompts followed by final total 5. Inputs 0, -1, -3 still use all three iterations and give final total 0. No positive contribution does not mean no final output.

worked.conclusion: Sequence, iteration and selection cooperate, but each controls a different part of the solution.

check.prompt: Independently write pseudocode to read four INTEGER values and total only those from 30 through 70 inclusive. Give the result for 29, 30, 70, 71.
check.answer:
DECLARE Index, Value, Total : INTEGER
Total ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 4
    INPUT Value
    IF (Value >= 30) AND (Value <= 70) THEN
        Total ← Total + Value
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total
// Final output: 100. All four inputs are read.

challenge.prompt: Modify the four-value task so it outputs both the qualifying sum and the number of qualifying values. State both results for 29, 30, 70, 71.
challenge.answer: Initialise Total and AcceptedCount to zero before the loop. Inside the qualifying IF, add Value to Total and add 1 to AcceptedCount. After the loop output Total and AcceptedCount. The results are 100 and 2.

learningCycle.takeaway: Read each input once, test it inside the loop, update only on the qualifying branch and output the final result after repetition.
learningCycle.bridge: A fixed count does not suit every task. Next, let a condition determine when input stops.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Stop a WHILE loop when its condition becomes false

leadVisual.title: Stop a WHILE loop when its condition becomes false

coreExplanation: INPUT Quantity supplies the first value for Quantity > 0. Without an initial input, the condition would try to use an unavailable value. Initialise the running total before any additions.
WHILE Quantity > 0 tests before its body. If the first input is 0, the body runs zero times. The final output is still reached after ENDWHILE.

Inside the body, add the current positive Quantity and read the next Quantity. Execution returns to the test with that new value. Omitting the new input would keep retesting the old positive value indefinitely.
For 2, 1, 0, only 2 and 1 enter the body. Zero makes the condition FALSE and exits. The total is 3, and a first input of zero leaves the initial total at 0.

learningCycle.observe: For this separate input task, positive whole numbers are quantities and 0 means “finish”. The list is 2, 1, 0. Zero is a stopping signal and must not be treated as another request.

stimulus.title: A stream with an end signal
items: Inputs: 2, 1, 0
Continue while Quantity > 0
Do not process the stopping value
What if the very first input is 0?

learningCycle.question: How can the desk collect quantities when nobody knows how many entries will arrive?

prerequisite.title: Separate a stopping signal from ordinary data
prerequisite.body: All inputs in this task are non-negative integers and the supplied stream eventually contains 0. A sentinel is a special value used to signal an end. Test the current input before deciding whether to process it.

steps.title: Read the first value before the test
steps.body: INPUT Quantity supplies the first value for Quantity > 0. Without an initial input, the condition would try to use an unavailable value. Initialise the running total before any additions.

steps.title: Use WHILE as a pre-condition loop
steps.body: WHILE Quantity > 0 tests before its body. If the first input is 0, the body runs zero times. The final output is still reached after ENDWHILE.

steps.title: Make progress towards another test
steps.body: Inside the body, add the current positive Quantity and read the next Quantity. Execution returns to the test with that new value. Omitting the new input would keep retesting the old positive value indefinitely.

steps.title: Keep the exit value out of processing
steps.body: For 2, 1, 0, only 2 and 1 enter the body. Zero makes the condition FALSE and exits. The total is 3, and a first input of zero leaves the initial total at 0.

worked.title: Trace each condition check
worked.setup: Read non-negative quantities until 0 and output their total. Trace 2, 1, 0.

steps.title: Prepare and enter
steps.body: Set Total to zero and read 2. Since 2 > 0 is TRUE, enter the body and add 2.

steps.title: Update the value used by the condition
steps.body: Read 1 at the end of the body. The next test is TRUE, so add 1 and obtain total 3. Then read 0.

steps.title: Exit and report once
steps.body: The test 0 > 0 is FALSE. Skip the body and output 3 after ENDWHILE.
steps.code:
DECLARE Quantity, Total : INTEGER
Total ← 0
INPUT Quantity
WHILE Quantity > 0
    Total ← Total + Quantity
    INPUT Quantity
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Total

worked.conclusion: A WHILE loop may execute zero times because its condition is tested before the body.

check.prompt: Trace the algorithm for input 0, then for 4, 0. Explain what happens if the input at the end of the body is removed.
check.answer: Input 0 gives final output 0 without entering the body. Inputs 4, 0 give final output 4. Removing the new input makes a positive first value repeat indefinitely, repeatedly adding that same value; the condition never receives the stopping value.

learningCycle.takeaway: A pre-condition loop repeats while its condition is true; its body must allow the stopping condition to be reached.
learningCycle.bridge: Some tasks need the first action to happen before the condition can be tested.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use REPEAT when the body must run at least once

leadVisual.title: Use REPEAT when the body must run at least once

coreExplanation: REPEAT starts the body immediately. Display the prompt and read Quantity inside the body, then test the input at UNTIL. No earlier input is needed for this structure.

UNTIL Quantity > 0 stops when the quantity is acceptable. A FALSE result repeats the body; a TRUE result leaves the loop. This stopping meaning is the opposite of a WHILE condition that is true while repetition continues.
After 0, Quantity > 0 is FALSE, so ask again. The same happens for -2. After 3 it becomes TRUE, so leave the loop with Quantity holding 3.

Use REPEAT when the body must run before the first test. Use WHILE when the condition may prevent every execution of the body. Equivalent solutions are possible if their input placement and condition polarity are adjusted together.

learningCycle.observe: A request-entry task must ask for a positive whole-number quantity. The buyer enters 0, then -2, then 3. All entries are INTEGER values, but only the last satisfies this exercise’s rule.

stimulus.title: Ask, then decide whether to stop asking
items: Attempt 1: 0 → ask again
Attempt 2: -2 → ask again
Attempt 3: 3 → accept
The task must ask at least once

learningCycle.question: How can a loop test a quantity only after it has asked the buyer for one?

prerequisite.title: This example checks a range, not a type
prerequisite.body: Assume every supplied input is an INTEGER and that a positive value will eventually be supplied. We only check positivity here; ticket availability will be checked separately. The input must happen before its value can be tested.

steps.title: Place the first action before the condition
steps.body: REPEAT starts the body immediately. Display the prompt and read Quantity inside the body, then test the input at UNTIL. No earlier input is needed for this structure.

steps.title: State the condition that ends repetition
steps.body: UNTIL Quantity > 0 stops when the quantity is acceptable. A FALSE result repeats the body; a TRUE result leaves the loop. This stopping meaning is the opposite of a WHILE condition that is true while repetition continues.

steps.title: Trace rejected and accepted attempts
steps.body: After 0, Quantity > 0 is FALSE, so ask again. The same happens for -2. After 3 it becomes TRUE, so leave the loop with Quantity holding 3.

steps.title: Choose a loop from the required first behaviour
steps.body: Use REPEAT when the body must run before the first test. Use WHILE when the condition may prevent every execution of the body. Equivalent solutions are possible if their input placement and condition polarity are adjusted together.

worked.title: Request a positive quantity
worked.setup: Prompt for an INTEGER Quantity until it is positive, then output the accepted quantity. Use attempts 0, -2, 3.

steps.title: Write the action and stopping rule
steps.body: Put the prompt and input after REPEAT. End with UNTIL Quantity > 0. The loop itself gives every attempt a prompt.

steps.title: Follow the three tests
steps.body: The tests after 0 and -2 are FALSE, so both repeat. The test after 3 is TRUE and stops. The body executes three times; its minimum possible count is one.

steps.title: Use the accepted value afterwards
steps.body: OUTPUT Quantity after the loop displays only the accepted value 3. Rejected inputs are not output as accepted requests.
steps.code:
DECLARE Quantity : INTEGER
REPEAT
    OUTPUT "Enter a positive quantity"
    INPUT Quantity
UNTIL Quantity > 0
OUTPUT Quantity

worked.conclusion: The REPEAT condition describes when to stop, and it is tested after the body.

check.prompt: Rewrite the positive-quantity task using WHILE. Include the first input and the condition that means “another attempt is needed”.
check.answer:
DECLARE Quantity : INTEGER
OUTPUT "Enter a positive quantity"
INPUT Quantity
WHILE Quantity <= 0
    OUTPUT "Enter a positive quantity"
    INPUT Quantity
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Quantity

challenge.prompt: The quantity must also fit PlacesLeft. State an UNTIL condition and explain what the program should do before the loop when PlacesLeft is 0.
challenge.answer: For positive PlacesLeft, use UNTIL (Quantity >= 1) AND (Quantity <= PlacesLeft). When PlacesLeft is 0, no quantity can satisfy that rule. Report that no places are available and skip the request loop; do not trap the buyer in endless attempts.

learningCycle.takeaway: REPEAT tests after the body and executes at least once. Its UNTIL condition is true when repetition finishes.
learningCycle.bridge: We can now translate loops between words, diagrams and pseudocode with their test positions intact.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Translate a written rule into pseudocode

leadVisual.title: Translate a written rule into pseudocode

coreExplanation: “Read” is an action and “quantity” is the data it obtains. “Multiply” names the processing, while quantity and price are its operands. This separates instructions from the values on which they operate.

Translate reading into INPUT Quantity. Translate the calculation into Total ← Quantity * TicketPrice. Translate displaying the answer into OUTPUT Total. Choose meaningful names and declare the types required by their roles.
Keep the multiplier 25.00 and the original operation order. Changing names consistently is acceptable, but changing the price, adding a discount or displaying only Quantity changes the algorithm.

Follow both versions for Quantity 2 and then Quantity 3. Each should produce 50.00 and 75.00 respectively. Matching one example is useful evidence, but you must also check that the statements preserve the general rule.

learningCycle.observe: A volunteer’s card says: “Read a positive ticket quantity. Multiply it by 25.00. Display the total.” The result must remain the same when those words become pseudocode.

stimulus.title: A rule with an order
items: Read the quantity
Multiply quantity by the fixed ticket price
Display the calculated total
Do not invent a discount or extra fee

learningCycle.question: Which parts of an English instruction must survive when we change its notation?

prerequisite.title: Reuse the effects of statements
prerequisite.body: INPUT obtains a value, assignment stores a calculated result and OUTPUT displays a value or literal. Structured English uses controlled natural-language steps to make operations and their grouping clear.

steps.title: Underline actions and data separately
steps.body: “Read” is an action and “quantity” is the data it obtains. “Multiply” names the processing, while quantity and price are its operands. This separates instructions from the values on which they operate.

steps.title: Choose one statement for each effect
steps.body: Translate reading into INPUT Quantity. Translate the calculation into Total ← Quantity * TicketPrice. Translate displaying the answer into OUTPUT Total. Choose meaningful names and declare the types required by their roles.

steps.title: Preserve every stated rule
steps.body: Keep the multiplier 25.00 and the original operation order. Changing names consistently is acceptable, but changing the price, adding a discount or displaying only Quantity changes the algorithm.

steps.title: Check equivalence with actual values
steps.body: Follow both versions for Quantity 2 and then Quantity 3. Each should produce 50.00 and 75.00 respectively. Matching one example is useful evidence, but you must also check that the statements preserve the general rule.

worked.title: Translate a two-output receipt
worked.setup: Structured English: read the buyer’s name and ticket quantity; calculate the total at 25.00 each; display the name followed by the total. Assume available tickets and a positive whole-number quantity.

steps.title: List the data roles
steps.body: BuyerName is STRING, Quantity is INTEGER and Total is REAL. TicketPrice is the fixed constant 25.00. The name is displayed but is not an operand in the multiplication.

steps.title: Translate in order
steps.body: Read BuyerName, then Quantity; calculate Total; output BuyerName and Total. The result can now be written as a complete listing.
steps.code:
CONSTANT TicketPrice = 25.00
DECLARE BuyerName : STRING
DECLARE Quantity : INTEGER
DECLARE Total : REAL
INPUT BuyerName
INPUT Quantity
Total ← Quantity * TicketPrice
OUTPUT BuyerName, Total

steps.title: Trace against the written rule
steps.body: For "Mina" and 2, display Mina followed by 50.00. Quoting "BuyerName" would display the identifier’s spelling instead of the buyer’s name and would fail the rule.

worked.conclusion: Translation changes the representation while preserving operations, data dependencies and results.

check.prompt: Independently translate: read a non-negative distance in kilometres and a positive speed in kilometres per hour; divide distance by speed; display the journey time in hours.
check.answer:
DECLARE Distance, Speed, Hours : REAL
INPUT Distance
INPUT Speed
Hours ← Distance / Speed
OUTPUT Hours

learningCycle.takeaway: Structured English and pseudocode must express the same defined operations in the same required order.
learningCycle.bridge: Next, the written rule will choose between two possible calculations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Draw and follow a simple decision

leadVisual.title: Draw and follow a simple decision

coreExplanation: Use a terminator for start and end, a parallelogram for input or output, a rectangle for processing, and a diamond for a decision. Put the actual operation or condition inside the shape.

Label the diamond’s exits consistently as Yes/No or True/False. For Student TRUE, follow the branch calculating Subtotal × 0.90. The labels represent the truth of the condition, not whether the outcome is desirable.
Connect both Total assignments to the shared output. The join does not execute both assignments; it gives either completed branch a next instruction. Connect the output forward to the end.

Trace one student and one non-student request. Every required input must be reached before it is used, and exactly one Total must be output. A correct-looking collection of shapes with a missing arrow is not a complete flowchart.

learningCycle.observe: Place a buyer at a decision with two labelled exits: TRUE for a student and FALSE for another buyer. Follow only one exit, then return to the shared instruction that displays the total.

stimulus.title: A path to one output
items: Start and obtain Quantity and Student
Calculate Subtotal
Decision: Student?
TRUE gives a discount; FALSE keeps the subtotal
Join the paths and display Total

learningCycle.question: Can someone follow the student-discount rule using arrows alone?

prerequisite.title: A diagram must describe execution
prerequisite.body: You already know what INPUT, assignment, OUTPUT and IF do. A flowchart expresses those operations with standard symbols and directed connections. Position on the page alone does not determine the next operation; follow arrowheads.

steps.title: Give each symbol a specific job
steps.body: Use a terminator for start and end, a parallelogram for input or output, a rectangle for processing, and a diamond for a decision. Put the actual operation or condition inside the shape.

steps.title: Use the condition to choose a labelled exit
steps.body: Label the diamond’s exits consistently as Yes/No or True/False. For Student TRUE, follow the branch calculating Subtotal × 0.90. The labels represent the truth of the condition, not whether the outcome is desirable.

steps.title: Show where the paths rejoin
steps.body: Connect both Total assignments to the shared output. The join does not execute both assignments; it gives either completed branch a next instruction. Connect the output forward to the end.

steps.title: Verify the arrows with two traces
steps.body: Trace one student and one non-student request. Every required input must be reached before it is used, and exactly one Total must be output. A correct-looking collection of shapes with a missing arrow is not a complete flowchart.

worked.title: Draw an entry-height decision
worked.setup: Read a whole-number Height in centimetres. Display Enter for a height of at least 120; otherwise display Wait. End after that message.

steps.title: Place the shared beginning
steps.body: Connect Start to an input parallelogram labelled INPUT Height, then to a diamond labelled Height >= 120.

steps.title: Draw both outcomes and the end
steps.body: Yes leads to an output parallelogram labelled OUTPUT "Enter". No leads to OUTPUT "Wait". Connect both outputs to End without an arrow from one output to the other.

steps.title: Check the boundary paths
steps.body: 119 follows No and displays Wait. 120 and 121 follow Yes and display Enter. Replacing >= with > would change the result at 120.

worked.conclusion: A flowchart records operations and control flow through connected symbols and labelled decisions.

check.prompt: Independently draw a flowchart: input Temperature; below zero output Frost, otherwise output Clear; then end. Afterwards write its equivalent pseudocode.
check.answer: Start → INPUT Temperature → decision Temperature < 0. Yes → OUTPUT "Frost" → End; No → OUTPUT "Clear" → End. Equivalent code: INPUT Temperature; IF Temperature < 0 THEN OUTPUT "Frost" ELSE OUTPUT "Clear" ENDIF, with Temperature declared as REAL. Zero follows the Clear branch.

learningCycle.takeaway: Use suitable symbols, arrowheads and labelled decision paths, then trace each possible outcome.
learningCycle.bridge: Some ticket rules require more than one condition to be true.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Preserve behaviour in all four conversions

leadVisual.title: Preserve behaviour in all four conversions

coreExplanation: Identify the input, update and stopping rule in the words. “Read three quantities” means three inputs, not one input reused three times. Write the initialisation before the loop and the final output after it.

Start at the terminator and follow arrows. Recover which paths repeat and when each condition is tested. A decision reached before the repeated input may represent WHILE; do not choose a loop solely because a diamond appears.

Choose symbols for each required operation and connect them in order. Show both exits of a decision and where each goes. For a repeated operation, show the return path and the exit to the final output.
Expand FOR Index ← 1 TO 3 into Index ← 1, a test Index <= 3, a repeated body, Index ← Index + 1 and a return to the test. When Index reaches 4, exit without reading a fourth quantity.

Trace quantities 2, 1, 3 in both representations. The intermediate totals must be 2, 3, 6 and the only final output 6. Also inspect the control paths; one matching example cannot excuse a missing branch.

learningCycle.observe: Four boxes show the same task in words, pseudocode and two possible diagram arrangements: read three quantities and output their sum. The layout can change, but the input count, additions and final output must agree.

stimulus.title: Things every representation must preserve
items: Total starts at 0
Exactly 3 new quantities are read
Each quantity is added once
One final output happens after repetition

learningCycle.question: How can different-looking representations read exactly the same inputs and produce the same outputs?

prerequisite.title: Track execution rather than appearance
prerequisite.body: You know sequence, decisions, FOR, WHILE and REPEAT. When a FOR loop becomes a flowchart, show the counter’s initial value, comparison and update explicitly. A different arrangement of boxes is acceptable if its directed paths preserve the algorithm.

steps.title: Translate Structured English into pseudocode
steps.body: Identify the input, update and stopping rule in the words. “Read three quantities” means three inputs, not one input reused three times. Write the initialisation before the loop and the final output after it.

steps.title: Translate a flowchart into pseudocode
steps.body: Start at the terminator and follow arrows. Recover which paths repeat and when each condition is tested. A decision reached before the repeated input may represent WHILE; do not choose a loop solely because a diamond appears.

steps.title: Draw from Structured English
steps.body: Choose symbols for each required operation and connect them in order. Show both exits of a decision and where each goes. For a repeated operation, show the return path and the exit to the final output.

steps.title: Draw from pseudocode
steps.body: Expand FOR Index ← 1 TO 3 into Index ← 1, a test Index <= 3, a repeated body, Index ← Index + 1 and a return to the test. When Index reaches 4, exit without reading a fourth quantity.

steps.title: Use a shared trace to compare results
steps.body: Trace quantities 2, 1, 3 in both representations. The intermediate totals must be 2, 3, 6 and the only final output 6. Also inspect the control paths; one matching example cannot excuse a missing branch.

worked.title: Convert the three-input total into a flowchart
worked.setup: Source pseudocode initialises Total to zero, repeats input and addition with FOR Index ← 1 TO 3, then outputs Total.

steps.title: Expand the hidden loop control
steps.body: After Start, use a processing rectangle for Total ← 0 and Index ← 1, then a diamond for Index <= 3.

steps.title: Connect the repeated path
steps.body: Yes leads to INPUT Quantity, then Total ← Total + Quantity, then Index ← Index + 1. The arrow returns to the same diamond, not to the initialisation.

steps.title: Connect and verify the exit
steps.body: No leads to OUTPUT Total and End. With 2, 1, 3 the total becomes 6; Index then becomes 4 and the next test exits.

worked.conclusion: The expanded diagram preserves the count-controlled loop even though it makes its control operations visible.

check.prompt:
Complete four independent tasks before comparing answers.

A — Structured English to pseudocode: read a non-negative whole-number Age. Display "Adult" for an age of at least 18; otherwise display "Minor". Display exactly one message.

B — Flowchart to pseudocode: use the supplied flowchart labelled B. Level is an INTEGER percentage from 0 to 100. Preserve both branch outputs and state the result for Level 20.

C — Structured English to flowchart: read a positive whole-number Quantity; multiply it by 25.00 and store the result in Total; display Total; end.

D — Pseudocode to flowchart: use the supplied listing labelled D. Draw the initialisation, loop test, counter update, return path and final output explicitly.

image.alt: Task B flowchart: Start, input Level, decision Level less than 20. Yes leads to output Refill; No leads to output No action. Both outputs lead to End.
image.caption: B — Supplied flowchart. Write the equivalent pseudocode before opening the answer.

check.code:
DECLARE I, Value, Total : INTEGER
Total ← 0
FOR I ← 1 TO 2
    INPUT Value
    Total ← Total + Value
NEXT I
OUTPUT Total
check.answer: A: declare and input Age; use IF Age >= 18 THEN OUTPUT "Adult" ELSE OUTPUT "Minor" ENDIF. B: declare and input Level; use IF Level < 20 THEN OUTPUT "Refill" ELSE OUTPUT "No action" ENDIF. Level 20 outputs No action. C: Start → input parallelogram for Quantity → processing rectangle Total ← Quantity * 25.00 → output parallelogram for Total → End. D: initialise Total=0 and I=1; test I<=2; Yes → input Value → add Value to Total → increment I → return to the test; No → output Total → End. Both diagrams require connected symbols and labelled decision exits where applicable.

challenge.prompt: A diagram returns from Index ← Index + 1 to Total ← 0 rather than to the condition. What behaviour changes?
challenge.answer: The accumulator is reset on later iterations, losing earlier inputs. If the same initialisation also resets Index, the loop may never progress to its exit. The return must go to the condition after the initialisation has run once.

learningCycle.takeaway: Conversions preserve operations, conditions, repetition counts and execution order, not just vocabulary or visual shape.
learningCycle.bridge: Next, use these conversion skills for a task with two distinct input phases.

steps.title: Expand the hidden loop control
steps.body: After Start, use a processing rectangle for Total ← 0 and Index ← 1, then a diamond for Index <= 3.

steps.title: Connect the repeated path
steps.body: Yes leads to INPUT Quantity, then Total ← Total + Quantity, then Index ← Index + 1. The arrow returns to the same diamond, not to the initialisation.

steps.body: No leads to OUTPUT Total and End. With 2, 1, 3 the total becomes 6; Index then becomes 4 and the next test exits.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate waiting from collecting data

leadVisual.title: Separate waiting from collecting data

coreExplanation: The first task consumes inputs until the first 27. It does not add any of those values. The second task starts after that signal and accumulates later values until 0.
A REPEAT input UNTIL Value = 27 reads at least once and stops on the start signal. A 0 encountered here does not satisfy Value = 27, so waiting continues.
After the waiting loop finishes, initialise Total to zero and input the next Value. Do not add the Value still holding the starting 27. Use WHILE Value <> 0 to control the collecting loop.
Inside collection, add the current Value and input the next one. A later 27 is added because it is not 0. Output the total only after the collecting loop exits.

learningCycle.observe: Read 0, 5, 27, 4, 27, 0. The first 27 starts collection and is not added. After that point, add values until 0. Before the first 27, even 0 must be ignored.

stimulus.title: Mark the phase boundary before calculating
items: Waiting: 0, 5
Start signal: first 27
Collected data: 4, 27
Stop signal: final 0
Expected total: 31

learningCycle.question: Can the same number mean “ignore” in one phase and “stop” in another?

prerequisite.title: A sentinel has a role within a phase
prerequisite.body: Inputs are INTEGER values and the supplied stream contains a start signal followed eventually by a stop signal. You can use two loops in sequence. The value 27 is a start signal only while waiting; after collection starts, a later 27 is ordinary data.

steps.title: Describe the two tasks separately
steps.body: The first task consumes inputs until the first 27. It does not add any of those values. The second task starts after that signal and accumulates later values until 0.

steps.title: Choose a loop for waiting
steps.body: A REPEAT input UNTIL Value = 27 reads at least once and stops on the start signal. A 0 encountered here does not satisfy Value = 27, so waiting continues.

steps.title: Read fresh data when collection begins
steps.body: After the waiting loop finishes, initialise Total to zero and input the next Value. Do not add the Value still holding the starting 27. Use WHILE Value <> 0 to control the collecting loop.

steps.title: Place the update and final output
steps.body: Inside collection, add the current Value and input the next one. A later 27 is added because it is not 0. Output the total only after the collecting loop exits.

worked.title: Trace both phases before drawing
worked.setup: Use input sequence 0, 5, 27, 4, 27, 0.

steps.title: Finish the waiting phase
steps.body: Read 0 and 5 without adding either. Reading the first 27 makes the waiting condition true and ends that phase. No collection total includes that 27.

steps.title: Collect the subsequent values
steps.body: Start Total at zero. Read 4 and add it to make 4; read the next 27 and add it to make 31; read 0 and exit without adding another value.

steps.title: Draw the phase transition
steps.body: The waiting loop’s successful exit leads to the collection initialisation and a fresh input. The collection test has its own return arrow through addition and new input, and its exit leads to OUTPUT Total.

worked.conclusion: Separate control phases preserve the changing role of each sentinel value.

check.prompt: Before seeing the official answer, draw the complete flowchart. Then trace 27, 0 and 0, 27, 27, 0. Give the totals and identify which 27 is added.
check.answer: The two-loop flowchart waits for the first 27, initialises Total, reads a fresh value, then adds and reads again while Value <> 0. Inputs 27, 0 give total 0. Inputs 0, 27, 27, 0 give total 27: the first 0 is ignored, the first 27 starts collection and the second 27 is added.

challenge.prompt: Write equivalent pseudocode using a waiting loop followed by a collecting loop.
challenge.answer:
DECLARE Value, Total : INTEGER
REPEAT
    INPUT Value
UNTIL Value = 27
Total ← 0
INPUT Value
WHILE Value <> 0
    Total ← Total + Value
    INPUT Value
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Total

learningCycle.takeaway: When input has phases, define each phase’s start, processing and stopping rules before joining their control flow.
learningCycle.bridge: Separating these responsibilities prepares us to name cooperating program modules.

workedExample.title: Trace both phases before drawing
workedExample.setup: Use input sequence 0, 5, 27, 4, 27, 0.

steps.title: Finish the waiting phase
steps.body: Read 0 and 5 without adding either. Reading the first 27 makes the waiting condition true and ends that phase. No collection total includes that 27.

steps.title: Collect the subsequent values
steps.body: Start Total at zero. Read 4 and add it to make 4; read the next 27 and add it to make 31; read 0 and exit without adding another value.

steps.title: Draw the phase transition
steps.body: The waiting loop’s successful exit leads to the collection initialisation and a fresh input. The collection test has its own return arrow through addition and new input, and its exit leads to OUTPUT Total.

workedExample.conclusion: Separate control phases preserve the changing role of each sentinel value.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Refine an unfinished step into programmable actions

leadVisual.title: Refine an unfinished step into programmable actions

coreExplanation: CompletePayment must either confirm a sufficiently paid sale or reject underpayment. Keep this result visible so that each expansion serves the same purpose rather than adding unrelated features.
Expand the step into obtain payment, compare it with Total, perform successful-sale updates or report failure. This first expansion exposes the decision but still leaves arithmetic to define.

On success, Change ← Paid - Total and PlacesLeft ← PlacesLeft - Quantity provide the missing calculations. On failure, display insufficient payment and leave PlacesLeft unchanged. Use Paid >= Total to include exact payment.

A leaf such as “process payment correctly” is still unresolved. A comparison, assignment or output with defined operands can be programmed. Trace exact payment and underpayment to check that the refined version preserves the parent task.

items: High-level step: complete payment
Known values: Quantity, PlacesLeft, Total
New input required: Paid
Success and failure must have different effects

worked.title: Refine a selected-number total in words
worked.setup: Read exactly four INTEGER values and total only those from 30 to 70 inclusive. This smaller teaching task prepares the control structure used by E072.

steps.title: Write the high-level outline
steps.body: Obtain the values, decide which qualify, accumulate their contributions and report the total. This describes the jobs but does not yet state initial values, loop count or the complete condition.

steps.title: Resolve each unfinished detail
steps.body: Set Total to zero. Read the next value. If it is at least 30 and at most 70, add it to Total. Repeat the reading and decision until four values have been input. Output Total afterwards.

steps.title: Test the finished refinement
steps.body: For 29, 30, 70, 71, only 30 and 70 contribute, giving 100. Read all four inputs even though two are rejected. For E072, apply its stated count and requested five-step response in words.

worked.conclusion: A final refinement states enough detail for implementation without requiring invented rules.

check.prompt: Refine “calculate the ticket total” through an intermediate level to programmable operations. Use fixed price 25.00 and a 10% student discount.
check.answer: Intermediate: obtain Quantity and Student; calculate the undiscounted amount; select the final amount; display it. Final: INPUT Quantity; INPUT Student; Subtotal ← Quantity * 25.00; IF Student THEN Total ← Subtotal * 0.90 ELSE Total ← Subtotal ENDIF; OUTPUT Total. Declare suitable variables and assume a positive available quantity.

challenge.prompt: A refinement says “repeat input; add qualifying values; display total”. Name four details it must resolve.
challenge.answer: State the initial total; the exact repetition count or stopping rule; the full qualifying condition; and whether the total is displayed inside or after the loop. Also ensure each repetition reads a new value.

learningCycle.takeaway: Repeatedly expand unresolved steps until the operations, conditions and execution order can be programmed.
learningCycle.bridge: Use the same method to assemble a complete ticket purchase and challenge its branches.
