knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine conditions without changing the rule

leadVisual.title: Combine conditions without changing the rule

coreExplanation: Use (Quantity >= 1) AND (Quantity <= PlacesLeft). With eight places, quantity 0 fails the first condition and 9 fails the second. Quantities 1 and 8 satisfy both, so both boundaries are included.

A separate example offers an invitation to a performer OR a helper. Performer OR Helper is TRUE if either or both values are TRUE. This invitation example does not alter the student-only ticket discount.

NOT Available is TRUE when Available is FALSE. To reject the complete valid-quantity rule, use NOT ((Quantity >= 1) AND (Quantity <= PlacesLeft)), or equivalently (Quantity < 1) OR (Quantity > PlacesLeft).
Quantity >= 1 OR Quantity <= 8 wrongly admits both 0 and 9: each satisfies one side. Evaluate values at and just outside each boundary, and vary Boolean inputs independently.

learningCycle.observe: There are eight places left. Compare requests for 0, 1, 8 and 9 tickets. A quantity must be positive and must fit the remaining capacity. State both answers before combining them.

stimulus.title: Two restrictions on one request
items: At least one ticket: Quantity >= 1
No more than the available places: Quantity <= PlacesLeft
PlacesLeft = 8
Test 0, 1, 8 and 9

learningCycle.question: Does a request qualify if it satisfies only one of the quantity restrictions?

prerequisite.title: Compare first, combine second
prerequisite.body: Each comparison produces TRUE or FALSE. A compound expression combines these complete truth-valued conditions. Quantities and PlacesLeft are INTEGER values; PlacesLeft is non-negative.

steps.title: Require both restrictions with AND
steps.body: Use (Quantity >= 1) AND (Quantity <= PlacesLeft). With eight places, quantity 0 fails the first condition and 9 fails the second. Quantities 1 and 8 satisfy both, so both boundaries are included.

steps.title: Use OR for genuine alternatives
steps.body: A separate example offers an invitation to a performer OR a helper. Performer OR Helper is TRUE if either or both values are TRUE. This invitation example does not alter the student-only ticket discount.

steps.title: Reverse a whole condition with NOT
steps.body: NOT Available is TRUE when Available is FALSE. To reject the complete valid-quantity rule, use NOT ((Quantity >= 1) AND (Quantity <= PlacesLeft)), or equivalently (Quantity < 1) OR (Quantity > PlacesLeft).

steps.title: Choose counterexamples before trusting the expression
steps.body: Quantity >= 1 OR Quantity <= 8 wrongly admits both 0 and 9: each satisfies one side. Evaluate values at and just outside each boundary, and vary Boolean inputs independently.

worked.title: Add a cancellation status to entry
worked.setup: Entry is allowed when a ticket has been paid for and is not cancelled. Let PaidTicket and Cancelled be BOOLEAN inputs.

steps.title: Translate each requirement
steps.body: PaidTicket represents the first requirement. NOT Cancelled represents the requirement that cancellation must be false.

steps.title: Combine and test
steps.body: Use PaidTicket AND NOT Cancelled. (TRUE, FALSE) allows entry; (TRUE, TRUE) rejects it; (FALSE, FALSE) also rejects it.

steps.title: Challenge a wrong connector
steps.body: PaidTicket OR NOT Cancelled accepts an unpaid but uncancelled ticket. That counterexample shows why OR changes the rule, even though it gives the right answer for a paid uncancelled ticket.

worked.conclusion: The English requirements determine the operator; successful results for one case do not establish equivalence.

check.prompt: Write a condition accepting a REAL parcel mass from 2 to 5 kg inclusive. Write its rejection condition and evaluate 1.9, 2, 5 and 5.1.
check.answer: Accept: (Mass >= 2) AND (Mass <= 5). Reject: (Mass < 2) OR (Mass > 5), equivalently NOT ((Mass >= 2) AND (Mass <= 5)). Acceptance results are FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE.

challenge.prompt: An invitation is allowed for a performer or helper, but never for a suspended person. Construct the expression and test Performer TRUE, Helper FALSE, Suspended TRUE.
challenge.answer: (Performer OR Helper) AND NOT Suspended. The stated case is FALSE. Without the parentheses, the suspension rule may not apply to both qualifying roles as intended.

learningCycle.takeaway: AND requires both conditions; OR allows either or both; NOT reverses a truth value. Test boundaries and counterexamples.
learningCycle.bridge: Next, use conditions to control when payment is requested and when ticket availability can change.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Put decisions in an order that preserves the rules

leadVisual.title: Put decisions in an order that preserves the rules

coreExplanation: Reject a quantity below one or above PlacesLeft. On that route, do not request student status or payment. Those values are needed only after a valid request reaches the calculation.
For a valid request, calculate the subtotal and apply the student decision. Store or receive the numeric Total and display it. A later comparison must use that value, not the text of a message.
Read Paid after displaying Total. Only if Paid >= Total should the program calculate change, subtract Quantity from PlacesLeft and confirm the sale. Underpayment leaves PlacesLeft unchanged.

A later decision can be reached only through the preceding arrows or branches. Checking a high threshold first and sending its false path directly to the end may make a middle band unreachable. Trace a failing example before proposing a repair.

learningCycle.observe: A student requests two tickets from eight available places. The amount due is 45.00, but the buyer tenders only 40.00. The price calculation succeeds; the sale does not.

stimulus.title: Calculation and confirmation are different events
items: Quantity 2; PlacesLeft 8; Student TRUE
Subtotal 50.00; Total 45.00
Paid 40.00 is insufficient
Expected result: no sale; PlacesLeft stays 8

learningCycle.question: Should the desk reduce PlacesLeft as soon as it calculates a price?

prerequisite.title: A returned value can be used later
prerequisite.body: Imagine giving Quantity and Student to a calculation box. It sends back the numeric Total for the caller to use in Paid >= Total. That is a returned value. Printing 45.00 on a screen does not by itself supply a numeric result to another calculation. We use this idea before formal module design.

steps.title: Check quantity before asking for later data
steps.body: Reject a quantity below one or above PlacesLeft. On that route, do not request student status or payment. Those values are needed only after a valid request reaches the calculation.

steps.title: Calculate and keep the amount due
steps.body: For a valid request, calculate the subtotal and apply the student decision. Store or receive the numeric Total and display it. A later comparison must use that value, not the text of a message.

steps.title: Place state changes inside the success branch
steps.body: Read Paid after displaying Total. Only if Paid >= Total should the program calculate change, subtract Quantity from PlacesLeft and confirm the sale. Underpayment leaves PlacesLeft unchanged.

steps.title: Trace conditions in their actual order
steps.body: A later decision can be reached only through the preceding arrows or branches. Checking a high threshold first and sending its false path directly to the end may make a middle band unreachable. Trace a failing example before proposing a repair.

worked.title: Compare two payments for the same request
worked.setup: Use independent runs with Quantity 2, PlacesLeft 8, Student TRUE and TicketPrice 25.00. First use Paid 40.00, then Paid 45.00.

steps.title: Follow the common path
steps.body: The request fits the eight places. Subtotal is 50.00; the returned or stored Total is 45.00. Display that amount and obtain payment.

steps.title: Trace the insufficient-payment run
steps.body: 40.00 >= 45.00 is FALSE. Display insufficient payment. Skip the availability update, so PlacesLeft remains 8.

steps.title: Trace exact payment
steps.body: 45.00 >= 45.00 is TRUE. Change is zero, PlacesLeft becomes 6 and the sale is confirmed. Exact payment belongs on the success branch.

worked.conclusion: The branch controls both the output and whether stored state is allowed to change.

check.prompt: A design subtracts Quantity from PlacesLeft before testing Paid >= Total. Explain its result for the underpaid request and correct the placement.
check.answer: The design wrongly reduces PlacesLeft from 8 to 6 even though payment is rejected. Move the subtraction into the sufficient-payment branch, after the payment condition succeeds. A failed payment must preserve 8 places.

challenge.prompt: For the separate bonus task, bands are 0 below 2000, 10 from 2000 through 4000, and 100 above 4000. Give a decision order and test both boundaries.
challenge.answer: First test ValueOfSales >= 2000. If FALSE, bonus is 0. If TRUE, test ValueOfSales > 4000: TRUE gives 100, FALSE gives 10. Values 2000 and 4000 both receive 10; 1999 receives 0 and 4001 receives 100.

learningCycle.takeaway: Trace every reachable path and place each action under the condition that authorises it.
learningCycle.bridge: We can process one request correctly. Next, repeat defined operations for several requests.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Assemble and test one complete ticket purchase

leadVisual.title: Assemble and test one complete ticket purchase

coreExplanation: Use Quantity and PlacesLeft as INTEGER; Student as BOOLEAN; Subtotal, Total, Paid and Change as REAL. Check the quantity, calculate the charge and complete payment. The fixed price belongs to the rule rather than to buyer input.
Input Quantity and PlacesLeft, then test (Quantity >= 1) AND (Quantity <= PlacesLeft). A false result outputs Unavailable and ends this request before obtaining Student or Paid.
Input Student, multiply Quantity by TicketPrice, then select the discounted or full subtotal. Output Total before reading Paid. Each path leading to the payment comparison has now assigned Total.

If Paid >= Total, calculate change and reduce PlacesLeft by Quantity, then output confirmation, change and remaining places. Otherwise output Insufficient payment. Both paths end without an accidental second update.

Include zero quantity, quantity above availability, zero available places, exact payment, underpayment and both student-status values. Check which inputs are consumed as well as the final numerical results.

learningCycle.observe: Compare a valid student request with insufficient payment, an exact-payment request and a request larger than the available places. Decide which inputs should be requested and when PlacesLeft may change before viewing the full algorithm.

items: TicketPrice = 25.00; students pay 90% of the subtotal
Quantity must be at least 1 and no greater than PlacesLeft
Read Paid only after displaying Total
Confirm and reduce places only when Paid >= Total
Typed inputs: INTEGER Quantity and PlacesLeft; BOOLEAN Student; non-negative REAL Paid

learningCycle.question: Does every successful and rejected purchase obey the same stated rules?

prerequisite.title: This program handles one request
prerequisite.body: PlacesLeft is initially a non-negative integer. Quantity may be an invalid integer such as 0, so the program must check its permitted range. All input types are assumed correct. This version does not store bookings or repeat for another buyer.

steps.title: Write the data and responsibility plan
steps.body: Use Quantity and PlacesLeft as INTEGER; Student as BOOLEAN; Subtotal, Total, Paid and Change as REAL. Check the quantity, calculate the charge and complete payment. The fixed price belongs to the rule rather than to buyer input.

steps.title: Finish both sides of the first decision
steps.body: Input Quantity and PlacesLeft, then test (Quantity >= 1) AND (Quantity <= PlacesLeft). A false result outputs Unavailable and ends this request before obtaining Student or Paid.

steps.title: Calculate and display the amount on the valid path
steps.body: Input Student, multiply Quantity by TicketPrice, then select the discounted or full subtotal. Output Total before reading Paid. Each path leading to the payment comparison has now assigned Total.

steps.title: Update only after sufficient payment
steps.body: If Paid >= Total, calculate change and reduce PlacesLeft by Quantity, then output confirmation, change and remaining places. Otherwise output Insufficient payment. Both paths end without an accidental second update.

steps.title: Choose cases that distinguish the branches
steps.body: Include zero quantity, quantity above availability, zero available places, exact payment, underpayment and both student-status values. Check which inputs are consumed as well as the final numerical results.

worked.title: Build the successful path, then challenge it
worked.setup: Quantity 2, PlacesLeft 8, Student TRUE and Paid 50.00. The price is 25.00 and the discount is 10%.

steps.title: Validate and calculate
steps.body: 2 is within 1 to 8. The subtotal is 50.00 and the student total is 45.00. Display 45.00, then obtain payment 50.00.

steps.title: Complete the successful payment
steps.body: 50.00 >= 45.00 is TRUE. Store Change = 5.00 and PlacesLeft = 6, then output Confirmed, 5.00 and 6.

steps.title: Change one input and retrace
steps.body: With Paid 44.00, the amount due is still 45.00, but payment fails and PlacesLeft stays 8. With Quantity 9, reject before reading student status or payment. These traces test different branches rather than just different arithmetic.

worked.conclusion: The complete algorithm must preserve rules, input dependencies and state on every path.

check.prompt: Independently write the full pseudocode for the stated single-purchase rules. Trace Quantity 1, PlacesLeft 1, Student FALSE, Paid 25.00; then trace Quantity 0, PlacesLeft 8.
check.answer:
CONSTANT TicketPrice = 25.00
DECLARE Quantity, PlacesLeft : INTEGER
DECLARE Student : BOOLEAN
DECLARE Subtotal, Total, Paid, Change : REAL
INPUT Quantity
INPUT PlacesLeft
IF (Quantity >= 1) AND (Quantity <= PlacesLeft) THEN
    INPUT Student
    Subtotal ← Quantity * TicketPrice
    IF Student THEN
        Total ← Subtotal * 0.90
    ELSE
        Total ← Subtotal
    ENDIF
    OUTPUT Total
    INPUT Paid
    IF Paid >= Total THEN
        Change ← Paid - Total
        PlacesLeft ← PlacesLeft - Quantity
        OUTPUT "Confirmed", Change, PlacesLeft
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Insufficient payment"
    ENDIF
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Unavailable"
ENDIF
// First case: 25.00; Confirmed, 0.00, 0.
// Second case: Unavailable; do not request Student or Paid.

challenge.prompt: Extend the design to three buyers without reinitialising the available places for every buyer. Where should the loop and stock initialisation go?
challenge.answer: Obtain the initial PlacesLeft once before the three-buyer loop. Inside the loop read the next Quantity and run the request, charge and payment logic using the current PlacesLeft. Update it only on successful payment. Do not input the original stock again or restore it at the start of each iteration.

learningCycle.takeaway: A complete solution connects a suitable model, defined data, precise rules and correct control flow.
learningCycle.bridge: Next, keep the design method while replacing the familiar ticket rules with a different calculation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Transfer refinement to a different set of rules

leadVisual.title: Transfer refinement to a different set of rules

coreExplanation: Keep Amount as the complete REAL input. WholeDollars is a derived INTEGER value. They have related but different jobs: the original amount chooses the band, while whole dollars determine how many units earn points.
Test Amount < 10 for rate 5. Otherwise, test Amount <= 100 for rate 7. The remaining case is above 100 and uses rate 10. Values exactly 10 and exactly 100 belong to the middle band.

Discard the fractional part to obtain WholeDollars, then calculate Points = WholeDollars × Rate. The chosen rate applies to the entire whole-dollar amount. Nothing in the rule asks for separate portions charged at different rates.

Write input, band selection, whole-dollar conversion, multiplication and output as explicit actions. Use 100.50 to detect the mistake of truncating before band selection: that error would choose rate 7 instead of 10.

learningCycle.observe: A separate shop awards points. Below 10 dollars the rate is 5 per whole dollar; from 10 through 100 it is 7; above 100 it is 10. A spend of 100.50 belongs to the highest band even though its whole-dollar part is 100.

stimulus.title: New scenario, new rules
items: Amount 99.77: middle band; 99 whole dollars
Amount 100.50: highest band; 100 whole dollars
Choose the band from the original amount
Apply that rate to all whole dollars; no progressive slices

learningCycle.question: Which order of operations matters when a reward uses both spending bands and whole dollars?

prerequisite.title: Discarding a fraction is not rounding
prerequisite.body: For a non-negative amount, taking its whole-dollar part removes the fractional part: 99.77 becomes 99. It does not become 100. This lesson can express that operation in words; do not invent an unspecified function name. These reward rules do not alter the ticket-price rules.

steps.title: Separate the original amount from the derived value
steps.body: Keep Amount as the complete REAL input. WholeDollars is a derived INTEGER value. They have related but different jobs: the original amount chooses the band, while whole dollars determine how many units earn points.

steps.title: Select exactly one rate
steps.body: Test Amount < 10 for rate 5. Otherwise, test Amount <= 100 for rate 7. The remaining case is above 100 and uses rate 10. Values exactly 10 and exactly 100 belong to the middle band.

steps.title: Apply the rate after obtaining whole dollars
steps.body: Discard the fractional part to obtain WholeDollars, then calculate Points = WholeDollars × Rate. The chosen rate applies to the entire whole-dollar amount. Nothing in the rule asks for separate portions charged at different rates.

steps.title: Refine and challenge the order
steps.body: Write input, band selection, whole-dollar conversion, multiplication and output as explicit actions. Use 100.50 to detect the mistake of truncating before band selection: that error would choose rate 7 instead of 10.

worked.title: Compare two nearby amounts
worked.setup: Apply the reward rules independently to 99.77 and 100.50.

steps.title: Choose rates from the original values
steps.body: 99.77 is at least 10 and no greater than 100, so its rate is 7. 100.50 is greater than 100, so its rate is 10.

steps.title: Obtain the whole-dollar quantities
steps.body: Discard the fractional parts: 99.77 gives 99 whole dollars and 100.50 gives 100. Keep each selected rate with its own original transaction.

steps.title: Calculate and verify
steps.body: 99 × 7 = 693 points. 100 × 10 = 1000 points. Rounding 99.77 to 100 would wrongly give 700; choosing a band after truncating 100.50 would also wrongly give 700.

worked.conclusion: Correct refinement preserves the meaning and required order of each transformation.

check.prompt: Give a five-step refinement in words for this calculation. Then state the points for Amount 10.00 and Amount 100.00.
check.answer: 1. Read Amount. 2. Choose rate 5 below 10, otherwise rate 7 up to and including 100, otherwise rate 10. 3. Discard the fractional dollar part to obtain WholeDollars. 4. Multiply WholeDollars by the selected rate. 5. Output Points. Amount 10.00 earns 70; Amount 100.00 earns 700.

challenge.prompt: A learner proposes “award 5 points for each of the first 10 dollars, then 7 for the next dollars”. Explain why that is a different algorithm.
challenge.answer: That proposal uses progressive slices. The stated rule selects one rate from the whole original amount and applies it to all whole dollars. For 99.77 the correct calculation is 99 × 7, not a sum of portions at different rates.

learningCycle.takeaway: A new scenario requires its own rules; refinement must preserve their boundaries, transformations and dependencies.
learningCycle.bridge: Finally, design a solution for an unfamiliar situation without copying the ticket algorithm.

coreExplanation: Retain requested quantity, available devices, payment and the fixed charging rule. Record the successful-hire count because the final output requires it. Poster colours and individual device serial numbers are outside this quantity-only task.

Use responsibilities for quantity checking, charge calculation and payment completion. A charge function can receive Quantity and return Quantity * 4.00 + 10.00. Refine each responsibility into statements; naming it alone is not an implementation.

Initialise DevicesLeft to 5 and SuccessfulHires to zero once before a three-iteration loop. Every iteration reads a fresh Quantity. Increment SuccessfulHires and reduce stock only after sufficient payment; then proceed to the next request.

Write pseudocode and a flowchart for the same solution. In the diagram, show the loop count explicitly and let each success or rejection route return to the next iteration. Translate one selected branch into Structured English without changing its conditions.

learningCycle.observe: A science club takes exactly three equipment-hire requests. Available devices begin at 5. Each accepted request costs 4.00 per device plus one 10.00 deposit per order. There is no student discount. Confirm only when the quantity fits and payment is sufficient.

items: Process exactly 3 requests; start with 5 devices
Quantity must be at least 1 and no greater than DevicesLeft
Charge = Quantity × 4.00 + 10.00 per accepted order
Display Charge, then read Paid, only for a quantity that fits
Success: reduce devices and output Confirmed with the change
Failure: output Unavailable or Insufficient payment; preserve the stock
After all requests, output the number of successful hires

prerequisite.title: Use the method without assuming the old rules
prerequisite.body: Quantity and DevicesLeft are INTEGER; Paid and Charge are REAL; supplied payment is non-negative and all input types are correct. Devices are not returned during these three requests. Attempt the design and its checks before opening a worked answer.

steps.title: Produce a purpose-specific model
steps.body: Retain requested quantity, available devices, payment and the fixed charging rule. Record the successful-hire count because the final output requires it. Poster colours and individual device serial numbers are outside this quantity-only task.

steps.title: Decompose and refine the work
steps.body: Use responsibilities for quantity checking, charge calculation and payment completion. A charge function can receive Quantity and return Quantity * 4.00 + 10.00. Refine each responsibility into statements; naming it alone is not an implementation.

steps.title: Place state and repetition deliberately
steps.body: Initialise DevicesLeft to 5 and SuccessfulHires to zero once before a three-iteration loop. Every iteration reads a fresh Quantity. Increment SuccessfulHires and reduce stock only after sufficient payment; then proceed to the next request.

steps.title: Create and compare representations

steps.title: Use evidence to identify the next learning need

worked.setup: Use three requests: Quantity 2 with Paid 20.00; Quantity 4; Quantity 3 with Paid 21.00. Start with 5 devices and zero successful hires.

steps.title: Trace a successful hire
steps.body: The first quantity fits. Charge is 2 × 4.00 + 10.00 = 18.00. Payment 20.00 succeeds, giving change 2.00, DevicesLeft 3 and SuccessfulHires 1. The deposit is charged once for the order.

steps.title: Trace a request that cannot be met
steps.body: Quantity 4 exceeds the current DevicesLeft 3. Reject without asking for payment. The two stored counts remain 3 devices and 1 successful hire.

steps.title: Trace underpayment and the final report
steps.body: Quantity 3 fits and requires 3 × 4.00 + 10.00 = 22.00. Paid 21.00 is insufficient, so stock and successful count remain unchanged. After all three requests, output SuccessfulHires = 1.

worked.conclusion: Independent design succeeds when the model, representations and traces all implement the new brief rather than the previous example.

check.prompt:
New independent brief: a parcel desk reads exactly five non-negative REAL masses. Accept masses from 2 to 5 kg inclusive. After all five inputs, output the accepted count. If that count is positive, also output the mean mass of the accepted parcels; otherwise output "No accepted parcels". All inputs have the stated type.

Produce an abstract model, an identifier table with purposes, named responsibilities with their data, complete pseudocode and a matching flowchart. Trace inputs 1.9, 2, 3.5, 5, 5.1 and a set with no accepted masses. Explain why the mean is calculated after the loop and why zero accepted parcels need a separate path.

challenge.prompt: Return to the equipment-hire brief. Write the complete three-request pseudocode and use a named deposit constant. Explain what changes if the deposit becomes 12.00 per order.
challenge.answer:
CONSTANT DevicePrice = 4.00
CONSTANT Deposit = 10.00
DECLARE RequestNumber, Quantity, DevicesLeft, SuccessfulHires : INTEGER
DECLARE Charge, Paid, Change : REAL
DevicesLeft ← 5
SuccessfulHires ← 0
FOR RequestNumber ← 1 TO 3
    INPUT Quantity
    IF (Quantity >= 1) AND (Quantity <= DevicesLeft) THEN
        Charge ← Quantity * DevicePrice + Deposit
        OUTPUT Charge
        INPUT Paid
        IF Paid >= Charge THEN
            Change ← Paid - Charge
            DevicesLeft ← DevicesLeft - Quantity
            SuccessfulHires ← SuccessfulHires + 1
            OUTPUT "Confirmed", Change
        ELSE
            OUTPUT "Insufficient payment"
        ENDIF
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Unavailable"
    ENDIF
NEXT RequestNumber
OUTPUT SuccessfulHires
// New deposit: change its constant definition to 12.00 and retest.
// For 2 paid 20; 4 unavailable; 3 paid 21: final count 1, stock 3.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Count seats and represent a price

leadVisual.title: Count seats and represent a price

coreExplanation: Seats can be 0, 1, 2 or 3. INTEGER represents whole numbers, including negative whole numbers. A separate rule must reject a negative seat count; choosing INTEGER alone does not enforce the booking rules.
A price can be 12.50 or 8.75. REAL allows a fractional part. A current price of 10.00 does not justify INTEGER if later prices may be fractional.
DECLARE Seats : INTEGER specifies a name and a type. Seats <- 3 explicitly gives it the value 3. Read <- as “is assigned”; it stores the right-hand value in the left-hand variable.

learningCycle.observe: Place three seat cards beside a price label of 12.50. Both facts use digits, but only one may take a fractional value. Decide which future values each fact must allow.

stimulus.title: One event booking
items: Seats requested: 3
Price per seat: 12.50
Another permitted price: 8.75

learningCycle.question: Why can a booking contain 3 seats and a price of 12.50, but not 3.5 seats?

prerequisite.title: Recall a variable
prerequisite.body: A variable is a named storage location whose value can change while a program runs. An identifier such as Seats is its name. A data type describes the values it can represent and the operations that are appropriate.

steps.title: Choose INTEGER for whole-number counts
steps.body: Seats can be 0, 1, 2 or 3. INTEGER represents whole numbers, including negative whole numbers. A separate rule must reject a negative seat count; choosing INTEGER alone does not enforce the booking rules.

steps.title: Choose REAL when fractions are allowed
steps.body: A price can be 12.50 or 8.75. REAL allows a fractional part. A current price of 10.00 does not justify INTEGER if later prices may be fractional.

steps.title: Declare before storing
steps.body: DECLARE Seats : INTEGER specifies a name and a type. Seats <- 3 explicitly gives it the value 3. Read <- as “is assigned”; it stores the right-hand value in the left-hand variable.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
DECLARE Price : REAL
Seats <- 3
Price <- 12.50

worked.title: Choose a type from the requirement
worked.setup: An event stores the number of tickets and the mass of equipment in kilograms. Today the mass happens to be 20.0.

steps.title: List possible values
steps.body: Tickets must be whole units, so choose INTEGER. Equipment can weigh 20.4 kg tomorrow, so choose REAL even though today’s reading has no fractional part.

steps.title: Check two invalid proposals
steps.body: A value of -2 is an INTEGER but is unsuitable as a booking count. A value of 2.5 is unsuitable for Seats because it is not a whole number. These are different reasons for rejection.

worked.conclusion: Choose the type from all permitted values, then apply any additional rules required by the task.

check.prompt: An event stores distances in whole centimetres only. Must Distance be REAL because distance is a measurement?
check.answer: No. INTEGER is suitable when the stated representation allows only whole centimetres. REAL is needed if fractional centimetres must be retained. Read the required unit and permitted precision.

learningCycle.takeaway: INTEGER represents whole numbers; REAL is suitable when fractional values are required.
learningCycle.bridge: Some values contain digits without representing a quantity. Treat those as text.

steps.body: A value of -2 is an INTEGER but is unsuitable as a booking count. A value of 2.5 is unsuitable for Seats because it is not a whole number. These are different reasons for rejection.

workedExample.conclusion: Choose the type from all permitted values, then apply any additional rules required by the task.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Preserve names, letters and leading zeros

leadVisual.title: Preserve names, letters and leading zeros

coreExplanation: A zone represented by exactly one letter fits CHAR. In Cambridge pseudocode a character literal uses single quotation marks, such as 'C'. A space or digit can also be one character.

A name and a booking code need STRING. A STRING can have one character, many characters, or no characters. Double quotation marks identify string literals; "C" is therefore a STRING even though it contains one character.

The string "0072" retains its leading zeros. The integer 72 represents a quantity and does not retain the four-character code. A telephone number is another identifier whose digits do not make arithmetic appropriate.

learningCycle.observe: Compare a name card Mina, a zone letter C and the printed code 0072. The code must keep all four characters and will not be added or multiplied.

stimulus.title: Details printed on a booking card
items: Name: Mina
Zone: C
Booking code: 0072

learningCycle.question: Should booking code 0072 be stored as the number 72?

prerequisite.title: Recall a literal
prerequisite.body: A literal is a value written directly in pseudocode. Its notation matters: 72 is an INTEGER literal, while "0072" is a STRING literal.

steps.title: Store one character with CHAR
steps.body: A zone represented by exactly one letter fits CHAR. In Cambridge pseudocode a character literal uses single quotation marks, such as 'C'. A space or digit can also be one character.

steps.title: Store a sequence with STRING
steps.body: A name and a booking code need STRING. A STRING can have one character, many characters, or no characters. Double quotation marks identify string literals; "C" is therefore a STRING even though it contains one character.

steps.title: Choose meaning over appearance
steps.body: The string "0072" retains its leading zeros. The integer 72 represents a quantity and does not retain the four-character code. A telephone number is another identifier whose digits do not make arithmetic appropriate.
steps.code:
DECLARE Name : STRING
DECLARE Zone : CHAR
DECLARE BookingCode : STRING
Name <- "Mina"
Zone <- 'C'
BookingCode <- "0072"

worked.title: Read the values without changing their types
worked.setup: Consider '7', "7", 7 and "".

steps.title: Use the notation
steps.body: '7' is one CHAR. "7" is a one-character STRING. 7 is an INTEGER. Their visual similarity does not make them interchangeable.

steps.title: Explain the empty value
steps.body: "" is an empty STRING with length zero. It is not the same as " ", which contains one space, and is not a valid character literal containing one character.

worked.conclusion: Read quotation marks and the required meaning before naming the type.

check.prompt: A zone can now be C, D or AB. Is CHAR still suitable, and why?
check.answer: No. AB needs two characters. Choose STRING for a field that must represent all three permitted zone labels.

learningCycle.takeaway: CHAR stores one character; STRING stores text, including digit sequences used as identifiers.
learningCycle.bridge: A yes/no state needs a logical value rather than a text label.

workedExample.title: Read the values without changing their types
workedExample.setup: Consider '7', "7", 7 and "".

steps.title: Use the notation
steps.body: '7' is one CHAR. "7" is a one-character STRING. 7 is an INTEGER. Their visual similarity does not make them interchangeable.

steps.title: Explain the empty value
steps.body: "" is an empty STRING with length zero. It is not the same as " ", which contains one space, and is not a valid character literal containing one character.

workedExample.conclusion: Read quotation marks and the required meaning before naming the type.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Store whether a booking is confirmed

leadVisual.title: Store whether a booking is confirmed

coreExplanation: BOOLEAN has exactly two values: TRUE and FALSE. FALSE is a meaningful stored state, not missing data. Use unquoted values; "FALSE" is text.
A declaration names the variable and its type but does not explicitly initialise it. Confirmed <- FALSE establishes the starting state. When confirmation arrives, assign TRUE.
A single BOOLEAN can answer a yes/no question. If a field must distinguish pending, confirmed and cancelled, those are three states and need a representation with more than two possible values.

learningCycle.observe: A booking moves from unconfirmed to confirmed. There are two possible answers to the question “Is it confirmed?” Predict the starting value and the later value.

stimulus.title: One yes/no question
items: Is the booking confirmed?
Before confirmation: no
After confirmation arrives: yes

learningCycle.question: What should Confirmed contain before the confirmation arrives?

prerequisite.title: Recall a condition
prerequisite.body: A condition is an expression evaluated as TRUE or FALSE. An IF statement performs its action only when its condition is TRUE. A BOOLEAN variable can store that result.

steps.title: Use the two Boolean values
steps.body: BOOLEAN has exactly two values: TRUE and FALSE. FALSE is a meaningful stored state, not missing data. Use unquoted values; "FALSE" is text.

steps.title: Assign the starting state
steps.body: A declaration names the variable and its type but does not explicitly initialise it. Confirmed <- FALSE establishes the starting state. When confirmation arrives, assign TRUE.
steps.code:
DECLARE Confirmed : BOOLEAN
Confirmed <- FALSE
Confirmed <- TRUE
IF Confirmed THEN
    OUTPUT "Booking confirmed"
ENDIF

steps.title: Check the number of states needed
steps.body: A single BOOLEAN can answer a yes/no question. If a field must distinguish pending, confirmed and cancelled, those are three states and need a representation with more than two possible values.

worked.title: Follow the state rather than the label
worked.setup: Confirmed starts as FALSE, then is assigned TRUE.

steps.title: Before the update
steps.body: IF Confirmed evaluates to FALSE, so the output is skipped. The variable still has a valid Boolean value.

steps.title: After the update
steps.body: The condition is TRUE, so the message appears. The stored value has changed; its declared BOOLEAN type has not.

worked.conclusion: Keep the data type, the current value and the decision made from that value separate.

check.prompt: Paid is BOOLEAN. Correct Paid <- "FALSE" and explain the correction.
check.answer: Write Paid <- FALSE. Without quotation marks, FALSE is a BOOLEAN literal. "FALSE" is a STRING and is incompatible with the declared type.

learningCycle.takeaway: Use BOOLEAN for a state with exactly two alternatives, and initialise it explicitly.
learningCycle.bridge: The event day is a calendar value, so its type and format also matter.

workedExample.title: Follow the state rather than the label
workedExample.setup: Confirmed starts as FALSE, then is assigned TRUE.

steps.title: Before the update
steps.body: IF Confirmed evaluates to FALSE, so the output is skipped. The variable still has a valid Boolean value.

steps.title: After the update
steps.body: The condition is TRUE, so the message appears. The stored value has changed; its declared BOOLEAN type has not.

workedExample.conclusion: Keep the data type, the current value and the decision made from that value separate.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Interpret a calendar date

leadVisual.title: Interpret a calendar date

coreExplanation: DATE represents a calendar date. In this course use the Cambridge dd/mm/yyyy convention: the first part is the day and the second part is the month. Thus 09/04/2027 represents 9 April 2027.
31/04/2027 has the expected pattern, but April has only 30 days. A matching pattern does not make an impossible date valid.
EventDate <- 09/04/2027 assigns a DATE literal. The value "09/04/2027" is a STRING literal because it is enclosed in double quotation marks.

learningCycle.observe: The booking desk uses dd/mm/yyyy. Read the day, month and year separately before deciding whether the whole date is valid.

stimulus.title: The desk uses dd/mm/yyyy
items: Proposed event date: 09/04/2027
Another proposed date: 31/04/2027
Text received: "09/04/2027"

learningCycle.question: Does 09/04/2027 mean 9 April or 4 September?

prerequisite.title: Recall text versus a typed value
prerequisite.body: Quotation marks denote a STRING literal. A date-shaped string is still text until it is interpreted as a date. Appearance alone does not establish the data type.

steps.title: State the date convention
steps.body: DATE represents a calendar date. In this course use the Cambridge dd/mm/yyyy convention: the first part is the day and the second part is the month. Thus 09/04/2027 represents 9 April 2027.
steps.code:
DECLARE EventDate : DATE
EventDate <- 09/04/2027

steps.title: Check the calendar as well as the format
steps.body: 31/04/2027 has the expected pattern, but April has only 30 days. A matching pattern does not make an impossible date valid.

steps.title: Separate a date from date-shaped text
steps.body: EventDate <- 09/04/2027 assigns a DATE literal. The value "09/04/2027" is a STRING literal because it is enclosed in double quotation marks.

worked.title: Read and check a booking day
worked.setup: A booking asks for 06/11/2027 using dd/mm/yyyy.

steps.title: Interpret the parts
steps.body: 06 is the day, 11 is the month and 2027 is the year: 6 November 2027.

steps.title: Assess a replacement
steps.body: Changing the day to 31 would give 31 November. November has 30 days, so reject that proposed date.

worked.conclusion: A DATE needs an unambiguous format and a valid calendar day.

check.prompt: A variable is assigned "12/05/2027". What type does the literal have?
check.answer: STRING. The double quotation marks make it text, even though its characters resemble a date.

learningCycle.takeaway: Use DATE for calendar values; read the format and literal notation carefully.
learningCycle.bridge: Now combine the types in one small sequence and trace its assignments.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace a declaration, an assignment and an update

leadVisual.title: Trace a declaration, an assignment and an update

coreExplanation: In DECLARE Seats : INTEGER, Seats is the identifier and INTEGER is its type. Seats <- 3 assigns the current value. Changing that value does not change the identifier or type.
For Seats <- Seats + 1, read the old Seats value 3, calculate 4, and store 4 on the left. The old 3 is replaced. For Total <- Seats * Price, Seats and Price are read while Total is changed.
The booking code keeps its leading zeros. Only Seats and Confirmed change after their initial assignments.

learningCycle.observe: Treat Seats as a labelled box containing 3. First read its old value, then calculate 3 + 1, then replace its contents. The assignment arrow describes a sequence, not a mathematical equation.

stimulus.title: Trace in statement order
items: DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
Seats <- 3
Seats <- Seats + 1

learningCycle.question: Why does Seats <- Seats + 1 make sense when Seats is 3?

prerequisite.title: Recall how to trace
prerequisite.body: A trace follows statements in execution order and records values after each statement. Initialise a variable before reading its old value. DECLARE alone is not an instruction to set it to zero.

steps.title: Name the three separate facts
steps.body: In DECLARE Seats : INTEGER, Seats is the identifier and INTEGER is its type. Seats <- 3 assigns the current value. Changing that value does not change the identifier or type.

steps.title: Evaluate the right side first
steps.body: For Seats <- Seats + 1, read the old Seats value 3, calculate 4, and store 4 on the left. The old 3 is replaced. For Total <- Seats * Price, Seats and Price are read while Total is changed.

steps.title: Trace a complete small program
steps.body: The booking code keeps its leading zeros. Only Seats and Confirmed change after their initial assignments.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
DECLARE Price : REAL
DECLARE BookingCode : STRING
DECLARE Confirmed : BOOLEAN
Seats <- 3
Price <- 12.50
BookingCode <- "0072"
Confirmed <- FALSE
Seats <- Seats + 1
Confirmed <- TRUE
OUTPUT Seats
OUTPUT BookingCode
OUTPUT Confirmed

worked.title: Record only changes caused by each statement
worked.setup: Start the program above with no values explicitly assigned.

steps.title: Trace the updates
steps.body: Seats becomes 3 and later 4. BookingCode becomes "0072" and is not changed. Confirmed becomes FALSE and later TRUE.

steps.title: Read the output
steps.body: The displayed values are 4, 0072 and TRUE on separate lines. The program does not display Price merely because it has been declared and assigned.

worked.conclusion: A trace records the effects of executed statements; it does not invent automatic values or outputs.

check.prompt: Seats is 2. After Seats <- Seats + 3 and Other <- Seats, which variable contains 5?
check.answer: Both Seats and Other contain 5 after the two assignments. The second assignment reads Seats and stores that value in Other; it does not move or remove the value from Seats.

learningCycle.takeaway: Declare the type, initialise the value, then evaluate each assignment from right to left.
learningCycle.bridge: One variable handles one value. A growing booking system also needs collections and saved data.

workedExample.title: Record only changes caused by each statement
workedExample.setup: Start the program above with no values explicitly assigned.

steps.title: Trace the updates
steps.body: Seats becomes 3 and later 4. BookingCode becomes "0072" and is not changed. Confirmed becomes FALSE and later TRUE.

steps.title: Read the output
steps.body: The displayed values are 4, 0072 and TRUE on separate lines. The program does not display Price merely because it has been declared and assigned.

workedExample.conclusion: A trace records the effects of executed statements; it does not invent automatic values or outputs.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish one value, a collection and a saved file

leadVisual.title: Distinguish one value, a collection and a saved file

coreExplanation: An ARRAY groups elements with a common declared type under one identifier. Names[1], Names[2] and Names[3] can retain different strings at the same time. The number inside brackets selects an element.
A file stores saved data for later use. Writing the names to a text file allows another execution to read them. Holding the names in an array alone does not save them between runs.

coreExplanation: A record is a composite data structure that groups related fields under one identifier. The fields can have different types. Their names explain which fact each value represents.
TYPE and ENDTYPE enclose the field declarations. BookingRecord is the name of the new type. This definition describes the structure; it does not yet create a booking variable.
DECLARE Booking : BookingRecord creates a variable with those fields. Another variable of BookingRecord has the same structure but can hold a different booking.

prerequisite.title: Recall names and types
prerequisite.body: STRING suits the name, INTEGER the seat count and BOOLEAN the payment state. A field is a named part of a record, with its own declared type.

steps.title: Group related fields
steps.body: A record is a composite data structure that groups related fields under one identifier. The fields can have different types. Their names explain which fact each value represents.

steps.title: Define a reusable record type
steps.body: TYPE and ENDTYPE enclose the field declarations. BookingRecord is the name of the new type. This definition describes the structure; it does not yet create a booking variable.
steps.code:
TYPE BookingRecord
    DECLARE Name : STRING
    DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
    DECLARE Paid : BOOLEAN
ENDTYPE

steps.title: Create a variable of that type
steps.body: DECLARE Booking : BookingRecord creates a variable with those fields. Another variable of BookingRecord has the same structure but can hold a different booking.

DECLARE AnotherBooking : BookingRecord

check.prompt: Can a record contain a STRING, an INTEGER and a BOOLEAN? Must every field have the same type?

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read and change a named field

leadVisual.title: Read and change a named field

coreExplanation: Booking.Seats means the Seats field inside the record variable Booking. BookingRecord names the type; Booking names one variable of that type. Use the variable name when accessing its current fields.
This complete example inputs two fields, explicitly initialises Paid, then changes only Seats.

Two variables can share a record type without sharing their current data. Updating AnotherBooking.Name does not instruct the program to update Booking.Name. The variable name identifies which record is being accessed.

learningCycle.observe: Mina adds a seat to an existing booking. Her name and payment state should remain as they were. Identify the precise field the program must update.
learningCycle.question: Which part changes when Booking.Seats is increased by one?

prerequisite.title: Recall assignment and INPUT
prerequisite.body: INPUT stores entered data in its destination. Assignment evaluates the right side and replaces the left-side value. OUTPUT reads and displays a value without changing it.

steps.title: Read the dot notation
steps.body: Booking.Seats means the Seats field inside the record variable Booking. BookingRecord names the type; Booking names one variable of that type. Use the variable name when accessing its current fields.

steps.title: Input, initialise and update fields
steps.body: This complete example inputs two fields, explicitly initialises Paid, then changes only Seats.
steps.code:
TYPE BookingRecord
    DECLARE Name : STRING
    DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
    DECLARE Paid : BOOLEAN
ENDTYPE
DECLARE Booking : BookingRecord
INPUT Booking.Name
INPUT Booking.Seats
Booking.Paid <- FALSE
Booking.Seats <- Booking.Seats + 1
OUTPUT Booking.Name
OUTPUT Booking.Seats
OUTPUT Booking.Paid

steps.title: Keep instances separate
steps.body: Two variables can share a record type without sharing their current data. Updating AnotherBooking.Name does not instruct the program to update Booking.Name. The variable name identifies which record is being accessed.

worked.conclusion: A field update changes the selected field of the selected record.

check.prompt: How would you display a booking’s name and then set its payment state to TRUE?
check.answer: Use OUTPUT Booking.Name followed by Booking.Paid <- TRUE. The first statement reads a field; the second changes a different field.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate an index from the value it selects

leadVisual.title: Separate an index from the value it selects

coreExplanation: Request names the collection. Request[2] names its second indexed element. That element currently contains 3. The index 2 and value 3 have different roles.
When Index contains 4, Request[Index] selects Request[4], whose value is 3. Changing Index changes which location is selected; it does not move the stored values.
Request[2] <- 9 replaces the value at index 2. It does not change the lower bound, the array length or the value at index 4.

learningCycle.observe: Five request cards contain 8, 3, 5, 3 and 1. Label their positions 1 to 5 above the cards. The second and fourth cards contain the same value but occupy different positions.
learningCycle.question: In Request[2] = 3, which number is the position and which is the stored request?

prerequisite.title: Recall a collection
prerequisite.body: An array groups elements of one declared type under one identifier. Each element is a storage location. An index selects a particular element.

steps.title: Read the whole array and one element
steps.body: Request names the collection. Request[2] names its second indexed element. That element currently contains 3. The index 2 and value 3 have different roles.

steps.title: Use a variable as the index
steps.body: When Index contains 4, Request[Index] selects Request[4], whose value is 3. Changing Index changes which location is selected; it does not move the stored values.

steps.title: Update one selected element
steps.body: Request[2] <- 9 replaces the value at index 2. It does not change the lower bound, the array length or the value at index 4.
steps.code:
DECLARE Request : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER
Request[2] <- 3
Request[2] <- 9
OUTPUT Request[2]

worked.title: Evaluate two accesses
worked.setup: Use the original five cards: [8, 3, 5, 3, 1]. Index contains 4.

steps.title: Read the first expression
steps.body: Request[Index] selects position 4 and gives 3.

steps.title: Evaluate the index expression first
steps.body: Request[Index - 1] uses index 3 and gives 5. Subtracting 1 from the index is not the same as subtracting 1 from the stored value.

worked.conclusion: Evaluate the expression inside the brackets first, then read the selected element.

check.prompt: Request[1] is 8. What changes after Request[1] <- Request[1] + 2?
check.answer: The value at index 1 becomes 10. The index remains 1, and no other element changes.

learningCycle.takeaway: An index identifies a position; the element at that position holds a value.
learningCycle.bridge: The declaration defines which index values are legal.

workedExample.title: Evaluate two accesses

knowledgeUnits.heading: Count inclusive bounds and reject invalid positions

leadVisual.title: Count inclusive bounds and reject invalid positions

coreExplanation: In ARRAY[3:7], 3 is the lower bound and 7 is the upper bound. Legal indices satisfy Index >= 3 AND Index <= 7. An access using 2 or 8 is outside the declaration.
The number of elements is upper bound - lower bound + 1. Here that gives 7 - 3 + 1 = 5. Capacity counts available positions, not how many meaningful values the program has entered so far.
A declaration does not explicitly supply every initial value. This complete example assigns an empty string to every legal element before displaying or changing it.

learningCycle.observe: Write the legal labels 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. There are five positions even though the upper bound is 7. The first legal index need not be zero or one.

stimulus.title: A declaration with non-zero lower bound
items: DECLARE Names : ARRAY[3:7] OF STRING
Proposed accesses: Names[2], Names[3], Names[7], Names[8]

learningCycle.question: How many elements are declared by ARRAY[3:7]?

prerequisite.title: Recall inclusive counting
prerequisite.body: Both endpoints are included in an array’s declared bounds. Upper minus lower measures the gaps; add one to count the positions.

steps.title: Identify each bound
steps.body: In ARRAY[3:7], 3 is the lower bound and 7 is the upper bound. Legal indices satisfy Index >= 3 AND Index <= 7. An access using 2 or 8 is outside the declaration.

steps.title: Calculate the capacity
steps.body: The number of elements is upper bound - lower bound + 1. Here that gives 7 - 3 + 1 = 5. Capacity counts available positions, not how many meaningful values the program has entered so far.

steps.title: Initialise before reading
steps.body: A declaration does not explicitly supply every initial value. This complete example assigns an empty string to every legal element before displaying or changing it.
steps.code:
DECLARE Names : ARRAY[3:5] OF STRING
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
FOR Index <- 3 TO 5
    Names[Index] <- ""
NEXT Index
Names[4] <- "Mina"
FOR Index <- 3 TO 5
    OUTPUT Names[Index]
NEXT Index

worked.title: Check a proposed final access
worked.setup: Names is declared ARRAY[3:5] OF STRING. A programmer proposes Names[6] <- "Mina".

steps.title: Count the elements
steps.body: There are 5 - 3 + 1 = 3 elements, labelled 3, 4 and 5.

steps.title: Reject the access by its index
steps.body: Index 6 is greater than the upper bound. The fact that "Mina" is a valid STRING does not make that array position valid.

worked.conclusion: Check both the selected position and the element type.

check.prompt: An array has bounds 0:99. How many elements does it contain, and is index 100 valid?
check.answer: It contains 99 - 0 + 1 = 100 elements. Index 100 is invalid because the greatest legal index is 99.

learningCycle.takeaway: Count inclusive bounds with upper - lower + 1 and keep every access inside them.
learningCycle.bridge: A loop can visit every valid position without repeating one statement for each value.

steps.title: Reject the access by its index

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose one index when one position identifies the value

leadVisual.title: Choose one index when one position identifies the value

coreExplanation: A list of five requests needs one position number to locate an item. A one-dimensional array is suitable: Request[1] through Request[5] retain the sequence.
Search, reverse output and sorting require access to earlier values. An array allows this repeated access. A running total alone cannot reconstruct the original requests.

If the only requirement is the final total, one current-value variable and an accumulator may suffice. Choose the structure from the required later operations, not merely because several inputs exist.

learningCycle.observe: The desk must later search the requests and display them in reverse arrival order. If each new input overwrites a single variable, the earlier requests will no longer be available.

stimulus.title: What will the next step need?
items: Inputs in arrival order: 8, 3, 5, 3, 1
Task A: display only their total.
Task B: display the third request later.

learningCycle.question: Why keep all five seat requests if the program can read one at a time?

prerequisite.title: Recall replacement by assignment
prerequisite.body: Reading another input into Request replaces that scalar value. An array provides a separate element for each retained value.

steps.title: Match one index to one position
steps.body: A list of five requests needs one position number to locate an item. A one-dimensional array is suitable: Request[1] through Request[5] retain the sequence.

steps.title: Retain values when later access needs them
steps.body: Search, reverse output and sorting require access to earlier values. An array allows this repeated access. A running total alone cannot reconstruct the original requests.

steps.title: Avoid storing values without a reason
steps.body: If the only requirement is the final total, one current-value variable and an accumulator may suffice. Choose the structure from the required later operations, not merely because several inputs exist.

worked.title: Compare two requirements
worked.setup: Both programs receive 8, 3, 5, 3 and 1.

steps.title: Only display the total
steps.body: A running Total can accumulate 20 while each current input is replaced. No later operation needs each individual value.

steps.title: Display the third request later
steps.body: Total = 20 cannot identify the third request. Store the inputs in an array so Request[3] remains available and gives 5.

check.prompt: A program must compare each day’s reading with the previous week after all readings are entered. Is retaining the readings useful?
check.answer: Yes. The later comparisons need individual earlier readings, so indexed storage is appropriate. A total alone would lose the required detail.

learningCycle.bridge: A FOR loop can fill, total or display that array using the same bounds.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace forward and reverse traversal

leadVisual.title: Trace forward and reverse traversal

coreExplanation: Use FOR Index <- 1 TO 5 to visit all five positions. INPUT Request[Index] stores each entered value in its own element. A later loop can revisit those stored values.
Start Total at 0 outside the loop. For [8, 3, 5, 3, 1], the successive totals are 8, 11, 16, 19 and 20. Resetting Total inside the loop would discard the previous additions.
After the input loop completes, start a new loop at the upper bound and use STEP -1. Each output reads the selected element. The stored array remains [8, 3, 5, 3, 1].

For the reverse phase, initialise Index to 5; test Index >= 1; on TRUE output Request[Index], subtract 1 and return to the test. On FALSE, finish. Complete the input phase before beginning the output phase.

learningCycle.observe: Keep cards [8, 3, 5, 3, 1] in their original positions. Read position 5, then 4, 3, 2 and 1. Only the order of visits changes.

stimulus.title: Keep the cards in their original positions

learningCycle.question: Must the array itself change to display its values in reverse order?

prerequisite.title: Recall FOR and an accumulator
prerequisite.body: FOR assigns successive index values and repeats its body. NEXT returns to the loop control. An accumulator stores a running result: Total <- Total + Value adds the current value to the old total. Set Total to 0 before adding the first value.

steps.title: Fill each legal position once
steps.body: Use FOR Index <- 1 TO 5 to visit all five positions. INPUT Request[Index] stores each entered value in its own element. A later loop can revisit those stored values.

steps.title: Trace the running total
steps.body: Start Total at 0 outside the loop. For [8, 3, 5, 3, 1], the successive totals are 8, 11, 16, 19 and 20. Resetting Total inside the loop would discard the previous additions.

steps.title: Reverse the visits without moving the data
steps.body: After the input loop completes, start a new loop at the upper bound and use STEP -1. Each output reads the selected element. The stored array remains [8, 3, 5, 3, 1].
steps.code:
DECLARE Request : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
FOR Index <- 1 TO 5
    INPUT Request[Index]
NEXT Index
Total <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 5
    Total <- Total + Request[Index]
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total
FOR Index <- 5 TO 1 STEP -1
    OUTPUT Request[Index]
NEXT Index

steps.title: Represent the same control flow in a flowchart
steps.body: For the reverse phase, initialise Index to 5; test Index >= 1; on TRUE output Request[Index], subtract 1 and return to the test. On FALSE, finish. Complete the input phase before beginning the output phase.

worked.title: Trace both directions
worked.setup: Input 8, 3, 5, 3 and 1 in that order.

steps.title: Finish input before output
steps.body: After input, all five elements are available. The total loop produces 20.

steps.title: Follow the reverse index
steps.body: The reverse loop uses indices 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and outputs 1, 3, 5, 3, 8. It stops before an attempted access at index 0.

worked.conclusion: Loop direction determines visit order; it does not automatically rearrange the array.

check.prompt: Why must the reverse output loop begin after all values have been entered?
check.answer: The first reverse output needs the last input value, and later outputs need the earlier stored values. Completing input first makes the entire sequence available for reverse traversal.

learningCycle.takeaway: Use the declared bounds for every traversal and initialise accumulators before their loops.
learningCycle.bridge: Sometimes the result should count matching elements instead of adding their values.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Count matches and combine conditions

leadVisual.title: Count matches and combine conditions

coreExplanation: Initialise Count to 0. When an element meets the condition, Count <- Count + 1 records one matching element. Adding the element’s value instead would calculate a total.
For requests [8, 3, 5, 3, 1] and threshold 5, the count becomes 1, stays 1, becomes 2, stays 2 and stays 2. The condition is evaluated for every element, even when the count does not change.

A test such as (Index MOD 2 = 0) AND ((Request[Index] = 3) OR (Request[Index] = 5)) requires an even index and one of the two permitted values. The brackets apply the even-index rule to the entire OR group.

learningCycle.observe: Only the requests containing 8 and 5 qualify. Their sum is 13, but there are two qualifying requests. Decide whether the task asks “how many?” or “how much altogether?”.

stimulus.title: Count requests of at least five seats
items: Requests: 8, 3, 5, 3, 1
Threshold: 5
Count starts at 0.

learningCycle.question: For requests [8, 3, 5, 3, 1], is the number of requests of at least 5 equal to 13?

prerequisite.title: Recall IF, comparisons and Boolean operators
prerequisite.body: IF runs its body only when the condition is TRUE. AND requires both conditions to be TRUE; OR requires at least one. MOD gives the remainder after integer division: 6 MOD 2 is 0, while 7 MOD 2 is 1.

steps.title: Increment a count by one
steps.body: Initialise Count to 0. When an element meets the condition, Count <- Count + 1 records one matching element. Adding the element’s value instead would calculate a total.
steps.code:
DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[1:4] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Threshold : INTEGER
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
FOR Index <- 1 TO 4
    INPUT Marks[Index]
NEXT Index
INPUT Threshold
Count <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 4
    IF Marks[Index] >= Threshold THEN
        Count <- Count + 1
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Count

steps.title: Trace both branches
steps.body: For requests [8, 3, 5, 3, 1] and threshold 5, the count becomes 1, stays 1, becomes 2, stays 2 and stays 2. The condition is evaluated for every element, even when the count does not change.

steps.title: Group combined conditions deliberately
steps.body: A test such as (Index MOD 2 = 0) AND ((Request[Index] = 3) OR (Request[Index] = 5)) requires an even index and one of the two permitted values. The brackets apply the even-index rule to the entire OR group.

worked.title: An even position with an accepted request value
worked.setup: Use [8, 3, 5, 3, 1] and accept value 3 or 5 only at even positions.

steps.title: Check index 2
steps.body: 2 MOD 2 = 0 is TRUE. Request[2] = 3 is TRUE, so the OR group is TRUE. TRUE AND TRUE qualifies: add one.

steps.title: Check index 3
steps.body: The value 5 satisfies the OR group, but 3 MOD 2 = 0 is FALSE. FALSE AND TRUE is FALSE, so this element does not qualify. Index 4 does qualify, giving count 2.

worked.conclusion: Evaluate each grouped condition, then combine their Boolean results.

check.prompt: A row satisfies both alternatives in an OR condition. Should one IF body run twice?
check.answer: No. The OR expression evaluates to one Boolean result, TRUE. The IF body executes once for that evaluation, so a count increments once.

learningCycle.takeaway: Count matching elements with + 1; use brackets to express the intended AND/OR grouping.
learningCycle.bridge: Finding a largest value needs a different starting value from a count.

workedExample.title: An even position with an accepted request value

leadVisual.title: Find a largest or smallest value safely

coreExplanation: For a non-empty array, set Largest and Smallest to Reading[1]. They are now actual input values. This works whether the inputs are positive, negative or mixed.

Start at index 2 because index 1 is already represented. Replace Largest only for a greater value, and Smallest only for a smaller value. Use two IF statements because each comparison has its own purpose.
After processing an element, Largest is the greatest value seen so far and Smallest is the least value seen so far. After the final element, the claim covers the entire array.

prerequisite.title: Recall selection and a running result
prerequisite.body: IF Reading[Index] > Largest updates Largest only when the new reading is greater. The other iterations must retain the best value already found.

steps.title: Use the first element as the initial candidate
steps.body: For a non-empty array, set Largest and Smallest to Reading[1]. They are now actual input values. This works whether the inputs are positive, negative or mixed.

steps.title: Process the remaining elements
steps.body: Start at index 2 because index 1 is already represented. Replace Largest only for a greater value, and Smallest only for a smaller value. Use two IF statements because each comparison has its own purpose.
steps.code:
DECLARE Reading : ARRAY[1:4] OF REAL
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Largest : REAL
DECLARE Smallest : REAL
FOR Index <- 1 TO 4
    INPUT Reading[Index]
NEXT Index
Largest <- Reading[1]
Smallest <- Reading[1]
FOR Index <- 2 TO 4
    IF Reading[Index] > Largest THEN
        Largest <- Reading[Index]
    ENDIF
    IF Reading[Index] < Smallest THEN
        Smallest <- Reading[Index]
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Largest
OUTPUT Smallest

steps.title: Explain the condition after each visit
steps.body: After processing an element, Largest is the greatest value seen so far and Smallest is the least value seen so far. After the final element, the claim covers the entire array.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Finish the inner loop before moving to the next row

leadVisual.title: Finish the inner loop before moving to the next row

coreExplanation: Row takes 1 then 2. For each Row value, Column starts at 1 and runs through 3. The visit order is [1,1], [1,2], [1,3], [2,1], [2,2], [2,3].
Scores[Row, Column] selects the current location. Using Scores[Row, 1] would repeatedly access only the first column. The nested loops themselves do not make a fixed access change.

RowTotal <- 0 is inside the outer loop but before the inner loop. It runs once per row. Resetting inside the inner loop would discard earlier values from the same row; resetting before both loops would combine rows.

learningCycle.observe: Trace a finger across the first row from columns 1 to 3, then return to column 1 of row 2. The column changes more often because its loop is inside the row loop.
learningCycle.question: After visiting [1, 3] in a two-row, three-column grid, which position comes next?

prerequisite.title: Recall the body of a loop
prerequisite.body: Every statement between FOR and NEXT belongs to that loop body. If another loop is inside it, that complete inner loop runs for each outer-loop value.

steps.title: Choose the outer and inner variables
steps.body: Row takes 1 then 2. For each Row value, Column starts at 1 and runs through 3. The visit order is [1,1], [1,2], [1,3], [2,1], [2,2], [2,3].

steps.title: Use both variables in the access
steps.body: Scores[Row, Column] selects the current location. Using Scores[Row, 1] would repeatedly access only the first column. The nested loops themselves do not make a fixed access change.
steps.code:
DECLARE Scores : ARRAY[1:2, 1:3] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Row : INTEGER
DECLARE Column : INTEGER
DECLARE RowTotal : INTEGER
FOR Row <- 1 TO 2
    RowTotal <- 0
    FOR Column <- 1 TO 3
        INPUT Scores[Row, Column]
        RowTotal <- RowTotal + Scores[Row, Column]
    NEXT Column
    OUTPUT RowTotal
NEXT Row

steps.title: Reset one row total for each new row

steps.title: Keep the grand total outside both loops
steps.body: GrandTotal starts at 0 once and accumulates all six elements. RowTotal resets once per row. They can be updated in the same inner loop because both totals need the current element.
steps.code:
DECLARE Scores : ARRAY[1:2, 1:3] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Row : INTEGER
DECLARE Column : INTEGER
DECLARE RowTotal : INTEGER
DECLARE ColumnTotal : INTEGER
DECLARE GrandTotal : INTEGER
GrandTotal <- 0
FOR Row <- 1 TO 2
    RowTotal <- 0
    FOR Column <- 1 TO 3
        INPUT Scores[Row, Column]
        RowTotal <- RowTotal + Scores[Row, Column]
        GrandTotal <- GrandTotal + Scores[Row, Column]
    NEXT Column
    OUTPUT RowTotal
NEXT Row
FOR Column <- 1 TO 3
    ColumnTotal <- 0
    FOR Row <- 1 TO 2
        ColumnTotal <- ColumnTotal + Scores[Row, Column]
    NEXT Row
    OUTPUT ColumnTotal
NEXT Column
OUTPUT GrandTotal

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare in order until a match or the end

leadVisual.title: Compare in order until a match or the end

coreExplanation: Linear search checks elements sequentially. It works on an unsorted array because it does not assume that greater or smaller values occupy a particular region.
Compare the current element with the target. If it does not match, move to the next legal index. If it matches and the requirement is first match, record that position and stop.

If every legal position has been checked without a match, report not found. For a 1-based array, 0 can be a not-found result because it is outside the legal index range. A question may specify -1 instead; follow that convention.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Write a search that stops safely

leadVisual.title: Write a search that stops safely

coreExplanation: Set Index to the lower bound and Position to the not-found sentinel. Position changes only when a match is found. Index advances only after a mismatch.

The loop condition tests Index <= 5 and Position = 0. Neither part accesses the array. The body therefore reads Values[Index] only when Index is in range, without depending on short-circuit evaluation.

A FOR loop might prevent a later match from overwriting the first result, yet continue through all remaining iterations. A suitable WHILE loop can stop immediately once Position changes from its sentinel.

A FUNCTION packages these search steps so they can be called with a search value. Its parameter SearchString receives that value; RETURN FoundAt sends the result back. The question supplies this wrapper. Focus on the comparisons, sentinel and loop; you do not need a new search method.

learningCycle.observe: Imagine searching for 9 when the final legal index is 5. After the final mismatch, Index becomes 6. The next loop test must stop before the body reads another element.

Initial Index = 1; Position = 0 means not found.

learningCycle.question: What prevents the search from reading past the final element?

prerequisite.title: Recall WHILE and a sentinel
prerequisite.body: WHILE tests its condition before each execution of the body. A sentinel is a reserved value with a special meaning, such as Position = 0 for not found. Choose a value that cannot be a valid result.

steps.title: Initialise both pieces of state
steps.body: Set Index to the lower bound and Position to the not-found sentinel. Position changes only when a match is found. Index advances only after a mismatch.

steps.title: Guard entry to the array access
steps.body: The loop condition tests Index <= 5 and Position = 0. Neither part accesses the array. The body therefore reads Values[Index] only when Index is in range, without depending on short-circuit evaluation.
steps.code:
DECLARE Values : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Target : INTEGER
DECLARE Position : INTEGER
FOR Index <- 1 TO 5
    INPUT Values[Index]
NEXT Index
INPUT Target
Index <- 1
Position <- 0
WHILE (Index <= 5) AND (Position = 0)
    IF Values[Index] = Target THEN
        Position <- Index
    ELSE
        Index <- Index + 1
    ENDIF
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Position

steps.title: Explain why a continued FOR loop can waste work
steps.body: A FOR loop might prevent a later match from overwriting the first result, yet continue through all remaining iterations. A suitable WHILE loop can stop immediately once Position changes from its sentinel.

steps.title: Read the supplied function wrapper in the question
steps.body: A FUNCTION packages these search steps so they can be called with a search value. Its parameter SearchString receives that value; RETURN FoundAt sends the result back. The question supplies this wrapper. Focus on the comparisons, sentinel and loop; you do not need a new search method.

steps.body: For ascending order, compare Values[Index] > Values[Index + 1]. If TRUE, exchange the values. Equal neighbours need no exchange. The greatest value encountered so far moves right after each relevant comparison.

steps.title: Preserve both values in a complete swap
steps.body: Save the left value in Temp, copy the right value to the left and copy Temp to the right. The three assignments exchange the originals without losing either.
steps.code:
Temp <- Values[Index]
Values[Index] <- Values[Index + 1]
Values[Index + 1] <- Temp

steps.title: Distinguish a comparison, a swap and a pass
steps.body: One comparison inspects one adjacent pair. It may or may not cause a swap. A pass visits every adjacent pair in the current unsorted region. One pass generally does not sort the entire array.

worked.title: Complete the first ascending pass
worked.setup: Start with [8, 3, 5, 1].

steps.title: Move the greatest value right
steps.body: Compare 8 and 3: [3, 8, 5, 1]. Compare 8 and 5: [3, 5, 8, 1]. Compare 8 and 1: [3, 5, 1, 8].

steps.title: Identify what is established
steps.body: 8 is now at its final last position. The prefix [3, 5, 1] is not sorted because 5 is still before 1. Another pass is needed.

worked.conclusion: One pass fixes the greatest remaining value at the right-hand end of the current region.

check.prompt: Why is Values[Index] <- Values[Index + 1] followed by Values[Index + 1] <- Values[Index] an incorrect swap?
check.answer: The first assignment overwrites the old left value. The second then copies the new left value back, leaving two copies of the old right value. Save the old left value in Temp before overwriting it.

learningCycle.takeaway: Bubble sort compares neighbours and uses a complete temporary-variable swap when they are out of order.
learningCycle.bridge: Repeat passes over a shrinking region and stop early when a full pass needs no swaps.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Finish the sort and detect an already ordered region

leadVisual.title: Finish the sort and detect an already ordered region

coreExplanation: If Last is the last index of the unsorted region, Index must stop at Last - 1 because the comparison also reads Index + 1. After the pass, decrement Last because its old final position is fixed.

Set Swapped to TRUE before the outer loop so the first pass can run. At each pass start, set it to FALSE. Set it to TRUE whenever a swap occurs. If it remains FALSE after the whole pass, all adjacent pairs in the remaining region were already in order.
The algorithm below fills the array, completes the sort and displays every sorted value. Last > 1 prevents a pass when fewer than two positions remain.

learningCycle.observe: After a pass on [3, 5, 1, 8], the final 8 need not be compared again. Keep a boundary for the unsorted region and a flag recording whether that pass made a change.

stimulus.title: State after the first pass
items: Current array: [3, 5, 1, 8]
Remaining unsorted region: indices 1 through 3
The next pass must record whether it makes a swap.

learningCycle.question: What does a complete pass with no swaps tell us?

prerequisite.title: Recall BOOLEAN flags and nested loops
prerequisite.body: A flag records whether an event has occurred. The outer WHILE controls passes, while the inner FOR controls adjacent comparisons within one pass. Reset the flag at the beginning of every pass.

steps.title: Keep the next neighbour inside the region
steps.body: If Last is the last index of the unsorted region, Index must stop at Last - 1 because the comparison also reads Index + 1. After the pass, decrement Last because its old final position is fixed.

steps.title: Reset and set Swapped at the correct times
steps.body: Set Swapped to TRUE before the outer loop so the first pass can run. At each pass start, set it to FALSE. Set it to TRUE whenever a swap occurs. If it remains FALSE after the whole pass, all adjacent pairs in the remaining region were already in order.

steps.title: Trace the complete algorithm
steps.body: The algorithm below fills the array, completes the sort and displays every sorted value. Last > 1 prevents a pass when fewer than two positions remain.
steps.code:
DECLARE Values : ARRAY[1:7] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Last : INTEGER
DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
DECLARE Swapped : BOOLEAN
FOR Index <- 1 TO 7
    INPUT Values[Index]
NEXT Index
Last <- 7
Swapped <- TRUE
WHILE (Last > 1) AND Swapped
    Swapped <- FALSE
    FOR Index <- 1 TO Last - 1
        IF Values[Index] > Values[Index + 1] THEN
            Temp <- Values[Index]
            Values[Index] <- Values[Index + 1]
            Values[Index + 1] <- Temp
            Swapped <- TRUE
        ENDIF
    NEXT Index
    Last <- Last - 1
ENDWHILE
FOR Index <- 1 TO 7
    OUTPUT Values[Index]
NEXT Index

worked.title: Finish sorting [8, 3, 5, 1]
worked.setup: Use the same algorithm with bounds 1:4.

steps.title: Track the boundary
steps.body: Pass 1 gives [3, 5, 1, 8] and Last becomes 3. Pass 2 gives [3, 1, 5, 8] and Last becomes 2. Pass 3 gives [1, 3, 5, 8] and Last becomes 1.

steps.title: Test a different starting order
steps.body: For [1, 3, 5, 8], the first complete pass makes no swaps. Swapped remains FALSE, so the next outer test ends the sort. The algorithm still checks the whole first pass before claiming the region is ordered.

worked.conclusion: The boundary avoids revisiting fixed values; the flag avoids further passes after a no-swap pass.

check.prompt: What happens if Swapped is never reset to FALSE at the beginning of a pass?
check.answer: Once any swap sets it to TRUE, that value can carry into later passes. A later no-swap pass would no longer be detected correctly, so the early-stop behaviour would be lost.

learningCycle.takeaway: A complete bubble sort repeats bounded passes and resets its swap flag for each pass.
learningCycle.bridge: When one row holds related facts, every swap must preserve the relationship between its columns.
