knowledgeUnits.heading: Move a row’s related values together

leadVisual.title: Move a row’s related values together

coreExplanation: For ascending speed, compare the speed in row Index with the speed in row Index + 1. Do not compare the sensor identifiers to decide the order when the requirement is order by speed. The question declares Reading[1:2000, 1:2] OF INTEGER.

When the speed comparison requires a swap, exchange column 1 and also exchange column 2. Use a temporary value for each exchange. Moving only the speed would attach a measurement to the wrong identifier.

NoSwaps starts TRUE at each pass and becomes FALSE after any swap. Its meaning is the opposite of Swapped. Continue another pass when swaps occurred and the unsorted boundary still contains a pair; do not copy a condition without checking the flag’s meaning.

The earlier scalar algorithm uses Last for the final right-hand index and loops to Last - 1. The exam version can use Boundary for the final left-hand comparison index: for 2000 rows, start Boundary at 1999 and loop Index from 1 to Boundary. Index + 1 then reaches at most 2000. Decrease Boundary after a pass.

With REPEAT, set NoSwaps to TRUE at the start of the pass and set it to FALSE after any swap. UNTIL NoSwaps = TRUE ends after a complete pass without a swap. The procedure wrapper groups these already-known operations; the task still needs complete loops and both column swaps.

learningCycle.observe: Use a two-column INTEGER table: rows (40, 7), (10, 3), (30, 9). The first column is a recorded speed and the second identifies its sensor. Each pair must remain together when rows change position.

stimulus.title: Each speed belongs to its sensor

learningCycle.question: If we sort a measured speed without its sensor identifier, which sensor will the row claim produced it?

prerequisite.title: Read the procedure wrapper and the loop condition
prerequisite.body: Reading[Row, 1] and Reading[Row, 2] are two elements in one row. PROCEDURE Sort() groups the sorting statements so they can be executed together; ENDPROCEDURE ends that group and CALL Sort() runs it. A REPEAT loop runs its body before testing UNTIL; it ends when that condition becomes TRUE.

steps.title: Compare the selected key column
steps.body: For ascending speed, compare the speed in row Index with the speed in row Index + 1. Do not compare the sensor identifiers to decide the order when the requirement is order by speed. The question declares Reading[1:2000, 1:2] OF INTEGER.

steps.title: Swap every related column
steps.body: When the speed comparison requires a swap, exchange column 1 and also exchange column 2. Use a temporary value for each exchange. Moving only the speed would attach a measurement to the wrong identifier.
steps.code:
IF Reading[Index, 1] > Reading[Index + 1, 1] THEN
    FOR Column <- 1 TO 2
        Temp <- Reading[Index, Column]
        Reading[Index, Column] <- Reading[Index + 1, Column]
        Reading[Index + 1, Column] <- Temp
    NEXT Column
    NoSwaps <- FALSE
ENDIF

steps.title: Read a flag with the opposite name
steps.body: NoSwaps starts TRUE at each pass and becomes FALSE after any swap. Its meaning is the opposite of Swapped. Continue another pass when swaps occurred and the unsorted boundary still contains a pair; do not copy a condition without checking the flag’s meaning.

steps.title: Translate the boundary convention
steps.body: The earlier scalar algorithm uses Last for the final right-hand index and loops to Last - 1. The exam version can use Boundary for the final left-hand comparison index: for 2000 rows, start Boundary at 1999 and loop Index from 1 to Boundary. Index + 1 then reaches at most 2000. Decrease Boundary after a pass.

steps.title: Transfer the termination condition
steps.body: With REPEAT, set NoSwaps to TRUE at the start of the pass and set it to FALSE after any swap. UNTIL NoSwaps = TRUE ends after a complete pass without a swap. The procedure wrapper groups these already-known operations; the task still needs complete loops and both column swaps.

worked.title: Preserve each sensor’s recorded speed
worked.setup: Start with (40, 7), (10, 3), (30, 9), ordered by arrival.

steps.title: Swap the first two complete pairs
steps.body: 40 is greater than 10. Exchange both columns, giving (10, 3), (40, 7), (30, 9). Sensor 7 still has speed 40.

steps.title: Complete the pass
steps.body: Compare 40 and 30 and exchange their complete rows. The result is (10, 3), (30, 9), (40, 7). A following no-swap pass confirms the remaining region is ordered.

steps.title: Assemble the complete procedure
steps.body: Assume the global array Reading[1:3, 1:2] already holds the three supplied rows. This procedure sorts them in place; CALL Sort() runs it. Follow the same comparisons as the table trace. For the 2000-row question, the initial Boundary becomes 1999. The question asks you to write a complete procedure, so include both loops and both column exchanges.
steps.code:
PROCEDURE Sort()
    DECLARE Index : INTEGER
    DECLARE Column : INTEGER
    DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
    DECLARE Boundary : INTEGER
    DECLARE NoSwaps : BOOLEAN
    Boundary <- 2
    REPEAT
        NoSwaps <- TRUE
        FOR Index <- 1 TO Boundary
            IF Reading[Index, 1] > Reading[Index + 1, 1] THEN
                FOR Column <- 1 TO 2
                    Temp <- Reading[Index, Column]
                    Reading[Index, Column] <- Reading[Index + 1, Column]
                    Reading[Index + 1, Column] <- Temp
                NEXT Column
                NoSwaps <- FALSE
            ENDIF
        NEXT Index
        Boundary <- Boundary - 1
    UNTIL (NoSwaps = TRUE) OR (Boundary < 1)
ENDPROCEDURE
CALL Sort()

worked.conclusion: The sorting key decides the order, but the entire logical row must move.

check.prompt: After sorting only column 1, the first row becomes (10, 7). What was lost?
check.answer: The association between the speed and its sensor was lost. In the original data, 10 belongs to sensor 3. Both columns must be exchanged whenever their rows are swapped.

learningCycle.takeaway: Sort by the required key and preserve each row’s related values during every swap.
learningCycle.bridge: The processed data is still working data. Save it in a file when a later program run will need it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Give the next run something to read

leadVisual.title: Give the next run something to read

coreExplanation: Files retain saved data between program executions and allow programs to read or share that saved data later. A text file stores a sequence of text lines that the program can read in order.
Line is a STRING variable used while processing one line. "Bookings.txt" identifies the file. READFILE transfers text into Line; WRITEFILE transfers a value from the program into the file.
Open the file with the required mode, perform the reading or writing and close the file. Use different modes for reading existing content, creating replacement content and adding to existing content.

learningCycle.observe: The running program has Mina and Jo in memory. Tomorrow’s program starts a new execution. A saved file provides the data that the new execution can read.

stimulus.title: The register is needed in two executions
items: Today: the running program holds Mina and Jo.
Tomorrow: a new program execution must recover those names.

learningCycle.question: What must happen before today’s booking register can be reopened tomorrow?

prerequisite.title: Recall working variables and saved data
prerequisite.body: A record or array organises values during execution. Its declaration alone does not save those values to persistent storage.

steps.title: Explain why a file is needed
steps.body: Files retain saved data between program executions and allow programs to read or share that saved data later. A text file stores a sequence of text lines that the program can read in order.

steps.title: Separate a variable from a file
steps.body: Line is a STRING variable used while processing one line. "Bookings.txt" identifies the file. READFILE transfers text into Line; WRITEFILE transfers a value from the program into the file.

steps.title: Plan the complete lifecycle
steps.body: Open the file with the required mode, perform the reading or writing and close the file. Use different modes for reading existing content, creating replacement content and adding to existing content.

worked.title: Follow one name between runs
worked.setup: Mina is entered today and must appear in tomorrow’s register.

steps.title: Save during the first run
steps.body: The program writes the text Mina to a file and closes it. The persistent file contains the line independently of the current Name variable.

steps.title: Recover during the next run
steps.body: The next program opens the file for reading and reads the line into a new variable. The program can then display or process Mina again.

worked.conclusion: Persistence requires a saved representation and later reading, not merely a larger array.

check.prompt: A program displays all booking names before it exits. Does displaying them also save them in a text file?
check.answer: No. OUTPUT displays data. Separate file operations are required to write a persistent file that a later run can read.

learningCycle.takeaway: Use files to retain data between program executions.
learningCycle.bridge: The opening mode determines whether writing replaces the old content or adds to it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose replacement or addition before writing

leadVisual.title: Choose replacement or addition before writing

coreExplanation: Opening FOR WRITE creates a new file or replaces the existing contents. Use it when the requirement is to produce a fresh register. It is unsuitable when the old lines must be retained.
Opening FOR APPEND places new writing after existing content. The program below adds one entered line and keeps the earlier lines.
CLOSEFILE completes the program’s use of that open file. It belongs after the writing loop, not before later writes. Do not assume OUTPUT Line writes to the file; use WRITEFILE.

learningCycle.observe: The existing register contains two lines: Mina and Jo. Compare the intended final files [Sam] and [Mina, Jo, Sam]. The choice of opening mode changes which result is produced.

stimulus.title: Existing Names.txt and a new arrival

learningCycle.question: To add Sam to a register containing Mina and Jo, should the program open it FOR WRITE?

prerequisite.title: Recall string values and one line
prerequisite.body: WRITEFILE writes the supplied text as a line to the open file. The variable supplying the line must already have a value. Opening, writing and closing are separate operations.

steps.title: Use WRITE for new replacement content
steps.body: Opening FOR WRITE creates a new file or replaces the existing contents. Use it when the requirement is to produce a fresh register. It is unsuitable when the old lines must be retained.
steps.code:
DECLARE Line : STRING
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
OPENFILE "Names.txt" FOR WRITE
FOR Index <- 1 TO 3
    INPUT Line
    WRITEFILE "Names.txt", Line
NEXT Index
CLOSEFILE "Names.txt"

steps.title: Use APPEND to preserve earlier lines
steps.body: Opening FOR APPEND places new writing after existing content. The program below adds one entered line and keeps the earlier lines.
steps.code:
DECLARE Line : STRING
INPUT Line
OPENFILE "Names.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "Names.txt", Line
CLOSEFILE "Names.txt"

steps.title: Close the file after its operations
steps.body: CLOSEFILE completes the program’s use of that open file. It belongs after the writing loop, not before later writes. Do not assume OUTPUT Line writes to the file; use WRITEFILE.

steps.title: Open FOR WRITE and write Sam
steps.body: The old contents are replaced. After closing, the file contains one line, Sam.

check.prompt: A daily report must contain only today’s results. Which mode fits that requirement?
check.answer: WRITE, because the report should contain a fresh set of results rather than retaining earlier results. APPEND is appropriate only when those earlier lines must remain.

learningCycle.bridge: Reading needs a different guard: check that another line exists before trying to read it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read every line, including a blank line

leadVisual.title: Read every line, including a blank line

coreExplanation: FOR READ uses existing content as input. The next read begins at the file’s current read position, initially before its first line. A read moves that position forward.
The loop reads only while NOT EOF is TRUE. An empty file therefore executes the body zero times. This avoids trying to read a line after all lines have been consumed.
A blank line makes Line equal to "". It still came from a successful READFILE and still contributes one to a line count. EOF is a state of the file position, not a particular text value.

learningCycle.observe: Names.txt contains three lines: Ada, an empty line and Bo. The empty second line is real content. The end of the file comes after the third line.
learningCycle.question: Is a blank line the same as the end of the file?

prerequisite.title: Recall WHILE and NOT
prerequisite.body: WHILE checks its condition before entering the body. NOT reverses a Boolean result. NOT EOF(filename) is TRUE when another line is available to read.

steps.title: Open in READ mode
steps.body: FOR READ uses existing content as input. The next read begins at the file’s current read position, initially before its first line. A read moves that position forward.

steps.title: Check EOF before each read
steps.body: The loop reads only while NOT EOF is TRUE. An empty file therefore executes the body zero times. This avoids trying to read a line after all lines have been consumed.
steps.code:
DECLARE Line : STRING
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
Count <- 0
OPENFILE "Names.txt" FOR READ
WHILE NOT EOF("Names.txt")
    READFILE "Names.txt", Line
    OUTPUT Line
    Count <- Count + 1
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "Names.txt"
OUTPUT Count

steps.title: Process an empty string as a line
steps.body: A blank line makes Line equal to "". It still came from a successful READFILE and still contributes one to a line count. EOF is a state of the file position, not a particular text value.

worked.title: Count three lines
worked.setup: The file lines are Ada, an empty string and Bo.

steps.title: Read all available lines
steps.body: Count begins at 0. Each successful read increments it: Ada gives 1, the blank line gives 2 and Bo gives 3.

steps.title: Stop after the last line
steps.body: At the next test, EOF is TRUE and NOT EOF is FALSE. Close the file and output 3. No fourth READFILE occurs.

worked.conclusion: Test the file state rather than treating blank content as a stop marker.

check.prompt: What does the same line-counting program output for an empty file?
check.answer: 0. EOF is already TRUE at the first loop test, so the body is skipped and Count remains at its initial value.

learningCycle.takeaway: Use NOT EOF before reading; a blank line is not the end of the file.
learningCycle.bridge: Combine writing, appending and reading to check a complete save-and-recover cycle.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace a complete save-and-recover cycle

leadVisual.title: Trace a complete save-and-recover cycle

coreExplanation: WRITE produces the initial three lines. APPEND adds a fourth. READ recovers all four. The STRING variable Line is reused for successive text values, but the file retains the full sequence.
Keep a separate record of the file contents and the current variables. A WRITEFILE changes saved content, while a READFILE updates Line and the read position.
The outputs are Ada, an empty line, Bo, Cy and then the count 4. The blank line remains part of the saved file. This checks more than merely observing that a write statement executed.

learningCycle.observe: The program writes Ada, a blank line and Bo, closes the file, reopens it to append Cy and finally reopens it for reading. Predict the order and count before tracing.

stimulus.title: Planned file operations
items: WRITE: Ada, an empty line, Bo
Close the file.
APPEND: Cy
Close, reopen FOR READ and count recovered lines.

learningCycle.question: After writing three lines and appending one line, how many reads should succeed?

prerequisite.title: Recall mode and read position
prerequisite.body: Each OPENFILE establishes the mode for that phase. Closing and reopening FOR READ starts reading the saved content from its beginning. A later APPEND does not replace previous lines.

steps.title: Separate the three phases
steps.body: WRITE produces the initial three lines. APPEND adds a fourth. READ recovers all four. The STRING variable Line is reused for successive text values, but the file retains the full sequence.

steps.title: Trace the complete program
steps.body: Keep a separate record of the file contents and the current variables. A WRITEFILE changes saved content, while a READFILE updates Line and the read position.
steps.code:
DECLARE Line : STRING
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
OPENFILE "Names.txt" FOR WRITE
WRITEFILE "Names.txt", "Ada"
WRITEFILE "Names.txt", ""
WRITEFILE "Names.txt", "Bo"
CLOSEFILE "Names.txt"
OPENFILE "Names.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "Names.txt", "Cy"
CLOSEFILE "Names.txt"
Count <- 0
OPENFILE "Names.txt" FOR READ
WHILE NOT EOF("Names.txt")
    READFILE "Names.txt", Line
    OUTPUT Line
    Count <- Count + 1
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "Names.txt"
OUTPUT Count

steps.title: Verify the result by reading it back
steps.body: The outputs are Ada, an empty line, Bo, Cy and then the count 4. The blank line remains part of the saved file. This checks more than merely observing that a write statement executed.

worked.title: Locate a destructive mode mistake
worked.setup: Suppose the second OPENFILE uses WRITE instead of APPEND.

steps.title: Trace the replacement
steps.body: The second WRITE opening discards the initial three-line content. Writing Cy leaves a file containing only Cy.

steps.title: Follow the effect into reading
steps.body: The later read loop succeeds once and outputs a count of 1. The error originates in the opening mode, even though the EOF loop itself is correct.

worked.conclusion: When a recovered result is wrong, trace both the earlier write mode and the later read loop.

check.prompt: Why should a file test compare the recovered content as well as checking the final line count?
check.answer: Two different files can have the same number of lines. Checking the values and their order confirms that the intended data was retained, not merely that the expected number of reads occurred.

learningCycle.takeaway: Trace file contents, mode and read position separately from the program’s current variables.
learningCycle.bridge: Files can also be read and rewritten in a different format.

steps.body: The second WRITE opening discards the initial three-line content. Writing Cy leaves a file containing only Cy.

steps.title: Follow the effect into reading
steps.body: The later read loop succeeds once and outputs a count of 1. The error originates in the opening mode, even though the EOF loop itself is correct.

workedExample.conclusion: When a recovered result is wrong, trace both the earlier write mode and the later read loop.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Transform complete records into output lines

leadVisual.title: Transform complete records into output lines

coreExplanation: For this specified file format, every record contains exactly three lines and the file contains complete records. After the EOF test, read all three fields in order before processing the next record.
Join the three strings with | when that character is excluded from every field by the file design. A separator that can occur inside a field would need an additional escaping or quoting rule.

The outer EOF check is sufficient here because complete three-line records are guaranteed. If incomplete records were possible, check for each remaining line and handle an incomplete record instead of blindly reading past EOF. Follow the given separator and format in the past paper.

learningCycle.observe: A teaching file stores each booking as three consecutive lines: name, event and seat code. Mina / Art / A3 is followed by Jo / Music / B2. Each group of three lines is one record.
learningCycle.question: How can three input lines become one output line without mixing two people’s details?

prerequisite.title: Recall concatenation and file positions
prerequisite.body: The operator & joins strings. READFILE advances the input position by one line; WRITEFILE writes one output line. A separator marks the boundary between fields in the combined line.

steps.title: Read one complete logical record
steps.body: For this specified file format, every record contains exactly three lines and the file contains complete records. After the EOF test, read all three fields in order before processing the next record.

steps.title: Join fields with an unambiguous separator
steps.body: Join the three strings with | when that character is excluded from every field by the file design. A separator that can occur inside a field would need an additional escaping or quoting rule.
steps.code:
DECLARE Name : STRING
DECLARE Event : STRING
DECLARE SeatCode : STRING
DECLARE Combined : STRING
OPENFILE "BookingFields.txt" FOR READ
OPENFILE "BookingRows.txt" FOR WRITE
WHILE NOT EOF("BookingFields.txt")
    READFILE "BookingFields.txt", Name
    READFILE "BookingFields.txt", Event
    READFILE "BookingFields.txt", SeatCode
    Combined <- Name & "|" & Event & "|" & SeatCode
    WRITEFILE "BookingRows.txt", Combined
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "BookingFields.txt"
CLOSEFILE "BookingRows.txt"

steps.title: Keep format assumptions explicit
steps.body: The outer EOF check is sufficient here because complete three-line records are guaranteed. If incomplete records were possible, check for each remaining line and handle an incomplete record instead of blindly reading past EOF. Follow the given separator and format in the past paper.

worked.title: Trace six input lines into two output lines
worked.setup: The input lines are Mina, Art, A3, Jo, Music and B2. No field contains |.

steps.title: Process the first record
steps.body: The first three reads give Mina, Art and A3. Write the single line Mina|Art|A3.

steps.title: Process the second record and finish
steps.body: The next three reads give Jo, Music and B2. Write Jo|Music|B2. The following EOF test ends the loop. Close both files; six input lines have become two output lines.

worked.conclusion: Use the record format to decide how many reads belong to one output record.

check.prompt: Why is a separator unsuitable if it can appear unescaped inside a name?
check.answer: A later reader could not reliably distinguish a field boundary from the same character belonging to the name. Choose a separator excluded by the data rules or define an escaping/quoting format.

learningCycle.takeaway: Read complete records, preserve field order and choose a separator that the file format can interpret reliably.
learningCycle.bridge: A file says where data is retained. An abstract data type says which operations a collection permits.

classroomSessions.focus: Distinguish an ADT’s contract from its representation and identify active versus stale data.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Specify data and permitted operations

leadVisual.title: Specify data and permitted operations

coreExplanation: An abstract data type, or ADT, consists of a collection of data and a set of operations on those data. Its definition specifies the permitted behaviour without requiring a particular storage implementation.

“Remove an item” is incomplete when several items exist. A waiting-request collection removes the earliest remaining arrival. An undo collection removes the latest remaining completed action. These are different contracts.
An empty collection cannot supply an item for removal. A fixed-capacity implementation may reject an addition when full. An unsuccessful operation must not silently damage the collection.

learningCycle.observe: One collection represents requests waiting in arrival order. Another represents completed changes that can be undone. Their stored labels can look similar while the required next removal differs.

stimulus.title: The same arrivals, two requirements
items: A, then B, then C are added.
Collection 1: serve the earliest waiting request.
Collection 2: undo the latest completed action.

learningCycle.question: If two collections contain A, B and C, must they remove A next?

prerequisite.title: Recall an operation
prerequisite.body: An operation is an action on data, such as adding an item, removing an item or inspecting one. State which item the operation acts on and what happens if the action is impossible.

steps.title: Define an abstract data type
steps.body: An abstract data type, or ADT, consists of a collection of data and a set of operations on those data. Its definition specifies the permitted behaviour without requiring a particular storage implementation.

steps.title: Make an operation precise
steps.body: “Remove an item” is incomplete when several items exist. A waiting-request collection removes the earliest remaining arrival. An undo collection removes the latest remaining completed action. These are different contracts.

steps.title: Include success and failure behaviour
steps.body: An empty collection cannot supply an item for removal. A fixed-capacity implementation may reject an addition when full. An unsuccessful operation must not silently damage the collection.

worked.title: Use the same labels with different rules
worked.setup: A, B and C are added in that order.

steps.title: Follow arrival order
steps.body: If removal must be earliest first, A is removed first, then B and then C.

steps.title: Follow undo order
steps.body: If removal must be latest first, C is removed first, then B and then A. The chosen operation rule determines the order.

worked.conclusion: Describe what an operation promises before deciding how its data will be stored.

check.prompt: Does saying “an ADT is an array” give a complete definition?
check.answer: No. An ADT specifies data and operations with defined behaviour. An array is one possible representation; the statement does not explain the permitted operations or their rules.

learningCycle.takeaway: An ADT specifies a collection of data and the operations on it.
learningCycle.bridge: An array implementation needs extra state to enforce those rules.

workedExample.title: Use the same labels with different rules
workedExample.setup: A, B and C are added in that order.

steps.title: Follow arrival order
steps.body: If removal must be earliest first, A is removed first, then B and then C.

steps.title: Follow undo order
steps.body: If removal must be latest first, C is removed first, then B and then A. The chosen operation rule determines the order.

workedExample.conclusion: Describe what an operation promises before deciding how its data will be stored.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate behaviour from its array representation

leadVisual.title: Separate behaviour from its array representation

coreExplanation: The array holds data. A top pointer, front and rear pointers, a count, or links describe which positions are active and the order in which operations access them.
Different implementations can satisfy the same ADT rules. Users of a stack still expect latest-in-first-out behaviour whether its internal storage uses an array or another representation.

For this part of the syllabus, explain how array positions and state change during ADT operations. Full implementation pseudocode is not required. Be precise about the checks, affected positions and resulting pointers.

learningCycle.observe: An array has five positions, but the collection contains only two active items. A pointer or count tells the program which positions belong to the current collection.
learningCycle.question: Can unused array cells still contain old values?

prerequisite.title: Recall capacity and logical contents
prerequisite.body: Capacity is the number of storage positions. The number of active items can be smaller. A stale value in an unused position is not automatically a member of the current collection.

steps.title: Give storage and state different jobs
steps.body: The array holds data. A top pointer, front and rear pointers, a count, or links describe which positions are active and the order in which operations access them.

steps.title: Preserve the same external behaviour
steps.body: Different implementations can satisfy the same ADT rules. Users of a stack still expect latest-in-first-out behaviour whether its internal storage uses an array or another representation.

steps.title: Describe operations at the required level
steps.body: For this part of the syllabus, explain how array positions and state change during ADT operations. Full implementation pseudocode is not required. Be precise about the checks, affected positions and resulting pointers.

worked.title: Interpret five physical positions
worked.setup: Cells 0 and 1 contain active values A and B. Cells 2, 3 and 4 contain old values from earlier use.

steps.title: Use the state to decide membership
steps.body: If the state defines only cells 0 and 1 as active, the collection contains two items, not five.

steps.title: Remove without relying on erasure
steps.body: An operation can make cell 1 inactive by updating the relevant pointer or count. Clearing its old value may help a display, but the state determines whether it remains a member.

worked.conclusion: Interpret the data together with the state that defines the active collection.

check.prompt: A display shows five non-blank array cells but Count is 2. Can you conclude that the ADT contains five items?
check.answer: No. Some displayed values may be stale. Follow the implementation’s pointers, links and count to identify the active items.

learningCycle.takeaway: An implementation must maintain state that makes its array obey the ADT’s operation rules.
learningCycle.bridge: A stack uses one end to make the most recent remaining item available first.

workedExample.title: Interpret five physical positions
workedExample.setup: Cells 0 and 1 contain active values A and B. Cells 2, 3 and 4 contain old values from earlier use.

steps.title: Use the state to decide membership
steps.body: If the state defines only cells 0 and 1 as active, the collection contains two items, not five.

steps.title: Remove without relying on erasure
steps.body: An operation can make cell 1 inactive by updating the relevant pointer or count. Clearing its old value may help a display, but the state determines whether it remains a member.

workedExample.conclusion: Interpret the data together with the state that defines the active collection.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use last in, first out for undo

leadVisual.title: Use last in, first out for undo

coreExplanation: Push adds a new item at the top. Pop removes and returns the current top item. Peek, when provided, reads the top item without removing it.
Last in, first out means the most recently added item still in the stack is removed next. It does not mean always removing the greatest value or the item with the greatest identifier.

An undo history stores completed changes so the latest change can be reversed first. Each entry must contain enough information to restore the previous state. Merely storing the word “undo” is not sufficient.

learningCycle.observe: Place action cards A, B and C on a pile in that order. The latest card C is at the top. Undoing the most recent action exposes the previous one.

stimulus.title: Completed actions
items: First: A
Next: B
Most recent: C
The user requests Undo once.

learningCycle.question: After booking A, then B, then C, which completed action should Undo reverse first?

prerequisite.title: Recall an ADT contract
prerequisite.body: The collection’s rules define where an addition and a removal occur. A stack has a top: both operations act at that end.

steps.title: Name the operations
steps.body: Push adds a new item at the top. Pop removes and returns the current top item. Peek, when provided, reads the top item without removing it.

steps.title: Explain LIFO
steps.body: Last in, first out means the most recently added item still in the stack is removed next. It does not mean always removing the greatest value or the item with the greatest identifier.

steps.title: Connect the rule to a use
steps.body: An undo history stores completed changes so the latest change can be reversed first. Each entry must contain enough information to restore the previous state. Merely storing the word “undo” is not sufficient.

worked.title: Push, pop and add another action
worked.setup: Start empty; push A, push B, push C, pop, then push D.

steps.title: Follow the first removal
steps.body: After three pushes, the bottom-to-top order is A, B, C. Pop returns C, leaving A, B.

steps.title: Continue from the remaining stack
steps.body: Push D produces A, B, D from bottom to top. The next pop returns D, followed by B and A. C is no longer present.

worked.conclusion: Always decide the next removal from the current stack, after all earlier operations have taken effect.

check.prompt: Why is a stack suitable for nested return order as well as undo?
check.answer: The most recently started unfinished activity must finish or return first. A stack makes its most recently added remaining entry available first, matching that order.

learningCycle.takeaway: A stack adds and removes at the top, giving last-in-first-out behaviour.
learningCycle.bridge: The array implementation records the top position and checks its bounds.

workedExample.title: Push, pop and add another action
workedExample.setup: Start empty; push A, push B, push C, pop, then push D.

steps.title: Follow the first removal
steps.body: After three pushes, the bottom-to-top order is A, B, C. Pop returns C, leaving A, B.

steps.title: Continue from the remaining stack
steps.body: Push D produces A, B, D from bottom to top. The next pop returns D, followed by B and A. C is no longer present.

workedExample.conclusion: Always decide the next removal from the current stack, after all earlier operations have taken effect.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Maintain the top pointer in an array

leadVisual.title: Maintain the top pointer in an array

coreExplanation: If Top = 4, the array-backed stack is full and the push must fail without changing data or Top. Otherwise increment Top and store the new item at that index. Incrementing first selects the new top slot.
If Top = -1, the stack is empty and no item can be read. Otherwise read or save the item at Top, then decrement Top. The old cell may still show a value but is no longer active.

If the interface permits editing the exposed top item, replace its data without changing Top. A buried item is not available through an ordinary top-only operation. To reach it using stack operations, pop the items above it, retain them, then restore them in the correct order.

A question may use indices 1 to 8 and Top = 0 for empty. The principle is unchanged: check the declared full/empty condition and use the stated meaning of Top. Do not copy the classroom sentinel into a different representation.

learningCycle.observe: Use a five-cell array indexed 0 to 4. Top points to the last occupied cell; an empty stack has Top = -1. State the convention before tracing any operation.

stimulus.title: Stack[0:4]; Top points to the last occupied cell

learningCycle.question: Which array position receives the next pushed value?

prerequisite.title: Recall an out-of-range sentinel
prerequisite.body: The value -1 is not a legal array index here. It represents an empty stack state and must never be used to read an item. The greatest legal index is 4.

steps.title: Describe a checked push
steps.body: If Top = 4, the array-backed stack is full and the push must fail without changing data or Top. Otherwise increment Top and store the new item at that index. Incrementing first selects the new top slot.

steps.title: Describe a checked pop
steps.body: If Top = -1, the stack is empty and no item can be read. Otherwise read or save the item at Top, then decrement Top. The old cell may still show a value but is no longer active.

steps.title: Describe a permitted edit
steps.body: If the interface permits editing the exposed top item, replace its data without changing Top. A buried item is not available through an ordinary top-only operation. To reach it using stack operations, pop the items above it, retain them, then restore them in the correct order.

steps.title: Translate a different pointer convention
steps.body: A question may use indices 1 to 8 and Top = 0 for empty. The principle is unchanged: check the declared full/empty condition and use the stated meaning of Top. Do not copy the classroom sentinel into a different representation.

worked.title: Trace a push and a pop
worked.setup: Array indices are 0:4. Active values are A at 0 and B at 1, so Top = 1.

steps.title: Push C
steps.body: The stack is not full. Increase Top to 2 and write C to cell 2. The active order is A, B, C.

steps.title: Pop once
steps.body: Read C from cell 2, then reduce Top to 1. A and B remain active. A second pop would read B, not the stale C in cell 2.

worked.conclusion: Each successful operation updates the data and top state consistently; each rejected operation preserves them.

check.prompt: In a 0:4 stack with Top = -1, what must happen before a pop attempts to read Stack[Top]?
check.answer: Detect the empty state and reject the pop. Stack[-1] is outside the array bounds and must not be read.

learningCycle.takeaway: Check full or empty first, then update the selected cell and Top in the required order.
learningCycle.bridge: Waiting requests need the opposite removal order: the earliest remaining arrival should be served first.

workedExample.title: Trace a push and a pop
workedExample.setup: Array indices are 0:4. Active values are A at 0 and B at 1, so Top = 1.

steps.title: Push C
steps.body: The stack is not full. Increase Top to 2 and write C to cell 2. The active order is A, B, C.

steps.title: Pop once
steps.body: Read C from cell 2, then reduce Top to 1. A and B remain active. A second pop would read B, not the stale C in cell 2.

workedExample.conclusion: Each successful operation updates the data and top state consistently; each rejected operation preserves them.

pastPaperCoverageNotes.E082: Traces circular queue pointers and counts active items across wrap-around. Read the question’s pointer convention before applying the classroom convention.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use first in, first out for waiting requests

leadVisual.title: Use first in, first out for waiting requests

coreExplanation: Enqueue adds at the rear. Dequeue removes and returns the front item. A peek operation, if provided, inspects the front without removing it.
First in, first out means the earliest added item still waiting is served next. This suits a printer processing jobs in arrival order or a waiting list that must respect arrival order.

Both collections can contain A, B and C. A queue removes A first; a stack removes C first. Select the structure from the required next operation, not from the labels or physical appearance of the data.

learningCycle.observe: Three request cards wait at the booking desk. New cards join the rear, while service takes the card at the front. Trace the waiting order after each arrival and departure.

stimulus.title: Waiting requests in arrival order
items: A arrives.
B arrives.
C arrives.
The desk is ready to serve one request.

learningCycle.question: If requests A, B and C arrive in that order, should C be served first?

prerequisite.title: Recall current membership
prerequisite.body: An item removed by an earlier operation is no longer in the collection. The next operation uses the remaining items and any later additions.

steps.title: Use different ends for addition and removal
steps.body: Enqueue adds at the rear. Dequeue removes and returns the front item. A peek operation, if provided, inspects the front without removing it.

steps.title: Explain FIFO
steps.body: First in, first out means the earliest added item still waiting is served next. This suits a printer processing jobs in arrival order or a waiting list that must respect arrival order.

steps.title: Compare the required rule with a stack
steps.body: Both collections can contain A, B and C. A queue removes A first; a stack removes C first. Select the structure from the required next operation, not from the labels or physical appearance of the data.

worked.title: Add a new request after service begins
worked.setup: Enqueue A, B and C; dequeue once; enqueue D.

steps.title: Serve the front
steps.body: The dequeue returns A. B becomes the earliest remaining request.

steps.title: Add at the rear
steps.body: D joins after C, leaving B, C, D in front-to-rear order. The next dequeue returns B.

worked.conclusion: Later arrivals join after existing waiting requests.

check.prompt: A printer job with a higher number arrives last. Does FIFO make it run first?
check.answer: No. FIFO follows arrival order, not numerical size or priority. The earliest remaining job is next unless a different scheduling rule is explicitly specified.

learningCycle.takeaway: A queue adds at the rear and removes from the front, preserving first-in-first-out order.
learningCycle.bridge: A circular array can maintain that logical order even when it crosses the final physical index.

workedExample.title: Add a new request after service begins
workedExample.setup: Enqueue A, B and C; dequeue once; enqueue D.

steps.title: Serve the front
steps.body: The dequeue returns A. B becomes the earliest remaining request.

steps.title: Add at the rear
steps.body: D joins after C, leaving B, C, D in front-to-rear order. The next dequeue returns B.

workedExample.conclusion: Later arrivals join after existing waiting requests.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Reuse released cells with circular pointers

leadVisual.title: Reuse released cells with circular pointers

coreExplanation: Count = 0 means empty and Count = 5 means full. A starting empty state can use Front = 0 and Rear = -1. These pointer values only make sense with the stated convention.
If Count = 5, reject the addition. Otherwise advance Rear, wrapping 4 to 0, store the new item there and increase Count. Existing waiting items remain in their current logical order.
If Count = 0, reject the removal. Otherwise read the item at Front, advance Front with the same wrap rule and decrease Count. The released cell becomes available for a later enqueue.

Some representations make Rear point to the next insertion position instead of the last inserted item. Such a design writes first and advances Rear afterwards. Read the question’s convention; do not mix the two operation orders.

learningCycle.observe: Use a five-cell array indexed 0:4. Front points to the next item for removal; Rear points to the last inserted item; Count records how many items are active. The next position after 4 wraps to 0.
learningCycle.question: If the rear reaches the final array cell, can the queue still use a free cell at index 0?

prerequisite.title: Recall physical position and logical order
prerequisite.body: The queue order is obtained by starting at Front and following Count consecutive circular positions. Sorting the physical indices would not necessarily give arrival order.

steps.title: State empty and full using Count
steps.body: Count = 0 means empty and Count = 5 means full. A starting empty state can use Front = 0 and Rear = -1. These pointer values only make sense with the stated convention.

steps.title: Describe enqueue
steps.body: If Count = 5, reject the addition. Otherwise advance Rear, wrapping 4 to 0, store the new item there and increase Count. Existing waiting items remain in their current logical order.

steps.title: Describe dequeue
steps.body: If Count = 0, reject the removal. Otherwise read the item at Front, advance Front with the same wrap rule and decrease Count. The released cell becomes available for a later enqueue.

steps.title: Recognise other rear conventions
steps.body: Some representations make Rear point to the next insertion position instead of the last inserted item. Such a design writes first and advances Rear afterwards. Read the question’s convention; do not mix the two operation orders.

worked.title: Cross the final index
worked.setup: Front = 3, Rear = 4 and Count = 2. A is at index 3 and B at index 4; all other cells are inactive.

steps.title: Enqueue C
steps.body: There is space. Rear wraps from 4 to 0, C is stored at 0 and Count becomes 3. Logical order is A at 3, B at 4, C at 0.

steps.title: Dequeue once
steps.body: Return A from index 3, move Front to 4 and reduce Count to 2. B at 4 is still before C at 0.

worked.conclusion: Wrapping changes the physical index sequence while preserving the arrival sequence.

check.prompt: After wrap-around, Front = 4, Rear = 1 and Count = 3 in a 0:4 array. Which indices are active in queue order?
check.answer: 4, 0 and 1. Start at Front and follow exactly Count circular positions. Indices 2 and 3 are inactive regardless of any old displayed values.

learningCycle.takeaway: A circular queue follows its pointer convention and active count across the array boundary.
learningCycle.bridge: Track a complete lifecycle and distinguish an edit from a removal or a new arrival.

workedExample.title: Cross the final index
workedExample.setup: Front = 3, Rear = 4 and Count = 2. A is at index 3 and B at index 4; all other cells are inactive.

steps.title: Enqueue C
steps.body: There is space. Rear wraps from 4 to 0, C is stored at 0 and Count becomes 3. Logical order is A at 3, B at 4, C at 0.

steps.title: Dequeue once
steps.body: Return A from index 3, move Front to 4 and reduce Count to 2. B at 4 is still before C at 0.

workedExample.conclusion: Wrapping changes the physical index sequence while preserving the arrival sequence.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Keep edits, removals and failed operations consistent

leadVisual.title: Keep edits, removals and failed operations consistent

coreExplanation: With a last-item Rear convention, follow from Front through the active sequence to Rear, using the count or the stated full/empty rule. Do not include stale values outside that active sequence.

If the queue interface allows correcting the current front item, update its data while leaving Front, Rear and Count unchanged. Ordinary FIFO enqueue/dequeue operations do not provide arbitrary middle removal. A requested maintenance edit must be explicitly supported and must preserve the waiting order.
An enqueue on a full queue and a dequeue on an empty queue fail without moving pointers or changing Count. Test the condition before any write or read that assumes an item or space exists.

learningCycle.observe: After a dequeue, the old data may remain visible in the released cell. Use Front and Count to decide membership before counting items or applying an edit.
learningCycle.question: Does a non-blank cell necessarily contain an item that is still waiting?

prerequisite.title: Recall data changes versus membership changes
prerequisite.body: Editing a value changes its contents. Enqueue and dequeue change which items belong to the queue. These actions need different state updates.

steps.title: Count active positions rather than visible labels
steps.body: With a last-item Rear convention, follow from Front through the active sequence to Rear, using the count or the stated full/empty rule. Do not include stale values outside that active sequence.

steps.title: Describe a permitted edit without reordering
steps.body: If the queue interface allows correcting the current front item, update its data while leaving Front, Rear and Count unchanged. Ordinary FIFO enqueue/dequeue operations do not provide arbitrary middle removal. A requested maintenance edit must be explicitly supported and must preserve the waiting order.

steps.title: Protect the state at both limits
steps.body: An enqueue on a full queue and a dequeue on an empty queue fail without moving pointers or changing Count. Test the condition before any write or read that assumes an item or space exists.

worked.title: Read a wrapped queue with old values
worked.setup: In a 0:4 array, Front = 4, Rear = 1, Count = 3. Active items are B at 4, C at 0 and D at 1. Cells 2 and 3 show old labels.

steps.title: Identify the active collection
steps.body: The queue contains three items in the order B, C, D. The two other labels do not count.

steps.title: Correct then serve the front
steps.body: If permitted, correcting B’s data changes cell 4 only. Dequeue then returns that corrected item, advances Front to 0 and reduces Count to 2; C and D remain in order.

worked.conclusion: Use the logical queue state to determine what may be read, edited or removed.

check.prompt: A full queue rejects a new request. Should Rear still advance to record the attempt?
check.answer: No. A rejected enqueue must leave Rear, Front, Count and active data unchanged. Moving Rear would describe an addition that did not occur.

learningCycle.takeaway: Membership comes from the queue state; edits preserve order and rejected operations preserve all state.
learningCycle.bridge: Some collections need insertion between existing items. Links can represent that logical order.

steps.title: Correct then serve the front

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read nodes, a head pointer and a null link

leadVisual.title: Read nodes, a head pointer and a null link

coreExplanation: A node contains a data item and a link to the next node. In an array implementation, parallel Data and Next arrays can store these parts at the same index. A record array is another possible representation.
Head identifies the first node. Read its data, then obtain the next node’s index from its link. Stop on the null link instead of treating null as an array position.

A linked list is useful when a sequence needs insertion or deletion between known neighbours without shifting every later data item. Finding an unknown position may still require following links from the head; links do not make every search immediate.

learningCycle.observe: Three activity nodes are stored at indices 3, 0 and 2. Head = 3; links lead 3 → 0 → 2 → -1. The programme order follows those links rather than the numerical index order.
learningCycle.question: Must the next activity in a programme occupy the next array index?

prerequisite.title: Recall an array index as a stored value
prerequisite.body: A pointer in this array representation stores the index of another node. It is different from the data stored in that node. Here -1 is the null link: it means there is no next node.

steps.title: Identify the parts of a node
steps.body: A node contains a data item and a link to the next node. In an array implementation, parallel Data and Next arrays can store these parts at the same index. A record array is another possible representation.

steps.title: Follow Head, then each link
steps.body: Head identifies the first node. Read its data, then obtain the next node’s index from its link. Stop on the null link instead of treating null as an array position.

steps.title: Connect the representation to a use
steps.body: A linked list is useful when a sequence needs insertion or deletion between known neighbours without shifting every later data item. Finding an unknown position may still require following links from the head; links do not make every search immediate.

worked.title: Read the programme in logical order
worked.setup: Use Head = 3 and the node table above.

steps.title: Follow the first two nodes
steps.body: Visit index 3: Welcome. Its Next value is 0, so visit index 0: Workshop. Its Next value is 2.

steps.title: Stop at the end
steps.body: Visit index 2: Questions. Next is -1, so stop. The logical sequence is Welcome, Workshop, Questions despite storage indices 3, 0, 2.

worked.conclusion: The links define the sequence; the array positions only locate its nodes.

check.prompt: If Data[1] contains an old title but no active link reaches index 1, is it necessarily part of the list?
check.answer: No. Membership depends on the active chain reachable from Head. An unreferenced cell can be inactive or part of a separate free list.

learningCycle.takeaway: A linked list consists of nodes with data and links; follow Head and the links until null.
learningCycle.bridge: An insertion must connect the new node without losing the old successor.

workedExample.conclusion: The links define the sequence; the array positions only locate its nodes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Insert, edit or remove a node between neighbours

leadVisual.title: Insert, edit or remove a node between neighbours

coreExplanation: Store Break in the new node. Set its Next to the old successor of Workshop, index 2. Then change Workshop’s Next from 2 to 1. The resulting chain passes through the new node and still reaches Questions.
To rename Workshop, locate its active node and replace its Data value. Leave its Next link and Head unchanged when the list order should remain the same.

To delete the new Break node, set Workshop’s Next to Break’s successor, 2. Break is no longer reachable from Head. Its physical slot must later be marked available for reuse; removing it from the active chain is only one part of managing storage.

learningCycle.observe: The active chain is Welcome at 3 → Workshop at 0 → Questions at 2 → null. A new node at index 1 is available for Break. Preserve a route to Questions while changing the links.

stimulus.title: Insert Break at available node 1 after Workshop

learningCycle.question: How can Break be placed between Workshop and Questions without moving their data cells?

prerequisite.title: Recall saving a value before overwriting it
prerequisite.body: As with a swap, an old link may be needed after an update. Read or retain the old successor before replacing the link that points to it.

steps.title: Insert after a known predecessor
steps.body: Store Break in the new node. Set its Next to the old successor of Workshop, index 2. Then change Workshop’s Next from 2 to 1. The resulting chain passes through the new node and still reaches Questions.

steps.title: Edit data without changing the chain
steps.body: To rename Workshop, locate its active node and replace its Data value. Leave its Next link and Head unchanged when the list order should remain the same.

steps.title: Bypass a node when deleting it
steps.body: To delete the new Break node, set Workshop’s Next to Break’s successor, 2. Break is no longer reachable from Head. Its physical slot must later be marked available for reuse; removing it from the active chain is only one part of managing storage.

worked.title: Preserve the successor during insertion
worked.setup: Before insertion, Next[0] = 2 and node 1 is available.

steps.title: Connect the new node forward
steps.body: Set Data[1] to Break and Next[1] to 2. At this moment, the old active chain still works because Next[0] has not yet changed.

steps.title: Connect the predecessor to the new node
steps.body: Set Next[0] to 1. The active indices are now 3 → 0 → 1 → 2 → -1. No other data value needed to shift.

worked.conclusion: Set the new node’s successor before replacing the predecessor’s old successor link.

check.prompt: What can go wrong if the predecessor is pointed at the new node before its old successor is retained?
check.answer: The only stored route to the old successor may be overwritten. The insertion can lose the rest of the active chain or accidentally create a self-link. Retain the successor before replacing the old link.

learningCycle.takeaway: Insertion links a new node between neighbours; deletion bypasses it; a data edit need not change links.
learningCycle.bridge: The first node has no predecessor, so operations at the head need a separate case.

steps.title: Connect the predecessor to the new node

workedExample.conclusion: Set the new node’s successor before replacing the predecessor’s old successor link.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Handle the first node, the last node and an empty list

leadVisual.title: Handle the first node, the last node and an empty list

coreExplanation: Point the new node’s Next at the old Head, then set Head to the new node. For an empty list, the old Head is null, so the new node becomes both the first and final node.
Retain the old head node’s index, then set Head to that node’s Next. If it was the only node, Head becomes null and the list is empty. The removed node can then be returned to available storage.
To append after a known final node, the new node’s Next must be null and the old final node must point to it. To delete a final node with a predecessor, set the predecessor’s Next to null.

learningCycle.observe: Head identifies Welcome. No earlier node points to Welcome, so there is no predecessor link to update. The external Head pointer must take the role of that link.

stimulus.title: A list with one remaining node
items: Head = 2
Data[2] = Questions
Next[2] = -1
Requested operation: remove the first node.

learningCycle.question: Which pointer must change when the first activity is removed?

prerequisite.title: Recall the null-link convention
prerequisite.body: Here Head = -1 means an empty list, and Next = -1 marks the final node. These values describe absence; they must not be dereferenced as valid indices.

steps.title: Insert at the head
steps.body: Point the new node’s Next at the old Head, then set Head to the new node. For an empty list, the old Head is null, so the new node becomes both the first and final node.

steps.title: Delete at the head
steps.body: Retain the old head node’s index, then set Head to that node’s Next. If it was the only node, Head becomes null and the list is empty. The removed node can then be returned to available storage.

steps.title: Handle the final node
steps.body: To append after a known final node, the new node’s Next must be null and the old final node must point to it. To delete a final node with a predecessor, set the predecessor’s Next to null.

worked.title: Remove the only remaining node
worked.setup: Head = 2, Data[2] = Questions and Next[2] = -1.

steps.title: Update the external pointer
steps.body: Save the removed index 2, then set Head to Next[2], which is -1. The active list is now empty.

steps.title: Check the next attempted removal
steps.body: Head is null, so reject another removal before reading Data[Head]. The old text in cell 2 does not make an active item remain.

worked.conclusion: Head operations update the external start pointer; end operations preserve a null final link.

check.prompt: An empty list receives its first node at index 4. What must Head and Next[4] become?
check.answer: Set Next[4] to the old null Head, -1, then set Head to 4. The single node is both first and last.

learningCycle.takeaway: Treat head, tail and empty cases explicitly so every active chain remains reachable and terminates.
learningCycle.bridge: A fixed array also needs a reliable record of which node slots are free.

workedExample.title: Remove the only remaining node
workedExample.setup: Head = 2, Data[2] = Questions and Next[2] = -1.

steps.title: Update the external pointer
steps.body: Save the removed index 2, then set Head to Next[2], which is -1. The active list is now empty.

steps.title: Check the next attempted removal
steps.body: Head is null, so reject another removal before reading Data[Head]. The old text in cell 2 does not make an active item remain.

workedExample.conclusion: Head operations update the external start pointer; end operations preserve a null final link.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Check state before changing an array-backed ADT

leadVisual.title: Check state before changing an array-backed ADT

coreExplanation: A push must not write above the upper bound. A pop must not read an empty stack. A circular queue must not overwrite its oldest waiting item when full or read a stale value when empty.

For a stack push, advance Top then write. For our last-inserted Rear queue, advance Rear with wrap, write and increment Count. The check is shared in purpose, but the implementation details are not interchangeable.

After a rejected operation, data and pointers must match their prior state. After a successful operation, membership count and access pointers must describe the new collection. A plausible diagram alone does not prove both conditions.

learningCycle.observe: Compare a full five-cell stack and a full five-cell queue. Both reject a further addition, but their successful-operation pointer rules differ.

stimulus.title: A five-cell implementation at its limit
items: Array bounds: 0:4
Stack: Top = 4
Queue: Count = 5
Requested operation: add one more item.

learningCycle.question: What must remain unchanged when an addition is rejected because the array is full?

prerequisite.title: Recall bounds and active-state conventions
prerequisite.body: A 0:4 array has five cells. In our stack Top = 4 means full and Top = -1 means empty. In our queue Count = 5 means full and Count = 0 means empty.

steps.title: Check before the potentially invalid access
steps.body: A push must not write above the upper bound. A pop must not read an empty stack. A circular queue must not overwrite its oldest waiting item when full or read a stale value when empty.

steps.title: Describe the successful state transition
steps.body: For a stack push, advance Top then write. For our last-inserted Rear queue, advance Rear with wrap, write and increment Count. The check is shared in purpose, but the implementation details are not interchangeable.

steps.title: Validate the complete state
steps.body: After a rejected operation, data and pointers must match their prior state. After a successful operation, membership count and access pointers must describe the new collection. A plausible diagram alone does not prove both conditions.

worked.title: Test the two boundaries of a five-cell stack
worked.setup: Start with an empty 0:4 stack, Top = -1.

steps.title: Fill and try one extra push
steps.body: Five successful pushes move Top through 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4. The sixth is rejected, keeping Top = 4 and all five active values unchanged.

steps.title: Empty and try one extra pop
steps.body: Five successful pops return the values in reverse order and move Top back to -1. The sixth pop is rejected and returns no stored item.

worked.conclusion: Test the operation immediately before the limit, at the limit and after a rejected attempt.

check.prompt: Why is it wrong to decrement a queue’s Count before checking whether the queue is empty?
check.answer: An empty-queue attempt would make Count negative and corrupt the state even though no item was removed. Check first, then update only when the operation can succeed.

learningCycle.takeaway: A failed operation preserves the state; a successful operation keeps the data and access state consistent.
learningCycle.bridge: For linked lists, “full” means there is no node left on the free chain.

workedExample.title: Test the two boundaries of a five-cell stack
workedExample.setup: Start with an empty 0:4 stack, Top = -1.

steps.title: Fill and try one extra push
steps.body: Five successful pushes move Top through 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4. The sixth is rejected, keeping Top = 4 and all five active values unchanged.

steps.title: Empty and try one extra pop
steps.body: Five successful pops return the values in reverse order and move Top back to -1. The sixth pop is rejected and returns no stored item.

workedExample.conclusion: Test the operation immediately before the limit, at the limit and after a rejected attempt.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Maintain the active list and the free list together

leadVisual.title: Maintain the active list and the free list together

coreExplanation: Head identifies the first active node; FreeHead identifies the first free node. Follow each chain to null. A free cell may contain old Data text, but its membership in the free chain means that text is not an active item.

If FreeHead is null, reject the insertion because the fixed array has no free node. Otherwise retain that index as NewNode and move FreeHead to the node’s old Next. Only then reuse NewNode’s link for the active insertion.

First remove the node from the active chain by updating its predecessor or Head. Then point the removed node’s Next to the old FreeHead and set FreeHead to the removed index. The node can now be allocated again.

For each physical node index, copy its data and outgoing pointer into matching array positions. Record Head and FreeHead separately. The question may use null = 0 with indices 1:8; follow that declared convention rather than this activity’s -1.

learningCycle.observe: In an array indexed 0:4, the active chain is Head = 3: 3 → 0 → 2 → -1. The free chain is FreeHead = 1: 1 → 4 → -1. Every slot belongs to exactly one of these chains.

stimulus.title: Two chains share the array storage
items: Active: Head = 3; 3 → 0 → 2 → -1
Free: FreeHead = 1; 1 → 4 → -1
Insert a new node after active node 0.

learningCycle.question: When node 1 becomes active, how can we still find the remaining free node 4?

prerequisite.title: Recall two uses of a link
prerequisite.body: In an active node, Next identifies the next active item. In a free node, Next identifies the next available slot. Reusing a node changes which chain its link belongs to, so retain the remaining free-chain pointer before overwriting that link.

steps.title: Read the two chains independently
steps.body: Head identifies the first active node; FreeHead identifies the first free node. Follow each chain to null. A free cell may contain old Data text, but its membership in the free chain means that text is not an active item.

steps.title: Allocate before linking into the active list
steps.body: If FreeHead is null, reject the insertion because the fixed array has no free node. Otherwise retain that index as NewNode and move FreeHead to the node’s old Next. Only then reuse NewNode’s link for the active insertion.

steps.title: Return a deleted node to the free chain
steps.body: First remove the node from the active chain by updating its predecessor or Head. Then point the removed node’s Next to the old FreeHead and set FreeHead to the removed index. The node can now be allocated again.

steps.title: Translate a diagram into parallel arrays
steps.body: For each physical node index, copy its data and outgoing pointer into matching array positions. Record Head and FreeHead separately. The question may use null = 0 with indices 1:8; follow that declared convention rather than this activity’s -1.

worked.title: Insert Break after Workshop and then remove it
worked.setup: Use the initial active and free chains above. Workshop occupies index 0.

steps.title: Preserve the rest of the free list
steps.body: Take NewNode = 1 and set FreeHead to old Next[1] = 4. The remaining free chain is now 4 → -1.

steps.title: Link the allocated node into the active list
steps.body: Store Break at Data[1]. Set Next[1] to Workshop’s old successor, 2; then set Next[0] to 1. The active chain becomes 3 → 0 → 1 → 2 → -1.

steps.title: Delete and release the node
steps.body: Set Next[0] to Next[1], which is 2. Set Next[1] to the old FreeHead, 4, then set FreeHead to 1. Both original chains are restored. Old Break text at Data[1] is inactive.

worked.conclusion: Preserve access to both chains throughout allocation and release.

check.prompt: Why must the old Next[FreeHead] be retained before the allocated node’s Next is changed?
check.answer: It is the link to the remaining free nodes. Overwriting it first can lose the rest of the free chain or make FreeHead point into the active list. Advance or save the free-chain pointer before reuse.

learningCycle.takeaway: Allocation and deletion must preserve both the active chain and the reusable free chain.
learningCycle.bridge: Bring the structures together by assigning each part of the booking system its own operation rule.

workedExample.title: Insert Break after Workshop and then remove it
workedExample.setup: Use the initial active and free chains above. Workshop occupies index 0.

steps.title: Preserve the rest of the free list
steps.body: Take NewNode = 1 and set FreeHead to old Next[1] = 4. The remaining free chain is now 4 → -1.

steps.title: Link the allocated node into the active list

steps.title: Delete and release the node
steps.body: Set Next[0] to Next[1], which is 2. Set Next[1] to the old FreeHead, 4, then set FreeHead to 1. Both original chains are restored. Old Break text at Data[1] is inactive.

workedExample.conclusion: Preserve access to both chains throughout allocation and release.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose dimensions and record fields for different facts

leadVisual.title: Choose dimensions and record fields for different facts

coreExplanation: Use a 2D BOOLEAN array for occupancy by row and seat. Use a 1D array of booking records for bookings located by one booking index. Each record can hold a STRING name and BOOLEAN Paid field.
Bookings[2].Paid first selects the second record and then its Paid field. It is different from a two-dimensional array access: .Paid is a named field, not a second numerical coordinate.
A single ordinary 2D array has one element type. Do not use it to claim that one column is STRING and another is BOOLEAN. A record preserves the different field types directly.

learningCycle.observe: One booking has a name and a payment state. The room has rows and seat positions. A collection of bookings and a grid of seats organise different kinds of relationships.

stimulus.title: Different facts need different accesses
items: One booking: name Mina, paid FALSE.
Booking collection: one numbered position per booking.
Seating plan: a row number and a seat position identify each seat.

learningCycle.question: Should a booking record and a seating plan use the same representation?

prerequisite.title: Recall record fields versus array elements
prerequisite.body: A record groups named fields that may have different types. An array has one declared element type and indexed positions. That element type can itself be a defined record type.

steps.title: Match each access to the required coordinates
steps.body: Use a 2D BOOLEAN array for occupancy by row and seat. Use a 1D array of booking records for bookings located by one booking index. Each record can hold a STRING name and BOOLEAN Paid field.

steps.title: Read an array-of-records access in two stages
steps.body: Bookings[2].Paid first selects the second record and then its Paid field. It is different from a two-dimensional array access: .Paid is a named field, not a second numerical coordinate.
steps.code:
TYPE BookingRecord
    DECLARE Name : STRING
    DECLARE Paid : BOOLEAN
ENDTYPE
DECLARE Bookings : ARRAY[1:2] OF BookingRecord
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
FOR Index <- 1 TO 2
    INPUT Bookings[Index].Name
    Bookings[Index].Paid <- FALSE
NEXT Index
Bookings[2].Paid <- TRUE
FOR Index <- 1 TO 2
    OUTPUT Bookings[Index].Name
    OUTPUT Bookings[Index].Paid
NEXT Index

steps.title: Avoid a type mismatch disguised as a table
steps.body: A single ordinary 2D array has one element type. Do not use it to claim that one column is STRING and another is BOOLEAN. A record preserves the different field types directly.

worked.title: Interpret one updated field
worked.setup: Input names Mina and Jo into the two-element record array.

steps.title: Trace initialisation
steps.body: Both Paid fields become FALSE. Bookings[1].Name is Mina and Bookings[2].Name is Jo.

steps.title: Apply the selected update
steps.body: Bookings[2].Paid <- TRUE changes only Jo’s payment field. The outputs are Mina, FALSE, Jo, TRUE on separate lines.

worked.conclusion: Choose dimensions for indexed relationships and fields for differently typed facts about one object.

check.prompt: Which access locates a seat by row and seat number, and which locates the name of the second booking?
check.answer: Occupied[Row, Seat] uses two indices for the seating grid. Bookings[2].Name selects one record by index and then selects its named field.

learningCycle.takeaway: Use the representation that matches how each fact is identified and what type it needs.
learningCycle.bridge: Collections of pending work and completed actions also need different removal rules.

leadVisual.title: Choose and combine FIFO, LIFO and linked order

coreExplanation: Use a queue for waiting requests, a stack for undo entries and a linked list when the activity programme needs insertion between known nodes. Justify each choice with the required operation rather than only naming a familiar example.

To transfer a stack into a queue, repeatedly pop the stack and enqueue the removed item. The first item placed in the queue is the original stack’s top item. Its arrival position is now governed by the queue.

Repeatedly dequeue and push onto the stack. The queue preserves the order in which the original stack was popped. Pushing that sequence builds a stack whose bottom-to-top order is reversed from the original.

When the queue’s rear pointer means next insertion position, store at Rear and then advance it. When Top means last occupied stack position, read before decrementing on pop and advance before storing on push. Follow any alternative directions or bounds stated by the supplied diagram.

learningCycle.observe: Requests must be served in arrival order, while completed changes must be undone in reverse completion order. A programme of activities may need insertion between known neighbours.

stimulus.title: Initial transfer state
items: Stack, bottom to top: A, B, C
Queue: empty, with sufficient capacity
Move all stack items to the queue, then move them back.

learningCycle.question: Why should the waiting list and the undo history not share the same removal rule?

prerequisite.title: Recall the three rules
prerequisite.body: A queue removes the earliest remaining arrival. A stack removes the latest remaining addition. A linked list follows its node links and supports controlled link changes to its sequence.

steps.title: Assign one responsibility to each collection
steps.body: Use a queue for waiting requests, a stack for undo entries and a linked list when the activity programme needs insertion between known nodes. Justify each choice with the required operation rather than only naming a familiar example.

steps.title: Trace a transfer by the source removal rule
steps.body: To transfer a stack into a queue, repeatedly pop the stack and enqueue the removed item. The first item placed in the queue is the original stack’s top item. Its arrival position is now governed by the queue.

steps.title: Transfer back using the queue rule
steps.body: Repeatedly dequeue and push onto the stack. The queue preserves the order in which the original stack was popped. Pushing that sequence builds a stack whose bottom-to-top order is reversed from the original.

steps.title: Read the question’s pointer meanings
steps.body: When the queue’s rear pointer means next insertion position, store at Rear and then advance it. When Top means last occupied stack position, read before decrementing on pop and advance before storing on push. Follow any alternative directions or bounds stated by the supplied diagram.

worked.title: Reverse a stack through a queue
worked.setup: The original stack contains A, B, C from bottom to top. The queue begins empty and has sufficient capacity.

steps.title: Empty the stack into the queue
steps.body: Pops return C, then B, then A. Enqueue in that order, so the queue contains C, B, A from front to rear.

steps.title: Empty the queue back into the stack
steps.body: Dequeues return C, B, A in that same order. Push each value. The final stack is C, B, A from bottom to top, so its next pop is A.

worked.conclusion: Track the returned item at every transfer and state which end each order describes.

check.prompt: After the two transfers, is the queue responsible for reversing the order of its own arrivals?
check.answer: No. The queue preserves its arrival order. The overall reversal results from first removing the original stack top-first and then pushing that sequence back onto the stack.

learningCycle.takeaway: Choose an ADT from its access rule and trace every transfer using the source and destination rules.
learningCycle.bridge: Finally follow one successful or rejected booking through all the affected structures.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow a booking from input to a consistent outcome

leadVisual.title: Follow a booking from input to a consistent outcome

coreExplanation: Validate the requested position, then check occupancy and the person’s existing membership. Assign a free seat or, under the stated waiting rule, enqueue a new person requesting an occupied seat. Reject a duplicate person or an addition to a full waiting queue without changing the state.

Before each successful change, push the previous seat and waiting-queue state. Both a seat assignment and a new waiting entry need an undo record because both change the system. Undo pops the latest entry and restores that previous state. A rejected attempt that changes nothing adds no entry.

When the task requires a persistent audit log, append a clearly formatted line and close the file. Saving the current complete register is a different requirement and may use a replacement file. Choose the mode from the desired final saved content.

Check the selected field and grid cell, the front-to-rear waiting order, the bottom-to-top undo order and the saved file content where applicable. A success message alone does not prove those values agree.

learningCycle.observe: The booking system has seat occupancy, waiting requests and an undo history. Assigning a free seat and adding someone to the waiting queue are both successful state changes. A rejected request changes neither collection and creates no undo entry.

stimulus.title: Two requests for one seat

Mina requests [1,2].
Jo later requests [1,2].
Waiting rule: queue a request whose seat is occupied.

prerequisite.title: Recall a state transition
prerequisite.body: Describe the values before an operation, the checks it makes and the values after it. Keep a saved log separate from an undo entry: a log records events, while undo needs the previous state required to reverse a successful change.

steps.title: Check before changing the booking
steps.body: Validate the requested position, then check occupancy and the person’s existing membership. Assign a free seat or, under the stated waiting rule, enqueue a new person requesting an occupied seat. Reject a duplicate person or an addition to a full waiting queue without changing the state.
