worked.title: Undo two different successful changes
worked.setup: The experiment uses a simplified one-dimensional list of seats 1:4. Seat 2 is initially free. Mina requests it, then Jo requests the same occupied seat.

steps.title: Trace the seat assignment
steps.body: Assign seat 2 to Mina and push the previous state. This creates one undo entry.

steps.title: Trace the successful waiting entry
steps.body: Keep Mina’s seat assignment and enqueue Jo at the rear. Save the prior state before this second change. There are now two undo entries. A repeated request from Jo would be rejected because Jo is already waiting and would add no third entry.

steps.title: Undo the changes one at a time
steps.body: The first Undo removes Jo’s waiting entry and leaves Mina in seat 2. A second Undo restores the state before Mina’s assignment, making seat 2 free. Each Undo restores the saved whole state rather than applying an unstated automatic promotion rule.

worked.conclusion: State the application’s rules, then check that every affected representation agrees with the outcome.

check.prompt: Why is storing only the text “booking changed” insufficient for a reliable undo entry?
check.answer: Undo must know which booking or seat changed and what its previous state was. A generic message does not contain enough information to restore that state.

learningCycle.takeaway: Match each structure to its responsibility and verify a complete, consistent state change.
learningCycle.bridge: Return to any check you could not explain without revealing its answer, then attempt the chapter’s combined practice.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Place each action at the right level

leadVisual.title: Place each action at the right level

coreExplanation: Declare Index, Value and Count as INTEGER. Set Count to 0 before any inputs, because no positive values have yet been observed.
Use FOR for the three slots. Read one fresh Value inside each iteration. Only IF Value > 0 should execute Count <- Count + 1. Do not change the rule to >= 0.

OUTPUT Count belongs after NEXT Index. This produces one completed result. Check that every sentence in the design has a corresponding operation and that no extra input, condition or output has been invented.

learningCycle.observe: The desk reads exactly three integer requests, counts those that are positive and displays the final count. Zero and negative requests still occupy input slots but do not increase the positive count.

stimulus.title: Structured English design
items: Set the positive-request count to zero.
Read three integers in turn.
For each positive integer, increase the count by one.
Display the completed count once.

learningCycle.question: Which actions happen once, which repeat and which happen only on one branch?

prerequisite.title: Recall counter and accumulator roles
prerequisite.body: Index identifies the current input slot. Count records how many inputs meet a condition. They may have different values even though both are INTEGER. A total of the input values would be a third, different quantity.

steps.title: Identify the required data and starting state
steps.body: Declare Index, Value and Count as INTEGER. Set Count to 0 before any inputs, because no positive values have yet been observed.

steps.title: Translate one repeated responsibility
steps.body: Use FOR for the three slots. Read one fresh Value inside each iteration. Only IF Value > 0 should execute Count <- Count + 1. Do not change the rule to >= 0.

steps.title: Put final reporting after repetition
steps.body: OUTPUT Count belongs after NEXT Index. This produces one completed result. Check that every sentence in the design has a corresponding operation and that no extra input, condition or output has been invented.
steps.code:
DECLARE Count, Index, Value : INTEGER
Count <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 3
    INPUT Value
    IF Value > 0 THEN
        Count <- Count + 1
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Count

worked.title: Translate first, then challenge the translation
worked.setup: Use inputs -2, 0 and 5.

steps.title: Trace the three decisions
steps.body: The tests are FALSE, FALSE and TRUE. Count stays 0, stays 0, then becomes 1. The loop still reads all three values.

steps.title: Distinguish a count from a total
steps.body: This design outputs 1, not 5. A different requirement to total positive values would use Total <- Total + Value. Read that distinction carefully in the real-paper task, which requires 100 inputs and a positive-number total.

worked.conclusion: A translation must preserve the specified operation, not merely use the right control-structure names.

check.prompt: If Count <- 0 is moved inside the loop, what is output for 2, 3, -1?
check.answer: 0 instead of 2. Each iteration resets Count, and the final negative value causes no increment.

learningCycle.takeaway: Translate the complete contract: starting state, repeated input, conditional work and final output.
learningCycle.bridge: A flowchart expresses the same obligations through arrows and decisions. Follow every edge before writing code.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Preserve both branches and the back edge

leadVisual.title: Preserve both branches and the back edge

coreExplanation: The graph explicitly sets Count to 0 and Index to 1. Its pre-condition test becomes WHILE Index <= 3.
INPUT Value occurs in the loop body. Put only the Count update inside IF Value > 0. Put Index <- Index + 1 after ENDIF so it runs for a positive, zero or negative value.
When Index reaches 4, the condition is FALSE. Continue to OUTPUT Count and then finish. There is no fourth input or return from End.

learningCycle.observe: Follow the No arrow from Value > 0 in the supplied three-input flowchart. It skips the count increment but still reaches the Index increment and the return to the loop test.

stimulus.title: Flowchart checkpoints
items: Initial state: Count 0, Index 1.
Loop test: Index <= 3.
Inner test: Value > 0.
Both inner paths advance Index before returning to the loop test.

learningCycle.question: Why must the flowchart advance Index after a non-positive input?

prerequisite.title: Recall a flowchart path
prerequisite.body: Arrows give execution order. A diamond selects a branch; a backward edge represents repetition; the End terminal has no outgoing execution path. A statement after a rejoin belongs to both branches.

steps.title: Translate the initialisation before the loop
steps.body: The graph explicitly sets Count to 0 and Index to 1. Its pre-condition test becomes WHILE Index <= 3.

steps.title: Translate the inner decision without swallowing the shared update
steps.body: INPUT Value occurs in the loop body. Put only the Count update inside IF Value > 0. Put Index <- Index + 1 after ENDIF so it runs for a positive, zero or negative value.

steps.title: Translate the exit and the terminal
steps.body: When Index reaches 4, the condition is FALSE. Continue to OUTPUT Count and then finish. There is no fourth input or return from End.
steps.code:
DECLARE Count, Index, Value : INTEGER
Count <- 0
Index <- 1
WHILE Index <= 3
    INPUT Value
    IF Value > 0 THEN
        Count <- Count + 1
    ENDIF
    Index <- Index + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Count

worked.title: Verify two representations of one design
worked.setup: Trace -2, 0, 5 through the graph and the direct WHILE translation.

steps.title: Track the two counters separately
steps.body: After each input, Index becomes 2, 3 and 4 while Count becomes 0, 0 and 1. The non-positive inputs still advance Index.

steps.title: Compare with the previous FOR version
steps.body: Both consume three inputs and output 1. The WHILE version makes the graph’s test and update explicit; the FOR version manages the known iteration sequence in its header and NEXT.

worked.conclusion: Check observable inputs, outputs and state changes along every path, not just a visually similar code layout.

check.prompt: What would happen if Index <- Index + 1 were placed inside IF Value > 0?
check.answer: A non-positive input would not advance the slot counter. The program could request more than three values and might fail to terminate if no positive values arrive.

learningCycle.takeaway: Translate both decision outcomes, shared updates, back edges and the final path to End.
learningCycle.bridge: The next extension calls supplied routines to process booking codes and generate useful numeric values.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Name and declare the data

leadVisual.title: Name and declare the data

coreExplanation: Seats describes a count; Price describes the cost of one seat. Names such as A and B give the reader less help. The same INTEGER type can represent a seat count or a loop counter, but those variables have different responsibilities.

Use INTEGER for whole seats, REAL for a price, STRING for a name or code, BOOLEAN for payment confirmation and CHAR for a single zone letter. DATE is available for a calendar day, using the declared calendar convention. A value containing digits is not necessarily a number for arithmetic.
Write DECLARE, the identifier, a colon and its data type. The next learning steps will give these variables values; declaration alone is not enough to calculate a receipt.

learningCycle.observe: Look at one request: Mina wants three seats at 12.50 each. The booking code is 0072 and payment is not yet confirmed. Describe each fact before writing any statements.

rows: A price that may have a fractional part

learningCycle.question: What must the program know before it can produce a booking receipt?

prerequisite.title: Recall variables and data types
prerequisite.body: In Section 10 a variable was a named storage location and its data type described the values it could represent. A declaration sets up that name and type. It does not automatically give the variable zero, an empty string or any other initial value.

steps.title: Choose names that explain the role
steps.body: Seats describes a count; Price describes the cost of one seat. Names such as A and B give the reader less help. The same INTEGER type can represent a seat count or a loop counter, but those variables have different responsibilities.

steps.title: Choose a type from the permitted values
steps.body: Use INTEGER for whole seats, REAL for a price, STRING for a name or code, BOOLEAN for payment confirmation and CHAR for a single zone letter. DATE is available for a calendar day, using the declared calendar convention. A value containing digits is not necessarily a number for arithmetic.

steps.title: Declare each variable before use
steps.body: Write DECLARE, the identifier, a colon and its data type. The next learning steps will give these variables values; declaration alone is not enough to calculate a receipt.
steps.code:
DECLARE Name, BookingCode : STRING
DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
DECLARE Price : REAL
DECLARE Paid : BOOLEAN
DECLARE Zone : CHAR
DECLARE EventDate : DATE

worked.title: Translate a booking card into declarations
worked.setup: The desk adds a zone, B, and the event date 12/05/2027 using dd/mm/yyyy.

steps.title: Explain the text choices
steps.body: BookingCode must keep 0072, so STRING is appropriate. Zone holds exactly one character, so CHAR is appropriate. If zones could include AB, Zone would need STRING.

steps.title: Separate type and current value
steps.body: DECLARE Seats : INTEGER permits integer values. It does not mean that Seats currently contains 3, or that negative integers are valid booking requests. Those are separate assignment and validation decisions.

worked.conclusion: Declare from the full data requirement, then explicitly obtain or assign the current value.

check.prompt: A room code is "003". Write a suitable declaration and explain why INTEGER would lose useful information.
check.answer: DECLARE RoomCode : STRING. The code identifies a room and must retain all three characters; interpreting it as integer 3 loses the leading zeros.

learningCycle.takeaway: A declaration establishes an identifier and data type; it does not supply an initial value.
learningCycle.bridge: Some values change between bookings, while a configured price stays fixed during the program run.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define a fixed value once

leadVisual.title: Define a fixed value once

coreExplanation: CONSTANT SeatPrice = 12.50 declares and initialises a named constant. Its value remains fixed during that execution. Use = in the declaration, not the assignment arrow.

SeatPrice explains why a number is being multiplied. A later version can change the single definition to 13.00; each use then follows the same revised rule. This reduces missed edits and inconsistent values.

Cambridge constant declarations use a literal: CONSTANT DoublePrice = SeatPrice * 2 is not the required declaration form. Calculate such a result into a suitably declared variable. A constant can be edited in source between versions, but cannot be reassigned during execution. In the following paper excerpt, IF branches choose which postal rate applies: read each branch as a conditional choice. The question here asks about the repeated rate values and their maintenance; writing those decisions is taught later.

learningCycle.observe: The receipt, booking summary and daily report all need the same price. Imagine that a later version uses 13.00 and one of three repeated numbers is overlooked.

stimulus.title: One rule used in three places
items: Receipt: multiply by 12.50.
Booking summary: multiply by 12.50.
Daily report: multiply by 12.50.

learningCycle.question: If every seat costs 12.50, should the program contain the literal 12.50 in every calculation?

prerequisite.title: Recall a literal
prerequisite.body: A literal is a value written directly in the program: 12.50 is numeric, "0072" is STRING, 'B' is CHAR and FALSE is BOOLEAN. Quotation marks and spelling affect the literal’s type.

steps.title: Give the literal a meaningful name
steps.body: CONSTANT SeatPrice = 12.50 declares and initialises a named constant. Its value remains fixed during that execution. Use = in the declaration, not the assignment arrow.
steps.code:
CONSTANT SeatPrice = 12.50
CONSTANT EventName = "School workshop"
CONSTANT MaximumSeats = 6

steps.title: Use the constant wherever its rule applies
steps.body: SeatPrice explains why a number is being multiplied. A later version can change the single definition to 13.00; each use then follows the same revised rule. This reduces missed edits and inconsistent values.

steps.title: Distinguish a fixed declaration from a calculation
steps.body: Cambridge constant declarations use a literal: CONSTANT DoublePrice = SeatPrice * 2 is not the required declaration form. Calculate such a result into a suitably declared variable. A constant can be edited in source between versions, but cannot be reassigned during execution. In the following paper excerpt, IF branches choose which postal rate applies: read each branch as a conditional choice. The question here asks about the repeated rate values and their maintenance; writing those decisions is taught later.

worked.title: Repair a rate that is repeated
worked.setup: A program uses 2.50 as the booking fee in four places.

steps.title: Declare the rate once
steps.body: Write CONSTANT BookingFee = 2.50 and replace the four fee literals with BookingFee. Retain other unrelated occurrences of 2.50; equal numbers do not necessarily mean the same rule.

steps.title: Explain the benefit in context
steps.body: A fee change needs one edit to the definition rather than four edits to the calculations. Each calculation still uses the same fee, and the identifier makes its purpose clear.

worked.conclusion: A useful explanation links the named constant to a specific maintenance task.

check.prompt: Correct CONSTANT Limit <- 6. Can the corrected constant later be changed by Limit <- 7 in the same run?
check.answer: Write CONSTANT Limit = 6. It cannot be reassigned in the same run; edit the constant definition for a different program version if the fixed rule changes.

learningCycle.takeaway: Use CONSTANT Identifier = Literal for a fixed named value, and reuse its meaningful name.
learningCycle.bridge: Variable values do change during a run. Follow each assignment to see exactly when the change occurs.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Read, calculate and replace a value

leadVisual.title: Read, calculate and replace a value

coreExplanation: For Seats <- Seats + 1, the right side reads the existing 3. This is why Seats must already have a value before the update.
The expression 3 + 1 produces 4. Store 4 in the variable named on the left, replacing its old 3. The variable’s name and declared type stay the same.
SavedSeats <- Seats copies the current value 3. It does not create a permanent connection. A later update to Seats leaves SavedSeats as 3.

learningCycle.observe: Mina first requests three seats, then adds one. Keep a copy of the original request in SavedSeats. Predict whether that copy also changes when Seats is updated.

stimulus.title: Trace these statements in order
items: Seats <- 3
SavedSeats <- Seats
Seats <- Seats + 1

learningCycle.question: When Seats contains 3, how can Seats <- Seats + 1 be correct?

prerequisite.title: Recall a trace
prerequisite.body: A trace records the state after each executed statement. Read <- as “is assigned”. Assignment is an action, not the mathematical assertion that two expressions are equal.

steps.title: Read the old value on the right
steps.body: For Seats <- Seats + 1, the right side reads the existing 3. This is why Seats must already have a value before the update.

steps.title: Calculate before storing
steps.body: The expression 3 + 1 produces 4. Store 4 in the variable named on the left, replacing its old 3. The variable’s name and declared type stay the same.

steps.title: Keep a copied value separate
steps.body: SavedSeats <- Seats copies the current value 3. It does not create a permanent connection. A later update to Seats leaves SavedSeats as 3.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats, SavedSeats : INTEGER
Seats <- 3
SavedSeats <- Seats
Seats <- Seats + 1
OUTPUT Seats
OUTPUT SavedSeats

worked.title: Follow a change without losing the original
worked.setup: Execute the complete program above.

steps.title: Record the two locations
steps.body: Seats receives 3, then SavedSeats receives that same value. Only the final assignment changes Seats.

steps.title: Read the output in order
steps.body: The first OUTPUT displays 4 and the second displays 3. Displaying a value does not remove it from its variable.

worked.conclusion: Trace the destination of each assignment; do not update other variables merely because they once contained the same value.

check.prompt: Seats is 5. After Saved <- Seats and Seats <- Seats - 2, what are the two values?
check.answer: Saved is 5 and Seats is 3. Saved keeps the value copied before the subtraction.

learningCycle.takeaway: Evaluate the right side using existing values, then store the result on the left.
learningCycle.bridge: Now replace a fixed starting assignment with keyboard input and produce a labelled receipt.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Obtain inputs before producing a result

leadVisual.title: Obtain inputs before producing a result

coreExplanation: OUTPUT "Enter seats" displays a prompt. INPUT Seats then obtains a value and stores it in Seats. The prompt does not itself read the value.
After INPUT, Seats has the entered quantity and SeatPrice has its constant value. Total <- Seats * SeatPrice calculates the product. Total must be REAL because the result may have a fractional part.

OUTPUT "Total: ", Total displays a label followed by the value. Commas separate output items; this is different from building a stored STRING. Assume the input is an integer at this stage; range validation is taught later.

learningCycle.observe: The seat price is fixed, but each attendee chooses a different quantity. Put the actions “ask”, “read”, “calculate” and “display” into a workable order.

stimulus.title: Receipt requirement
items: Each seat costs 12.50.
Read one integer seat quantity.
Display the calculated total with a label.

learningCycle.question: What must happen before the program can display the total booking cost?

prerequisite.title: Recall sequence
prerequisite.body: Statements run in order unless a control structure changes that order. A calculation cannot use an input that has not yet been read. A prompt is output text telling the user what to enter.

steps.title: Ask and read are separate operations
steps.body: OUTPUT "Enter seats" displays a prompt. INPUT Seats then obtains a value and stores it in Seats. The prompt does not itself read the value.

steps.title: Calculate from defined values
steps.body: After INPUT, Seats has the entered quantity and SeatPrice has its constant value. Total <- Seats * SeatPrice calculates the product. Total must be REAL because the result may have a fractional part.

steps.title: Display the result explicitly
steps.body: OUTPUT "Total: ", Total displays a label followed by the value. Commas separate output items; this is different from building a stored STRING. Assume the input is an integer at this stage; range validation is taught later.
steps.code:
CONSTANT SeatPrice = 12.50
DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
DECLARE Total : REAL
OUTPUT "Enter seats"
INPUT Seats
Total <- Seats * SeatPrice
OUTPUT "Total: ", Total

worked.title: Produce the first receipt
worked.setup: The user enters 3 at the prompt.

steps.title: Follow the data dependency
steps.body: INPUT stores 3 in Seats. The multiplication reads 3 and 12.50, producing 37.5, which is stored in Total.

steps.title: Explain the visible result
steps.body: The final output displays Total: followed by 37.5. A display format with two decimal places is a separate presentation requirement; the calculated amount is the same as 37.50.

worked.conclusion: The full sequence is declaration and constant definition, prompt and input, calculation, then output.

check.prompt: A program declares Seats and immediately executes Total <- Seats * 12.50 before INPUT Seats. Why is the calculation unsafe?
check.answer: Seats has not yet been given a value. Move INPUT Seats before the multiplication, and declare Total as REAL before using it.

learningCycle.takeaway: INPUT stores an entered value; assignment stores a calculated value; OUTPUT displays a value.
learningCycle.bridge: Different pricing rules need different expression grouping. Build those expressions before adding decisions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Group a calculation to match the rule

leadVisual.title: Group a calculation to match the rule

coreExplanation: Without brackets, 3 * 12.50 + 2.00 first gives 37.50 and then adds the single fee. Operators of the same precedence are evaluated left to right in these examples.
For a fee on every seat, calculate 12.50 + 2.00 before multiplying by 3. Parentheses express that grouping explicitly rather than relying on a verbal description.
The / operator gives real division: 7 / 2 is 3.5. Dividing a booking total by its positive seat count gives a per-seat amount. A divisor must not be zero.

learningCycle.observe: Three seats cost 12.50 each. Compare a receipt with one booking fee against a receipt with a fee on every seat. The same numbers can describe different calculations.
learningCycle.question: Is a 2.00 charge added once per booking or once per seat?

prerequisite.title: Recall assignment
prerequisite.body: An assignment calculates its right side first. Arithmetic uses +, -, * and /. Choose a REAL result when fractional values may occur.

steps.title: Apply multiplication and division before addition and subtraction
steps.body: Without brackets, 3 * 12.50 + 2.00 first gives 37.50 and then adds the single fee. Operators of the same precedence are evaluated left to right in these examples.

steps.title: Use parentheses for a combined per-item amount
steps.body: For a fee on every seat, calculate 12.50 + 2.00 before multiplying by 3. Parentheses express that grouping explicitly rather than relying on a verbal description.

steps.title: Keep real division separate from whole-group counting
steps.body: The / operator gives real division: 7 / 2 is 3.5. Dividing a booking total by its positive seat count gives a per-seat amount. A divisor must not be zero.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
DECLARE Price, Fee, Total : REAL
Seats <- 3
Price <- 12.50
Fee <- 2.00
Total <- Seats * (Price + Fee)
OUTPUT Total

worked.title: Explain both receipts
worked.setup: Use Seats 3, Price 12.50 and Fee 2.00.

steps.title: Calculate a fee on every seat
steps.body: 3 * (12.50 + 2.00) = 3 * 14.50 = 43.50. The 4.00 difference comes from two extra fee charges.

worked.conclusion: A correct expression implements the wording of the rule, not just a plausible numerical answer.

check.prompt: Calculate 2 + 3 * 4 and (2 + 3) * 4. Why do they differ?
check.answer: The results are 14 and 20. In the first expression multiplication occurs first; in the second, parentheses require the addition first.

learningCycle.takeaway: Translate the charging rule into grouping, then evaluate before assigning.
learningCycle.bridge: A time slot needs complete hours and remaining minutes, which are different from real division.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Separate complete groups from a remainder

leadVisual.title: Separate complete groups from a remainder

coreExplanation: Minutes DIV 60 gives the number of complete hours. For non-negative integer Minutes and positive divisor 60, this is 2 for 125. DIV is not rounding to the nearest integer.
Minutes MOD 60 gives 5. The remainder must be at least 0 and less than 60 in this example. At exactly 120 minutes, it is 0.
Hours * 60 + Remaining must equal Minutes. Both result variables are INTEGER. These examples use non-negative quantities and positive divisors, so no signed-remainder convention is needed.

learningCycle.observe: Make as many complete groups of 60 minutes as possible. Two groups use 120 minutes, leaving 5. A decimal hour value answers a different question.

stimulus.title: Split a duration
items: Total minutes: 125
Minutes per complete hour: 60

learningCycle.question: How do 125 booking minutes become 2 hours and 5 minutes?

prerequisite.title: Recall integer and real division
prerequisite.body: 125 / 60 is a REAL calculation. When the task asks for a number of complete groups and a remainder, use integer quotient and remainder operations.

steps.title: Use DIV for the quotient
steps.body: Minutes DIV 60 gives the number of complete hours. For non-negative integer Minutes and positive divisor 60, this is 2 for 125. DIV is not rounding to the nearest integer.

steps.title: Use MOD for what remains
steps.body: Minutes MOD 60 gives 5. The remainder must be at least 0 and less than 60 in this example. At exactly 120 minutes, it is 0.

steps.title: Check by rebuilding the original value
steps.body: Hours * 60 + Remaining must equal Minutes. Both result variables are INTEGER. These examples use non-negative quantities and positive divisors, so no signed-remainder convention is needed.
steps.code:
DECLARE Minutes, Hours, Remaining : INTEGER
INPUT Minutes
Hours <- Minutes DIV 60
Remaining <- Minutes MOD 60
OUTPUT Hours, " hours and ", Remaining, " minutes"

worked.title: Test below and at an exact hour
worked.setup: Evaluate durations 59, 60 and 125 minutes.

steps.title: Separate quotient and remainder
steps.body: 59 gives 0 and 59; 60 gives 1 and 0; 125 gives 2 and 5.

steps.title: Reject swapped operators
steps.body: Using MOD for Hours would report five hours for 125 minutes. Using DIV for Remaining would report two minutes. The reconstruction exposes both errors.

worked.conclusion: Use the quotient to count complete groups and the remainder to describe the ungrouped part.

check.prompt: Twenty-seven chairs are packed in groups of 8. State 27 DIV 8 and 27 MOD 8.
check.answer: 27 DIV 8 is 3 and 27 MOD 8 is 3. Three complete groups use 24 chairs and three chairs remain.

learningCycle.takeaway: For these non-negative quantities, Value = (Value DIV GroupSize) * GroupSize + (Value MOD GroupSize).
learningCycle.bridge: Arithmetic produces values. A comparison asks a question about those values and produces TRUE or FALSE.

steps.title: Separate quotient and remainder

steps.title: Reject swapped operators
steps.body: Using MOD for Hours would report five hours for 125 minutes. Using DIV for Remaining would report two minutes. The reconstruction exposes both errors.

workedExample.conclusion: Use the quotient to count complete groups and the remainder to describe the ungrouped part.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Turn a boundary into a Boolean value

leadVisual.title: Turn a boundary into a Boolean value

coreExplanation: “At most” uses <= and includes equality. Seats <= Available is TRUE when Seats equals Available. Using < would reject the exact-fit booking.
= tests equality; <> tests inequality; < and > are strict; <= and >= include equality. In Allowed <- Seats <= Available, the arrow assigns the result of the comparison.
Choose a value immediately below, at and immediately above the limit. A current correct result is not enough to establish that the rule covers its whole allowed range.

learningCycle.observe: Place requests for 5, 6 and 7 beside an available-seat count of 6. Say the rule in words before choosing the comparison symbol.
learningCycle.question: If six seats remain, should a request for exactly six be accepted?

prerequisite.title: Recall BOOLEAN
prerequisite.body: A BOOLEAN value is TRUE or FALSE. A comparison evaluates two values and produces one Boolean result. It does not assign a new value unless it is used on the right of an assignment.

steps.title: Match the words to the boundary
steps.body: “At most” uses <= and includes equality. Seats <= Available is TRUE when Seats equals Available. Using < would reject the exact-fit booking.

steps.title: Recognise the comparison operators
steps.body: = tests equality; <> tests inequality; < and > are strict; <= and >= include equality. In Allowed <- Seats <= Available, the arrow assigns the result of the comparison.

steps.title: Test around the boundary
steps.body: Choose a value immediately below, at and immediately above the limit. A current correct result is not enough to establish that the rule covers its whole allowed range.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats, Available : INTEGER
DECLARE Fits : BOOLEAN
Seats <- 6
Available <- 6
Fits <- Seats <= Available
OUTPUT Fits

worked.title: Explain an exact-fit request
worked.setup: Available is 6. The condition is Seats <= Available.

steps.title: Substitute each request
steps.body: 5 <= 6 is TRUE; 6 <= 6 is TRUE; 7 <= 6 is FALSE.

steps.title: Expose the wrong operator
steps.body: With Seats < Available, only the middle result changes to FALSE. Testing only 5 and 7 would miss the exact-fit defect.

worked.conclusion: The equality part of <= or >= is a requirement, not an optional detail.

check.prompt: Write a condition for at least 18 years of age. Is Age = 18 an equivalent condition?
check.answer: Use Age >= 18. Age = 18 accepts only the single age 18 and rejects older people.

learningCycle.takeaway: Write the full comparison and test both sides of every included or excluded boundary.
learningCycle.bridge: Most real rules ask more than one question. Combine the Boolean results explicitly.

steps.title: Substitute each request

steps.title: Expose the wrong operator

workedExample.conclusion: The equality part of <= or >= is a requirement, not an optional detail.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine restrictions with AND, OR and NOT

leadVisual.title: Combine restrictions with AND, OR and NOT

coreExplanation: AND is TRUE only when both operands are TRUE. For a valid paid booking, use ((Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6)) AND Paid. A failure of any restriction makes the whole result FALSE. In the experiment, the adjustable Available value replaces the fixed upper limit 6, so the rule is (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= Available) AND Paid.
An invalid quantity is (Seats < 1) OR (Seats > 6). Either excluded region makes it invalid. OR is inclusive: if both operands are TRUE, the result is still TRUE.
NOT Paid is TRUE when Paid is FALSE. Parentheses make the intended grouping clear. An expression such as Active OR NOT Active is always TRUE, whichever Boolean value Active has.

learningCycle.observe: A valid quantity is from 1 to 6 inclusive. Confirmation also requires payment. Examine a paid request for 0 seats: one fact is acceptable, but the whole booking is not.

stimulus.title: Confirmation rules
items: Seats must be at least 1.
Seats must be at most 6.
Paid must be TRUE.

learningCycle.question: What must be true before the desk confirms a request?

prerequisite.title: Recall comparisons
prerequisite.body: Each full comparison returns TRUE or FALSE. Write Seats on both sides of a range test: (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6). Do not use the mathematical shorthand 1 <= Seats <= 6 in Cambridge pseudocode.

steps.title: Require every restriction with AND
steps.body: AND is TRUE only when both operands are TRUE. For a valid paid booking, use ((Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6)) AND Paid. A failure of any restriction makes the whole result FALSE. In the experiment, the adjustable Available value replaces the fixed upper limit 6, so the rule is (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= Available) AND Paid.

steps.title: Accept either alternative with OR
steps.body: An invalid quantity is (Seats < 1) OR (Seats > 6). Either excluded region makes it invalid. OR is inclusive: if both operands are TRUE, the result is still TRUE.

steps.title: Reverse a result with NOT
steps.body: NOT Paid is TRUE when Paid is FALSE. Parentheses make the intended grouping clear. An expression such as Active OR NOT Active is always TRUE, whichever Boolean value Active has.

worked.title: Evaluate and then simplify for every input
worked.setup: Seats is 3, Available is 4 and Paid is TRUE. Then consider the general expression (Active OR NOT Active) AND NOT Exempt.

steps.title: Substitute one booking
steps.body: (Seats <= Available) AND Paid becomes TRUE AND TRUE, so it is TRUE. Changing only Paid to FALSE makes it FALSE.

steps.title: Separate an example result from a general equivalence
steps.body: Active OR NOT Active is TRUE for Active FALSE and for Active TRUE. The whole general expression is therefore equivalent to NOT Exempt. Writing TRUE would be wrong when Exempt is TRUE.

worked.conclusion: Evaluate each part before combining it, and justify a simplification for all possible relevant values.

check.prompt: Why does (Seats >= 1) OR (Seats <= 6) fail as a validation rule? Give a rejected quantity that it wrongly accepts.
check.answer: For Seats 0, the second comparison is TRUE, so OR gives TRUE. For Seats 7, the first is TRUE. Use AND to require both boundaries at the same time.

learningCycle.takeaway: AND joins required restrictions; OR joins alternatives; NOT reverses a Boolean result.
learningCycle.bridge: A Boolean expression gives an answer. Selection uses that answer to decide which statements execute.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow a numeric function from input to result

leadVisual.title: Follow a numeric function from input to result

coreExplanation: A built-in function is provided by the language environment; a library routine supplies a reusable operation through its documented interface. For either, check the arguments and result before use. INT(4.8) returns the INTEGER 4 under the supplied contract. RAND(6) returns a REAL, so 2.75 is a possible result but 6 is excluded.
In INT(RAND(6)), first generate a real value. INT then takes its integer part. For these non-negative results, the possible integers are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.
Adding 1 gives the required 1 to 6 inclusive. Generate a fixed target once before a guessing loop if every attempt is meant to find the same target.

learningCycle.observe: A simulation chooses one of six demonstration desks. First inspect the supplied contract: RAND(6) can produce a fractional number from 0 inclusive to 6 exclusive.

rows: REAL value at least 0 and less than X

learningCycle.question: Why does RAND(6) alone not produce a whole-number desk label from 1 to 6?

prerequisite.title: Recall an expression value
prerequisite.body: An expression produces a value for assignment, output or another expression. A function call can occupy that position because it returns a value. The values supplied inside its parentheses are arguments.

steps.title: Read accepted types and the result
steps.body: A built-in function is provided by the language environment; a library routine supplies a reusable operation through its documented interface. For either, check the arguments and result before use. INT(4.8) returns the INTEGER 4 under the supplied contract. RAND(6) returns a REAL, so 2.75 is a possible result but 6 is excluded.

steps.title: Evaluate an inner call before its enclosing call
steps.body: In INT(RAND(6)), first generate a real value. INT then takes its integer part. For these non-negative results, the possible integers are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

steps.title: Shift the range after conversion
steps.body: Adding 1 gives the required 1 to 6 inclusive. Generate a fixed target once before a guessing loop if every attempt is meant to find the same target.
steps.code:
DECLARE Desk : INTEGER
Desk <- INT(RAND(6)) + 1
OUTPUT Desk

worked.title: Check the extreme possible outcomes
worked.setup: Consider generated values 0.0 and 5.999.

steps.title: Follow the lower outcome
steps.body: INT(0.0) gives 0; adding 1 gives desk 1.

steps.title: Follow the upper end
steps.body: INT(5.999) gives 5; adding 1 gives desk 6. RAND never supplies 6, so the expression cannot produce desk 7.

worked.conclusion: Follow each returned value and its type; the outside operation receives the inside result.

check.prompt: What are the smallest and largest results of INT(RAND(4)) + 2?
check.answer: 2 and 5. INT produces 0 through 3, then adding 2 shifts the interval.

learningCycle.takeaway: Use the supplied numeric contract to derive both the result type and its possible range.
learningCycle.bridge: String routines have equally precise contracts: positions, lengths and returned types all matter.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Extract a part of a booking code

leadVisual.title: Extract a part of a booking code

coreExplanation: LENGTH(Code) returns 7. Spaces and punctuation count as characters too. LENGTH("") returns 0 for an empty string.

For the supplied MID(Text, Start, Count), Start is one-based and Count is the number of characters, not an ending position. MID(Code, 4, 4) returns "0072". Keep the requested range within the string unless a task defines other behaviour.

RIGHT(Code, 2) returns "72", a STRING. The character routines UCASE(Letter) and LCASE(Letter) accept a CHAR and return its upper- or lower-case CHAR under the Cambridge guide: UCASE('b') gives 'B' and LCASE('Q') gives 'q'. The experiment instead supplies TO_UPPER(Text) for a STRING; read that separate interface before calling it.

learningCycle.observe: Number the characters from 1. The first digit is at position 4 and four digits must be retained, including both leading zeros.
learningCycle.question: Which arguments extract 0072 from the booking code ART0072?

prerequisite.title: Recall STRING and CHAR
prerequisite.body: A STRING is a sequence of characters; a CHAR is one character. A one-character STRING and a CHAR are different types unless the supplied task explicitly permits interchange. An extracted digit string does not automatically become a number.

steps.title: Read LENGTH as a character count
steps.body: LENGTH(Code) returns 7. Spaces and punctuation count as characters too. LENGTH("") returns 0 for an empty string.

steps.title: Use the MID start and count correctly
steps.body: For the supplied MID(Text, Start, Count), Start is one-based and Count is the number of characters, not an ending position. MID(Code, 4, 4) returns "0072". Keep the requested range within the string unless a task defines other behaviour.

steps.title: Distinguish extraction from conversion
steps.body: RIGHT(Code, 2) returns "72", a STRING. The character routines UCASE(Letter) and LCASE(Letter) accept a CHAR and return its upper- or lower-case CHAR under the Cambridge guide: UCASE('b') gives 'B' and LCASE('Q') gives 'q'. The experiment instead supplies TO_UPPER(Text) for a STRING; read that separate interface before calling it.
steps.code:
DECLARE Code, Digits : STRING
Code <- "ART0072"
Digits <- MID(Code, 4, 4)
OUTPUT LENGTH(Code)
OUTPUT Digits
OUTPUT RIGHT(Code, 2)

worked.title: Extract without dropping leading zeros
worked.setup: Trace the complete program above.

steps.title: Identify the requested slice
steps.body: Starting at character 4 and taking four gives positions 4, 5, 6 and 7: "0072".

steps.title: Read the output types
steps.body: The outputs are integer 7, string "0072" and string "72". Quotation marks in this explanation identify the types; they need not be printed as part of the displayed output.

worked.conclusion: Label character positions before writing a substring expression.

check.prompt: Under the supplied one-based MID contract, what is MID("CAMBRIDGE", 2, 3)?
check.answer: "AMB": start at the second character and take three characters, positions 2 through 4.

learningCycle.takeaway: Read the supplied position convention and count exactly the characters requested.
learningCycle.bridge: Extracted strings can be joined into a new label without changing their order or leading zeros.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Build a stored label by concatenation

leadVisual.title: Build a stored label by concatenation

coreExplanation: Concatenation places the second string directly after the first. "ART" & "-" gives "ART-". The operator does not add an automatic space or punctuation.
"00" & "72" gives "0072". It does not calculate the number 72. & joins strings; AND combines Boolean values. Do not interchange those operators.
Build Label using extracted parts, then OUTPUT Label. An OUTPUT statement with comma-separated items can display a similar result, but does not itself create a stored combined STRING.

learningCycle.observe: Separate the three-letter activity code from the four-digit identifier, then place a hyphen between the two strings.

stimulus.title: Three pieces of one label
items: Prefix: "ART"
Separator: "-"
Digits: "0072"

learningCycle.question: How can ART0072 become the label ART-0072 without treating its digits as a number?

prerequisite.title: Recall an assignment result
prerequisite.body: The right side of an assignment may itself contain function calls. Each call supplies a returned value, then the surrounding expression combines those values.

steps.title: Use & to concatenate strings
steps.body: Concatenation places the second string directly after the first. "ART" & "-" gives "ART-". The operator does not add an automatic space or punctuation.

steps.title: Keep text joining separate from arithmetic and logic
steps.body: "00" & "72" gives "0072". It does not calculate the number 72. & joins strings; AND combines Boolean values. Do not interchange those operators.

steps.title: Store the complete label when it will be reused
steps.body: Build Label using extracted parts, then OUTPUT Label. An OUTPUT statement with comma-separated items can display a similar result, but does not itself create a stored combined STRING.
steps.code:
DECLARE Code, Prefix, Digits, Label : STRING
Code <- "ART0072"
Prefix <- MID(Code, 1, 3)
Digits <- RIGHT(Code, 4)
Label <- Prefix & "-" & Digits
OUTPUT Label

worked.title: Predict both contents and length
worked.setup: Use Code "ART0072".

steps.title: Follow the intermediate strings
steps.body: Prefix becomes "ART", Digits becomes "0072" and Label becomes "ART-0072".

steps.title: Check the character count
steps.body: The label has 3 + 1 + 4 = 8 characters. The hyphen counts; leading zeros remain part of the final string.

worked.conclusion: Construct a label from explicitly ordered strings and separators.

check.prompt: What is LENGTH("A" & " " & "B")? Would omitting " " give the same string?
check.answer: The length is 3 and the string is "A B". Omitting the space gives "AB", whose length is 2.

learningCycle.takeaway: Concatenation combines strings in order; every separator must be supplied explicitly.
learningCycle.bridge: A paper may supply a routine with a new name or different types. Its definition controls how to use it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Take one of two paths

leadVisual.title: Take one of two paths

coreExplanation: IF Seats <= Available THEN starts a decision. If the expression is TRUE, execute its indented block. With no ELSE, a FALSE result simply skips that block.
The ELSE block runs only when the same condition is FALSE. One IF/ELSE chooses exactly one branch, so it cannot display both messages in a single execution.
ENDIF marks where both paths rejoin. Statements after ENDIF run whichever branch was chosen.

learningCycle.observe: There are four seats left. Compare a request for three with a request for five. In each run, choose exactly one message.

stimulus.title: Two alternatives
items: If the request fits, display "Seats available".
Otherwise, display "Not enough seats".
Assume Seats is a positive integer in this example.

learningCycle.question: What should the desk display when a request needs more seats than are available?

prerequisite.title: Recall a Boolean condition
prerequisite.body: Seats <= Available evaluates to TRUE or FALSE without changing either variable. IF uses that result to choose the next statements.

steps.title: Write the TRUE action after THEN
steps.body: IF Seats <= Available THEN starts a decision. If the expression is TRUE, execute its indented block. With no ELSE, a FALSE result simply skips that block.

steps.title: Use ELSE for the alternative
steps.body: The ELSE block runs only when the same condition is FALSE. One IF/ELSE chooses exactly one branch, so it cannot display both messages in a single execution.

steps.title: Close the decision before continuing
steps.body: ENDIF marks where both paths rejoin. Statements after ENDIF run whichever branch was chosen.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats, Available : INTEGER
Available <- 4
INPUT Seats
IF Seats <= Available THEN
    OUTPUT "Seats available"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Not enough seats"
ENDIF
OUTPUT "Check complete"

worked.title: Trace both paths and their shared continuation
worked.setup: Run the program once with 3 and once with 5.

steps.title: Request three seats
steps.body: 3 <= 4 is TRUE. Display Seats available, skip ELSE, then display Check complete.

steps.title: Request five seats
steps.body: 5 <= 4 is FALSE. Skip the THEN output, display Not enough seats, then display Check complete.

worked.conclusion: A trace follows only the selected branch, then continues after ENDIF.

check.prompt: What is displayed for Seats 4? What happens if <= is replaced with <?
check.answer: With <= the exact-fit request displays Seats available, then Check complete. With < it incorrectly displays Not enough seats, then Check complete.

learningCycle.takeaway: IF/ELSE chooses between alternatives; ENDIF joins their paths.
learningCycle.bridge: A second rule may matter only after the first has succeeded. Place that decision inside the appropriate branch.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Reach an inner decision only when needed

leadVisual.title: Reach an inner decision only when needed

coreExplanation: Seats <= Available determines whether the payment decision is reached. The outer FALSE branch handles the failure immediately.

Inside THEN, IF Paid selects Confirmed or Payment needed. Its ENDIF closes the inner decision before ELSE introduces the outer false branch. The experiment offers another nested rule: first reject Seats < 1, then check whether the positive request exceeds Available. Its three outcomes are invalid quantity, insufficient seats or a confirmed request.
Two separate IF statements are tested independently and may both execute. An exclusive classification should use appropriate IF/ELSE branches rather than two overlapping tests.

learningCycle.observe: The desk first checks availability. If the request fits, it checks payment; otherwise it reports a lack of seats without entering the payment branch.
learningCycle.question: Should payment confirmation matter when no seats are available?

prerequisite.title: Recall a branch
prerequisite.body: A block inside a branch is executed only if that branch is reached. Each IF has its own matching ENDIF; indentation makes the relationships visible.

steps.title: Put the first restriction outside
steps.body: Seats <= Available determines whether the payment decision is reached. The outer FALSE branch handles the failure immediately.

steps.title: Nest the payment decision in the TRUE branch
steps.body: Inside THEN, IF Paid selects Confirmed or Payment needed. Its ENDIF closes the inner decision before ELSE introduces the outer false branch. The experiment offers another nested rule: first reject Seats < 1, then check whether the positive request exceeds Available. Its three outcomes are invalid quantity, insufficient seats or a confirmed request.

steps.title: Distinguish nesting from independent decisions
steps.body: Two separate IF statements are tested independently and may both execute. An exclusive classification should use appropriate IF/ELSE branches rather than two overlapping tests.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats, Available : INTEGER
DECLARE Paid : BOOLEAN
Available <- 4
INPUT Seats
INPUT Paid
IF Seats <= Available THEN
    IF Paid THEN
        OUTPUT "Confirmed"
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Payment needed"
    ENDIF
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Not enough seats"
ENDIF

worked.title: Follow the outer decision before the inner one
worked.setup: Use the complete program with (Seats, Paid) equal to (5, TRUE), (4, FALSE) and (3, TRUE).

steps.title: Trace the paths
steps.body: The outputs are Not enough seats, Payment needed and Confirmed respectively. In the first run, Paid has been input but its inner condition is not evaluated.

steps.title: Explain an overlapping classification
steps.body: IF Seats >= 3 followed by IF Seats >= 5 executes both blocks for Seats 5. If only one classification is required, test the larger threshold first and put the other test in its ELSE branch.

worked.conclusion: Use the structure to express which decisions depend on earlier decisions.

check.prompt: In the booking program, which ELSE belongs to IF Paid, and what message does it control?
check.answer: The indented ELSE before the inner ENDIF belongs to IF Paid. It outputs Payment needed only after the availability test succeeded and Paid was FALSE.

learningCycle.takeaway: An inner IF runs only along the outer branch containing it; independent IF statements can both act.
learningCycle.bridge: When a menu chooses among values of one identifier, CASE can show the alternatives more directly.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose a menu action with CASE

leadVisual.title: Choose a menu action with CASE

coreExplanation: Write CASE OF Choice, put each label before a colon, and close with ENDCASE. There is no break statement in Cambridge pseudocode.
OTHERWISE supplies the default branch. A range label such as 1 TO 5 includes both endpoints. Prefer clear, non-overlapping intended alternatives.

If a supplied CASE first handles values below 30, a later clause for values below 20 is unreachable: every such value already matched the earlier clause. If all values are covered, OTHERWISE is also unreachable. Follow the original code rather than silently repairing it.

learningCycle.observe: The booking menu offers 1 for a new booking and 2 for viewing the register. A value such as 0 must produce a defined response.
learningCycle.question: How can one menu value select exactly one action?

prerequisite.title: Recall exclusive alternatives
prerequisite.body: An IF/ELSE follows one selected branch. CASE similarly selects an alternative based on one identifier, rather than treating every label as an independent IF.

steps.title: Name the identifier after CASE OF
steps.body: Write CASE OF Choice, put each label before a colon, and close with ENDCASE. There is no break statement in Cambridge pseudocode.

steps.title: Provide a response for unmatched values
steps.body: OTHERWISE supplies the default branch. A range label such as 1 TO 5 includes both endpoints. Prefer clear, non-overlapping intended alternatives.
steps.code:
DECLARE Choice : INTEGER
INPUT Choice
CASE OF Choice
    1 : OUTPUT "New booking"
    2 : OUTPUT "View register"
    OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "Invalid option"
ENDCASE

steps.title: Check the order when reading overlapping supplied clauses
steps.body: If a supplied CASE first handles values below 30, a later clause for values below 20 is unreachable: every such value already matched the earlier clause. If all values are covered, OTHERWISE is also unreachable. Follow the original code rather than silently repairing it.

worked.title: Explain both a working menu and an unreachable clause
worked.setup: First input Choice 2. Then consider ordered ranges: below 30; below 20; 30 to 40 inclusive; above 40.

steps.title: Trace the menu
steps.body: Choice 2 matches its label and displays View register. OTHERWISE is skipped.

steps.title: Test a value in the narrower range
steps.body: 15 is below 20 but is also below 30, so the earlier clause is selected. Values below 30, 30 through 40 and above 40 already cover all possibilities, leaving none for OTHERWISE.

worked.conclusion: A branch is reachable only if some permitted input reaches it after the preceding alternatives have been considered.

check.prompt: For CASE labels 1 TO 5 and 6 TO 7 followed by OTHERWISE, which branch receives 5, 7 and 8?
check.answer: 5 selects the first range; 7 selects the second; 8 selects OTHERWISE. Both range endpoints are included.

learningCycle.takeaway: CASE OF selects by one identifier; check labels, order, coverage and the default path.
learningCycle.bridge: The desk can now process one request. Repetition lets it apply the same actions to several requests.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Count the executions of a FOR loop

leadVisual.title: Count the executions of a FOR loop

coreExplanation: FOR Index <- 1 TO 3 visits 1, 2 and 3. With the default positive step of 1, the upper endpoint is included when reached.
Every statement before the matching NEXT Index belongs to the body. Let FOR manage its control variable; do not add a separate Index <- Index + 1 inside the body.
1 TO 1 executes once. 1 TO 0 with the default positive step executes zero times because the start is already beyond the endpoint. FOR does not guarantee a first body execution.

learningCycle.observe: Lay out three numbered request cards. The loop control variable identifies the current card; its value is not the seat quantity requested on that card.

stimulus.title: Known request slots
items: First iteration: Index 1
Second iteration: Index 2
Third iteration: Index 3

learningCycle.question: How many booking slots are processed by FOR Index <- 1 TO 3?

prerequisite.title: Recall sequence and selection
prerequisite.body: Sequence performs statements in order and selection chooses a path. Iteration repeats a block. A count-controlled loop is suitable when its iteration count is determined before it begins.

steps.title: Write the inclusive bounds
steps.body: FOR Index <- 1 TO 3 visits 1, 2 and 3. With the default positive step of 1, the upper endpoint is included when reached.

steps.title: Place the repeated action inside the loop
steps.body: Every statement before the matching NEXT Index belongs to the body. Let FOR manage its control variable; do not add a separate Index <- Index + 1 inside the body.
steps.code:
DECLARE Index : INTEGER
FOR Index <- 1 TO 3
    OUTPUT "Process booking ", Index
NEXT Index
OUTPUT "All slots complete"

steps.title: Check zero and one iteration
steps.body: 1 TO 1 executes once. 1 TO 0 with the default positive step executes zero times because the start is already beyond the endpoint. FOR does not guarantee a first body execution.

worked.title: Count a non-one starting range
worked.setup: Change the header to FOR Index <- 2 TO 5.

steps.title: List the body values
steps.body: The body uses 2, 3, 4 and 5, giving four executions. For a step of 1 and an increasing valid range, the count is End - Start + 1.

steps.title: Keep the final output outside
steps.body: All slots complete appears once after all four body executions. Moving it inside would print it four times.

worked.conclusion: Count the values used by the body; do not assume a specific control-variable value after the completed loop.

check.prompt: How many times do the bodies run for 3 TO 3 and 3 TO 2 with the default step?
check.answer: One execution for 3 TO 3 and zero for 3 TO 2.

learningCycle.takeaway: A FOR loop controls a predetermined sequence of counter values, including an endpoint it reaches.
learningCycle.bridge: Each iteration can read a new request and add it to a running total.

workedExample.title: Count a non-one starting range
workedExample.setup: Change the header to FOR Index <- 2 TO 5.

steps.title: List the body values
steps.body: The body uses 2, 3, 4 and 5, giving four executions. For a step of 1 and an increasing valid range, the count is End - Start + 1.

steps.title: Keep the final output outside
steps.body: All slots complete appears once after all four body executions. Moving it inside would print it four times.

workedExample.conclusion: Count the values used by the body; do not assume a specific control-variable value after the completed loop.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Keep a total across iterations

leadVisual.title: Keep a total across iterations

coreExplanation: Set Total <- 0 before the loop. No seats have been counted yet. Setting it to zero inside the loop would discard the result from earlier iterations.
INPUT Seats must be inside so that each slot obtains a new request. Reading once before the loop would repeatedly add the same request.
OUTPUT Total after NEXT gives one final total. A count of bookings and a total of seats are different: three bookings can request nine seats.

learningCycle.observe: Three requests ask for 3, 2 and 4 seats. After each request, keep the earlier total and add only the newly read quantity.
learningCycle.question: Where must Total start at zero so that three requests are added together?

prerequisite.title: Recall an update
prerequisite.body: Total <- Total + Seats reads the old total and the current request, then stores their sum. Total therefore needs an initial value before the first addition.

steps.title: Initialise the accumulator once
steps.body: Set Total <- 0 before the loop. No seats have been counted yet. Setting it to zero inside the loop would discard the result from earlier iterations.

steps.title: Read and add inside each iteration
steps.body: INPUT Seats must be inside so that each slot obtains a new request. Reading once before the loop would repeatedly add the same request.

steps.title: Report after the complete traversal
steps.body: OUTPUT Total after NEXT gives one final total. A count of bookings and a total of seats are different: three bookings can request nine seats.
steps.code:
DECLARE Index, Seats, Total : INTEGER
Total <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 3
    INPUT Seats
    Total <- Total + Seats
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total

worked.title: Trace every addition
worked.setup: Enter 3, 2 and 4.

steps.title: Preserve the earlier sum
steps.body: Total begins as 0, becomes 3 after the first request, 5 after the second and 9 after the third.

steps.title: Expose a reset in the wrong place
steps.body: If Total <- 0 is the first line of the body, the totals become 3, 2 and 4. The final output is only the last request, 4.

worked.conclusion: Initialisation, repeated input and final reporting belong at different levels of the program.

check.prompt: If the loop runs from 1 TO Count and Count is 0, what does the correctly initialised program output?
check.answer: It outputs 0. The body reads no requests and the accumulator keeps its initial value.

learningCycle.takeaway: Initialise before the loop, obtain and process each value inside it, and report the completed result after it.
learningCycle.bridge: Some known sequences increase by more than one or run backwards. STEP controls that sequence.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Control direction and step size

leadVisual.title: Control direction and step size

coreExplanation: STEP 3 adds 3 each iteration; STEP -2 subtracts 2. The sign must move the control value toward the intended endpoint.
2 TO 8 STEP 3 uses 2, 5 and 8. 5 TO 0 STEP -2 uses 5, 3 and 1, then stops before the next value would pass the endpoint.
STEP 0 is unsuitable because it never changes the counter. A descending step with a start below the endpoint has no permitted body values, such as 0 TO 5 STEP -1.

learningCycle.observe: Move a marker from 6 toward 0, subtracting 2 on every move. Then try the same movement starting at 5 and notice that it never lands on 0.

stimulus.title: Two descending sequences
items: Start 6, end 0, step -2: 6, 4, 2, 0
Start 5, end 0, step -2: 5, 3, 1

learningCycle.question: How can a display visit seat labels 6, 4, 2 and 0?

prerequisite.title: Recall inclusive bounds
prerequisite.body: An endpoint is permitted when the sequence reaches it. Inclusive does not mean that a sequence with a larger step must land exactly on that endpoint.

steps.title: Give a positive or negative step
steps.body: STEP 3 adds 3 each iteration; STEP -2 subtracts 2. The sign must move the control value toward the intended endpoint.

steps.title: List the sequence before counting it
steps.body: 2 TO 8 STEP 3 uses 2, 5 and 8. 5 TO 0 STEP -2 uses 5, 3 and 1, then stops before the next value would pass the endpoint.

steps.title: Reject a step that cannot progress
steps.body: STEP 0 is unsuitable because it never changes the counter. A descending step with a start below the endpoint has no permitted body values, such as 0 TO 5 STEP -1.
steps.code:
DECLARE SeatLabel : INTEGER
FOR SeatLabel <- 6 TO 0 STEP -2
    OUTPUT SeatLabel
NEXT SeatLabel

worked.title: Trace both endpoints and an overshoot
worked.setup: Compare 8 TO 2 STEP -3 with 8 TO 1 STEP -3.

steps.title: First sequence
steps.body: The body values are 8, 5 and 2. The endpoint is reached exactly.

steps.title: Second sequence
steps.body: The body values remain 8, 5 and 2. The next value would be -1, which is below the endpoint 1, so there is no body execution at 1 or -1.

worked.conclusion: Direction and step determine the visited values; the endpoint only sets the allowed limit.

check.prompt: List the values visited by 1 TO 6 STEP 2.
check.answer: 1, 3 and 5. The next value 7 is beyond 6, so 6 is not visited.

learningCycle.takeaway: Choose start, end and a non-zero step together, then trace the actual values used.
learningCycle.bridge: A seating grid needs both a row and a seat number. That requires an inner loop for every outer value.

steps.title: First sequence
steps.body: The body values are 8, 5 and 2. The endpoint is reached exactly.

steps.title: Second sequence
steps.body: The body values remain 8, 5 and 2. The next value would be -1, which is below the endpoint 1, so there is no body execution at 1 or -1.

workedExample.conclusion: Direction and step determine the visited values; the endpoint only sets the allowed limit.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Complete the inner loop for every row

leadVisual.title: Complete the inner loop for every row

coreExplanation: Row identifies the outer iteration and Seat identifies the inner one. Reusing Row for both loops would interfere with the outer sequence.
For Row 1, Seat visits 1, 2, 3. Only after NEXT Seat completes does NEXT Row advance Row to 2; the inner header then starts Seat at 1 again.

The body above runs 2 * 3 = 6 times. In an array task, the same pattern may write Flags[Row, Seat]. A one-dimensional Boolean array such as CheckTotal[0:35] instead uses one computed index; its bounds include both 0 and 35, giving 36 elements.

learningCycle.observe: Visit all seats in the first row before moving to row 2. The inner seat counter starts again for the new row.
learningCycle.question: Which seat follows row 1, seat 3 in a two-row, three-seat grid?

prerequisite.title: Recall array indices
prerequisite.body: An array index selects an element. A two-dimensional position needs two indices. FOR counters can generate these indices, but the counter value and the stored element value are different facts.

steps.title: Use a separate control variable for each responsibility
steps.body: Row identifies the outer iteration and Seat identifies the inner one. Reusing Row for both loops would interfere with the outer sequence.

steps.title: Restart the inner loop on each outer iteration
steps.body: For Row 1, Seat visits 1, 2, 3. Only after NEXT Seat completes does NEXT Row advance Row to 2; the inner header then starts Seat at 1 again.
steps.code:
DECLARE Row, Seat, Count : INTEGER
Count <- 0
FOR Row <- 1 TO 2
    FOR Seat <- 1 TO 3
        OUTPUT Row, ",", Seat
        Count <- Count + 1
    NEXT Seat
NEXT Row
OUTPUT Count

steps.title: Connect the counters to array updates
steps.body: The body above runs 2 * 3 = 6 times. In an array task, the same pattern may write Flags[Row, Seat]. A one-dimensional Boolean array such as CheckTotal[0:35] instead uses one computed index; its bounds include both 0 and 35, giving 36 elements.

worked.title: Prepare to enumerate score combinations
worked.setup: A quiz allows 0 to 5 easy answers worth 3 each and 0 to 4 hard answers worth 5 each.

steps.title: List possible contributions
steps.body: Easy points are 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. Hard points are 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. Nested loops must include zero because either category may have no correct answer.

steps.title: Use the sum as a Boolean-array index
steps.body: Initialise CheckTotal[0:35] to FALSE. For every pair of contributions set CheckTotal[EasyPoints + HardPoints] to TRUE. There are 6 * 5 pairs; different pairs may reach the same total, so this does not imply 30 distinct scores.

worked.conclusion: A nested traversal generates combinations; initialise the result structure before recording those combinations.

check.prompt: How often does an inner loop 1 TO 4 run when the outer loop is 1 TO 3? Which pair follows (2,4)?
check.answer: Its body runs 12 times overall. The pair after (2,4) is (3,1), because the inner counter restarts for the next outer value.

learningCycle.takeaway: Finish all inner iterations for each outer value, and distinguish combinations from distinct results.
learningCycle.bridge: A known count suits FOR. An input stream that stops when a signal arrives needs a condition-controlled loop.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Check before processing the next request

leadVisual.title: Check before processing the next request

coreExplanation: INPUT Seats before WHILE supplies the value used by the first condition. WHILE Seats <> 0 means continue while the value is not the sentinel.
When Seats is 0, the body is skipped. If that happens on the first test, the body executes zero times and Total remains 0.
After adding the current request, read another Seats value. ENDWHILE returns to the condition. Omitting this input can leave Seats unchanged and cause endless repetition.

learningCycle.observe: The desk reads positive seat requests until the integer 0 signals the end. Compare the streams 3, 2, 4, 0 and just 0. The stopping marker is not a booking.

stimulus.title: Two possible streams
items: Requests then stop: 3, 2, 4, 0
Stop immediately: 0
Only positive quantities are ordinary requests in this task.

learningCycle.question: How can a stream end before any booking has been processed?

prerequisite.title: Recall a sentinel
prerequisite.body: A sentinel is a special value that marks the end of input. Its meaning comes from the stated task. Here 0 ends the stream; in another task 0 could be ordinary data.

steps.title: Obtain the first value before testing it
steps.body: INPUT Seats before WHILE supplies the value used by the first condition. WHILE Seats <> 0 means continue while the value is not the sentinel.

steps.title: Process only after a TRUE test
steps.body: When Seats is 0, the body is skipped. If that happens on the first test, the body executes zero times and Total remains 0.

steps.title: Read the next value inside the body
steps.body: After adding the current request, read another Seats value. ENDWHILE returns to the condition. Omitting this input can leave Seats unchanged and cause endless repetition.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats, Total : INTEGER
Total <- 0
INPUT Seats
WHILE Seats <> 0
    Total <- Total + Seats
    INPUT Seats
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Total

worked.title: Trace the marker before the addition

steps.title: Follow the ordinary values
steps.body: Tests on 3, 2 and 4 are TRUE. The additions produce totals 3, 5 and 9.

steps.title: Follow the exit
steps.body: The next INPUT stores 0. The next test is FALSE, so no addition occurs and OUTPUT displays 9. If the first input is 0, OUTPUT displays 0.

worked.conclusion: A pre-condition loop can process no data, because its condition is tested before the body.

check.prompt: INPUT Seats is followed by WHILE Seats <> 0 containing only OUTPUT Seats. What happens for first input 3?
check.answer: Seats stays 3, so the condition remains TRUE and 3 is displayed repeatedly. Read a new Seats value inside the loop so a later 0 can end it.

learningCycle.takeaway: WHILE continues on TRUE, tests before the body, and needs a path that changes its tested state.
learningCycle.bridge: When an input attempt must happen before it can be checked, put the test after the body instead.

workedExample.title: Trace the marker before the addition

steps.title: Follow the ordinary values
steps.body: Tests on 3, 2 and 4 are TRUE. The additions produce totals 3, 5 and 9.

steps.title: Follow the exit
steps.body: The next INPUT stores 0. The next test is FALSE, so no addition occurs and OUTPUT displays 9. If the first input is 0, OUTPUT displays 0.

workedExample.conclusion: A pre-condition loop can process no data, because its condition is tested before the body.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Obtain an attempt before checking it

leadVisual.title: Obtain an attempt before checking it

coreExplanation: REPEAT begins the body immediately. INPUT Seats supplies a value before the program tries to test it. This post-condition loop executes its body at least once.
UNTIL (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6) expresses the acceptance condition. FALSE repeats the body; TRUE ends the loop. This is the opposite polarity from WHILE.
Place the booking calculation or update after UNTIL so rejected attempts do not affect totals.

learningCycle.observe: A user tries 0, then 7, then 3. The first two attempts are outside the allowed interval. Only the final 3 may become an accepted booking.
learningCycle.question: How can the desk keep asking until the seat quantity is from 1 to 6?

prerequisite.title: Recall a range condition
prerequisite.body: A quantity is inside 1 to 6 inclusive when (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6). Assume the input operation supplies integers; checking whether typed text can be converted to an integer is outside this example.

steps.title: Perform the required first attempt
steps.body: REPEAT begins the body immediately. INPUT Seats supplies a value before the program tries to test it. This post-condition loop executes its body at least once.

steps.title: Stop when the UNTIL condition is TRUE
steps.body: UNTIL (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6) expresses the acceptance condition. FALSE repeats the body; TRUE ends the loop. This is the opposite polarity from WHILE.

steps.title: Use the accepted value after the loop
steps.body: Place the booking calculation or update after UNTIL so rejected attempts do not affect totals.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
REPEAT
    OUTPUT "Enter seats from 1 to 6"
    INPUT Seats
UNTIL (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6)
OUTPUT "Accepted seats: ", Seats

worked.title: Separate attempts from accepted data
worked.setup: Execute with attempts 0, 7, 3.

steps.title: Test each attempt
steps.body: For 0 the lower comparison fails; for 7 the upper comparison fails. The body repeats after both. For 3 both are TRUE, so the loop stops.

steps.title: Read the final state
steps.body: There were three inputs but one accepted booking quantity. Seats retains 3 and the final result output reports the accepted value.

worked.conclusion: Validation retries obtain a replacement attempt; they do not automatically create additional bookings.

check.prompt: How many body executions occur if the first input is 6? What if UNTIL uses Seats < 1 OR Seats > 6?
check.answer: The valid first input gives one execution. The proposed outside-range condition reverses the rule: it stops on an invalid input instead of an accepted one.

learningCycle.takeaway: REPEAT runs first and stops when UNTIL becomes TRUE.
learningCycle.bridge: Compare test position and condition meaning together before converting one loop form to another.

workedExample.title: Separate attempts from accepted data
workedExample.setup: Execute with attempts 0, 7, 3.

steps.body: For 0 the lower comparison fails; for 7 the upper comparison fails. The body repeats after both. For 3 both are TRUE, so the loop stops.

steps.title: Read the final state

workedExample.conclusion: Validation retries obtain a replacement attempt; they do not automatically create additional bookings.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match the test position and its meaning

leadVisual.title: Match the test position and its meaning

coreExplanation: For validation, stop when the value is valid. A REPEAT loop directly uses that stopping condition; a WHILE loop needs the continuation condition that the value is invalid.
A WHILE version must read the first attempt before testing it, then read replacements in the body. It can implement the same validation task, but needs different setup.

A sentinel can be the first input. A bare REPEAT that adds a value before checking the sentinel would wrongly process it once. Add a suitable guard or use WHILE; changing only the keyword is insufficient.

learningCycle.observe: For a booking quantity, “still invalid” and “now valid” are opposite questions. One condition permits another attempt; the other ends the attempts.
learningCycle.question: Does changing WHILE to UNTIL without changing the condition preserve a program?

prerequisite.title: Recall complement conditions
prerequisite.body: The complement of (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6) is (Seats < 1) OR (Seats > 6). Both comparison boundaries and the connecting operator change.

steps.title: Write the required stopping event in words
steps.body: For validation, stop when the value is valid. A REPEAT loop directly uses that stopping condition; a WHILE loop needs the continuation condition that the value is invalid.

steps.title: Provide a value before a pre-condition test
steps.body: A WHILE version must read the first attempt before testing it, then read replacements in the body. It can implement the same validation task, but needs different setup.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
OUTPUT "Enter seats from 1 to 6"
INPUT Seats
WHILE (Seats < 1) OR (Seats > 6)
    OUTPUT "Try again"
    INPUT Seats
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Seats

steps.title: Check whether zero processed items are possible
steps.body: A sentinel can be the first input. A bare REPEAT that adds a value before checking the sentinel would wrongly process it once. Add a suitable guard or use WHILE; changing only the keyword is insufficient.

worked.title: Compare the same validation stream
worked.setup: Use 0, 7, 3 with the WHILE program above and the earlier REPEAT program.

steps.title: Compare consumed values
steps.body: Both programs read three attempts and retain 3. The WHILE body runs twice because the initial input is outside it; the REPEAT body runs three times.

steps.title: State the comparison precisely
steps.body: The accepted value and number of inputs agree. The shown prompt text differs, so the two displayed message sequences are not identical. Specify which required behaviour is being compared.

worked.conclusion: Equivalent input processing does not imply identical body counts or identical display messages.

check.prompt: For WHILE NOT Finished and REPEAT … UNTIL Finished, what does Finished = TRUE mean?
check.answer: It prevents entry to another WHILE body and ends the REPEAT loop after its current body. The test positions remain different.

learningCycle.takeaway: Choose the test position, define initial state and use the correct continuation or stopping condition.
learningCycle.bridge: Now choose a loop from a problem’s actual constraints, including limits on attempts or storage.
