knowledgeUnits.heading: Justify the structure from the requirement

leadVisual.title: Justify the structure from the requirement

coreExplanation: Four receipts give four iterations. “The number of repetitions is known before the loop begins” is the reason; merely saying “FOR repeats” is not a useful justification.
A sentinel stream may contain no ordinary data. Reading before a WHILE test naturally excludes a first sentinel without processing it.

A menu option must be entered before validation. REPEAT naturally captures that order. A correctly initialised WHILE solution can also work; suitability does not imply that every other structure is impossible.

learningCycle.observe: Compare printing four receipts, accepting requests until 0, and asking for one valid menu option. All repeat actions, but their stopping information differs.

rows: Count unknown; first input may be 0
At least one attempt is required

learningCycle.question: Which fact tells you whether FOR, WHILE or REPEAT is the clearest choice?

prerequisite.title: Recall the three structures
prerequisite.body: FOR controls a predetermined counter sequence. WHILE tests a continuation condition before the body. REPEAT tests a stopping condition after the body.

steps.title: Use FOR for a known count or sequence
steps.body: Four receipts give four iterations. “The number of repetitions is known before the loop begins” is the reason; merely saying “FOR repeats” is not a useful justification.

steps.title: Use WHILE when processing may be skipped
steps.body: A sentinel stream may contain no ordinary data. Reading before a WHILE test naturally excludes a first sentinel without processing it.

steps.title: Use REPEAT when an attempt must occur first
steps.body: A menu option must be entered before validation. REPEAT naturally captures that order. A correctly initialised WHILE solution can also work; suitability does not imply that every other structure is impossible.

worked.title: Write a reason that belongs to the question
worked.setup: A sensor supplies readings until -999; the number of readings is unknown.

steps.title: Name a suitable structure
steps.body: A condition-controlled loop is suitable. For a first marker that must be excluded, use WHILE Reading <> -999 with the initial input before the loop.

steps.title: Connect behaviour to the requirement
steps.body: The input determines when processing stops, and the first input may already be the marker. A guessed FOR count would either stop too early or ask for unwanted readings.

worked.conclusion: An exam justification should name the relevant count or stopping behaviour and connect it to the context.

check.prompt: A loop displays 20, 15, 10, 5, 0. Which structure fits and why?
check.answer: FOR with 20 TO 0 STEP -5 fits because the complete sequence is predetermined before execution.

learningCycle.takeaway: Justify a loop with the problem’s known count, required first action and stopping event.
learningCycle.bridge: Some tasks stop either on success or when an attempt limit is reached. Both restrictions must control continuation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Stop after success or the final attempt

leadVisual.title: Stop after success or the final attempt

coreExplanation: Password <- "" makes the first success test FALSE, and Attempts <- 0 records that no attempt has been made. Both variables have values before WHILE reads them.
(Password <> "open") AND (Attempts < 3) permits another input only when the previous input failed and fewer than three attempts have occurred.

After INPUT Password, increment Attempts. The next test can stop on the new success or on the reached limit. OR in the WHILE condition would allow continuation when only one restriction remained true.

learningCycle.observe: Compare success on attempt 1, success on attempt 3 and three failures. A fourth input must never be requested.

stimulus.title: Two reasons to stop
items: The entered code is "open".
Or, three attempts have been made.
Another attempt is needed only while the code is wrong AND attempts remain.

learningCycle.question: How can a desk access-code check allow at most three attempts and stop early on success?

prerequisite.title: Recall AND and OR
prerequisite.body: To continue, both permissions must hold. To stop, either stopping event is enough. This example illustrates loop logic only; it is not a model of a production authentication system.

steps.title: Give the tested state initial values
steps.body: Password <- "" makes the first success test FALSE, and Attempts <- 0 records that no attempt has been made. Both variables have values before WHILE reads them.

steps.title: Require both continuation conditions
steps.body: (Password <> "open") AND (Attempts < 3) permits another input only when the previous input failed and fewer than three attempts have occurred.

steps.title: Count every completed attempt exactly once
steps.body: After INPUT Password, increment Attempts. The next test can stop on the new success or on the reached limit. OR in the WHILE condition would allow continuation when only one restriction remained true.
steps.code:
DECLARE Password : STRING
DECLARE Attempts : INTEGER
Password <- ""
Attempts <- 0
WHILE (Password <> "open") AND (Attempts < 3)
    INPUT Password
    Attempts <- Attempts + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Password = "open", Attempts

worked.title: Check success at the limit
worked.setup: Inputs are "x", "y", "open".

steps.title: Trace the first two attempts
steps.body: Attempts becomes 1 and 2, while the password remains wrong. Both continuation conditions are TRUE before the next input.

steps.title: Trace the third test
steps.body: The third input succeeds and Attempts becomes 3. Both continuation conditions are now FALSE. The final output reports TRUE and 3, with no fourth input.

worked.conclusion: Count attempts after they occur, and stop when either another attempt is unnecessary or the limit is reached.

check.prompt: A post-condition version uses UNTIL. Write its stopping condition.
check.answer: (Password = "open") OR (Attempts >= 3). Success or an exhausted attempt allowance is sufficient to stop.

learningCycle.takeaway: Multiple stopping events usually become AND-connected permissions in WHILE, or OR-connected stopping conditions in UNTIL.
learningCycle.bridge: An input buffer has another limit: the program must never store beyond its declared capacity.

workedExample.title: Check success at the limit
workedExample.setup: Inputs are "x", "y", "open".

steps.title: Trace the first two attempts
steps.body: Attempts becomes 1 and 2, while the password remains wrong. Both continuation conditions are TRUE before the next input.

steps.title: Trace the third test
steps.body: The third input succeeds and Attempts becomes 3. Both continuation conditions are now FALSE. The final output reports TRUE and 3, with no fourth input.

workedExample.conclusion: Count attempts after they occur, and stop when either another attempt is unnecessary or the limit is reached.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Stop safely at a sentinel or full storage

leadVisual.title: Stop safely at a sentinel or full storage

coreExplanation: Start Count at 0 and read the first request. Continue only while Count < 3 and Seats <> 0. Both values are simple scalar variables, so evaluating either comparison does not risk an invalid array access.
Increment Count, then write Requests[Count]. Reaching Count 3 is allowed: it is the final valid array element, not an overflow.
Read the next Seats only if Count < 3. This avoids requesting an unnecessary fourth value after the buffer is full.

learningCycle.observe: The buffer accepts positive requests until sentinel 0 or until three ordinary requests have been stored. Compare 0, then 2,0, and finally 2,3,4.
learningCycle.question: How can a three-slot request buffer stop without storing 0 or asking for a fourth request?

prerequisite.title: Recall bounded array access
prerequisite.body: An ARRAY[1:3] has valid indices 1, 2 and 3. Count records how many entries are stored. The sentinel is a control signal, so it must be checked before storage.

steps.title: Separate storage capacity from the next value
steps.body: Start Count at 0 and read the first request. Continue only while Count < 3 and Seats <> 0. Both values are simple scalar variables, so evaluating either comparison does not risk an invalid array access.

steps.title: Store only an ordinary request
steps.body: Increment Count, then write Requests[Count]. Reaching Count 3 is allowed: it is the final valid array element, not an overflow.

steps.title: Check remaining capacity before asking again
steps.body: Read the next Seats only if Count < 3. This avoids requesting an unnecessary fourth value after the buffer is full.
steps.code:
DECLARE Requests : ARRAY[1:3] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Seats, Count : INTEGER
Count <- 0
INPUT Seats
WHILE (Count < 3) AND (Seats <> 0)
    Count <- Count + 1
    Requests[Count] <- Seats
    IF Count < 3 THEN
        INPUT Seats
    ENDIF
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Count

worked.title: Prepare the same reasoning for a flowchart
worked.setup: The real-paper task uses 20 REAL values and sentinel 99.9 rather than this three-request buffer.

steps.title: Trace an immediate sentinel
steps.body: If the first value is 99.9, follow the stop path before any array assignment. No stored-value count or array index should advance as though data had been accepted.

steps.title: Trace the last permitted storage
steps.body: The twentieth ordinary value must be stored. Advance the next-position index to 21, then stop before an invalid access. Read the exact placement of further INPUT operations when comparing the supplied flowchart alternatives.

worked.conclusion: Verify sentinel-first, partial-fill and exactly-full paths; they expose different placement errors.

check.prompt: Why is “stop when Count = 3 before storing the third request” wrong?
check.answer: It can stop after only two stored requests if Count describes the next position. Define the counter’s meaning precisely and trace the last permitted storage before the stop test.

learningCycle.takeaway: Check a sentinel before storing and check remaining capacity before requesting more data.
learningCycle.bridge: You now know the required constructs. Translate an entire supplied design while preserving its order and every path.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Define an action and call it when needed

leadVisual.title: Define an action and call it when needed

coreExplanation: Begin PROCEDURE Heading() and finish ENDPROCEDURE. The empty parentheses show that this procedure has no parameters.
CALL Heading() transfers execution into the procedure body. At ENDPROCEDURE, execution resumes immediately after the call. Defining a procedure does not invoke it.
Printing a heading is an effect. The caller does not need a returned value to use in a calculation, so a procedure is appropriate. Reuse also gives one place to maintain the heading.

learningCycle.observe: The desk wants the same heading before different booking outputs. Define that action once, then decide exactly where to call it.

stimulus.title: One reusable action
items: Action name: Heading
Required effect: display "School bookings"
No information needs to be supplied to this action.

learningCycle.question: Does writing a procedure definition immediately print its receipt?

prerequisite.title: Recall a routine call
prerequisite.body: A supplied routine has an interface the caller follows. A user-defined procedure gives your own action a name and interface. Its definition describes the action; a call performs it.

steps.title: Write the procedure definition
steps.body: Begin PROCEDURE Heading() and finish ENDPROCEDURE. The empty parentheses show that this procedure has no parameters.

steps.title: Invoke the action with CALL
steps.body: CALL Heading() transfers execution into the procedure body. At ENDPROCEDURE, execution resumes immediately after the call. Defining a procedure does not invoke it.

steps.title: Choose a procedure for an action
steps.body: Printing a heading is an effect. The caller does not need a returned value to use in a calculation, so a procedure is appropriate. Reuse also gives one place to maintain the heading.
steps.code:
PROCEDURE Heading()
    OUTPUT "School bookings"
ENDPROCEDURE
CALL Heading()
OUTPUT "First request"
CALL Heading()
OUTPUT "Second request"

worked.title: Follow the return point after each call
worked.setup: Execute the complete program above.

steps.title: Enter the first call
steps.body: The first call outputs School bookings, then returns to OUTPUT "First request".

steps.title: Enter the second call
steps.body: The second call runs the same body again, then returns to OUTPUT "Second request". The definition is shared, but each call is a separate execution.

worked.conclusion: A named procedure packages an action; CALL determines when that action occurs.

check.prompt: A program defines Heading() but never contains CALL Heading(). Is its heading output?
check.answer: No. A definition alone does not execute the procedure body.

learningCycle.takeaway: Define an action with PROCEDURE … ENDPROCEDURE and invoke it with CALL.
learningCycle.bridge: The same receipt action can handle different bookings if its caller supplies values as arguments.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match arguments to ordered parameters

leadVisual.title: Match arguments to ordered parameters

coreExplanation: ShowBooking has Name : STRING followed by Seats : INTEGER. BYVAL supplies copied values; the next group traces that mechanism in detail.

CALL ShowBooking("Mina", 3) supplies two compatible arguments in the declared order. The caller’s variable names need not match the parameter names. CALL ShowBooking(3, "Mina") reverses incompatible types.
Heading() needs none; ShowSeats(BYVAL Seats : INTEGER) needs one; ShowBooking needs two. Choose parameters from the information needed by the action, not from every variable in the main program.

learningCycle.observe: The action stays the same, but the name and quantity differ. Put those varying values into an interface rather than hard-coding them in the body.
learningCycle.question: How can one procedure display Mina’s three seats and Jo’s two seats?

prerequisite.title: Recall parameter versus argument
prerequisite.body: A parameter is an identifier declared in a subprogram header. An argument is an actual value, expression or variable supplied by a call. Position pairs each argument with its parameter.

steps.title: Write an ordered, typed interface
steps.body: ShowBooking has Name : STRING followed by Seats : INTEGER. BYVAL supplies copied values; the next group traces that mechanism in detail.

steps.title: Match count, order and type
steps.body: CALL ShowBooking("Mina", 3) supplies two compatible arguments in the declared order. The caller’s variable names need not match the parameter names. CALL ShowBooking(3, "Mina") reverses incompatible types.

steps.title: Recognise zero, one and several parameters
steps.body: Heading() needs none; ShowSeats(BYVAL Seats : INTEGER) needs one; ShowBooking needs two. Choose parameters from the information needed by the action, not from every variable in the main program.
steps.code:
PROCEDURE ShowBooking(BYVAL Name : STRING, BYVAL Seats : INTEGER)
    OUTPUT Name, " requested ", Seats, " seats"
ENDPROCEDURE
DECLARE Attendee : STRING
DECLARE Requested : INTEGER
Attendee <- "Mina"
Requested <- 3
CALL ShowBooking(Attendee, Requested)
CALL ShowBooking("Jo", 2)

worked.title: Match by position, not spelling
worked.setup: Trace CALL ShowBooking(Attendee, Requested).

steps.title: Pair the arguments
steps.body: Attendee supplies its value "Mina" to parameter Name. Requested supplies its value 3 to parameter Seats.

steps.title: Explain the body’s view
steps.body: The body uses the parameter identifiers Name and Seats to display Mina requested 3 seats. It does not require caller variables with those same names.

worked.conclusion: The interface is the agreement between caller and procedure: name, ordered parameters, types and passing modes.

check.prompt: For PROCEDURE ShowAmounts(BYVAL First : INTEGER, BYVAL Amount : INTEGER), which argument in CALL ShowAmounts(Score, 4) corresponds to Amount?
check.answer: The second argument, 4, corresponds to Amount. Score corresponds to First by its first position.

learningCycle.takeaway: A parameter belongs to the definition; an argument belongs to a call and is matched by position.
learningCycle.bridge: Passing a value copies it. Changing that copy does not change the original caller variable.

workedExample.title: Match by position, not spelling

steps.title: Pair the arguments

knowledgeUnits.heading: Change a copy without changing the caller

leadVisual.title: Change a copy without changing the caller

coreExplanation: On CALL PreviewExtra(Seats), the argument’s current value is copied into Quantity. The procedure can read it without sharing the caller’s storage. The experiment uses ShowBooking(BYVAL Quantity : INTEGER) to display a supplied quantity and return to a caller output; the worked PreviewExtra below additionally changes the copy to expose the distinction.
Quantity <- Quantity + 2 makes the parameter 5. OUTPUT Quantity displays 5 inside the procedure, but Seats remains 3.
After ENDPROCEDURE, OUTPUT Seats displays 3. A display action is not a return value and does not assign anything to Seats.

learningCycle.observe: Place a caller box labelled Seats beside a separate parameter box labelled Quantity. At the call, copy the value 3 into Quantity, then change only the parameter box.
learningCycle.question: If a procedure adds two to its BYVAL parameter, must the caller’s Seats also increase?

prerequisite.title: Recall value copying
prerequisite.body: SavedSeats <- Seats copied a scalar value without creating a permanent link. BYVAL likewise supplies a copy to a parameter for that call.

steps.title: Create the parameter’s copy
steps.body: On CALL PreviewExtra(Seats), the argument’s current value is copied into Quantity. The procedure can read it without sharing the caller’s storage. The experiment uses ShowBooking(BYVAL Quantity : INTEGER) to display a supplied quantity and return to a caller output; the worked PreviewExtra below additionally changes the copy to expose the distinction.

steps.title: Trace assignments to the parameter separately
steps.body: Quantity <- Quantity + 2 makes the parameter 5. OUTPUT Quantity displays 5 inside the procedure, but Seats remains 3.

steps.title: Return to the caller’s original state
steps.body: After ENDPROCEDURE, OUTPUT Seats displays 3. A display action is not a return value and does not assign anything to Seats.
steps.code:
PROCEDURE PreviewExtra(BYVAL Quantity : INTEGER)
    Quantity <- Quantity + 2
    OUTPUT Quantity
ENDPROCEDURE
DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
Seats <- 3
CALL PreviewExtra(Seats)
OUTPUT Seats

worked.title: Explain why two outputs differ
worked.setup: The complete program prints one value inside the procedure and one afterwards.

steps.title: Inside the procedure
steps.body: The copied Quantity changes from 3 to 5 and its output is 5.

steps.title: After the call
steps.body: Caller Seats still contains 3, so the second output is 3. CALL PreviewExtra(3) is also a valid value argument because the literal can be copied.

worked.conclusion: A procedure may change a BYVAL parameter locally while leaving the caller’s scalar value unchanged.

check.prompt: Would CALL PreviewExtra(Seats + 1) be possible for this BYVAL parameter, and what starting value would Quantity receive?
check.answer: Yes. With Seats 3, the expression evaluates to 4 and that value is copied into Quantity. Seats itself remains 3.

learningCycle.takeaway: BYVAL copies the argument’s value; assignments to that parameter do not update caller scalar storage.
learningCycle.bridge: When an action must update a caller accumulator, explicitly pass that storage by reference.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Supply a result to the calling expression

leadVisual.title: Supply a result to the calling expression

coreExplanation: FUNCTION Charge(Quantity : INTEGER) RETURNS REAL declares one parameter and a REAL result. Function parameters are passed by value by default in Cambridge pseudocode; do not design a function interface that relies on BYREF parameters.
RETURN Quantity * 12.50 evaluates the expression and ends the current function call with that result. RETURNS in the header names a type; RETURN in the body supplies a value.

Total <- Charge(Seats) receives the result. OUTPUT Charge(Seats) + 2.00 uses it in a larger expression. Do not write CALL Charge(Seats); CALL invokes a procedure. The experiment extends the interface to Charge(Quantity : INTEGER, PriceEach : REAL), called as Charge(Seats, Price), so you can change both inputs. The second argument supplies the per-seat price that is fixed at 12.50 in the worked program.

learningCycle.observe: The receipt needs a numeric amount, not just a message printed elsewhere. Follow the input quantity into a function and the returned amount back to the calling expression.

stimulus.title: A function call has a result

learningCycle.question: How can a charge calculation supply a number for Total <- Charge(Seats)?

prerequisite.title: Recall a procedure effect
prerequisite.body: CALL ShowBooking(…) performs an action. A function instead provides a typed return value that can be used in an assignment, calculation, output or condition.

steps.title: Declare the result type in the header

The second argument supplies the per-seat price that is fixed at 12.50 in the worked program.

FUNCTION Charge(Quantity : INTEGER) RETURNS REAL

ENDFUNCTION

knowledgeUnits.heading: Implement a function from a precise interface

leadVisual.title: Implement a function from a precise interface

coreExplanation: The header gives the name, ordered parameter identifiers and types, and return type. Parameters belong to the definition; arguments belong to a particular call. A receiving variable such as Matches is part of the caller, not a parameter.

Initialise Count to 0, traverse positions 1 through LENGTH(Text), compare the extracted character with Letter, and increment only on a match. Declarations inside the function make Index and Count local working variables.
RETURN Count belongs after NEXT Index. A return inside the loop would stop the function before all characters had been examined. An empty string gives zero iterations and returns the initial 0.

learningCycle.observe: The caller already has the text and target character. The function must count matches and return an integer; it should not ask the user to input those values again.

rows: FUNCTION CountLetter(Text : STRING, Letter : CHAR) RETURNS INTEGER

learningCycle.question: Which facts must caller and function agree on when counting a character in a code?

prerequisite.title: Recall string traversal
prerequisite.body: LENGTH gives the character count and a one-based MID(Text, Index, 1) extracts the current character as a one-character STRING. For this supplied counting task, the paper permits comparison with its CHAR argument. Upper- and lower-case letters remain distinct.

steps.title: Read the header as an agreement
steps.body: The header gives the name, ordered parameter identifiers and types, and return type. Parameters belong to the definition; arguments belong to a particular call. A receiving variable such as Matches is part of the caller, not a parameter.

steps.title: Build the body from familiar parts
steps.body: Initialise Count to 0, traverse positions 1 through LENGTH(Text), compare the extracted character with Letter, and increment only on a match. Declarations inside the function make Index and Count local working variables.

steps.title: Return only after the complete count
steps.body: RETURN Count belongs after NEXT Index. A return inside the loop would stop the function before all characters had been examined. An empty string gives zero iterations and returns the initial 0.
steps.code:
FUNCTION CountLetter(Text : STRING, Letter : CHAR) RETURNS INTEGER
    DECLARE Index, Count : INTEGER
    Count <- 0
    FOR Index <- 1 TO LENGTH(Text)
        IF MID(Text, Index, 1) = Letter THEN
            Count <- Count + 1
        ENDIF
    NEXT Index
    RETURN Count
ENDFUNCTION
DECLARE Matches : INTEGER
Matches <- CountLetter("aAba", 'a')
OUTPUT Matches

worked.title: Trace a case-sensitive count
worked.setup: Call CountLetter("aAba", 'a').

steps.title: Compare each position
steps.body: The characters are a, A, b and a. The counts after each comparison are 1, 1, 1 and 2. Converting all text to lower case would change the required rule.

steps.title: Distinguish all three names
steps.body: Text and Letter are formal parameters. "aAba" and 'a' are arguments. Matches is the caller variable that receives the returned 2.

worked.conclusion: The interface states what crosses the call boundary; local variables carry out the internal calculation.

check.prompt: What should CountLetter("", 'a') return? What happens if Count is not initialised?
check.answer: It should return 0 because the loop body runs zero times. Without Count <- 0, the return reads a value that was never established.

learningCycle.takeaway: Match argument order and types, use local working state, and return the completed result.
learningCycle.bridge: Returning before the end is sometimes intentional: a successful first-match search should finish immediately.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Return on success and stop unnecessary searching

leadVisual.title: Return on success and stop unnecessary searching

coreExplanation: A function returning BOOLEAN must supply TRUE when the action succeeds and FALSE when no free slot exists. A path that reaches the end without the promised result is incomplete.

After filling the first free slot, RETURN TRUE ends the function immediately, even from inside a FOR loop. It does not merely leave the IF or wait for later iterations. Put RETURN FALSE after the loop for the no-slot path.

Once the first slot is filled, visiting remaining slots is unnecessary and could fill multiple entries if the update is repeated. An early return both preserves the “first unused record only” rule and avoids scanning the remaining positions. A match at slot 1 needs one check; a full 7000-record array still needs all 7000 checks.

learningCycle.observe: Three slots contain "Mina", an empty string and an empty string. A new request from Jo should fill the first empty slot only.
learningCycle.question: When a booking is stored in the first free slot, why must the search stop immediately?

prerequisite.title: Recall arrays of records from Section 10
prerequisite.body: An array element can hold a record with several fields. Booking[Index].Name accesses the Name field of one indexed record. In the real-paper task Loan[Index] is a record with StudentID, BookID and OnLoan fields. The supplied rule defines unused as StudentID = ""; a returned book with OnLoan FALSE still has a historical record.

steps.title: Give every execution path a result
steps.body: A function returning BOOLEAN must supply TRUE when the action succeeds and FALSE when no free slot exists. A path that reaches the end without the promised result is incomplete.

steps.title: Use RETURN to finish the entire call
steps.body: After filling the first free slot, RETURN TRUE ends the function immediately, even from inside a FOR loop. It does not merely leave the IF or wait for later iterations. Put RETURN FALSE after the loop for the no-slot path.

steps.title: Explain the concrete efficiency gain
steps.body: Once the first slot is filled, visiting remaining slots is unnecessary and could fill multiple entries if the update is repeated. An early return both preserves the “first unused record only” rule and avoids scanning the remaining positions. A match at slot 1 needs one check; a full 7000-record array still needs all 7000 checks.

worked.title: Build and trace a complete first-match function
worked.setup: For this small teaching example, an INTEGER function reads a three-element array declared outside the function and reports the first unused position: 0 means no free slot. Names is a global variable in this example, available to both the function and the main program.

steps.title: Use a returned position to isolate the search
steps.body: FirstFree has no parameters: it reads the explicitly declared global Names array and returns only the first empty position. Index is declared inside the function and is local to that call. The caller then decides whether to write a booking. This establishes the same shared-array context supplied for Loan in the following paper.
steps.code:
DECLARE Names : ARRAY[1:3] OF STRING
FUNCTION FirstFree() RETURNS INTEGER
    DECLARE Index : INTEGER
    FOR Index <- 1 TO 3
        IF Names[Index] = "" THEN
            RETURN Index
        ENDIF
    NEXT Index
    RETURN 0
ENDFUNCTION
DECLARE Position : INTEGER
Names[1] <- "Mina"
Names[2] <- ""
Names[3] <- ""
Position <- FirstFree()
IF Position <> 0 THEN
    Names[Position] <- "Jo"
ENDIF
OUTPUT Position

steps.title: Follow success and failure
steps.body: With the shown data, Index 1 fails the empty test and Index 2 returns 2; the caller changes only Names[2]. With all three names occupied, the loop finishes and returns 0, so no array element is changed.

worked.conclusion: The following paper combines this first-match rule with updates to its supplied global array of loan records. Those updates are explicit side effects; the BOOLEAN return reports whether they succeeded.

check.prompt: Why must the real-paper NewLoan function test StudentID = "" rather than OnLoan = FALSE?
check.answer: A record for a returned book can have OnLoan FALSE while still retaining its StudentID and BookID. Overwriting it would lose history; only an empty StudentID identifies an unused record.

learningCycle.takeaway: Place RETURN where the required result is complete: after traversal for a full count, or immediately on a first-match success.
learningCycle.bridge: Efficiency means removing identifiable unnecessary work while preserving the required results and effects.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine a repeated unchanged decision

leadVisual.title: Combine a repeated unchanged decision

coreExplanation: The second identical comparison repeats a result already known for the same Seats value. The claim is about removing one comparison, not a measured execution-time percentage.
Increment GroupCount, then output Group booking inside one IF. Keep the original order. A final output of GroupCount remains after ENDIF.
If intervening code changed Seats, the two original tests might differ. Moving an output outside the branch would change the false path. Reducing code length alone does not establish correctness.

learningCycle.observe: A group booking must increment GroupCount and display a group message. Both actions currently use the same unchanged threshold test.

stimulus.title: Repeated work
items: Test Seats >= 3; if TRUE, increment GroupCount.
Test Seats >= 3 again; if TRUE, display "Group booking".
Seats does not change between these tests.

learningCycle.question: If Seats has not changed, why test Seats >= 3 twice?

prerequisite.title: Recall independent IF statements
prerequisite.body: Two separate IF conditions are evaluated independently. If their expression and all its inputs are unchanged, their truth values agree, but the order of their actions can still matter.

steps.title: Identify the redundant operation precisely
steps.body: The second identical comparison repeats a result already known for the same Seats value. The claim is about removing one comparison, not a measured execution-time percentage.

steps.title: Keep both actions in the same selected block
steps.body: Increment GroupCount, then output Group booking inside one IF. Keep the original order. A final output of GroupCount remains after ENDIF.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats, GroupCount : INTEGER
INPUT Seats
GroupCount <- 0
IF Seats >= 3 THEN
    GroupCount <- GroupCount + 1
    OUTPUT "Group booking"
ENDIF
OUTPUT GroupCount

steps.title: Check whether combining is safe
steps.body: If intervening code changed Seats, the two original tests might differ. Moving an output outside the branch would change the false path. Reducing code length alone does not establish correctness.

worked.title: Compare below, at and above the threshold
worked.setup: Test Seats 2, 3 and 4.

steps.title: Check the false path
steps.body: Seats 2 must produce no group message and final count 0 in both versions.

steps.title: Check true paths and output order
steps.body: Seats 3 and 4 must first display Group booking and then 1. The revised version uses one comparison instead of two while preserving these effects.

worked.conclusion: An efficiency claim should identify removed work and demonstrate preserved behaviour.

check.prompt: Would replacing >= 3 with > 3 while combining the tests preserve the program?
check.answer: No. Seats 3 would no longer increment the count or display the group message. The boundary rule would change.

learningCycle.takeaway: Combine repeated conditions only when their inputs and required action order permit it.
learningCycle.bridge: A calculation can also be reused if all of its operands stay fixed across repetition.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate a fixed amount once

leadVisual.title: Calculate a fixed amount once

coreExplanation: Seats and Price are read before the copy loop and remain fixed. Multiplying them inside every iteration performs avoidable repeated work.

Assign Cost <- Seats * Price before repetition, then OUTPUT Cost in each iteration. For a positive Copies count, this uses one multiplication instead of Copies multiplications while keeping every required receipt output.

The guard avoids a new calculation when Copies is zero, matching an original zero-iteration loop. If each iteration instead reads a new Seats quantity, its charge changes and that multiplication must remain after the new input.

learningCycle.observe: One booking has three seats at 12.50. Printing several copies changes neither Seats nor Price, so every multiplication produces the same 37.5.
learningCycle.question: Should printing three identical copies of one receipt multiply Seats by Price three times?

prerequisite.title: Recall a loop-invariant value
prerequisite.body: A calculation is invariant across a loop when its inputs remain unchanged, so it produces the same result each iteration. Check when the inputs become available before moving it.

steps.title: Locate the unchanged operands
steps.body: Seats and Price are read before the copy loop and remain fixed. Multiplying them inside every iteration performs avoidable repeated work.

steps.title: Reuse the calculated result
steps.body: Assign Cost <- Seats * Price before repetition, then OUTPUT Cost in each iteration. For a positive Copies count, this uses one multiplication instead of Copies multiplications while keeping every required receipt output.
steps.code:
DECLARE Seats, Copies, Index : INTEGER
DECLARE Price, Cost : REAL
INPUT Seats
INPUT Price
INPUT Copies
IF Copies > 0 THEN
    Cost <- Seats * Price
    FOR Index <- 1 TO Copies
        OUTPUT Cost
    NEXT Index
ENDIF

steps.title: Update both results for each current value
steps.body: Read Requests[Index] into Seats once, add Seats to Total and increment GroupCount when Seats >= 3. Both accumulators begin at 0.
steps.code:
DECLARE Requests : ARRAY[1:5] OF INTEGER
DECLARE Index, Seats, Total, GroupCount : INTEGER
FOR Index <- 1 TO 5
    INPUT Requests[Index]
NEXT Index
Total <- 0
GroupCount <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 5
    Seats <- Requests[Index]
    Total <- Total + Seats
    IF Seats >= 3 THEN
        GroupCount <- GroupCount + 1
    ENDIF
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total, GroupCount

Total <- 0
Groups <- 0

    IF Seats >= 3 THEN

prerequisite.title: Recall call notation and modes
prerequisite.body: Use ValidSeats(Seats) as a Boolean expression in UNTIL. Use CALL RecordBooking(Seats, Total, Groups) for the action. The quantity is copied; the two accumulators must be passed by reference.

steps.title: Define the exact interfaces
steps.body: ValidSeats declares RETURNS BOOLEAN and returns the same inclusive condition as the inline version. RecordBooking declares its read-only Quantity BYVAL and both changed accumulators BYREF.

steps.title: Match arguments and retain control placement
steps.body: Each call supplies arguments in the declared order. The procedure remains after UNTIL and inside FOR. Refactoring into a subprogram does not change when the update should happen.
steps.code:
FUNCTION ValidSeats(Quantity : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN
    RETURN (Quantity >= 1) AND (Quantity <= 6)
ENDFUNCTION
PROCEDURE RecordBooking(BYVAL Quantity : INTEGER, BYREF RunningTotal : INTEGER, BYREF GroupCount : INTEGER)
    RunningTotal <- RunningTotal + Quantity
    IF Quantity >= 3 THEN
        GroupCount <- GroupCount + 1
    ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE
DECLARE Index, Seats, Total, Groups : INTEGER
Total <- 0
Groups <- 0
FOR Index <- 1 TO 3
    REPEAT
        INPUT Seats
    UNTIL ValidSeats(Seats)
    CALL RecordBooking(Seats, Total, Groups)
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total, Groups

coreExplanation: Ask users what the program must do. Agree that the input is an INTEGER, 1–6 inclusive is accepted, and every other integer is rejected. Record the messages, independent-request assumption and any constraints. The specification now determines what correct means.

coreExplanation: Waterfall normally settles and reviews one planned stage before proceeding to the next. Requirements lead to design, then implementation and testing. Written outputs establish a common basis for the people responsible for each stage.
Stable price rules make it practical to agree the calculation early. The bursar can review the requirement and design; the team can plan milestones and trace each test to an approved rule.

If the working form reveals that school groups require a discount, the team may need to revise requirements, calculations, code and tests. Returning to earlier work is possible, but completed work can need substantial revision. Users may see useful working software only late in the process.

coreExplanation: Iterative development repeats analysis, design, coding and testing through successive versions. For this cycle, the aim is to explain a rejection clearly, while retaining the agreed range.

prerequisite.title: Recall definitions and execution order
prerequisite.body: A declaration establishes a variable and type, not a starting value. Execution begins with the main call here. A procedure finishes at ENDPROCEDURE; a function’s RETURN gives control and a value back to the waiting expression.

steps.code:
PROCEDURE ReadBooking(BYREF Seats : INTEGER, BYREF Price : REAL)
    INPUT Seats
    INPUT Price
ENDPROCEDURE

FUNCTION CalculateCharge(BYVAL Quantity : INTEGER, BYVAL PriceEach : REAL) RETURNS REAL
    RETURN Quantity * PriceEach
ENDFUNCTION

PROCEDURE DisplayCharge(BYVAL Amount : REAL)
    OUTPUT Amount
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE BookingController
    DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
    DECLARE Price, Total : REAL
    CALL ReadBooking(Seats, Price)
    Total <- CalculateCharge(Seats, Price)
    CALL DisplayCharge(Total)
ENDPROCEDURE

CALL BookingController

steps.body: Every module has the same responsibility as its chart box. The same values travel in the same direction. A program with matching names but a BYVAL reader, missing return assignment or reversed call order does not implement the same design.

steps.title: Finish the visible action
steps.body: DisplayCharge receives 37.50, displays it and returns. BookingController then finishes. The experiment also allows repeated display calls; changing the number of copies changes output count, not the calculated charge.

A labelled arrow shows transfer direction. An unfilled circle denotes a data couple; a filled circle denotes a control couple, such as a Boolean flag controlling a choice. steps.title: Translate the control as well as the interfaces
steps.body: The parent’s loop surrounds the ProcessOrder call; the IF belongs inside CalculateCost. The complete example includes definitions and all caller connections.
steps.code:
PROCEDURE ReadOrder(BYREF Quantity : INTEGER, BYREF UnitPrice : REAL, BYREF Member : BOOLEAN)
    INPUT Quantity
    INPUT UnitPrice
    INPUT Member
ENDPROCEDURE

FUNCTION StandardCost(Quantity : INTEGER, UnitPrice : REAL) RETURNS REAL
    RETURN Quantity * UnitPrice
ENDFUNCTION

FUNCTION MemberCost(Quantity : INTEGER, UnitPrice : REAL) RETURNS REAL
    RETURN Quantity * UnitPrice * 0.90
ENDFUNCTION

FUNCTION CalculateCost(Quantity : INTEGER, UnitPrice : REAL, Member : BOOLEAN) RETURNS REAL
    IF Member THEN
        RETURN MemberCost(Quantity, UnitPrice)
    ELSE
        RETURN StandardCost(Quantity, UnitPrice)
    ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

PROCEDURE DisplayCost(BYVAL Cost : REAL)
    OUTPUT Cost
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE ProcessOrder()
    DECLARE Quantity : INTEGER
    DECLARE UnitPrice : REAL
    DECLARE Member : BOOLEAN
    DECLARE Cost : REAL
    CALL ReadOrder(Quantity, UnitPrice, Member)
    Cost <- CalculateCost(Quantity, UnitPrice, Member)
    CALL DisplayCost(Cost)
ENDPROCEDURE

PROCEDURE ProcessBatch()
    DECLARE OrderCount : INTEGER
    DECLARE Index : INTEGER
    INPUT OrderCount
    IF OrderCount = 0 THEN
        OUTPUT "No orders"
    ELSE
        FOR Index <- 1 TO OrderCount
            CALL ProcessOrder()
        NEXT Index
    ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

CALL ProcessBatch()

steps.title: Second repeated call

check.answer: There are zero reader calls when OrderCount is 0. For one member order only MemberCost executes; the alternative StandardCost call is skipped.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Keep the current state between events

leadVisual.title: Keep the current state between events

coreExplanation: A state-transition diagram uses a node for each state and directed arrows for transitions. A starting arrow identifies the initial state. Begin the booking model in Draft, before consuming any event.

For a valid request, Submit moves Draft to Pending. Pay moves Pending to Confirmed. Cancel moves Pending or Confirmed back to Draft. Read the event only against outgoing arrows from the current state.

In this teaching model, events not assigned a change leave the state unchanged. Pay in Draft therefore stays Draft; Submit in Confirmed stays Confirmed. Such a self-loop consumes an event without moving to a different state. That rule is explicitly specified here; do not invent missing transitions in another question.

A state diagram shows event-dependent behaviour over time. It does not divide the program into callable modules. The same booking system can have both a structure chart and a state diagram, each documenting a different aspect.

Such a self-loop consumes an event without moving to a different state. That rule is explicitly specified here; do not invent missing transitions in another question.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Distinguish three different failures

leadVisual.title: Distinguish three different failures

coreExplanation: A missing THEN or mismatched loop ending prevents the construct being read correctly. Use translator feedback or a syntax checker to locate the malformed statement, then inspect the surrounding block. Error reporting may identify where the problem was noticed rather than its original cause.

The correct rule accepts Seats 6 when Available is 6. A complete condition using Seats < Available rejects it. The code can translate and finish, but the result disagrees with the requirement. Compare actual output with an independently expected output.

Total / Groups with Groups 0 attempts division by zero. An array access outside its declared bounds can also cause a run-time error. Whether the failure occurs depends on the path and values reached during execution.

Use clear requirements, small modules, meaningful names and consistent indentation. Review interfaces and boundary cases; validate or guard inputs before unsafe operations. Then use translator checks, code review and purposeful tests. None of these alone proves the complete program correct.

learningCycle.observe: The same phrase, “it does not work”, hides three different causes. Identify what was observed before proposing a repair.

rows: The translator rejects an IF with no THEN
The program runs but rejects a valid request for 6

learningCycle.question: Which problem concerns grammar, which concerns the rule, and which occurs during execution?

prerequisite.title: Recall translation and execution
prerequisite.body: A translator checks whether code follows the language rules. Execution performs its operations on actual values. Correct grammar does not prove that those operations implement the specification.

steps.title: Syntax: the statement does not follow the language rules
steps.body: A missing THEN or mismatched loop ending prevents the construct being read correctly. Use translator feedback or a syntax checker to locate the malformed statement, then inspect the surrounding block. Error reporting may identify where the problem was noticed rather than its original cause.

steps.title: Logic: valid instructions produce the wrong behaviour
steps.body: The correct rule accepts Seats 6 when Available is 6. A complete condition using Seats < Available rejects it. The code can translate and finish, but the result disagrees with the requirement. Compare actual output with an independently expected output.

steps.title: Run time: an invalid operation occurs when executing
steps.body: Total / Groups with Groups 0 attempts division by zero. An array access outside its declared bounds can also cause a run-time error. Whether the failure occurs depends on the path and values reached during execution.

steps.title: Reduce the chance of a fault and expose remaining faults
steps.body: Use clear requirements, small modules, meaningful names and consistent indentation. Review interfaces and boundary cases; validate or guard inputs before unsafe operations. Then use translator checks, code review and purposeful tests. None of these alone proves the complete program correct.

worked.title: Match each report to evidence
worked.setup: The required average is total seats divided by the number of bookings; zero bookings must display No data.

steps.title: Classify without guessing
steps.body: A is syntax because the IF lacks required grammar. B is logic because a valid input produces the wrong decision. C is run time because execution attempts a forbidden division.

steps.title: Choose a useful next check
steps.body: For A inspect the complete IF/ELSE/ENDIF block. For B trace exactly Seats 6, not only an ordinary value such as 3. For C inspect Groups immediately before division and test the zero-booking path.

worked.conclusion: A useful error label is supported by the observed cause, not just by a failed test.

check.prompt: A program translates successfully and charges 25.00 for three seats costing 12.50 each. What kind of error does this evidence suggest, and what is the expected charge?
check.answer: It suggests a logic error: the completed calculation disagrees with the required multiplication. The expected charge is 3 * 12.50 = 37.50.

learningCycle.takeaway: Syntax concerns language rules; logic concerns the required result; run-time errors arise from invalid executed operations.
learningCycle.bridge: An error category narrows the search. A trace shows the exact point where values or decisions diverge.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace from the symptom to its cause

leadVisual.title: Trace from the symptom to its cause

coreExplanation: Use Seats 6 and Available 6. Record the exact input, expected Accepted and actual Rejected. Keeping one failing example removes unrelated interactions and allows the same fault to be checked after repair.

Seats is 6 and Available is 6, so the input has been read correctly. Evaluate the existing comparisons. Seats >= 1 is TRUE, but Seats < Available is FALSE. This is the first discrepancy with the inclusive specification.

TRUE AND FALSE is FALSE, so the ELSE branch produces Rejected. The output statement is doing what that branch tells it to do. Changing the word Rejected would hide the symptom and break other cases; the upper comparison is the cause.

For division by zero, inspect the denominator and the path that allowed 0 to reach the division. For an array failure, compare the current index with the declared bounds before the access. For an unreachable branch, list possible expression results and the alternatives already covered.

learningCycle.observe: The ordinary case passes. The exact-fit case fails. Read the quantity, evaluate both comparisons, then inspect which branch executes.
learningCycle.question: What is the first decision that differs from the intended algorithm?

prerequisite.title: Recall a trace and a breakpoint
prerequisite.body: A dry run follows statements manually. A breakpoint pauses an executing program before or at a selected statement; stepping advances execution, and a watch displays selected variable values. Neither operation repairs code automatically.

steps.title: Reproduce the failure with a small test
steps.body: Use Seats 6 and Available 6. Record the exact input, expected Accepted and actual Rejected. Keeping one failing example removes unrelated interactions and allows the same fault to be checked after repair.

steps.title: Inspect state just before the decision
steps.body: Seats is 6 and Available is 6, so the input has been read correctly. Evaluate the existing comparisons. Seats >= 1 is TRUE, but Seats < Available is FALSE. This is the first discrepancy with the inclusive specification.

steps.title: Follow the discrepancy to its consequence
steps.body: TRUE AND FALSE is FALSE, so the ELSE branch produces Rejected. The output statement is doing what that branch tells it to do. Changing the word Rejected would hide the symptom and break other cases; the upper comparison is the cause.

steps.title: Apply the same method to other paths
steps.body: For division by zero, inspect the denominator and the path that allowed 0 to reach the division. For an array failure, compare the current index with the declared bounds before the access. For an unreachable branch, list possible expression results and the alternatives already covered.

worked.title: Explain why an OTHERWISE is unreachable
worked.setup: Index is a non-negative integer. CASE OF Index MOD 2 already contains alternatives 0 and 1.

steps.title: Recall what MOD returns
steps.body: MOD gives the remainder after integer division. Dividing a non-negative integer by 2 can leave only remainder 0 or 1.

steps.title: Check coverage before blaming execution
steps.body: Both possible values already select named alternatives. No input in the stated domain reaches OTHERWISE. This conclusion comes from the expression’s possible values, not from simply failing to observe the branch in one test.

worked.conclusion: Locate a cause by comparing the first incorrect state or decision with the requirement.

check.prompt: The output is wrong, but the input and intermediate total are correct. Why should you inspect the next calculation or branch before rewriting the whole program?
check.answer: The earliest difference narrows the cause. Correct earlier state is evidence that those parts should be preserved while inspecting the operation that first produces an incorrect value or path.

learningCycle.takeaway: Reproduce the fault, inspect state, and locate the first departure from the intended behaviour.
learningCycle.bridge: A focused correction still needs evidence that it fixes the original failure and preserves other required cases.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Correct the cause and repeat the right tests

leadVisual.title: Correct the cause and repeat the right tests

coreExplanation: Use <= for the inclusive upper limit, leaving the correct lower bound and output branches intact. For a syntax error, restore the missing or matching keyword at the correct block position. Do not move a statement merely to silence an error message without understanding its role.
For a zero count, test the denominator before dividing. Putting the guard after the division is too late.

For the range repair, 6 must now pass. Check 5 remains accepted, 7 remains rejected, 1 remains accepted and 0 remains rejected. Record the new version and results while retaining the original failure record.

In the next paper, & joins string or character operands. Index is INTEGER, so convert it with NUM_TO_STR(Index) before concatenation, or use comma-separated OUTPUT items. Its supplied TO_UPPER and TO_LOWER routines accept STRING arguments; follow that insert rather than assuming another routine interface. An array declared from 1 to 200 has no element 0.

If a repair changes loop initialisation, trace the first and last valid array positions. Changing an initial index from 0 to 1 may skip the first element when the loop also increments before access. Understand the existing flow before applying a plausible-looking correction.

learningCycle.observe: A patch that accepts every quantity would pass that one test. Choose additional inputs that distinguish a genuine repair from this new fault.

prerequisite.title: Recall a boundary and regression
prerequisite.body: A boundary is where a rule changes its decision. A regression is a previously correct required behaviour broken by a change. Repeating relevant old tests helps detect it.

steps.title: Amend the smallest responsible operation
steps.body: Use <= for the inclusive upper limit, leaving the correct lower bound and output branches intact. For a syntax error, restore the missing or matching keyword at the correct block position. Do not move a statement merely to silence an error message without understanding its role.

steps.title: Guard an unsafe calculation before it happens
steps.body: For a zero count, test the denominator before dividing. Putting the guard after the division is too late.
steps.code:
DECLARE Total : REAL
DECLARE Groups : INTEGER
INPUT Total
INPUT Groups
IF Groups > 0 THEN
    OUTPUT Total / Groups
ELSE
    OUTPUT "No data"
ENDIF

steps.title: Recheck the full path affected by the change
steps.body: If a repair changes loop initialisation, trace the first and last valid array positions. Changing an initial index from 0 to 1 may skip the first element when the loop also increments before access. Understand the existing flow before applying a plausible-looking correction.

steps.title: Explain what the evidence supports
steps.body: These cases expose the identified off-by-one mistake and protect nearby behaviour. They do not establish every possible feature of the whole booking system; keep testing proportional to the affected responsibility.

worked.conclusion: A repair is supported by a reproduced failure, a causal change and relevant retest evidence.

coreExplanation: Choose exact input values and follow the written statements in execution order. Record changing variables, condition results and outputs in a trace table. The aim is to predict what this implementation actually does, even if it is wrong.

The requirement says the total should be 3 + 2 + 4 = 9. Compare that expected result with the trace. A trace can reveal repeated initialisation, a missing update or a wrong stopping condition without executing the code.

In a walkthrough, the author explains the design or code step by step to others. Reviewers question assumptions, conditions and interfaces. They may trace sample values, but a walkthrough is the collaborative review activity, not merely another name for an individual trace.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Choose from the specification or the code

leadVisual.title: Choose from the specification or the code

coreExplanation: Select cases from the specification without relying on internal code structure. For a 1–6 rule, input 6 must be accepted regardless of how the programmer wrote the condition. This can expose wrong results or failures during execution.

Inspect code to choose inputs that exercise particular statements, branches or paths. For an IF Paid condition, TRUE and FALSE exercise both alternatives. For a loop, consider no iterations where possible, one iteration and several iterations.

Black-box tests can miss an internal branch that the chosen requirements examples never reach. White-box branch coverage can execute incorrect logic without proving the requirements are satisfied. Use independent expected outcomes in both methods; successful coverage is evidence of execution, not proof of correctness.

learningCycle.observe: It is how test cases are selected. Both testers can compare actual output with expected output, and the same input might be useful to both.

rows: IF Paid THEN confirm ELSE ask for payment
Use Paid TRUE and FALSE to execute both branches

prerequisite.title: Recall a path through IF
prerequisite.body: Only one IF/ELSE branch executes on a particular test. A passing test for the TRUE branch does not tell you what the FALSE branch will do.

steps.title: Black-box: start from required inputs and outputs

steps.title: White-box: use the implementation structure
steps.body: Inspect code to choose inputs that exercise particular statements, branches or paths. For an IF Paid condition, TRUE and FALSE exercise both alternatives. For a loop, consider no iterations where possible, one iteration and several iterations.

steps.title: Explain what each result does and does not show
steps.body: Black-box tests can miss an internal branch that the chosen requirements examples never reach. White-box branch coverage can execute incorrect logic without proving the requirements are satisfied. Use independent expected outcomes in both methods; successful coverage is evidence of execution, not proof of correctness.

steps.title: Derive the black-box case

steps.body: White-box inputs 3 and 7 execute both acceptance and rejection branches. Both results can be correct even though the inclusive endpoint is wrong. Add the boundary case because branch coverage alone missed that requirement.

check.prompt: A tester looks at an IF and chooses inputs to execute each branch. Is this white-box or black-box, and why does passing both cases not prove the inclusive limit is correct?
check.answer: It is white-box because the code structure guided the choice. Values can exercise both branches without being exactly at the boundary; an incorrect < can still pass those tests.

learningCycle.takeaway: Black-box selects from the specification; white-box selects using the internal structure.
learningCycle.bridge: Even correctly tested modules can fail when their interfaces are connected.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Test a caller before its real module is ready

leadVisual.title: Test a caller before its real module is ready

coreExplanation: A module may calculate correctly in isolation, yet integration can reveal reversed arguments, a wrong returned type or values sent to the wrong place. Integration testing checks cooperating modules and their interfaces when they are combined.

A stub stands in for an unfinished called module. It uses the required interface and supplies a controlled response, such as a fixed TRUE. A separate FALSE version lets the caller’s other branch be exercised.

A TRUE stub makes every entered quantity produce Accepted because that is its programmed response. This can show that the caller handles TRUE, but it does not verify the required range or the missing implementation. Change the controlled return to FALSE to check the other branch.
The real ValidSeats function returns (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6). Test 0 and 7 expecting Rejected, and 3 and 6 expecting Accepted. The caller, parameter interface and real result now need to agree.

learningCycle.observe: Give the caller a controlled TRUE response, then a controlled FALSE response. Identify which part is being exercised and which part is still absent.

stimulus.title: The booking interface is ready first

TRUE should display Accepted; FALSE should display Rejected.

learningCycle.question: How can you check both caller branches without pretending that the real validation has been implemented?

prerequisite.title: Recall a Boolean function interface
prerequisite.body: A function header states the ordered parameters and return type. The caller uses the returned BOOLEAN in its condition. Replacing a function safely requires preserving the interface expected by that caller.

steps.title: Separate a module from its connections
steps.body: A module may calculate correctly in isolation, yet integration can reveal reversed arguments, a wrong returned type or values sent to the wrong place. Integration testing checks cooperating modules and their interfaces when they are combined.

steps.title: Substitute a small temporary stub
steps.body: A stub stands in for an unfinished called module. It uses the required interface and supplies a controlled response, such as a fixed TRUE. A separate FALSE version lets the caller’s other branch be exercised.
steps.code:
FUNCTION ValidSeats(BYVAL Seats : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN
    RETURN TRUE
ENDFUNCTION

DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
INPUT Seats
IF ValidSeats(Seats) THEN
    OUTPUT "Accepted"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Rejected"
ENDIF

steps.title: Keep the claim within the evidence
steps.body: A TRUE stub makes every entered quantity produce Accepted because that is its programmed response. This can show that the caller handles TRUE, but it does not verify the required range or the missing implementation. Change the controlled return to FALSE to check the other branch.

steps.title: Replace the stub and retest the integration
steps.body: The real ValidSeats function returns (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6). Test 0 and 7 expecting Rejected, and 3 and 6 expecting Accepted. The caller, parameter interface and real result now need to agree.
steps.code:
FUNCTION ValidSeats(BYVAL Seats : INTEGER) RETURNS BOOLEAN
    RETURN (Seats >= 1) AND (Seats <= 6)
ENDFUNCTION

DECLARE Seats : INTEGER
INPUT Seats
IF ValidSeats(Seats) THEN
    OUTPUT "Accepted"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Rejected"
ENDIF

steps.title: Use the controlled versions

steps.title: Check the connected real version

If all still display Accepted, inspect the selected implementation, returned Boolean and caller branch. Use the white-box view to identify which caller branches were visited; use the black-box view to judge outcomes from the specification.

worked.conclusion: A stub enables progress on a caller while making the unverified responsibility explicit.

check.prompt: A stub returns TRUE for every Seats value and all caller tests pass. What still needs to be tested after the real function replaces it?

learningCycle.takeaway: A stub preserves an interface but supplies a controlled temporary response; integration must be checked after replacement.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Test in controlled and real user environments

leadVisual.title: Test in controlled and real user environments

coreExplanation: Alpha testing takes place within the developing organisation or another controlled test environment, typically with internal testers and sometimes invited users. Problems can be investigated while the developers control the setup.

Beta testing makes a trial version available to selected users in their real environments. Their equipment, data and workflows can expose problems the development setup did not reproduce. Gather specific feedback and defect reports for the next change.

Use controlled testing when you need reproducible conditions and close inspection. Use beta feedback when you need evidence from real user environments. A beta release may still contain defects; distributing it does not itself mean that the customer has accepted the finished system.

learningCycle.observe: The completed screen now meets different equipment, users and work patterns. Compare the level of control and the source of feedback in the two trials.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Decide whether the agreed requirements are met

leadVisual.title: Decide whether the agreed requirements are met

coreExplanation: Acceptance testing checks the completed system against agreed requirements so the customer can decide whether to accept it. Include the outputs and constraints that the agreement specifies, not only the developer’s favourite features.

An acceptance test can be black-box because its cases come from required behaviour rather than code. Acceptance identifies the customer-decision purpose; black-box identifies the basis for selecting the cases.

If the system rejects a valid maximum request, record the failure and resolve it before claiming that requirement is met. A new requested feature needs an agreed change; it should not silently replace an existing acceptance criterion.

learningCycle.observe: A pleasant interface can still calculate the wrong amount. The customer needs repeatable evidence against the actual requirements, not just a general impression.
learningCycle.question: What distinguishes “staff like it” from accepting the agreed system?

prerequisite.title: Recall the test plan

steps.title: Use customer requirements as the basis

worked.conclusion: Acceptance connects the end of the current delivery to the requirements agreed at its beginning.

learningCycle.takeaway: Acceptance testing supplies the customer with evidence against the agreed requirements.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Plan the whole testing approach

leadVisual.title: Plan the whole testing approach

coreExplanation: A test strategy describes the overall approach: what will be tested, the methods and sequence, significant risks, responsibilities, environments, resources and completion criteria. A test plan then makes the work concrete and repeatable with schedules and individual cases.

Review and dry-run calculations; select black-box range cases and white-box branch cases; use a stub while the availability module is absent; check integration after replacement. Plan user trials and acceptance with their participants and environments.

Name who prepares cases, runs them, investigates failures and decides whether the completion criteria are met. Record environment and version so another tester can reproduce a failure. Define what must pass rather than using “we tested for an hour” as a release criterion.

prerequisite.title: Recall method, data and expected result

steps.title: Set scope, priorities and stages

knowledgeUnits.heading: Challenge ordinary values and both limits

leadVisual.title: Challenge ordinary values and both limits

coreExplanation: Normal data represents typical permitted input, such as Seats 3. It should be accepted. It establishes an ordinary working path but may not challenge a limit.

Abnormal data violates the requirement. For this integer input contract, 0 and 7 are outside the permitted range and should be rejected. Text and fractional values are separate type-validation cases only when the stated input source can supply them.

Extreme valid values are the minimum and maximum permitted values, here 1 and 6. Boundary testing also considers values immediately around the decision boundaries, such as 0, 1, 2 and 5, 6, 7. State the actual value and expected result so different naming conventions do not obscure the test.

For strings, a length limit concerns the number of characters, not the numeric value of the text. For real values, the useful neighbouring inputs depend on stated precision. With one decimal place, -5.1, -5.0 and -4.9 can challenge -5.0; there is no universal next real value found by adding 1.

learningCycle.observe: Predict each decision first. Then test the exact upper limit against an implementation using < instead of <=. Explain why an ordinary accepted value might miss the mistake.

prerequisite.title: Recall inclusive limits
prerequisite.body: Inclusive means the endpoint is allowed. For an INTEGER range, the nearest integer below 1 is 0 and the nearest above 6 is 7. Available does not decrease in this independent-request model.

steps.body: Extreme valid values are the minimum and maximum permitted values, here 1 and 6. Boundary testing also considers values immediately around the decision boundaries, such as 0, 1, 2 and 5, 6, 7. State the actual value and expected result so different naming conventions do not obscure the test.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Test distinct behaviours with complete sequences

leadVisual.title: Test distinct behaviours with complete sequences

coreExplanation: 99 alone tests immediate termination and a zero total. 3, 99 tests one update. 3, 2, 4, 99 tests repeated accumulation. Three lists with different numbers can still test the same behaviour if their structure is identical.

For a routine counting odd and even data, use an all-odd sequence to check the even count stays zero, an all-even sequence to check the odd count stays zero, and an immediate sentinel to check both start at zero. Choose according to the outputs actually required.

If asked for valid sequences, obey the stated type, sign and terminating sentinel. Do not insert an invalid value just because abnormal testing exists elsewhere. Include each sequence’s purpose and independently predicted output when useful.

Several data items can reveal an accumulator reset inside a loop. An immediate sentinel can reveal processing before the termination check. A sequence containing only one category can expose an unintended update to the other category.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Follow a change after delivery

leadVisual.title: Follow a change after delivery

coreExplanation: Real use can expose faults not found before delivery. Operating systems, devices, libraries or external rules can change. Users may need additional functions or better performance. Maintenance changes delivered software so that it remains useful under these circumstances.

Confirm the new 1–8 rule and its reason before editing. Identify every dependent location: the interface guidance, validation condition, documentation and test cases. A change request should distinguish a new requirement from a defect in the old one.

After the approved change, 7 and 8 should be accepted, while 9 should be rejected. Old 0 must remain rejected and old ordinary values must remain accepted. Change expectations because the requirement changed, not because an arbitrary patch happens to produce them.

learningCycle.observe: Predict what happens if only the help text changes. Then predict what happens if only the code changes. Neither change alone keeps the user instruction, behaviour and evidence aligned.

stimulus.title: A new booking-desk message
items: The delivered system follows the agreed maximum of 6 seats per request.

The input hint still says 1–6, the code still checks <= 6, and the old maximum test still uses 6.

learningCycle.question: Which connected parts must change before the new rule is consistently supported?

prerequisite.title: Recall requirement, implementation and test
prerequisite.body: A required limit determines the design, comparison, user guidance and expected boundary results. The new limit is a revised requirement; it does not mean the original 1–6 implementation was faulty.

steps.title: Explain why maintenance continues
steps.body: Real use can expose faults not found before delivery. Operating systems, devices, libraries or external rules can change. Users may need additional functions or better performance. Maintenance changes delivered software so that it remains useful under these circumstances.

steps.title: Record what changed and why
steps.body: Confirm the new 1–8 rule and its reason before editing. Identify every dependent location: the interface guidance, validation condition, documentation and test cases. A change request should distinguish a new requirement from a defect in the old one.

steps.title: Update affected evidence coherently
steps.body: After the approved change, 7 and 8 should be accepted, while 9 should be rejected. Old 0 must remain rejected and old ordinary values must remain accepted. Change expectations because the requirement changed, not because an arbitrary patch happens to produce them.

worked.title: Check the new maximum without losing the minimum

steps.title: List changed and retained behaviour
steps.body: Inputs 7 and 8 deliberately change from rejection to acceptance. Input 6 still passes. Input 0 still fails. The next rejected upper neighbour is now 9.

steps.title: Prepare a coherent revision
steps.body: Revise the displayed range and upper comparison to 8, update the specification and expected cases, then repeat the revised boundary cases and relevant unchanged cases. Record which version implements which rule.

worked.conclusion: A maintenance change includes its impact on users, code and evidence.

check.prompt: A revised limit makes input 7 valid. Is changing its expected result from Rejected to Accepted always hiding a defect?
check.answer: No. It is correct when an approved requirement changed from maximum 6 to maximum 8. It would hide a defect if the original 1–6 requirement still applied and the expected result were changed merely to match faulty code.

learningCycle.takeaway: Maintenance responds to change after delivery and keeps all affected parts consistent.
learningCycle.bridge: Classify a maintenance task by the reason for the change, not by the file that receives it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Classify the cause of the change

leadVisual.title: Classify the cause of the change

coreExplanation: Corrective maintenance restores behaviour the system should already provide. Repairing a wrong total or an existing response-time violation is corrective because the original requirement was not met.

Adaptive maintenance lets a program work with changed operating systems, hardware, library interfaces, external rules or operational circumstances. A new printer interface requires an adaptation even if the old printer support was correct.

Perfective maintenance improves functionality, efficiency or usability beyond the currently satisfied requirements. An extra report or a faster already-compliant search can be perfective. Classify from the stated reason, not from the word “faster” alone.

“Fix duplicate charges, support a new printer and add a chart” contains three different causes. A changed tax rate could be corrective if the old value was already wrong, or adaptive if a new external rule changes it. The same edited line can serve different maintenance purposes.

learningCycle.observe: Look for the cause stated in each ticket. The number of edited lines, adding a function or changing a screen does not determine the category.

rows: Fix the charge for exactly 6 seats
The original calculation requirement is not met
Users want an improvement to a working report

learningCycle.question: Why can all three tickets change code but belong to different categories?

prerequisite.title: Recall old and revised requirements
prerequisite.body: A defect means the program fails a requirement that already applied. A new environment or improvement request can create a new requirement even when the old behaviour was correct.

steps.title: Corrective: repair an existing fault
steps.body: Corrective maintenance restores behaviour the system should already provide. Repairing a wrong total or an existing response-time violation is corrective because the original requirement was not met.

steps.title: Adaptive: respond to the changed environment
steps.body: Adaptive maintenance lets a program work with changed operating systems, hardware, library interfaces, external rules or operational circumstances. A new printer interface requires an adaptation even if the old printer support was correct.

steps.title: Perfective: improve a delivered system
steps.body: Perfective maintenance improves functionality, efficiency or usability beyond the currently satisfied requirements. An extra report or a faster already-compliant search can be perfective. Classify from the stated reason, not from the word “faster” alone.

steps.title: Split mixed requests and ask what changed
steps.body: “Fix duplicate charges, support a new printer and add a chart” contains three different causes. A changed tax rate could be corrective if the old value was already wrong, or adaptive if a new external rule changes it. The same edited line can serve different maintenance purposes.

worked.title: Explain why a correct program still needs adaptation
worked.setup: The booking program calls a printer library. A system update replaces the library’s interface.

steps.title: Identify the external change
steps.body: The old program worked with the old interface. Its caller now needs the replacement interface, so the trigger is environmental change rather than a newly discovered old fault.

steps.title: Give a contextual consequence
steps.body: Update the printer call and any affected data handling, then test the connection. The same reasoning applies to a factory program when its control hardware or a library it uses changes.

worked.conclusion: A classification earns its explanation by linking the change to the stated cause.

check.prompt: A search already meets its required response time. Users request a faster version. Then a different search is found to exceed its existing required time. Classify the two changes.
check.answer: The requested improvement to the already-compliant search is perfective. Repairing the search that violates an existing response-time requirement is corrective.

learningCycle.takeaway: Corrective repairs a fault; adaptive responds to external change; perfective improves a delivered system.
learningCycle.bridge: To implement any of these changes safely, first understand the current program and its dependencies.
